ceqa-3ef4630f5d8d92a380.name: Turnout on the Friant-Kern Canal at Big Dry Creek Project (California Endangered Species Act Incidental Take Permit No. 2081-2024-067-04, Amendment No. 1)
ceqa-3ef4630f5d8d92a380.projectTitle: Turnout on the Friant-Kern Canal at Big Dry Creek Project
ceqa-3ef4630f5d8d92a380.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has issued an amended ITP (No. 2081-2024-067-04), pursuant to Section 2081(b) of the Fish and Game Code to the Fresno Irrigation District (FID). The Project includes the construction of a new water diversion facility (turnout) and associated infrastructure at the Friant-Kern Canal to divert water from the Friant-Kern Canal into Big Dry Creek for groundwater recharge. Amendment No. 1 adds western spadefoot (Spea hammondii) as a Covered Species, reduces the Project Area, reduces the corresponding amount of compensatory mitigation for California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense), adds nightwork, and extends the expiration date of the ITP. The Project will result in impacts to 2.74 acres of California tiger salamander habitat including temporary impacts to 2.61 acres and the permanent removal of 0.13 acres of grassland upland habitat. The Project will result in impacts to 3.24 acres of western spadefoot habitat including temporary impacts to 3.08 acres and the permanent removal of 0.13 acres of grassland upland habitat and 0.16 acres of upland stream habitat. The Project is expected to result in incidental take of California tiger salamander which is designated as a threatened species under CESA and western spadefoot which is a state candidate pursuant to CESA. The ITP referenced above as issued by CDFW authorizes incidental take of species listed under CESA that may occur as a result of Project implementation.

ceqa-1fc8e05b9f158aebbe.name: Dakota/Hayes Elementary School Removal Action Workplan
ceqa-1fc8e05b9f158aebbe.projectTitle: Dakota/Hayes Elementary School Removal Action Workplan
ceqa-1fc8e05b9f158aebbe.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-1fc8e05b9f158aebbe.description: Project Description: The project consists of implementing the Dakota/Hayes Elementary School Removal Action Workplan (RAW) to address elevated levels of organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), lead, arsenic, and dioxins/furans in soil at 5710 & 5796 West Dakota Avenue (Project Site) in the City of Fresno. The remediation identified in the RAW consists of excavation and off-site disposal of approximately 370 cubic yards of soil. Background: The Project Site consists of approximately 32.57-acres and is comprised of five parcels identified by the County of Fresno as Assessor’s Parcel Numbers (APNs): 511-011-21 (10-acre), 511-011-22 (10-acre), 511-011-27 (7.39-acre), 511-011-28 (2.59-acre), and 511-011-29 (2.59-acre). Based on a review of historical documentation (topographic maps, aerial photographs), the Project Site was used for agricultural purposes from at least 1937 to approximately 2023. Currently, the Project Site contains one small, vacant residential structure. Approximately six acres of the land are planted with inactive grapevines for raisin production, while the remainder is fallow. The Project Site is bordered to the north and west by agricultural land and rural residences; to the east by a rural residence, beyond which is a residential neighborhood; and to the south by West Dakota Avenue, beyond which is a residential neighborhood and a vacant field. Previous Investigations: In December 2022, a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) was completed for the Project Site. The Phase I ESA identified recognized environmental conditions (RECs) associated with historical agricultural activities and building structures, noting the potential for asbestos-containing material (ACM), lead-based paint (LBP), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and residual pesticides in soil. To further evaluate these impacts, a Preliminary Environmental Assessment (PEA) was conducted in July 2024. The investigation identified elevated concentrations of organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), dioxins/furans, arsenic, and lead in the soil. The concentrations of these chemicals exceed DTSC screening levels and pose a potential risk to human health, necessitating the proposed removal action. Project Activities: The remedial measures described in the RAW consist of the excavation and off-site disposal of approximately 370 cubic yards of contaminated soil from five designated Areas of Concern (AOC-1 through AOC-5) associated with a former residence, a former outbuilding, an existing structure, and burn areas, extending up to 2.5 feet below ground surface (bgs). Staged soils will be covered with plastic sheeting during non-work hours to prevent dust generation and runoff. It is estimated that approximately 31 truckloads will be required to transport the soil to a California-licensed receiving facility for disposal. Following excavation, confirmation soil sampling will be conducted to ensure established cleanup goals are achieved. If necessary, additional localized excavation will be performed. Upon completion, the excavated areas will be backfilled utilizing on-site soils, as the need for imported fill material is not anticipated. However, any imported fill, if required, will be verified in accordance with current DTSC advisories. The fieldwork portion of the project is estimated to take approximately 15 to 30 days to complete. Project-related air pollutant emissions from excavation and disposal activities are subject to compliance with all applicable requirements of the San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District (SJVAPCD). Although a formal SJVAPCD Dust Control Plan is not required due to the project’s size, best management practices will be strictly implemented such as water spraying, covering stockpiled soil, and truck tracking controls. To prevent fugitive dust generation and off-site drift, excavation areas will be actively managed using soil wetting techniques and continuous air monitoring at a minimum of two downwind fence line locations. Work will be suspended if site action levels for dust are exceeded.
ceqa-1fc8e05b9f158aebbe.crossStreets: West Dakota Avenue & North Hayes Avenue

ceqa-da7ca90b9f5236bda3.name: 2028 Amendments to the California Green Building Standards Code Pursuant to Senate Bill 745
ceqa-da7ca90b9f5236bda3.projectTitle: 2028 Amendments to the California Green Building Standards Code Pursuant to Senate Bill 745
ceqa-da7ca90b9f5236bda3.description: In response to the Drought-Resistant Buildings Act (SB 745), the Building Standards Commission (BSC) is proposing amendments to CALGreen, Part 11 of Title 24.The proposed amendments are intended to reduce potable water use in new nonresidential buildings by elevating certain existing voluntary water-efficiency measures to mandatory requirements. The proposed requirements would provide multiple compliance options to accommodate varying building types and regional conditions throughout California. If adopted, the amendments would be incorporated into the 2028 CALGreen, scheduled for publication on July 1, 2028, and would take effect on January 1, 2029.The Project consists of changes to building design and construction requirements that would apply statewide. Accordingly, the geographic scope of the Project encompasses the entire State of California. Although CALGreen establishes requirements applicable to new construction, the Project does not propose, authorize, or induce the construction of any new buildings or development. Rather, CALGreen regulates how applicable buildings and improvements are designed and constructed when such construction occurs; it does not determine where or when new construction takes place.

ceqa-5bac0b438deec2e8cc.description: The proposed Project involves the development of a 271 single-family residential subdivision on an approximately 53.43-acre portion of APN 012-190-255T and 012-160-255T (Project Site). Currently, the Project is located outside of the City of Mendota’s city limits and the City of Mendota’s Sphere of Influence. In addition to the 271 single-family residential lot tentative subdivision map (TSM), the Project includes a request to amend the City’s Sphere of Influence (SCI) and annex the Project site into the City. The Project proposes to amend the existing Low Density Residential land use designation for APN 012-190-255T to Medium Density Residential while concurrently amending the City’s Official Zoning Map to prezone APN 012-190-255T to the PH zone district (Single-Fami/Medium Density Residential), which is consistent with the proposed Medium Density Residential General Plan land use designation. Additionally, the Project proposes to prezone APN 012-160-255T to the P-F zone district (Public Facilities) which is consistent with the current Public Facility General Plan land use designation. The application also requests the Project be processed as a Planned Development to provide flexibility from the normally required development standards of the R-l zone district. Upon approval of the Project the City of Mendota City Council, the amendment of the City’s SCI and annexation of the Project site would be initiated with the Fresno County Local Agency Formation Commission (Fresno LAFCO). In addition to development of the subdivision, the Project would extend Amador Avenue to Belmont Avenue with one lane in each direction. The Project would also include a new permanent storm drainage basin, approximately 4.21 acres in size, located immediately north of the subdivision (on APN 012-160-ZSST) to accommodate storm water runoff generated by the Project. Additionally, approximately one-half mile of new sewer main piping and manholes will extend the existing Westside Sewer Interceptor trunk line from its current terminus on the northside of the existing residential subdivision along Amador Avenue to the southern end of the development

ceqa-8c71da867706448a0e.description: The Project would include the construction of a new, one-story, approximately 8,600-gross-square-foot (GSF) meats processing laboratory building. The new lab facility would consist of dry storage, cooler, freezer storage, raw meat preparation area, commercial kitchen and packing area, restrooms, an office, and a meeting/training/teaching room. The building and associated facilities would support teaching activities for Agricultural Sciences and Technology Program students. Operation of the Project would include meat processing, product preparation, training workshops, and educational seminars during regular hours with some evening or weekend hours. There would no public sales of meat products or public events at the facility. The facility would replace the current undersized processing space in the Animal Science Multipurpose Facility. The Project would include 30 new parking spaces and new electrical, natural gas, stormwater, water, and sewer service connections to existing utility infrastructure near the Project site. The campus is required to comply with the Region-wide Municipal Separate Storm Sewer Systems (MS4) permit issued by the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB) in 2016, and the Storm Water Quality Management Program (SWQMP), adopted in 2013. The Project site is less than 1 acre, so it would not require compliance with the applicable Construction General Permit. The site would be landscaped with drought-tolerant plantings. The Project would be designed to meet Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Silver equivalent and would, at a minimum, comply with Title 24 Building, Energy and Green Buildings Standards. Exterior lighting would adhere to LEED–New Construction (NC) guidelines for light pollution reduction and energy efficiency. The Project would include roof-mounted photovoltaic panels. A Minor Master Plan Revision would be required to locate the new building footprint on the campus; this would be required as part of the Project approval. While this is a new building, it replaces an existing use and program space located within the existing Animal Science Multipurpose Facility (Building 252) and is located in an area with other agricultural buildings and facilities. The Project is subject to and incorporates applicable mitigation measures in the Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program (MMRP) adopted in conjunction with certification of the Campus Master Plan Revision Environmental Impact Report (EIR) (State Clearinghouse Number 1994032022) by the CSU Board of Trustees in 1994. Applicable mitigation measures address cultural resources, drainage and flooding, and hazardous materials, and would be implemented during Project construction and/or operation.

ceqa-de0c8bb59fa8f81535.name: CEMEX Rockfield Quarry Modification Project Environmental Impact Report No. 7763 and Unclassified Conditional Use Permit Application Nos. 3666 and 3667
ceqa-de0c8bb59fa8f81535.projectTitle: CEMEX Rockfield Quarry Modification Project - Environmental Impact Report No. 7763 and Unclassified Conditional Use Permit Application Nos. 3666 and 3667
ceqa-de0c8bb59fa8f81535.description: CEMEX Construction Materials Pacific LLC (the “Applicant”) has applied to the County of Fresno Department of Public Works and Planning (County) for two Unclassified Conditional Use Permits (CUP Application Nos. 3666 and 3667) to allow the Rockfield Quarry a continuation and modification of its current aggregate (rock, sand, and gravel) mining and processing operations. The project is generally located at two separate sites approximately two miles apart, The first, the Plant Site, is located on the west side of North Friant Road between North Willow Avenue and Little Dry Creek, and the second, the Quarry Site, is located on the west side of North Friant Road between Bluff View Avenue and Lost Lake Road. The County is the lead agency for preparation of the Environmental Impact Report (EIR No. 7763) for this project and is circulating the Final EIR, including the proposed responses to comments, to public agencies that commented on the Draft EIR pursuant to Section 15088(b) of the CEQA Guidelines. PROJECT LOCATION The project site is located at two sites: 13475 N. Friant Road and 14765 North Friant Road, Fresno, CA 93636, between North Friant Road and the San Joaquin River, in an unincorporated portion of Fresno County. Continued surface mining disturbances are planned on the two locations, the Plant Site and the Quarry Site, as described below: • Plant Site (CUP 3666): CEMEX’s current Plant Site is located on approximately 138.5 acres on the west side of North Friant Road, approximately 1.5 miles north of the City of Fresno and approximately 0.7 mile north of the intersection of North Willow Avenue and North Friant Road. The Plant Site includes approximately 126.6 acres owned by the Applicant (APNs 300-070-56S, 57S, 58S, and 60S) and approximately 11.9 acres owned by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (portions of APNs 300-070-43ST, 48ST, and 50ST). • Quarry Site (CUP 3667): CEMEX’s current Quarry Site is located on approximately 352.4 acres on the west side of N. Friant Road (APNs 300-040-19 & 20, 300-080-01S, 300-250-12 & portion of 300-310-01) approximately 2.0 miles north of CEMEX’s current Plant Site and approximately 2.0 miles south of the unincorporated community of Friant. PROJECT DESCRIPTION The Applicant is requesting a continuation and modification of its current aggregate (rock, sand, and gravel) mining and processing operations. The Project includes the following two project life stages that are estimated to span 100 years: Stage 1: - Continue concurrent operations at both the Quarry Site and the Plant Site for up to 30 years. - At the Plant Site, the existing aggregate processing plant would continue to be used to wash, screen, crush and sort aggregate mined on site. - At the Quarry Site the hard rock deposit that lies beneath the alluvial deposit currently being mined, would be mined. Excavation of the hard rock would require drilling and blasting and would occur to a depth of approximately 600-feet below ground surface (bgs). - An aggregate processing plant would be added to the Quarry Site to wash, screen, crush, and sort the hard rock to be mined on site. - Aggregate products produced at the Quarry Site used at the asphalt and ready-mix plants at the Plant Site would be transported approximately 2 miles south to the Plant Site via Friant Road in the same manner as the raw aggregate currently being transported from the Quarry Site to the Plant Site for the existing operations. - Other aggregate products produced at the Quarry site not used by the asphalt and ready-mix plants at the Plant Site would be sold directly from the quarry. - The existing asphalt plant at the Plant Site would be replaced with a modern Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA) plant. - Periodic use of a portable crushing plant to recycle come-back concrete would continue with the addition of asphalt recycling and import of concrete debris to recycle into crushed miscellaneous base (CMB) and asphalt debris to be recycled asphalt product (RAP). - Mine the remaining alluvial deposit at the Plant Site to a depth of approximately 85-feet below ground surface (bgs). - Relocation of the plant operations at the Plant Site to the Quarry Site in less than 30 years to recover the deposit beneath the plants. - Upon approval of project permits, the combined annual sales of aggregate from both sites are estimated to ramp up from the 1.4 MT allowed under the current permits to 2.0 MT in approximately five years and up to 3.0 MT in approximately 10 years. - When mining is completed at the Plant Site, reclamation would consist of approximately 138.5 acres of open space, riparian and open water wildlife habitat. Stage 2: - Continue hard rock mining and processing operations only at the Quarry Site for approximately 70 more years. The ready-mix concrete plant and the hot-mix asphalt plant would be relocated from the Plant Site to the Quarry Site. - The periodic use of a portable plant to recycle concrete and asphalt debris (including imported) into CMB and RAP would be added to the Quarry Site. - All aggregate products produced at the Quarry site would be used by the on-site asphalt and ready-mix plants or sold directly from the Quarry Site. The interplant haul would cease. - Stage 2 operations are estimated to have annual aggregate sales of 3.0 MT. - Reclamation of the Quarry Site would create approximately 352.4 acres of open space, riparian and open water wildlife habitat.
ceqa-de0c8bb59fa8f81535.crossStreets: Plant Site: North Friant Rd/North Willow Ave; Quarry Site: North Friant Rd/Bluff View Ave

ceqa-1f175c0f45aa290f29.name: Environmental Review No. 8980 - California Climate Investments-Shaded Fuel Breaks
ceqa-1f175c0f45aa290f29.projectTitle: Environmental Review No. 8980 - California Climate Investments-Shaded Fuel Breaks
ceqa-1f175c0f45aa290f29.description: The proposed project consists of establishing two shaded fuel breaks along Auberry Road and Peterson Road in eastern Fresno County. The Auberry Road Shaded Fuel Break totals approximately 315 acres, and the Peterson Road Shaded Fuel Break totals approximately 234 acres (see attached map). Vegetation treatment will generally occur within 200 feet of each road centerline, creating a 400-foot-wide gap in fuel continuity. Standing dead trees will be assessed and marked by, or under the direct supervision of, a Registered Professional Forester (RPF) for removal and disposal. Smaller-diameter trees and slash may be chipped and broadcast on-site to a depth not exceeding six inches, masticated on-site, or hauled off-site for legal disposal. Woody brush will be removed to reduce horizontal and vertical fuel continuity. Targeted herbicide may be used for long-term maintenance and prevention of ladder-fuel regrowth in accordance with all applicable federal, state, and local laws, regulations, and label requirements. A licensed Pest Control Advisor will recommend the appropriate herbicide, and a contractor holding a Qualified Applicator License will apply the material. Selective retention and spacing of sprouting hardwoods and seedlings and saplings of mortality-impacted species, including ponderosa pine and sugar pine, will promote canopy shade, with treatment targeting an average crown spacing of at least 20 feet. RPFs will prepare detailed treatment plans, layout design, and silvicultural prescriptions. Watercourses and wet areas will be flagged and buffered in accordance with California Forest Practice Rules, with equipment limitation and exclusion zones established as appropriate. The project is intended to reduce community wildfire hazards and promote a healthier forest landscape. Funding is provided by the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection's Wildfire Prevention Grants Program as part of the California Climate Investments Program.

ceqa-7f85b18940c194bac8.name: BirdReturns
ceqa-7f85b18940c194bac8.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Habitat Conservation Planning
ceqa-7f85b18940c194bac8.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife (Headquarters), Habitat Conservation Planning Branch - Sacramento
ceqa-7f85b18940c194bac8.description: The BirdReturns program funds several successful and established habitat incentive programs including the Spring Wetlands, Semi-Permanent and Permanent Wetlands, Farmlands, Fall Wetlands, Winter Habitat and Tricolored Blackbird Colony Protection Programs. In partnership with the Migratory Bird Conservation Partnership, which includes the non-governmental agencies, The Nature Conservancy, Point Blue Conservation Science, and Audubon California, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife will oversee the administration of funds and implementation of the programs. These programs provide high-value habitat for migratory and resident waterbirds during specific windows of their annual cycle by incentivizing private landowners (private wetland owners and agricultural producers) to manage water to meet waterbirds specific needs. Not only do these practices provide waterbird habitat, but they are also beneficial for landowners and improve California’s climate resiliency by recharging groundwater, allowing flexibility during drought scenarios, reducing flood risk, controlling weeds, improving wetland habitat, and improving recreation benefits for rural communities.

ceqa-305a5e735afe844855.name: P25-03460 Cal Color Dryer Expansion - Development Permit
ceqa-305a5e735afe844855.description: For the environmental analysis, this addendum analyzes the change contemplated from the original Project. The original Mitigated Negative Declaration (Original MND), State Clearinghouse Number 2022080501, adopted by the City of Fresno on August 22, 2022, considered a minor expansion of the existing California Natural Color operations. Since the Original IS/MND was approved, California Natural Color has identified a need for further expansion of their operations. Specifically, California Natural Color will expand their existing dryer and dry storage warehouse by constructing a 28,000 sq. ft. expansion that will connect the existing Dryer building and Dry Storage warehouse. The new expansion will be approximately 150’ x 150’ with a first story of approximately 17,700 sq. ft. and a second story of approximately 10,300 sq. ft. Combined with the existing Dryer and Dry Storage Warehouse, which is 18,700 sq. ft. with one (1) dryer, this will create a total building area of approximately 46,700 sq. ft. with a total of five (5) dryers. The expansion would provide the necessary space to accommodate four (4) additional dryers over the next four (4) years. The Project would consist of a new building with utility connections to existing site infrastructure, new grading and paving, new parking stalls, and relocation of perimeter fencing and gates to accommodate the new building layout, and a proposed lot line adjustment between parcels owned by E & J Gallo Winery. See Attachment A for the site plans. Building The face of the new building is over 300 feet back from the property line and is located behind other existing buildings. It is a steel building with metal siding and metal roof, consistent with other buildings at the facility. It is 30 feet tall at the eaves and under 40 feet tall at the highest point. There are no exterior windows, and exterior doors are limited to control access into this building. As a food ingredient production facility, sanitary design is important to keep the interior spaces clean and washable. The dryers are located on the second floor to allow for the dried flakes that are produced to drop directly into milling machines that grind the products into uniform particle size powders. The facility uses and stores some materials that are classified as hazardous. This includes CIP cleaning chemicals for sanitizing equipment and piping, washing down rooms, and foot baths. Gallo will complete a dust hazard analysis to identify and address hazard concerns of the milled product. Utilities The new building will use electricity, potable water, natural gas, steam, and compressed air. All these utilities will be served by the facility’s existing infrastructure, without the need for upgrades from utility providers. Storm drainage and wastewater from the process will be collected and treated using existing onsite storm basins and wastewater treatment systems; no modifications to those systems are anticipated. No additional restrooms or break areas are planned with this expansion, as this space will be served by adjacent amenities. Therefore, no additional sanitary sewer waste is generated with this project. Site & Traffic The building will occupy an area on the east side of the facility that is currently an asphalt paved area used for circulation of trucks accessing the loading dock that is just southwest of the proposed expansion. There is ample space in the northeast area of the facility to accommodate truck navigation and staging that are displaced by this new building. Two landscape islands will be reduced to accommodate the truck navigation around the building. The perimeter fence and gate on the east side of the facility will be relocated but will maintain the same aesthetic and same level of security as the existing entry gate. Over the course of the next five years, an increase of approximately 2 inbound trucks per day delivering raw materials and 2 outbound trucks per day shipping finished goods is expected, which will have a negligible impact to traffic and operations in and around the facility. There are currently 95 employees and 5 new employees are expected with this expansion. In addition, minimal daily impact on visitors are expected at this facility as a result of this expansion. The facility will handle similar traffic to the current operation, and will allow for access by the semi-trucks for delivery and shipment of goods. Fire lanes will also be maintained for access by emergency services personnel. The revised Project would not have a significant impact. It may be determined that: (1) No substantial changes are proposed in the revised Project which require major revisions to the Original MND due to the involvement of new significant environmental effects or a substantial increase in the severity of previously identified significant effects; (2) No substantial changes will occur with respect to the circumstances under which the Project is undertaken which will require major revisions of the Original MND due to the involvement of new significant environmental effects or a substantial increase in the severity of previously identified significant effects; and, (3) No new information, which was not known and could not have been known with the exercise of reasonable diligence at the time the Original MND was adopted has become available. Analysis for this determination is detailed in the section below. Therefore, the City of Fresno has determined that an addendum to the Original MND is appropriate given that none of the conditions described in Section 15162 of the CEQA Guidelines calling for preparation of a subsequent negative declaration have occurred; and, new information added is only for the purposes of providing minor changes or additions, in accordance with Section 15164 of the CEQA Guidelines.

ceqa-a8d63eff1d241a1cd7.name: Norseman Elementary School Modernization
ceqa-a8d63eff1d241a1cd7.description: The Fresno Unified School District proposes the Norseman Elementary School Modernization Project to modernize the existing 12.4-acre Norseman Elementary School campus and associated adjacent rights-of-way using Measure H bond funding. The project includes demolition, reconstruction, and renovation of aging facilities; construction of new classroom, early learning, and administration buildings; modernization of existing campus buildings; upgrades to outdoor learning and recreation areas; and improvements to parking, circulation, and student drop-off areas. The project would demolish approximately 27,850 square feet of existing buildings and construct approximately 28,500 square feet of new facilities, resulting in approximately 64,100 square feet of total campus space. Limited off-site traffic safety improvements may also occur within adjacent public rights-of-way. Construction is anticipated to occur between June 2028 and August 2029 and would be phased to allow the school to remain operational. The project would not increase student enrollment or campus capacity and would be designed in compliance with applicable state building, accessibility, energy efficiency, and safety standards.

ceqa-2a5aa7794f23d3b16b.name: Calwa Elementary School Reconstruction
ceqa-2a5aa7794f23d3b16b.description: The District proposes to implement the Calwa Elementary School Reconstruction Project (the "project") using Measure H bond funds. The existing campus buildings, constructed between 1945 and 1970, are among the oldest in the District and no longer meet current District standards or adequately serve student needs. The project would involve selective demolition and reconstruction of certain campus buildings, while other buildings would undergo interior renovation. Construction would occur in two overlapping phases while instruction remains in session. The project’s purpose is to replace and renovate facilities that no longer meet current building, accessibility, and educational standards. The proposed campus reconstruction would include a new Multipurpose Room (MPR), Administration Office, and Early Learning Building, as well as interior renovations to seven existing buildings. Site improvements would include a new parking lot with a student drop-off loop in the northwest portion of the campus, a staff parking lot in the southeast, a bus drop-off loop in the south, and redeveloped play areas in the north and northeast. The project would not increase student enrollment or overall campus capacity. Instead, it would provide students and staff with equitable access to modern, energy-efficient, accessible, and safe facilities that are consistent with other recently modernized District campuses. Construction is anticipated to begin in June 2028 and end in August 2030.

ceqa-11d0901cad10186834.description: The 21st District Agricultural Association / Big Fresno Fair proposes to construct the Big Fresno Community Cooling Corridor at the Big Fresno Fairgrounds. The Project consists of nature-based cooling and communityserving improvements within the existing developed footprint of the fairgrounds, including expanded tree canopy through the planting of native and drought-tolerant shade trees; shade structures and shade sails over existing pedestrian gathering and circulation areas; hydration stations, misters, and passive cooling elements along the existing pedestrian network; green stormwater and low-impact landscape improvements; and interpretive signage, wayfinding, and cultural/educational elements developed in consultation with local California Native American tribes. Purpose: reduce extreme-heat vulnerability at the fairgrounds, expand tree canopy in a disadvantaged and climate-vulnerable community, and strengthen the fairgrounds' capacity to serve as a public gathering venue and emergency response and resiliency hub. The Project is sited within the existing developed footprint of the fairgrounds and does not expand the operational envelope of the facility. Beneficiaries: residents of the City of Fresno and Fresno County (including populations identified as vulnerable to extreme-heat and other climate hazards under CalEnviroScreen and Healthy Places Index screens for the census tracts encompassing the fairgrounds); approximately 500,000 annual Big Fresno Fair visitors plus year-round fairground event attendees; local California Native American tribes participating in the Project's cultural and educational elements; and first responders and displaced residents using the fairgrounds as an emergency response and resiliency site during wildfire smoke, extreme-heat, flood, and other declared events.

ceqa-d37be43309228f31a1.description: The proposed Project involves the development of a 271 single-family residential subdivision on an approximately 53.43-acre portion of APN 012-190 255T and 012-160-ZSST (Project Site). Currently, the Project is located outside of the City of Mendota’s city limits and the City of Mendota’s Sphere of Influence. In addition to the 271 single-family residential lot tentative subdivision map (TSM), the Project includes a request to amend the City’s Sphere of Influence (SCI) and annex the Project site into the City. The Project proposes to amend the existing Low Density Residential land use designation for APN 012-190-255T to Medium Density Residential while concurrently amending the City’s Official Zoning Map to prezone APN 012-190-255T to the R-1 zone district (Single-Family/Medium Density Residential), which is consistent with the proposed Medium Density Residential General Plan land use designation. Additionally, the Project proposes to prezone APN 012-160-ZSST to the P-F zone district (Public Facilities) which is consistent with the current Public Facility General Plan land use designation. The application also requests the Project be processed as a Planned Development to provide flexibility from the normally required development standards of the R-l zone district. Upon approval of the Project the City of Mendota City Council, the amendment of the City’s SCI and annexation of the Project site would be initiated with the Fresno County Local Agency Formation Commission (Fresno LAFCo). In addition to development of the subdivision, the Project would extend Amador Avenue to Belmont Avenue with one lane in each direction. The Project would also include a new permanent storm drainage basin, approximately 4.21 acres in size, located immediately north of the subdivision (on APN 012-160-ZSST) to accommodate storm water runoff generated by the Project. Additionally, approximately one-half mile of new sewer main piping and manholes will extend the existing Westside Sewer Interceptor trunk line from its current terminus on the northside of the existing residential subdivision along Amador Avenue to the southern end of the development.

ceqa-4f195c29814cd46a83.name: Replacement Tire Efficiency Program
ceqa-4f195c29814cd46a83.description: Notice of Determination for the Replacement Tire Efficiency Program. Assembly Bill 844 (Nation, Chapter 645, Statutes of 2003) requires the CEC to develop and maintain a replacement tire efficiency program under Public Resources Code (PRC) sections 25770–25773. Pursuant to PRC sections 25770–25773, CEC staff designed the Replacement Tire Efficiency Program (RTEP) to ensure that replacement tires sold in California are at least as energy-efficient, on average, as original equipment tires on new passenger vehicles and light-duty trucks. The RTEP seeks to improve the energy efficiency of replacement tires through the establishment of minimum performance standards, as well as a consumer-focused efficiency rating system, for replacement tires for passenger cars and light-duty trucks sold in California. The amended proposed minimum standards would apply to the sale of new replacement tires starting with those manufactured on or after January 1, 2029, with a more stringent level coming into effect on January 1, 2033 (referred to as Phase I and Phase II, respectively).

ceqa-41d31d607f0feb48ab.name: California High-Speed Train Project: Fresno to Bakersfield Major Amendment No. 35; California Endangered Species Act Incidental Take Permit No. 2081-2015-024-04

ceqa-41d31d607f0feb48ab.description: The Project involves the construction of the California HST alignment. This Major Amendment No. 35 updates Tables 10 and 10A, adds Covered Activities, modifies several speciesspecific ITP Conditions of Approval and adds new species-specific Conditions of Approval. The Project is expected to result in incidental take of California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense, CTS), Tipton kangaroo rat (Dipodomys nitratoides nitratoides, TKR), San Joaquin antelope squirrel (Ammospermophilus nelsoni, SJAS), Swainson’s hawk (Buteo swainsoni, SWHA), San Joaquin kit fox (Vulpes macrotis mutica, SJFK), western burrowing owl (Athene cunicularia hypugaea, BUOW), and blunt-nosed leopard lizard (Gambelia sila, BNLL) (collectively, the Covered Species). CTS, SJAS, SWHA, and SJKF are species designated as threatened, TKR is designated as endangered, and BUOW are designated as a candidate species under the California Endangered Species Act (CESA). BNLL is designated as endangered under CESA and is fully protected under Fish and Game Code. The ITP referenced above as issued by CDFW authorizes incidental take of species listed under CESA that may occur as a result of Project implementation.

ceqa-8a7c6bdd2cc86f2fdd.name: California High-Speed Rail Central Valley Heavy Maintenance Facility Project
ceqa-8a7c6bdd2cc86f2fdd.projectTitle: California High-Speed Rail Central Valley Heavy Maintenance Facility Project
ceqa-8a7c6bdd2cc86f2fdd.description: The Authority proposes to construct and operate an HMF to support the full range of Phase 1 (San Francisco – Los Angeles/Anaheim) HSR operation and maintenance activities, including crewing, servicing, heavy repairs, and storage of trains, while also providing accommodations for staff and operations management. Key components of both HMF alternatives include: Two independent points of access to the HSR mainline; Stabling tracks to provide designated parking areas for trainsets that are not in active service; Servicing platforms to support regular interior cleaning and to prepare trains for service, crew platforms and support structures, exterior cleaning, and support structures; Vehicle maintenance shops to include support for regular ongoing light and heavy maintenance of trainsets, low-speed dynamic testing, static testing, and switching, coupling, uncoupling, and lifting of train cars. The vehicle maintenance shops would also include a wheel reprofiling track support shops and offices and areas for storage of materials and equipment; A component shop campus to support long-term operational resilience of the Phase 1 HSR system and domestic supply-chain security for HSR critical parts, components, and specialist services; A solar array and battery energy storage system consisting of solar panels mounted on racks that would generate and store energy to support the HMF operations; Additional areas, such as parking lots (employee and visitor), access roads (including improvements to the adjacent roadway network), stormwater detention ponds, utilities, fences, and other facilities, that could include, but would not be limited to, cart storage facilities, crew transfer buildings, a cleaning crew building, a waste facility for waste products awaiting off-site disposal, a substation, and an emergency generator. Page 5 of 9 The preparation of this Central Valley HMF Project EIR will involve development of preliminary engineering designs and assessment of environmental effects associated with the construction, operation, and maintenance of the proposed project. The Central Valley HMF Project EIR will examine a range of HMF alternative sites, as well as a No Project Alternative. This project-level EIR will describe site-specific environmental impacts, identify specific mitigation measures to address those impacts, and incorporate design practices to avoid and minimize potentially significant environmental impacts. The Authority will assess the site characteristics, size, nature, and timing of proposed site-specific projects to determine whether impacts can be avoided or mitigated. The EIR will identify and evaluate the impacts from construction, operation, and maintenance of the HMF. Information and documents regarding this HSR environmental review process will be available through the Authority's website: hsr.ca.gov/CVHMF-environmental-documents.
ceqa-8a7c6bdd2cc86f2fdd.crossStreets: East Malaga Avenue & South Cedar Ave (Fresno); CA-43 & Iona Ave (Hanford).See attached NOC maps.

ceqa-fdb540d4dfba2c187e.description: The Westlands Water District (District) proposes to implement a contract for application of a copper based molluscicide to the District’s existing water infrastructure, specifically at lateral numbers 7R and 4L. The application is intended to eradicate and prevent immediate resettlement of the Golden Mussel on the treated pipeline infrastructure. Pursuant to a vendor agreement, the project would apply a properly registered molluscicide that is effective in the treatment of Golden Mussels and for use on raw water for agricultural and municipal use. Applications would start as soon as possible and continue through December of 2026, but may be stopped sooner if desired control is achieved. The project will require assessment of mussel mortality and regular water quality monitoring. The application is intended to mitigate and prevent further damage to the District’s infrastructure, limit the spread of the Golden Mussel, and minimize threats to property, essential public services, and the environment. The project will also require a budget augmentation to fund Division 3 (Operations and Maintenance) expenses.

ceqa-203885eabca8b376bd.name: North-to-South Water Transfers Subsequent El R to the 2019 Long-Term Water Transfers Final ElR
ceqa-203885eabca8b376bd.projectTitle: North-to-South Water Transfers Subsequent El R to the 2019 Long-Term Water Transfers Final ElR
ceqa-203885eabca8b376bd.agency: San Luis and Delta Mendota Water Authority
ceqa-203885eabca8b376bd.agencyName: San Luis and Delta Mendota Water Authority
ceqa-203885eabca8b376bd.description: The North-to-South Water Transfers Subsequent EIR (SEIR) will evaluate a range of alternatives for potential single-year water transfers over a multi-year period to facilitate responsible transfers when climate or water resource variability limit water supply availability in Central Valley Project-dependent areas. Transfers would occur through agreements between willing Sellers and Buyers. Each potential transfer must be proposed, reviewed, and approved by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation on an annual basis. The project location includes the counties that overlap with the Buyers’ and Sellers’ Service Areas and at reservoirs used for release transfers. Affected counties include Alameda, Butte, Colusa, Contra Costa, El Dorado, Fresno, Glenn, Kings, Merced, Placer, Sacramento, Shasta, Stanislaus, Sutter, San Benito, Santa Clara, Tehama, and Yolo counties. The San Luis & Delta-Mendota Water Authority (SLDMWA) plans to prepare a SEIR to the 2019 Long-Term Water Transfers Final EIR (LTWT EIR). In April 2020, SLDMWA certified the LTWT EIR. Since certification, changes have been proposed to the project that warrant consideration in a subsequent EIR to assess the potential effects of the project with the proposed changes (consistent with California Public Resources Code, § 21166 and State CEQA Guidelines, 14 CCR § 15162). Specifically, the SEIR will consider a revised list of participating sellers and transfer quantities. The LTWT EIR retains its informational value regarding the environmental effects of the project. Preparation of the SEIR will evaluate the potential environmental effects of the project as revised and ensure that any new or substantially more severe environmental impacts are addressed through the CEQA process.

ceqa-58c2085c8ee444249a.name: Helms Pumped Storage Project, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Project No. 2735
ceqa-58c2085c8ee444249a.projectTitle: Relicensing of Helms Pumped Storage Project
ceqa-58c2085c8ee444249a.description: The Proposed Project covered by this Notice of Determination involves the FERC relicensing of Pacific Gas and Electric Company’s (PG&E) Helms Pumped Storage Project (Project). PG&E has applied for a new FERC license for the Proposed Project, under which it proposes to: (1) continue to operate the Helms Pumped Storage Project; (2) replace and rehabilitate existing recreation facilities; (3) designate approximately 36 miles of existing roads and approximately one mile of existing trails as Project roads and trails; (4) modify the FERC Project boundary to more accurately define lands necessary for Project operation and maintenance activities under a new FERC Project license; and (5) implement new protection, mitigation, and enhancement plans and measures. The Project transfers water to and from Courtright Lake (upper reservoir) and Lake Wishon (lower reservoir) for power generation and water storage. The Project's two intake-discharge structures are normally underwater, and all Project facilities and structures used to exchange water between the two reservoirs are underground. Courtright Lake and Lake Wishon are impounded by Courtright Dam and Wishon Dam, respectively, all of which are licensed facilities of PG&E’s Haas-Kings River Hydroelectric Project. The Project includes Courtright Intake-Discharge Structure; Wishon Intake-Discharge Structure; Tunnels 1, 2, and 3; Helms Penstocks; Lost Canyon Pipe; Helms Powerhouse; Helms Switchyard; approximately 65 miles of transmission and distribution lines; approximately 38 miles of non-recreational Project roads and trails; three helicopter landing zones; an 80-acre wildlife habitat management area; 12 recreational facilities near Courtright Lake and Lake Wishon; and ancillary support facilities.

ceqa-b59f786bba384e9b80.name: (RFFCP2022) Tribal Capacity Building Program – Big Sandy Rancheria (SNC1741-RFFCP)
ceqa-b59f786bba384e9b80.projectTitle: (RFFCP2022) Tribal Capacity Building Program – Big Sandy Rancheria (SNC1741-RFFCP)
ceqa-b59f786bba384e9b80.description: Sierra Nevada Conservancy (SNC) would award grant agreement #1741-RFFCP (RFFCP2022) Tribal Capacity Building Program – Big Sandy Rancheria to Big Sandy Rancheria of Western Mono Indians to partner with the Bureau of Indian Affairs to maintain existing fuel breaks around Big Sandy Rancheria. Utilizing tribal crews, hand, and mechanical treatments, the Proposed Project would reduce hazardous fuels on 70-80 acres of previous established shaded fuel breaks. Potential specific treatment activities to maintain the fuel break would include thinning of ladder fuels and overgrown vegetation, removal of dead and downed woody debris, hand thinning, mechanical thinning, lop & scatter, mastication, and chipping, and maintenance of defensible space around homes and structures. The fuel breaks were originally established between 2022 and 2024, and this project is maintenance activities within the existing fuel break footprints.

ceqa-67e0dc000f84751490.name: Rosemary Solar and Energy Storage System Complex Project

ceqa-67e0dc000f84751490.description: The Rosemary Solar Project (Project) will construct and operate a 140-megawatt (MW) photovoltaic (PV) solar and battery energy storage facility on approximately 1,212 acres of land located in an agricultural area of unincorporated Fresno County west of State Route 145, approximately 25 miles southwest of Fresno, 6 miles east of Cantua Creek, and 5 miles south of San Joaquin on the south side of Kamm Avenue between South El Dorado Avenue and South Yuba Avenue. The Project consists of three interconnected generation sites, an on-site substation, to an approximate 2-mile transmission line connecting to the Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) Crescent Substation. The Project plans to upgrade the utility infrastructure including reconducting 5-miles of PG&E transmission lines and the eventual decommissioning of the facility at the end of its operational life.

ceqa-f2e60a75c7502d91cb.name: SB 1013 Addition of New Beverage Containers Permanent Regulations
ceqa-f2e60a75c7502d91cb.projectTitle: SB 1013 Addition of New Beverage Containers Permanent Regulations
ceqa-f2e60a75c7502d91cb.agency: California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery
ceqa-f2e60a75c7502d91cb.agencyName: Resources Recycling and Recovery, Department of (CalRecycle)
ceqa-f2e60a75c7502d91cb.description: In 2022, the Legislature enacted Senate Bill 1013 (2021-2022 Reg. Session, Chapter 610 of the Statutes of 2022), Public Resources Code sections 14504, 14560, and 14561, to expand the types of beverages and beverages containers that are eligible for redemption as part of the BCRP. Prior to the passage of SB 1013, chapter 5, division 2, title 14 of the California Code of Regulations (“14 CCR”) established a framework for the BCRP that includes a system of payments and procedures among a variety of program participants. This regulatory framework is built upon the previously eligible beverages and beverage containers. Since the Bottle Bill was enacted, there have been a number of amendments to PRC section 14504 to expand the type of beverages covered by the Act. Immediately prior to the passage of Senate Bill 1013 (2021-2022 Reg. Session, Chapter 610 of the Statutes of 2022) (“SB 1013”), certain types of beverages were covered by the Act where in a beverage container primarily consisting of aluminum, glass, plastic, or bimetal. The covered beverage types excluded the following: wine, distilled spirits, wine and distilled spirit coolers exceeding 7 percent alcohol by volume, certain large fruit and juice containers, milk, medical food, and infant formula.? Prior to SB 1013 being chaptered, CRV had increased to 5 cents for a beverage container less than 24 ounces, and 10 cents for a beverage container 24 ounces or larger. CalRecycle has developed a proposed regulation to establish administrative procedures to enable CalRecycle to fulfill its responsibilities under SB 1013.

ceqa-58940aca3bd2bbf437.name: Norseman Elementary School Modernization
ceqa-58940aca3bd2bbf437.description: The Fresno Unified School District proposes the Norseman Elementary School Modernization Project to modernize the existing 12.4-acre Norseman Elementary School campus and associated adjacent rights-of-way using Measure H bond funding. The project includes demolition, reconstruction, and renovation of aging facilities; construction of new classroom, early learning, and administration buildings; modernization of existing campus buildings; upgrades to outdoor learning and recreation areas; and improvements to parking, circulation, and student drop-off areas. The project would demolish approximately 27,850 square feet of existing buildings and construct approximately 28,500 square feet of new facilities, resulting in approximately 64,100 square feet of total campus space. Limited off-site traffic safety improvements may also occur within adjacent public rights-of-way. Construction is anticipated to occur between June 2028 and August 2029 and would be phased to allow the school to remain operational. The project would not increase student enrollment or campus capacity and would be designed in compliance with applicable state building, accessibility, energy efficiency, and safety standards.

Lead agencies and responsible agencies such as local land use and planning agencies, local enforcement agencies, and CalRecycle may use the CEQA document in considering subsequent discretionary actions.

ceqa-d24f18143dad8eec78.name: Adopt Emergency Regulations to Amend Title 22, California Code of Regulations, Division 4.5, Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 6
ceqa-d24f18143dad8eec78.projectTitle: Adopt Emergency Regulations to Amend Title 22, California Code of Regulations, Division 4.5, Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 6
ceqa-d24f18143dad8eec78.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-d24f18143dad8eec78.description: The Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) proposes to approve an emergency rulemaking amendment to add to the existing list of Covered Electronic Devices (CED’s) within the California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 66260.201(e). This emergency rulemaking will amend the list of CED’s to include the new devices and provide clarity to impacted entities. The amended regulations will safeguard California’s environment against potential hazardous constituents found in discarded electronic devices and expand financial incentives for proper end-of-life management which will lead to an increase in the amount of CED’s recycled and decrease the amount of hazardous electronic waste illegally disposed of in landfills. Background: California enacted the Electronic Waste Recycling Act (Act) of 2003 through Senate Bill 20, which was amended through Senate Bill 50 in 2005 to incentivize collectors and recyclers to provide ample opportunities to California residents for recycling, thereby discouraging the illegal disposal of hazardous electronic waste in landfills and establish a funding system for the collection and recycling of certain electronic waste identified as the Covered Electronic Waste Recycling Program (Program). A CED is a video display device containing a screen greater than four inches, measured diagonally, that is found to exhibit the hazardous waste characteristic of toxicity when discarded. The Program requires consumers to pay a fee on all CED’s at the time of retail purchase. Retailers can also elect to pay the fee on behalf of consumers. The retailers remit the fees they collect to the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA). CDTFA deposits the fees into a designated account used to provide payments to approved collectors and recyclers for the recovery, processing, and recycling of CED’s. The Act tasks the California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery (CalRecycle) with administering the payment system for collectors and recyclers. The Act also tasks DTSC with (a) developing regulations for the proper management of discarded CED’s, (b) identifying in regulations any devices that exhibit, or are presumed to exhibit, the hazardous waste characteristic of toxicity as a CED, and (c) conducting inspections and compliance activities. Under Health and Safety Code section 25214.10.1 subsection (c), DTSC has the authority to presume that devices are hazardous waste when discarded. Thus, based on DTSC’s presumption authority and the analytical testing data of components commonly used in the manufacture of video display devices as described below, DTSC has identified that these devices are CED’s and are hazardous waste when discarded. In 2021, DTSC’s Environmental Chemistry Lab conducted analytical testing on six different device categories that met the definition of a CED under Public Resources Code section 42463. Specifically, DTSC tested the printed circuit boards and screen materials from these devices. Analytical testing results concluded that these devices exhibit the hazardous waste characteristic of toxicity identified in Article 4 of chapter 11 and exceed the California hazardous waste total threshold concentrations described in section 66261.24(a)(2)(A) for copper, lead, and nickel. Therefore, these devices are deemed hazardous wastes when discarded and were added to the list of CED’s in emergency regulations, OAL reference# R-021-09E (readopted in 2023 and 2025). Project Activities: The proposed rulemaking will add five new device categories to the list of CED’s found in Chapter 11, Appendix X, Subsection (c) and Chapter 10, Subsection 66260.201(e). The new device categories consist of the following: • Portable gaming devices with an integrated screen; • Home surveillance monitors with an integrated or dedicated screen; • Smart mirrors and any other mirrors capable of displaying video; • Digital picture frames capable of displaying video; and • Smart remote controllers with an integrated screen capable of displaying video.

ceqa-6c4ca42db85045cde4.name: Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment Project at CAL TRANS D6 Coalinga
ceqa-6c4ca42db85045cde4.projectTitle: Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment Project at CAL TRANS D6 Coalinga
ceqa-6c4ca42db85045cde4.description: The project consists of installing the Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE) infrastructure for fleet vehicles use. This initiative is designed to create a fully operational system that will eventually support one dual port and one single port, pedestal-mounted Electric Vehicle Charging Stations (EVCS). Note that the installation of the EVCS themselves is outside our current scope and may be handled by others at a later date. As part of this project, three parking stalls will be specially stenciled and restriped. Clear signage will be installed to indicate that these stalls are reserved for electric vehicle use, ensuring easy identification and proper use The project involves the installation of buried conduits, fixed bollards, wheel stops, and new electrical equipment, including all necessary wiring, to deliver a complete and functional system. Electrical power for the EVSE will be drawn from an existing source already available at the site. All aspects of the work, including waste disposal, will be conducted in strict compliance with all applicable laws, regulations, and ordinances. The work will involve pavement saw cutting, trenching, backfilling, and restoring the affected lot surface to its original condition once the installation is complete.

ceqa-c62759f5b7c7afe430.name: Pulse Flows Component of the Water Storage Investment Program (WSIP) Groundwater Projects
ceqa-c62759f5b7c7afe430.projectTitle: Pulse Flows Component of the Water Storage Investment Program (WSIP) Groundwater Projects
ceqa-c62759f5b7c7afe430.description: The Pulse Flows Component is defined by the following DWR actions: (1) Release of the pulse flows from Lake Oroville into the Low Flow Channel of the Feather River, with the goal of improving habitat conditions for listed salmonids, as well as improving spawning and migration conditions for other listed and non-listed native fish species. (2) Implementation of the WSIP Operational Exchange Process that develops water used for pulse flow releases. (3) Diversion and conveyance of water to Kern Fan and Willow Springs that would be stored, in part, for ecosystem benefit. Implementation of the Pulse Flows Component would not require construction of any new facilities in addition to those previously analyzed in the three WSIP Groundwater Projects’ EIRs. Existing facilities would be used, with operations modified to support the pulse flow releases. The Pulse Flows Component study area analyzed in this Draft SEIR extends approximately 575 miles from Lake Oroville in Northern California to the WSIP Groundwater Projects in the San Joaquin Valley and Southern California.

ceqa-f86865f98ca0c4aeb9.name: Sweet Destination Environmental Assessment No. 2026-07 for Conditional Use Permit Application No. 2025-04
ceqa-f86865f98ca0c4aeb9.projectTitle: Sweet Destination Environmental Assessment No. 2026-07 for Conditional Use Permit Application No. 2025-04
ceqa-f86865f98ca0c4aeb9.description: Conditional Use Permit Application No. 2025-04 pertains to authorizing the potential for sales of beer, wine, and distilled spirits for off-site consumption within an existing approximately 2,600 square-feet, specialty candy and gift shop. The existing establishment, named Sweet Destination is requesting a Type 21 ABC License (Off-Sales General), so they can offer beer, wine and distilled spirits in their gift baskets. ABC’s description of a Type 21 License is as follows: Type 21 – Off-Sale General Issued to retail stores. Authorizes the sale of beer, wine and distilled spirits for consumption off the premises where sold. Minors are allowed on the premises. The current hours of operation for the store are 6 am to 8 pm, 6 days a week. The proposed alcohol sales will be during Sweet Destination’s operating hours of 6 am to 8 pm. Alcohol will be stored in a locked display and behind a locked door in a cold storage room. No exterior changes to the existing building or site plan are proposed. Security camera system will be installed with interior and exterior cameras to monitor activities. The project is consistent with the 2030 General Plan Community Commercial Planned Land Use and the CC (Central & Community Commercial) zone district.

ceqa-dc89a8bd804d1a8a49.name: New Fresno Courthouse Project
ceqa-dc89a8bd804d1a8a49.description: The proposed Project would involve demolition of the existing Sheriff Administration and South Annex Jail buildings and construction of an approximately 413,000 SF-square-foot courthouse on the 2.09-acre parcel, which includes 36 courtrooms, support spaces, and secure parking for judicial officers. The support spaces would include, but are not limited to, judicial chambers, clerks’ offices, jury assembly and deliberation rooms, temporary in-custody holding, administrative office space, parking loading dock, and secure prisoner sallyport. Secured parking would be provided for judicial officers only, no staff or public parking is included as part of the Project scope. Visitors to the new courthouse would utilize available off-site public parking owned by the City in the surrounding area. The Project would implement sustainable elements throughout its design, construction, operation, and maintenance. The Project would be designed for sustainability and, at a minimum, to the standards of a Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Silver certified rating. The Project will be delivered through a Design-Build process. Although final plans have not yet been prepared, the Project is anticipated to include demolition of existing buildings and site preparation, grading, building construction, paving, and architectural finishing activities. The Judicial Council, acting as the Judicial Branch of State government, is not subject to local land use regulations; however, the Judicial Council, as appropriate, considers local policies in evaluating whether the proposed Project’s impacts would be significant.

ceqa-2064ab9df40950a4a3.name: Safer Consumer Products: Adding para-Phenylenediamine (PPD) Derivatives to the Candidate Chemicals List (Regulation Reference Number R-2024-07R)
ceqa-2064ab9df40950a4a3.projectTitle: Safer Consumer Products: Adding para-Phenylenediamine (PPD) Derivatives to the Candidate Chemicals List (Regulation Reference Number R-2024-07R)
ceqa-2064ab9df40950a4a3.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-2064ab9df40950a4a3.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted by California Health and Safety Code sections 25252, 25253, and 58012, approved a regulatory amendment to amend section 69502.2 to article 2, chapter 55, division 4.5 of title 22, California Code of Regulations (CCR). This regulatory action will add para-phenylenediamine (PPD) derivatives to the Candidate Chemicals List (article 2 of the Safer Consumer Products Regulations). Background: DTSC’s Safer Consumer Products Regulations, adopted in 2013, strive to reduce toxic chemicals in products and create safer substitutes for hazardous ingredients in consumer products sold in California. The regulations emphasize safer products and healthier lives by reducing or eliminating use of toxic chemicals, while allowing manufacturers to determine how to best address human health or environmental concerns related to their products. These regulations specify a process for adding chemicals to the Candidate Chemicals List (22 CCR 69502.2(b)). The regulations require DTSC to evaluate and prioritize product/Candidate Chemical combinations and to add these product/Candidate Chemical combinations to the Priority Products List (article 11 of the Safer Consumer Products Regulations). Project Activities: DTSC adopted a rule adding PPD derivatives to the Candidate Chemicals List based on findings that (1) there are potential exposures to PPD derivatives, and (2) there is potential for one or more of these PPD derivative exposures to contribute to or cause adverse impacts. Listing one or more chemicals as a Candidate Chemical does not place regulatory obligations on chemical manufacturers or on product manufacturers that use the chemical(s). However, it does give DTSC the option of regulating the chemical(s) in specific consumer products in the future, based on certain findings. A Candidate Chemical that is the basis for a product being listed as a Priority Product is designated as a Chemical of Concern for that product. A chemical’s presence on the Candidate Chemicals List also affects the regulatory responses that the Safer Consumer Products Program can select for a Priority Product following the Alternatives Analysis phase. DTSC selects Priority Products based on the potential risk of exposure to the Chemical(s) of Concern in the product and the potential for this exposure to contribute to or cause widespread or significant adverse impacts to people or the environment.

The Kerckhoff Hydroelectric Project is comprised of Kerckhoff Dam, Kerckhoff Reservoir, Kerckhoff 1 Powerhouse and associated facilities, Kerckhoff 2 Powerhouse and associated facilities, the Smalley Cove Recreation Area, helicopter landing zones, roads, and gages. ceqa-4f79c2bccb6c1f5881.name: Vista Ranch Project
ceqa-4f79c2bccb6c1f5881.description: The proposed project would expand the City of Clovis Sphere of Influence (SOI) to include the approximately 952-acre project site, which is currently outside of the SOI boundary (SOI Expansion). The proposed project would also adopt a comprehensive Vista Ranch Master Plan (Master Plan) to guide development within approximately 507 acres of the project site, and the proposed project would implement the Vista Ranch Development (Vista Ranch Development), which would develop approximately 368 acres of the Master Plan Area with mixed uses over a build-out period of approximately 10 years. The SOI Expansion and Master Plan are analyzed at a program-level; however, the Vista Ranch Development is analyzed at the project-level. The Vista Ranch Development would construct a mixed-use development anticipated to provide up to 2,718 residential units, including single- and multi-family units at varying densities. The Vista Ranch Development is planned to center on a mixed-use village core area surrounded by higher-density residential development, with lower residential densities toward the edges of the development, transitioning to surrounding rural/agricultural use. Within the Vista Ranch Development, new public and private roadways would enable access and circulation. The Vista Ranch Development would also include an extensive trail system.

ceqa-7de14120860ce3eb6a.agency: California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery
ceqa-7de14120860ce3eb6a.agencyName: Resources Recycling and Recovery, Department of (CalRecycle)
ceqa-7de14120860ce3eb6a.description: The Used Mattress Recovery and Recycling Act (Public Resources Code [PRC] sections 42985-42994) requires a mattress recycling organization to submit a mattress recycling plan to CalRecycle for CalRecycle’s approval. The mattress recycling plan must be designed to establish a convenient and cost-effective program to reduce illegal dumping, increase recycling, and substantially reduce public agency costs for the end-of-life management of used mattresses. Mattress Recycling Council (MRC), a nonprofit mattress recycling organization established by mattress manufacturers, renovators, and retailers, designs and implements the mattress stewardship program described in its plan. Since 2015, MRC has collected and managed used mattresses in California by establishing public no-cost drop-off sites, funding the collection of illegally dumped mattresses, and coordinating with retailers to offer pickup of used mattresses when new mattresses are delivered to consumers. On February 13, 2026, MRC submitted to CalRecycle a new mattress recycling plan, titled Used Mattress Recovery and Recycling Plan. CalRecycle conditionally approved the plan on May 13, 2026.

ceqa-6e055ce2705144d370.name: City of Coalinga Continuous GPS (CGPS) and Monitoring Well Installation
ceqa-6e055ce2705144d370.projectTitle: City of Coalinga Continuous GPS (CGPS) and Monitoring Well Installation
ceqa-6e055ce2705144d370.description: Description of Nature, Purpose and Beneficiaries of Project: In 2014, the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) was signed into law requiring local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs) to manage groundwater in their service area that necessitates the development of an adequate network of appropriately spaced groundwater monitoring wells. With secured funding, the Department of Water Resources (DWR) has established the Technical Support Services (TSS) program to help GSAs meet their SGMA requirements by providing services to install groundwater monitoring wells, conduct downhole video logging, and training on methods to accurately monitor groundwater levels. The CGPS installation consists of installing a single CGPS station. The CGPS station will continuously measure the three-dimensional position at the site with the focus of monitoring for vertical movement, also known as land subsidence. A total area of 20' x 40' for equipment with a 50' x 50' staging area for vehicles and equipment is needed. The drilled holes will penetrate approximately 35' into the subsurface where stainless pipe is lowered and then grout is pumped through the legs to anchor the monument. The total height of the CGPS station equipment is approximately 6' tall. The Well Installation Project consists of installing a single, nested groundwater monitoring well. The well site location is TBD but will be marked by Underground Service Alert, then hand tools will be used to excavate to a minimum depth of 5'. The driller will use a truck-mounted drill rig to drill a pilot hole while using a mud cleaner to filter out solids and return drilling mud to the drill bit. When the pilot hole is at the desired depth, the driller will expand the borehole to a diameter of approximately 14". The nested well will consist of two or three PVC casings, and the base of each well, from the bottom up, will consist of sand, a filter pack, and a bentonite seal. Cement will be pumped from the support truck to place the sanitary seal in accordance with state and county requirements. A raised well monument and concrete pad approximately four square feet and four inches tall with four approximately 4-foot-high metal crash posts will be installed at ground level to protect the well from potential damage, or the well will be installed in a flush-mounted vault in accordance with county road ordinance. DWR or GSA staff may visit the well on a quarterly schedule to collect data. Operation and maintenance will be minimal and may consist of periodic servicing of equipment and replacing batteries as needed. Access to the well location will be by existing paved and dirt roads. Once installed, this facility will become part of the GSA's monitoring program.
ceqa-6e055ce2705144d370.crossStreets: South Alpine Avenue/Lost Hills Road (Hwy 33) and Firestone Road
