ceqa-53d9426554541737dd.name: Crystal Clean, LLC (formerly Heritage-Crystal Clean, LLC) – Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Renewal
ceqa-53d9426554541737dd.projectTitle: Bakersfield Transfer, Inc. Hazardous Waste Permit
ceqa-53d9426554541737dd.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-53d9426554541737dd.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20 is approving an Addendum to a previously adopted Initial Study/Negative Declaration for renewal of a Hazardous Waste Facility Permit (Permit) for Crystal Clean, LLC (formerly Heritage-Crystal Clean, LLC). DTSC prepared an Addendum pursuant to a previously adopted 2015 Initial Study/Negative Declaration (IS/ND) due to minor changes and updates to the CEQA Guidelines. The Permit Renewal will authorize continued storage and treatment of hazardous waste. In addition, Crystal Clean, LLC (Crystal Clean) proposes additional capacity and flexibility of containers in Units 3 and 4 to facilitate waste acceptance and movement of oily water; installation of two (2) 18,000-gallon storage containers in Unit 5-3 (T-5 and T-6) on the existing concrete pad; expansion of testing capabilities of water from storm water and tank/container rinse water; and administrative waste code changes. The Permit does not include any significant changes in operations and no construction or ground disturbing activities are proposed. Crystal Clean is located at 1620 East Brundage Lane in Bakersfield, California 93307. Background: Crystal Clean is located on an approximately 4.3-acre parcel that is shared with Sierra International Machinery, which occupies the majority of the parcel and surrounds the facility to the east and south. Crystal Clean is a treatment and storage facility whose operations include the collection and storage of used oil, used antifreeze, oily water, contaminated petroleum sludge, and oily solids from offsite generators (gas stations, oil changers, auto repair shops, etc.); treating used oil and oily water to meet recycled oil standards; and treatment of contaminated petroleum sludge. Crystal Clean receives these hazardous wastes via tanker trucks, vacuum trucks, railcars, and in containers from off-site generators. Wastes are consolidated by type and stored in permitted tanks and storage areas before being treated and/or shipped to an offsite facility. Crystal Clean consists of six permitted hazardous waste transfer and storage units; Tank Farm (Unit 1), Drum Storage Area (Unit 2), Roll-Off Bin Storage Area (Unit 3), Drum Loading/Unloading Area (Unit 4), and Truck and Railcar Loading/Unloading Area (Unit 5). There are no proposed changes to current hazardous waste storage and treatment activities with the proposed Permit Renewal other than the: Addition of two (2) portable containers with capacities less than 20,000 gallons each and the addition of four (4) 20-cubic yard roll-off bins in Unit 3 (Roll-Off Bin Storage Area); • Flexibility of containers in Units 3 and 4 to facilitate waste acceptance and movement of oily water; • Installation of two (2) 18,000-gallon storage tanks Oily Water Tank (Tank 5) and Recycled Oil Tank (Tank 6) in Sub-Unit 5-3 on an existing concrete pad; • Expansion of the testing capabilities of waste determination testing on collected stormwater and tank/container rinse water accumulated on site, to determine if the water meets requirements of the facility’s wastewater discharge permit and would then be managed accordingly based on the analytical results; and • Administrative waste code changes, specifically the addition of waste code #181 to Unit 2 (Drum Storage Area) and Unit 4 (Drum Loading/Unloading Area) as an acceptable waste stream. • Change the name of the Facility from Heritage-Crystal Clean, LLC to Crystal Clean, LLC; Bakersfield Transfer, Inc. (BTI), the predecessor to Crysal Clean, was issued their first Permit by DTSC in 2010, which allowed them to store used oil, used antifreeze, oily water and oily solids only with no treatment of used oil. On May 26, 2010, BTI submitted a new Permit application to DTSC for a California-Only Hazardous Waste Facility Permit which allowed BTI to treat used oil and certify the treated used oil as “recycled oil” in accordance with California Health & Safety Code Section 25250.1. DTSC circulated an IS/ND (State Clearinghouse Number 2015031014) for public comment in March of 2015 and filed a Notice of Determination (State Clearinghouse Number 2015031014) in July of 2015 for approval of the Permit. DTSC issued a Permit effective July 28, 2015, reflecting certification of these new Permit conditions. DTSC approved a Permit modification request for a change in ownership from BTI to Heritage-Crystal Clean, LLC on August 13, 2021, and filed a Notice of Determination on August 16, 2021 (State Clearinghouse Number 2015031014). This Addendum is to the previously adopted IS/ND and has been prepared to address activities associated with the Permit enewal request and to amend the analysis of the previously adopted 2015 IS/ND due to updates to the CEQA Guidelines, not as a result of project changes. The Permit Renewal will authorize the Facility to continue operating as a commercial hazardous waste storage and treatment facility and implement the proposed changes. All other operating activities of the Facility will continue as previously approved. This Permit Renewal does not include any construction, ground disturbing activities, or other operational changes and all previous Permit requirements will remain in effect. This Permit Renewal will not result in any new or substantially more severe significant impacts on the environment.

ceqa-a731f369fb2ba5da6d.description: DWR will work with a Contractor to perform repairs to the California Aqueduct. Work will include repairing concrete liner by filling voids on the water side of the embankment. Damaged panels will be craned to roadway for offsite disposal. Work will require the following equipment: (1) Rig to install new inner casing string, Cement unit to cement the casing, Wireline unit to perforate the well. Deliveries are limited to water and new casing. All travel to/from the project location will occur on established roadways and no expansion is required. The speed limit while on SPR property is 15 mph. Dust is controlled via water trucks pursuant to SPR’s Dust Control Plan. The existing well pad can accommodate all associated equipment, materials storage, and operations including deliveries and personnel parking. Any undisturbed vegetation will be avoided, and all work will occur on the existing disturbed pad only. No expansion of the existing well pad, road, staging areas or pipelines is required. ceqa-160e4fbb1cb5c051ac.name: 347648_464-00-0025_HWOC_UIC
ceqa-160e4fbb1cb5c051ac.description: Holmes Western Oil Corporation (HWOC) proposes to initiate a new steamflood and cyclic steam Underground Injection Control (UIC) project through the conversion of 12 existing production wells to steam injection wells, 30 production wells to cyclic steam wells, and 4 existing production wells to temperature observation wells. These conversions require no change to the casing of the wellbores and will not require notices of intention (NOIs). Additionally, HWOC proposes to transfer 26 cyclic steam wells from placeholder UIC project No. 46400393. The proposed project is located in an area containing existing well pads, roadways, pipelines, and facilities in a densely developed existing oil field. Well pads and roadways are maintained with a 10-foot vegetation buffer for everyday operations and fire control. No new roadways are required. No new permanent facilities will be constructed, and no expansion of associated facilities will be required. The proposed project consists of the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division (CalGEM) issuing one new project approval letter (PAL) to HWOC for the new UIC project No. 464-00-0025, located within the Midway-Sunset Oil Field in Kern County. The list of injection wells that would be associated with the new UIC project are included in Attachment 1.

ceqa-17bc1f7e2e2829ee62.name: Riverview Market Commercial Project
ceqa-17bc1f7e2e2829ee62.description: The Project involves construction and operation of the Riverview Market, a commercial retail center, that would encompass 405,531 square feet of total building space. The specific businesses and/or tenants that would ultimately occupy each of the buildings are not fully known at this time. However, it is assumed that larger anchor building’s interior to the Project site would be occupied by markets, retail uses, storage uses, and a health club. The outer building pads would be occupied by smaller retail tenants, a medical office, drive-thru, fast casual and sit-down restaurants, a car wash, and a gas station with 20 dual-sided pumps. Other Project components include vehicular access and circulation improvements (both on- and off-site); surface parking areas and drive aisles; pedestrian access and circulation improvements; various landscape, hardscape, and lighting improvements; green space/park improvements; site and tenant signage; and infrastructure and utility improvements.

ceqa-0368aa42d6cd789bef.projectTitle: Aratina Solar Project by 64NB 8ME LLC (8Minute Energy) Response to Comments
ceqa-0368aa42d6cd789bef.description: The Project includes the construction, operation, and maintenance of a photovoltaic solar facility that will include service roads, photovoltaic panels supported on solar trackers, a power collection system, communication cables, overhead and underground transmission lines, electrical switchyards, substations, battery energy storage system, weather stations and operations and maintenance facilities. The Project will result in permanent impacts throughout the 1,376-acre Project area of desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizzii), Mohave ground squirrel (Xerospermophilus mohavensis), and western burrowing owl (Athene cunicularia hypugaea) habitat. The Project is expected to result in incidental take of desert tortoise, Mohave ground squirrel, and western burrowing owl; the former two species are designated as endangered and threatened species, respectively, and the latter species is designated as a candidate for listing, under the California Endangered Species Act. The ITP referenced above as issued by CDFW authorizes incidental take of species listed under CESA that may occur as a result of Project implementation. Major Amendment No. 2 modifies the Permittee list and adds take coverage for western burrowing owl.

ceqa-48b1561b22fd1c6134.projectTitle: Agreement among DWR, TLBWSD and KCWA for Transfer and Storage of a Portion of TLBWSD’s SWP water in Rosedale-Rio Bravo WSD's Water Banking & Exchange Program
ceqa-48b1561b22fd1c6134.description: The project is for the delivery and storage of up to 10,000 acre-feet of Tulare’s State Water Project water (SWP Water) to the Rosedale-Tulare Banking and Exchange Program by December 31, 2026, and for recovery of a portion of that stored water less applicable losses through December 31, 2036. For every two acre-feet of Tulare’s SWP Water delivered for storage, one acre-foot of that water will be retained by Rosedale. The Rosedale-Tulare Banking and Exchange Program is in effect through December 31, 2036, or until Tulare has recovered all of its stored water.

ceqa-ff9fee57fde4685970.name: 2026 KCAG RTP/SCS
ceqa-ff9fee57fde4685970.projectTitle: 2026 Regional Transportation Plan and Sustainable Communities Strategy
ceqa-ff9fee57fde4685970.description: The proposed project is the 2026 KCAG RTP/SCS, which will be an update to the 2022 RTP/SCS. KCAG, by state and federal mandate, is required to develop a comprehensive minimum 20-year plan for the region’s transportation system. The 2026 RTP/SCS will cover the planning period through the year 2049. The EIR is intended to comply with CEQA. It will also require coordination with or reference to: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act the Federal Clean Air Act; the California Clean Air Act; California SB 375; California SB 743; California Assembly Bill 32, and California Senate Bill 32. The EIR will consider the 2026 RTP/SCS programmed projects and preferred SCS scenario, a No Project alternative, the SCS alternative scenarios carried forward, and any alternatives to address identified significant impacts. The EIR will evaluate the potential impacts of implementing the policies and programs in the RTP in accordance with CEQA and will concentrate on the long-term environmental impacts of the RTP/SCS that extend to the 2049 planning horizon. The 2026 RTP/SCS EIR will be prepared as a program-level document that analyzes the effects of proposed actions for all modes of transportation, including other issues and concerns such as transportation control measures and demand management and intelligent transportation systems. As a Programmatic EIR, it will be prepared at a level of detail necessary to facilitate effective tiering by lead agencies for future transportation and development projects, particularly regarding potential SB 375 streamlining.

ceqa-867b7d31457c425e3b.description: The applicant is proposing to amend a previously approved Conditional Use Permit (CUP) for a 250 megawatt (MW) commercial solar photovoltaic facility with 250 MW battery storage to be located at 24900 Nevada Ave., Stratford, Assessor’s Parcel Numbers 026-300-034, 026-320-006, -010, -011, -017, -020, -021, -022, -023, -024, and 026-330-037. This CUP was approved by the Kings County Planning Commission on April 6, 2026. The proposed amendment is to refine language in Mitigation Measure BIO-3 (Protection of Burrowing Owls) contained in the Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (IS/MND) that was adopted for the project. The proposed revisions to MM BIO-3 are solely intended to remove ambiguity and to provide needed clarity regarding the mitigation requirements. The proposed revisions represent technical changes that do not reflect new significant impacts, or increased severity of previously identified significant impacts, to the burrowing owl. An addendum to the IS/MND has been prepared as part of the CUP amendment. No changes to the previously approved development plan, construction, or operating characteristics of the Westlands VI Solar Project are proposed.

The first modification is to realign the on-site segment of the gen-tie line to run along the southeast side of Avenal Cutoff Rd. for approximately 1.4 miles from the northeast corner of the Project Site southwestward to the relocated project substation. The second modification is to change the location of the project operations center to an approximately 13-acre area of the Project Site located on the north side of Laurel Ave. approximately 0.3 miles east of Avenal Cutoff Rd. The third modification is to add a steel storage building (approximately 120 ft by 60 ft or 7,200 sf) to the project operations center for the storage of spare parts. ceqa-23340cbe8c80723013.description: The field division plans to install a 120v receptacle and lighting for the chemical injection system for the Golden Mussel Mitigation Project. This work will involve excavating a 2-feet wide by 2-feet deep by 1,180-feet long trench. The trench will start at Check Site 22 of the State Water Project and run along the secondary aqueduct access road. The trench will terminate at the start of the Coastal Branch. A backhoe will be used to dig the trench. Once PVC conduit is installed, the trench will be backfilled. All work will take place within the DWR right-of-way. This work is necessary to provide power to the chemical injection system, which is needed to protect the California aqueduct from invasive mussels.

ceqa-622313453497e85502.name: Amendment to Include 2025 San Joaquin River Restoration Program Recapture Water as an additional source of Non-Project Water and to Allow the United States
ceqa-622313453497e85502.projectTitle: Conveyance of Non-Project Water to Tulare Lake Basin Water Storage District (SWP #26007)
ceqa-622313453497e85502.description: [PROJECT TITLE CONTINUED]:Bureau of Reclamation to Make Non-Project Water Available to the Department of Water Resources at Banks Pumping Plant under SWP #26007 (SWP #26007-A) The original Agreement, SWP #26007, provides for the conveyance of up to 82,204 acre-feet of Central Valley Project (CVP) water (Non-Project Water) to Tulare, including up to 20,000 acre-feet of Lower Tule River Irrigation District’s (Lower Tule’s) 2026 San Joaquin River Restoration Program Recapture Water. The Non-Project Water is to be made available by the United States Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) to DWR at O’Neill Forebay by February 28, 2027 for subsequent delivery by DWR to Tulare by December 31, 2027. This Amendment adds Lower Tule’s 2025 San Joaquin River Restoration Program Recapture Water as part of the 20,000 acre-feet of San Joaquin River Restoration Program Recapture Water originally approved. Furthermore, for operational flexibility between DWR and Reclamation, this Amendment adds Banks Pumping Plant as an additional location where Reclamation could provide the Non-Project Water to DWR.

ceqa-17f68510d99e506c6f.name: Conditional Use Permit No. 25 (Bar E Dairy)
ceqa-17f68510d99e506c6f.projectTitle: Conditional Use Permit No. 25-10 (Bar E Dairy)
ceqa-17f68510d99e506c6f.description: The applicant is proposing to construct a vermifiltration system to produce higher quality process water for reuse, storage, and land application on an existing dairy. The proposed system will include: one (1) earthen berm in an existing wastewater retention pond, two (2) wastewater lift stations, and seven (7) wastewater processing beds with a total area of 151,480 sq. ft, a 30,296 sq. ft. material processing area, and a 111,400 sq. ft. manure storage area. The dairy facility is also replacing existing equipment with the construction and installation of one (1) wastewater process pit, two (2) mechanical separators, three (3) concrete push walls, one (1) wastewater lift station, and a 21,645 sq. ft. concrete slab for manure handling. The project site is located at 6740 Corona Ave., Kingsburg, Assessor’s Parcel Numbers 002-070-068 and 091.

ceqa-5b2431930ac5c42a5b.name: New City Park
ceqa-5b2431930ac5c42a5b.description: The City of Lemoore proposes to acquire and develop approximately 2.76 acres as a new public neighborhood park known as Cinnamon Park. The site currently contains a residence and associated improvements. The residence and improvements would be removed as part of park development. The current planning program includes a multi-generational splash pad; musical/sensory playground; pump track; 2 to 4 pickleball courts; walking/fitness loop; outdoor fitness stations; pollinator and wellness garden; multi-use turf/open green space; prefabricated public restroom; approximately 0.23-acre parking area; shade sails/structures; benches and picnic tables; trash receptacles and related furnishings; at least 40 trees; drought-tolerant landscaping and water-efficient irrigation; lighting; fencing; accessible circulation; stormwater improvements; and necessary utility connections. The final configuration will be refined through community-based planning and subsequent design.

ceqa-19300172671b780e86.name: Bonadelle Lacey Ave Residential Project
ceqa-19300172671b780e86.description: Project Description: The proposed Project includes an annexation, prezoning, and residential development on a 16.65-acre site immediately west of the City of Hanford. The proposed Project site is within the City’s Sphere of Influence and annexation is proposed for the entire 16.65-acre Project site, and includes Assessor Parcel Numbers (APN) 011-010-003, -004, -005, -006, -007, -008 and -009. APNs 011-010-007, -008 and -009 total 2.77 acres in size and are currently developed with rural residences. See Figure 2. No development is proposed for these 2.77 acres. A Tentative Subdivision Map is proposed for the remaining 13.88 acres, which would divide the site into 78 single family residential lots, ranging in size from 4,172 to 10,367 square feet square feet. Access roads, lighting, landscaping and other associated improvements will be constructed, per City Standards within the proposed Project site and along the future Aquifer Drive alignment along the eastern site boundary. Construction will include the connection to City water, storm drain and sewer within the development, along with other utilities such as electric and communication lines. Along with the Tentative Subdivision Map, a Planned Unit Development (PUD) may be required to allow for wider garage widths than the small-lot provisions of the City of Hanford’s Municipal Code Sections 17.10.100 and 17.12.100 allow. The development of 78 single-family residential units is allowable under the current General Plan Land Use Designation and City of Hanford Zone District.

ceqa-c0fc36051ef591e483.projectTitle: Conditional Use Permit No. 25-01 (Sentry Ag Services/Dixie Creek Ranch Dairy Expansion)
ceqa-c0fc36051ef591e483.description: The applicant is proposing to expand the herd size and footprint of an existing dairy located at 3601 Lacey Blvd., Hanford, Assessor’s Parcel Number 016-090-012. The proposal includes a herd expansion to increase the previously permitted herd size by 1,500 head of cattle (500 head of milk cows and 1,000 head of dry cows) bringing the total herd size to 8,000 head (10,920 animal units) at the Dixie Creek Ranch Dairy. The dairy has acquired additional land adjacent to the facility to increase the capacity for land application. Additionally, the proposal includes the construction of two (2) new Saudi-style barns (approximately 1,200 ft. by 105 ft. for 127,000 sq. ft. each), and a new feed center and manure drying area on the east side of the dairy facility. The feed center bays will be 80,000 sq. ft. on 5 acres, and the new manure drying area will be located on 13 acres. Operation activities are anticipated to remain essentially unchanged from the existing operation with only a slight increase in operational truck trips.

ceqa-51afeb13390d8f38d4.projectTitle: Pool 2 Coastal Branch Secondary Road Erosion Repair
ceqa-51afeb13390d8f38d4.description: San Joaquin Field Division plans to fill and compact an erosion along the secondary access road of Pool 2. A dump truck will be used to haul in fill material. A backhoe will be used to fill and compact the erosion. A water truck may be used to control dust and aid in compaction. A compaction wheel may be used. All work will take place by the road. All staging will take place on paved or graveled surfaces. All work will take place within the DWR right-of-way. This work is necessary to maintain the structural integrity of the access road and the California aqueduct.

ceqa-4a134b610416ae780d.name: BHPP Holding Pond Culvert Connection Repair
ceqa-4a134b610416ae780d.projectTitle: BHPP Holding Pond Culvert Connection Repair
ceqa-4a134b610416ae780d.description: San Joaquin Field Division plans to repair the culvert connecting Badger Hill Pumping Plant pond 1 and 2. They also plan to fill and compact the erosion created from the leaky culvert. A backhoe will be used to excavate, fill, and compact dirt. A compaction wheel may be used to aid in compaction. A dump truck will be used to bring in fill material. A water truck may be used to aid in compaction and control dust. All work will take place by the road. All staging will take place on existing dirt roads. All work will take place within the DWR right-of-way. This work is necessary to maintain the ponds and pond access roads.

ceqa-1e9c366b608d45824a.name: 2025 Urban Water Management Plan (UWMP)
ceqa-1e9c366b608d45824a.description: The UWMP serves as a comprehensive planning document intended to evaluate and ensure the reliability of the City's water supply. It supports long-term resource planning, promotes water conservation, and establishes a framework for managing water shortages and drought conditions. The 2025 UWMP includes the following key components:1. Development of a long-term strategy for managing current and projected water demands; 2. Evaluation of potable and non-potable water supplies, including supply constraints under regulatory and hydrologic conditions; 3. Assessment of water supply reliability under normal, single dry-year, and multiple dry-year (five consecutive years) scenarios through the year 2050; 4. Preparation of a Drought Risk Assessment (DRA) that analyzes water supply and demand under a modeled five-year drought scenario; and 5. Inclusion of a Water Shortage Contingency Plan (WSCP), which identifies response actions to reduce demand and increase supply during water shortage conditions.

ceqa-5547b8959e07748044.name: Site Plan Review No. 26-05 (Gomez Goat Dairy)
ceqa-5547b8959e07748044.projectTitle: Site Plan Review No. 26-05 (Gomez Goat Dairy)
ceqa-5547b8959e07748044.description: The applicant is proposing to establish a goat dairy at a former bovine dairy/heifer feedlot facility located at 16501 Colony Rd., Lemoore, Assessor’s Parcel Number 004-280-083. Improvements to the facility will be completed in two (2) phases: 1) onboarding and 2) expansion. The proposal for the onboarding phase includes the remodel and/or reconstruction of the existing milk barn (2,220 sf), milk house (525 sf), and holding pen (2,700 sf) to accommodate goats. A corral shade (30,900 sf) is proposed to be installed to cover the goat housing area. The herd size for onboarding is proposed to be 1,860 milking goats, 186 dry goats, and 635 support stock for a total herd size of 2,681 goats, which equates to 536 animal units (AU) for Phase 1. The proposal for the expansion phase includes constructing additional milk stations in the milk barn, adding feed lanes and shading to the existing open corrals (141,225 sf total), and constructing a commodity barn (5,500 sf) and truck scale (1,050 sf). The proposed herd size for the expansion is 4,080 milking goats, 408 dry goats, and 1,392 support stock, for a total herd size of 5,880 goats, which equates to 1,176 AU for Phase 2. The existing concrete separation pits and earthen storage ponds will continue to be used, and an incinerator will be installed for mortality management.

ceqa-2200297112811c47ff.name: Conditional Use Permit No. 25-04 (Rex Solaire Solar and Storage Project)
ceqa-2200297112811c47ff.projectTitle: Conditional Use Permit No. 25-04 (Rex Solaire Solar and Storage Project)
ceqa-2200297112811c47ff.description: The Kings County Community Development Agency has received an application for a land development permit that proposes to construct, operate, and eventually decommission a utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) solar power generation and energy storage facility on approximately 20,600 acres. The Project consists of tracking solar PV panel arrays with a nominal output of up to 2,800 megawatts (MW) alternating current (AC) at the point of interconnection and battery energy storage with a capacity of up to 11.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh). Other project components include project substations, an underground collection system, and a gen-tie line that would connect the project substations to up to two switchyards located adjacent to the Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) transmission corridor. The project would also include telecommunication facilities and an operations and maintenance facility.

ceqa-6f2c0992e936c1b9a3.name: Site Plan Review No. 26-06 (AMPS Solar)
ceqa-6f2c0992e936c1b9a3.description: The applicant is proposing to establish a solar module assembly facility located at 10652 Jackson Ave., Hanford, Assessor’s Parcel Numbers 028-030-021 & 036. The solar module assembly facility (up to 8 gigawatts) includes production line installation inside an existing industrial facility with no building expansion or structural changes. There are no hazardous manufacturing processes proposed. The project proposal is limited to interior equipment installation and solar module assembly operations within existing buildings. Operations will include automated assembly lines, packaging, warehousing, shipping, receiving, and related office and support uses. Phase 1 will include assembly lines in Warehouse #1 and Warehouse #2 and finished product storage and distribution in Warehouse #3 and Warehouse #4. Phase 2 includes future expansion of assembly into Warehouse #3 and/or Warehouse #4 if needed. There will be an estimated 10-20 truck trips per day during operations. The facility will operate up to 24 hours a day, seven days a week, depending on demand, and will have approximately 200 employees per shift.

ceqa-b44be1a48343067336.name: Naval Air Station Lemoore Broadcast Burn Assist
ceqa-b44be1a48343067336.projectTitle: Naval Air Station Lemoore Broadcast Burn Assist
ceqa-b44be1a48343067336.agency: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
ceqa-b44be1a48343067336.agencyName: Forestry and Fire Protection, Department of
ceqa-b44be1a48343067336.description: The United States Naval Air Station Lemoore proposes to request assistance from the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) to perform prescribed burns within approximately 105 acres of Naval Air Station Lemoore. The prescribed burn will aim to reduce the accumulation of dry annual grasses, reduce wildland fire starts, and provide live fire training for Naval Air Station Federal Fire and cooperating agencies. The prescribed burn would occur annually between late spring and fall to maximize effectiveness. Approximate timing of the burn is dependent on fuel type, weather conditions and prescription burn requirements.

ceqa-f303d600fe83e5c8f2.name: Millennium Estates Residential Project
ceqa-f303d600fe83e5c8f2.description: The Project Applicant intends to develop up to 211 single-family residential units on an approximately 30.9-acre site. Access roads, lighting, landscaping and other associated improvements will be constructed, per City Standards within the proposed Project site and along the future 12 ½ Avenue alignment (to be named Aquifer Drive). Construction will include the connection to City water, storm drain and sewer within the development with connection to existing lines in 12 ½ Avenue (to be named Aquifer Drive) and Millennium Way, along with other utilities such as electric and communication lines. Entitlements needed to accommodate the proposed Project include a Tentative Subdivision Map and a Planned Unit Development to accommodate a variety of lot sizes and modified setbacks. The proposed Project is consistent with the General Plan density of between two to ten units per acre in the Low Density Residential category. The proposed Project density is 6.82 units per acre. Site Circulation Vehicular access to the Project will be from future Millennium Way, which bisects the property and 12 ½ Avenue (to be named Aquifer Drive) to the east. Future connections have been provided to the north and west of the property. Each single-family residence will include a two-car garage. Construction Phasing The Project is anticipated to be developed in three phases over three years total. Project Location The Project site is located on the west side of the City of Hanford along 12 ½ Avenue approximately 0.18 miles south of the intersection of West Lacey Boulevard and 12 ½ Avenue. The Project lies in the northwest quarter of Section 34 of Township 18 South, Range 21 East, Mount Diablo Base Line and Meridian of the Hanford, California 7.5-minute USGS quadrangle Project #: (TT 949; PUD 47-25)

ceqa-a5b5ba6cd5acb84441.name: 2024-2032 Kings County Multijurisdictional Housing Element Update for the County of Kings and Cities of Avenal, Corcoran, and Hanford
ceqa-a5b5ba6cd5acb84441.projectTitle: 2024-2032 Kings County Multijurisdictional Housing Element Update for the County of Kings and Cities of Avenal, Corcoran, and Hanford
ceqa-a5b5ba6cd5acb84441.description: Adopted through Kings County General Plan Amendment 26-02, City of Avenal General Plan Amendment 2026-01, City of Corcoran General Plan Amendment 26-01, and City of Hanford General Plan Amendment 2026-01. The General Plan is Kings County’s and the Cities of Avenal’s, Corcoran’s, and Hanford’s primary planning policy document and includes state-mandated “elements” that set forth objectives, principles, standards, and goals to guide orderly development. The purpose of the Housing Element is to identify the housing needs of all economic segments of the community and describe the action the County and Cities intend to take to facilitate the preservation and development of adequate housing to meet those needs. State law established requirements for updating Housing Elements on an eight-year cycle. The 6th Cycle Housing Element update is for the 2024-2032 planning period. Full Title: 2024-2032 Kings County Multijurisdictional Housing Element Update for the County of Kings and Cities of Avenal, Corcoran, and Hanford, adopted through Kings County General Plan Amendment 26-02, City of A venal General Plan Amendment 2026-01, City of Corcoran General Plan Amendment 26-01, and City of Hanford General Plan Amendment 2026-01

ceqa-0fb0bbdc4203b16cc5.name: Caltrans D6 Comcast Encroachment Permit # 06-26-6-BB-0226
ceqa-0fb0bbdc4203b16cc5.description: The California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) will issue an encroachment permit to Comcast to install new aerial and underground fiber optic cable along State Route 41 in Kings County. The purpose of the project is to connect fiber optic infrastructure located outside the Caltrans right-of-way. Work would occur along State Route 41 between postmiles 45.144 and 47.565 in unincorporated Kings County, north of the city of Lemoore. Work for the project includes installation of aerial and underground fiber optic and vaults. 8,648 feet of fiber optic cable would be installed aerially on existing utility poles. This portion of the work would also include installation of 15 anchors and 8 new risers on existing poles. 3,019 feet of fiber optic cable would be installed underground within new 2-inch conduit. Of that, 2,620 feet of conduit would be installed via open trenching and 399 feet would be installed using horizontal directional drilling (HDD). Boring would occur between the edge of pavement and the limit of the Caltrans right-of-way, and would also extend beneath the roadway. The conduit would be installed at a depth of approximately 48 inches below the ground surface.One vault 30"X48"36" would be installed along the underground portion of the alignment. The project would not require removal of trees. Ruderal vegetation along State Route 41 would be temporarily disturbed or removed during excavation of bore pits and vault installation, as well as from vehicle parking and construction staging. All work would occur during daytime hours; no night work is proposed. The maximum depth of excavation is 48 inches below the ground surface.

During the peak season, approximately 20 trucks per day are anticipated, which could increase to 30 trucks per day in the future. The facility will operate six (6) days a week during the peak season with approximately 4,676 truck trips, which could increase to 7,015 trips in the future. Gypsum will be stored in a designated area on site to prevent dust generation, contamination, and runoff. This storage area will be managed in compliance with air quality and stormwater control regulations to minimize environmental impacts. The enriched compost will be sold to local farmers, providing them with a high-quality, affordable soil amendment that supports healthier crop yields and sustainable farming practices. The facility’s operations ensure that gypsum sales will not interfere with existing composting activities or create significant additional impacts on traffic, noise, or air quality.

ceqa-2ee38b04043e322771.name: Lift Station 9A
ceqa-2ee38b04043e322771.description: The City of Lemoore is undertaking improvements to its wastewater collection system in the areas served by the Carmel and Viera Lift Stations. To address existing capacity limitations and accommodate future growth, the City plans to construct a new lift station—Lift Station 9A—at the current Carmel Lift Station site located on the east side Carmel Drive (see Figure1). This new facility is designed to accommodate projected peak flows through 2040 and serve as a replacement for both of those lift stations. The project also includes installation of a new gravity sewer main that will redirect wastewater from the Viera lift station to the new lift station. ceqa-4e087f8cc58d6b2683.name: Heroes Park Project
ceqa-4e087f8cc58d6b2683.description: The proposed project would include the demolition of the existing structures and construction of a 40-acre regional park that would include various recreation features and site amenities. The proposed project would consist of an amphitheater that would include a stage, concrete dance floor, tiered seating, and speakers as well as allow for temporary lighting; the amphitheater would host events such as concerts, plays, and celebratory events. Additional recreational elements would include an outdoor skate park, dog park, multi-use athletic fields with stadium lighting, a disc golf course, a pickleball court complex with speakers and full-court outdoor basketball courts. The new park would feature a playground, outdoor fitness equipment area, a trail loop, a community learning garden, picnic areas, and a central plaza with water fountain. Public art pieces would be placed throughout the site to honor community heroes. The proposed project would include landscaping and open space areas throughout the site. The proposed project would operate seven days a week between the hours of 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m. The proposed project would include the installation of lighting throughout the project site to enhance visibility and ensure public safety. Perimeter fencing would be installed around the project site to restrict access during non-operational hours. Ingress/egress would be provided via three new driveways. The proposed project would include the construction of a bus stop in the northern part of the project site along the eastbound side of Grangeville Boulevard. Additionally, the proposed project would include off-site improvements consisting of a new two-lane collector street, 9th Avenue, along the western boundary of the site, that extends south from Grangeville Boulevard and features sidewalks on both sides. Associated utility and right-of-way infrastructure would be developed in accordance with City of Hanford standards and regulations.

ceqa-2604145fd985b05f6d.name: Eaton Canyon Fire Recovery and Resilience Project
ceqa-2604145fd985b05f6d.projectTitle: Eaton Canyon Fire Recovery and Resilience Project
ceqa-2604145fd985b05f6d.agency: Los Angeles County Department of Parks & Recreation
ceqa-2604145fd985b05f6d.description: The Eaton Fire, the second most destructive wildfire in California’s history, left Eaton Canyon, one of Los Angeles County’s most iconic natural areas and an important ecological resource, severely degraded and at an increased risk for future fires due to ongoing habitat conversion from native shrublands to nonnative vegetation. The fire also increased erosion and sediment transport, altered hydrologic conditions, and degraded riparian and upland habitats that support wildlife, water quality, and watershed function. By removing and controlling fire-promoting nonnative vegetation, restoring native vegetation communities, and fostering community stewardship through outreach, habitat management, and volunteer programs, the proposed work will increase the resilience of Eaton Canyon to future wildfires and enhance safety for visitors and surrounding communities. The proposed work aligns with Los Angeles County’s (County) restoration goals, integrates Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK), and establishes Eaton Canyon as a model for climate-adaptive ecological restoration in the San Gabriel foothills. Overarching Goal Over a 5-year period, the County and its partners will implement a resilient, climate-adapted post-fire restoration and ecosystem recovery program guided by science-based management, TEK, and community stewardship. The project will focus on restoring the ecological integrity, hydrologic function, cultural significance, and public access of the 190-acre Eaton Canyon Natural Area following the 2025 Eaton Fire. Proposed work focuses on the reduction of sedimentation, improvement of water quality, enhancement of habitat for sensitive species through native plant establishment and nonnative plant control, and long-term resiliency in one of the County’s most visited natural areas, establishing Eaton Canyon as a national model for post-fire climate-adaptive ecological restoration. Primary Goal 1: Restore Native Vegetation and Suppress Invasives Restore native plant communities and habitat quality throughout Eaton Canyon by controlling invasive species and promoting the recovery of native vegetation. This goal will support recovery of sensitive habitats, strengthen wildlife corridors, and increase resilience to future disturbances, including wildfires. Objective 1.1. Restore and enhance up to 66 acres of fire-affected habitat through revegetation of burned hillslopes, alluvial fans, riparian corridors, and upland plant communities using locally adapted, climate-resilient native species. Objective 1.2. Reduce invasive plant cover to less than 15% relative cover across restoration areas within five years through early detection, rapid response, and sustained control and removal of priority invasive species. Objective 1.3. Protect and enhance habitat conditions for sensitive plant and wildlife species by conserving existing populations, improving ecological connectivity, and strengthening wildlife corridors. Objective 1.4. Develop long-term native plant and seed resources through expansion of onsite seed banking and nursery capacity to support continued restoration and climate resilience. Primary Goal 2. Reduce Sediment Mobilization, Stabilize Trails, and Provide Public Access Reduce erosion and sediment mobilization from trails, roads, and disturbed hillslopes while providing safe and sustainable public access throughout Eaton Canyon through trail stabilization, revegetation, and runoff management. Objective 2.1. Reduce erosion and sediment transport from trails, roads, and disturbed hillslopes through installation of trail stabilization and runoff-management features. Objective 2.2. Stabilize up to 16 acres of burned habitat through revegetation with climate-resilient native vegetation to reduce soil loss and improve watershed function. Objective 2.3. Improve understanding of post-fire geomorphic processes through long-term monitoring of channel cross-sections and sediment transport dynamics in Eaton Wash and its tributaries. Objective 2.4. Enhance native vegetation recruitment and long-term slope stability through integrated invasive species management and restoration treatments. Primary Goal 3. Restore Hydrology and Riparian Habitat Restore hydrologic and riparian functions within Eaton Wash and its tributaries by supporting natural channel processes and recovery of native riparian vegetation. Objective 3.1. Restore natural hydrologic processes by reducing runoff velocity, increasing sediment retention, and improving infiltration within tributary channels and alluvial fan systems. Objective 3.2. Enhance seasonal water availability and floodplain connectivity in the mainstem channel through implementation and maintenance of low-tech process-based restoration features. Objective 3.3. Reestablish native riparian vegetation communities to improve channel stability, water quality, habitat complexity, and ecosystem resilience. Objective 3.4. Increase watershed resilience by restoring riparian ecosystem functions that support biodiversity, groundwater recharge, and long-term post-fire recovery. Primary Goal 4. Monitoring, Maintenance, Adaptive Management, and Tribal Science Ensure the long-term success and sustainability of restoration activities through the development and implementation of a comprehensive monitoring, maintenance, and adaptive management framework that incorporates Western Science and Traditional Ecological Knowledge (Tribal Science). Objective 4.1. Implement a science-based monitoring program to evaluate ecological recovery, vegetation establishment, wetland condition, invasive species dynamics, and geomorphic change throughout the project. Objective 4.2. Maintain restoration investments through routine site inspections, invasive species control, replacement plantings, and repair of restoration infrastructure. Objective 4.3. Apply adaptive management principles by using monitoring results to refine restoration strategies, improve effectiveness, and respond to changing environmental conditions. Objective 4.4. Integrate Traditional Ecological Knowledge into restoration planning, implementation, monitoring, and stewardship through meaningful and sustained partnerships with Tribal communities. Primary Goal 5. Public Access, Trails, Interpretive Signage, and Community Engagement Enhance public access and community engagement through improvements of existing trails, development of ADA-accessible public access opportunities on the Plateau, installation of interpretive signage, and community engagement programs that foster education, stewardship, and connection to Eaton Canyon. Objective 5.1. Improve safe and inclusive public access to Eaton Canyon through restoration of trail infrastructure and expansion of ADA-accessible recreation opportunities where feasible. Objective 5.2. Increase public understanding of wildfire recovery, watershed processes, native ecosystems, and Indigenous stewardship through interpretive signage and educational programming. Objective 5.3. Engage community members, schools, and local organizations in hands-on restoration activities, including seed collection, planting, and stewardship events. Objective 5.4. Build long-term community stewardship capacity by supporting local native plant propagation and volunteer-based restoration programs that contribute directly to ecosystem recovery. Following the fire, this refuge for biodiversity and valuable resource for surrounding communities faces destabilized soils, invasive species proliferation, impaired hydrology, and a loss of riparian and upland habitat. Without immediate intervention, post-fire erosion and colonization by invasive plants will cause long-term ecological decline, threaten downstream water quality, compromise habitat for special-status species, and increase fire risk.

ceqa-4da5922d1a8d5efb23.name: 853464_0100006_SoCalGas_UGS
ceqa-4da5922d1a8d5efb23.description: Southern California Gas Company proposes to Rework existing Gas Storage well Fernando Fee 32-A at Aliso Canyon UGS 0100006. The intent of this project is to inspect the well integrity and remediate identified conditions as part of the Storage Integrity Management Program (SIMP). After reviewing well history, available directional surveys and inspection logs, and current wellbore configuration (casing size, restrictions, perforations, liner, etc.), a plan has been developed to return the well to service. This project includes pulling completion equipment, cleaning to total depth, performing punch and inject, and probable casing expansions as proposed and with approval from CalGEM, performing integrity tests, and running new completion tubing. Temporary equipment such as a mud pump and return bins will be utilized. No permanent facilities will be constructed during the process, and no expansion of associated facilities will be required. All waste material, including brine kill fluid, will be properly disposed of as non-hazardous or hazardous waste, as appropriate, at a facility licensed to accept the waste. The established oil field surrounding the project location consists of graded pads, wells, oilfield equipment and roadways with areas of undisturbed non-native grasses and California sage brush vegetation. The proposed project consists of the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division (CalGEM) approving 1 permit for Southern California Gas Company (S4700) to rework the well listed below, in the Aliso Canyon Gas Field. API # Well Name 0403721872 Fernando Fee 32-A

ceqa-efbf8fd99ce0c547f3.name: Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project
ceqa-efbf8fd99ce0c547f3.projectTitle: Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project
ceqa-efbf8fd99ce0c547f3.description: The proposed Modified Project would accommodate construction and utility installation activities for the Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project consisting of: Demolition of the Berths D52-54 Transit Shed on Pier D along Pico Avenue; Extension of an existing 36-inch diameter sewer line along West 12th Street between Harbor Avenue and Fashion Avenue; Relocation of the Control Point Foote Wye east of the Dominguez Channel to be compatible with mainline rail track configurations in the Control Point Crucero; Installation of conduit to extend an existing rail signal in the Control Point Foote Wye area; Closure of Grant Street (between Schley Avenue and Farragut Avenue) and Southern Pacific Drive (between Schley Avenue and Perry Avenue) in the City of Los Angeles; Construction of water and sewer lines on West Water Street near Interstate 710; Designation of temporary construction staging and laydown areas near the Dominguez Channel Rail Bridge, south of West Anaheim Street and west of Jackson Avenue, north and east of Carrack Avenue, and beneath the Long Beach International Gateway Bridge accessed from West Pier D Street; pavement restriping and installation of signage at the southbound I-710 Exit 1B offramp off Pico Avenue; and removal/abandonment of Sewer Main Line, north of the Toyota Logistics Services building at Pier B. Operational activities of the Pier B On-Dock Rail Support Facility Project would remain the same as discussed and analyzed in the certified EIR. Minor additions and changes to the Pier B Project consist of the following 10 areas: 1 - Berths D52-D54 Transit Shed Demolition. Demolition of the entire Transit Shed at Pier D Berths 52-54, located in the southeast portion of the project area, west of Pico Avenue, to accommodate realignment of Pico Avenue and site reconfigurations on the west side of existing Pico Avenue. The 2025 Draft SEIR proposed partial demolition of the Transit Shed, which is deemed infeasible due to cost, engineering and constructability complexities related to maintaining the remainder of the building’s integrity after partial removal of the façade and easterly portion of the Transit Shed. Thus, total demolition of the Transit Shed is now proposed. 2 - West 12th Street Sewer Line Installation. Extension of a 36-inch-diameter sewer along West 12th Street between Harbor Avenue and Fashion Avenue. 3 - Control Point Foote Wye Track Relocation and Rail Signal Extension. Relocation of the Control Point (CP) Foote Wye, east of the Dominguez Channel to be compatible with the revised mainline track configurations in the CP Crucero area. Relocation, removal, and/or protection-in-place of water, gas, storm drain, electrical, communication, and oil utilities would accommodate the relocated rail tracks. Grant Street (between approximately Schley Avenue and Farragut Avenue) and Southern Pacific Drive (between approximately Schley Avenue and Perry Avenue), within the City of Los Angeles, require closure to accommodate track realignment work. Installation of conduit to support extension of the railroad signal in the CP Foote Wye Area, west of Pennington Avenue, east of the Dominguez Channel, north of Grant Street. An existing rail signal shelter adjacent to the Dominguez Channel would be demolished. 4 - West Water Street Utility Connections. Construction of sewer and water lines on West Water Street, near the I-710 interchange at Ocean Boulevard. 5 - Dominguez Channel Rail Bridge Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Area (.03 acres) for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to the construction of the security wall under the existing and widened Dominguez Channel Rail Bridge. 6 - Pavement Restriping. Restriping and signage at the southbound I-710 Exit 1B offramp, and adjacent to Queen’s Wharf Restaurant off Pico Avenue. 7 - Anaheim Street Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Area (2.5 acres) used for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to construction, south of West Anaheim Street and west of Jackson Avenue. 8 - Carrack Avenue Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Area (12.3 acres) used for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to construction, north and east of Carrack Avenue, east of an Oil Operating Area, and south of the Toyota Logistics Services lot. 9 - Pier B Sewer Main Line Removal/Abandonment. Removal/Abandonment of a COLA-owned 27-inch sewer main line, north of the Toyota Logistics Services building at Pier B near the intersection of Pier B Street and Carrack Avenue. As part of the sewer work, POLB would take ownership of the sewer to remove/abandon it in place and would install and maintain a new manhole at the point of connection (POC) between the existing POLB/COLA sewer. Approximately 275 feet of the sewer within Southern California Edison’s (SCE) right-of-way is proposed to be removed, and approximately 2,389 ft of sewer within Toyota Logistics Services’ parking lot at Pier B is proposed to be abandoned. 10 - West Pier D Street Construction Staging and Laydown Area. Two areas (totaling 4.9 acres) for temporary construction equipment staging and laydown for contractor activities related to construction, beneath the Long Beach International Gateway Bridge, accessed from West Pier D Street.

ceqa-fb4043ca054dabf96f.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 5 - South Coast, San Diego
ceqa-fb4043ca054dabf96f.description: The Ballona Wetlands Ecological Reserve is located in Southern California, south of Marina del Rey and east of Playa del Rey. It extends roughly from the Marina Freeway (State Route 90) to the east, the Westchester bluffs to the south, Playa del Rey to the west, and Fiji Way to the north. The project site is held by the State of California (by CDFW and the State Lands Commission). The site is bisected by and includes a channelized span of Ballona Creek. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Works–Flood Control District (collectively, LACFCD) owns and operates the Ballona Creek channel and levee system, which are features of the Los Angeles County Drainage Area (LACDA) project authorized by Congress in 1990. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, in cooperation with the LACFCD, constructed the Ballona Creek channel and levees within the Ballona Reserve as part of the LACDA project. Seeking to restore degraded wetland habitat and functions within the Ballona Reserve, CDFW is proposing a large-scale effort to restore, enhance, and establish native coastal wetland and upland habitats on approximately 566 acres within the Ballona Reserve; these efforts would require incidental work on adjacent property.

ceqa-b7fa05be0acfc459cf.name: Los Angeles County General Hospital Campus Master Plan
ceqa-b7fa05be0acfc459cf.projectTitle: Los Angeles County General Hospital Campus Master Plan
ceqa-b7fa05be0acfc459cf.agency: County of Los Angeles Department of Economic Opportunity
ceqa-b7fa05be0acfc459cf.agencyName: County of Los Angeles Department of Economic Opportunity
ceqa-b7fa05be0acfc459cf.description: The Proposed Project involves implementation of the proposed Los Angeles County General Hospital Campus Master Plan. which would guide the long-term redevelopment of approximately 30.8 acres of the Project Site. including adaptive reuse of the 1.2-million-sguare-foot General Hospital Building. The Proposed Project seeks to maintain flexibility for the County to redevelop other parts of the Project Site (the approximately 51.1 acres outside of the Master Plan area) with potential County-initiated projects in the future. The Proposed Project includes the demolition of existing buildings, structures, storage containers, modular buildings, pavement, utilities, and landscaping to allow for the development of approximately 8.1 million square feet of new uses. Additionally, the Proposed Project involves seismic retrofit, selective demolition, and major improvements to facilitate adaptive reuse of the General Hospital Building and the area surrounding the building. known as the Los Angeles General Hospital-Acute Unit Historic District. The Proposed Project includes utility infrastructure improvements, circulation and transportation demand management strategies, parking, and open space and landscaping. With respect to utility infrastructure improvements, the Project Site would undergo comprehensive updates to the infrastructure network on the Project Site to meet the needs of the proposed land uses, including potable water lines, sewer lines, stormwater system, electrical lines, natural gas, and steam infrastructure. This would include decommissioning and demolition of existing outdated and inefficient energy and water distribution/collection systems, including the existing West Central Plant, consistent with assumptions in the 2014 Master Plan EIR. The Proposed Project may include development of a new centralized energy distribution system (utility plant) or a broader system of electrical and natural gas infrastructure. The Proposed Project under consideration and evaluated in the Draft SEIR represents a new proposed Master Plan that would govern redevelopment on approximately 30.8 acres of the Project Site and would largely supersede the prior Master Plan that was approved by the County. Portions of the Project Site not subject to the proposed Master Plan would continue to be governed by the previously approved 2014 Master Plan and its associated development parameters. However, because development within the remainder of the Project Site would continue pursuant to the 2014 Master Plan, the Draft SEIR evaluates potential environmental impacts associated with development across the entire Project Site to ensure that a full range of potential redevelopment on the Project Site is considered.

ceqa-129eb5f5a0e2f218ad.name: Fulton Playfield Multi-Benefit Infiltration Project
ceqa-129eb5f5a0e2f218ad.projectTitle: Enhanced Watershed Management Programs (EWMP) Program EIR
ceqa-129eb5f5a0e2f218ad.description: The Fulton Playfield Multi-Benefit Infiltration Project proposes incorporating infiltration elements into the existing Greenflag Detention Basin (Basin) to add water quality and volume reduction benefits to the Basin without compromising the flood control function. The Project includes modification to the existing diversion weir box by creating two chambers (diversion and bypass chambers) to divert stormwater to the Basin during storm events and installation of approximately 12 infiltration drywells adjacent to the Basin. The existing flap gates will be replaced with sliding gates to maintain the stormwater in the Basin and to allow infrequent manual dewatering if needed. When the Basin is filled during large storm events, excess stormwater runoff will flow downstream via the existing weir wall into the overflow chamber and existing storm drain. Parkway greening (bioretention cells) is proposed along both sides of Rindge Lane and west side of Earle Lane to capture and treat street flows that are not currently tributary to the project. An ocean-friendly garden is proposed along the north perimeter between the Playfield and Ripley Avenue to treat street runoff and provide public education on green stormwater management practice. Park enhancement, such as outdoor fitness equipment, will also be implemented as part of the Project per community stakeholder input. The Los Angeles County Flood Control District is acting as a Responsible Agency for the Project for the issuance of a Use and Maintenance Agreement. The City of Redondo Beach (Lead Agency) certified the District's Enhanced Watershed Management Program Environmental Impact Report (PEIR) on June 16, 2015. The District conducted a review of the Project in light of the PEIR, that was certified by the County of Los Angeles Board of Supervisors, as the governing body of the District, on May 26, 2015. The Notice of Determination for the Enhanced Watershed Management Program PEIR was submitted to the State Clearinghouse (File No. 2014081106) and filed with the Los Angeles County Clerk on May 27, 2015. Based on this review, project-specific impacts do not meet any of the conditions in State California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15162 or Section 15163. No new environmental documentation is required under Section 15168(c)(2) of the State CEQA Guidelines.

ceqa-e43dc2994eb03a3713.name: State Route 71 Freeway Upgrade and Interchange Improvement Project
ceqa-e43dc2994eb03a3713.projectTitle: State Route 71 Freeway Upgrade and Interchange Improvement Projects
ceqa-e43dc2994eb03a3713.description: This project involves upgrading SR 71 from a combination of 4-lane expressway and 6-lane freeway into an 8-lane freeway, with 3 mixed-flow lanes and 1 High Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) lane in each direction between Interstate 10 and the Los Angeles/San Bernardino County line in both counties. This will be achieved by widening or restriping to add either one or two lanes depending on the location. Additional improvements include replacing two railroad overhead bridges with raised profiles to meet current vertical clearance standards, replacing an existing pedestrian overcrossing, and eliminating local crossings between Mission Boulevard (Blvd) and Rio Rancho Road. The project will also repave the roadway, reconstruct on- and off-ramps at Valley and Mission Blvd, as well as the southbound Rio Rancho Road off-ramp. In addition, paving and striping 0.2 miles into San Bernardino County to maintain HOV lane continuity. Furthermore, the project includes constructing soundwalls and retaining walls, installing Permanent Best Management Practices, and shifting the centerline alignment westward from Mission Blvd to Old Pomona Road to minimize right of way impacts.

ceqa-3923fb9f75ff32733b.name: Open Space Element Update
ceqa-3923fb9f75ff32733b.description: The Open Space Element Update (Project) is an amendment to the City's General Plan involving updates to the existing Parks and Recreation Element, which will be renamed the “Open Space Element.” The Open Space Element Update is in response to Senate Bill (SB) 1425, which requires local jurisdictions to address equitable access to open space, climate resilience, and rewilding opportunities in the open space element of the general plan. The Project addresses SB 1425 through updated background information, inventories, goals, policies, and implementation actions related to parks, recreation, and open space in West Hollywood. The Project includes information regarding disadvantaged communities, existing park service levels, current rewilding and urban greening efforts, and ongoing or planned parks and open space initiatives. The Project also includes revised and new policy direction intended to guide future decisions regarding parks, recreational facilities, and open space, with particular attention to equitable access, climate resilience, and rewilding. The Project is a policy document and does not approve or authorize any site-specific park, recreation, or open space improvement projects. The Project does not approve land acquisition, rezoning, subdivisions, construction, or funding for any specific capital improvement. Any future physical improvement or discretionary actions that may be pursued to implement the Project would be subject to separate review under the California Environmental Quality Act, as applicable.

ceqa-1ad1bf77c2b67534d5.name: Amend Sections 28.06 and 28.65, Title 14, CCR Re: Recreational Gear Restrictions for White Shark (90-day Emergency Extension)
ceqa-1ad1bf77c2b67534d5.projectTitle: Amend Sections 28.06 and 28.65, Title 14, CCR Re: Recreational Gear Restrictions for White Shark (90-day Emergency Extension)
ceqa-1ad1bf77c2b67534d5.description: The proposed project would extend the emergency amendments to Title 14, California Code of Regulations (CCR), sections 28.06 and 28.65 regarding finfish fishing gear restrictions and the take of white sharks. The proposed extension would continue the requirement to immediately release hooked white sharks and prohibit removing white sharks from the water. The proposed extension would also continue the also prohibit the use of wire or metallic lines or leaders or hooks greater than one and one-half inches in maximum inside diameter when fishing from the shoreline (including beaches, banks, piers, jetties, breakwaters, docks, and other man-made structures connected to the shore) or within 1,000 yards of the mean high tide line in ocean waters south of Pigeon Point (San Mateo County, 37° 11' N. lat.). This project extends the emergency rule originally adopted at the June 17-18, 2026 Fish and Game Commission meeting (Office of Administrative Law File Number 2026-0626-01E). The El Nino conditions that prompted the emergency are continuing and anticipated to increase through the fall, necessitating an extension of the emergency regulations. The extension of the emergency amendments are necessary to further protect white sharks from illegal fishing activities and to help prevent incidents between hooked white sharks and ocean users in the same vicinity. White sharks are an important apex predator in the marine ecosystem and are protected under state and federal fishing regulations. There have been several incidents involving pier and beach anglers either intentionally targeting white sharks or accidentally hooking them with very heavy fishing gear; the incidents have resulted in the death of at least three white sharks this year. Additionally, in 2014, a swimmer was bitten by a white shark that had been hooked by a pier angler. This year, a forecasted strong El Niño oceanic event is anticipated to increase the presence of white sharks in California coastal waters, which will increase their availability to anglers and the potential for human interactions with hooked sharks. Young white sharks are already being observed in significantly higher numbers in southern California. Because of this, an emergency situation exists that requires an immediate need to curtail illegal targeted fishing for white sharks, help ensure accidentally hooked sharks are released alive, and help prevent another incident where a hooked shark bites an ocean user or the heavy gear used to catch such sharks entangles a person in the water.

ceqa-42d50ac08f2e31f3bc.name: Valencia Water Reclamation Plant Outfall 001 Spillway Emergency Repair
ceqa-42d50ac08f2e31f3bc.projectTitle: Valencia Water Reclamation Plant Outfall 001 Spillway Emergency Repair
ceqa-42d50ac08f2e31f3bc.description: The Valencia Water Reclamation Plant (VWRP) is one of two water reclamation plants owned by the Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District and serves the City of Santa Clarita and a portion of unincorporated Los Angeles County. Continuous operations of the VWRP are critical for the ability of the SCVSD to provide essential service to over 200,000 residents. The Outfall 001 is currently the only outfall utilized by VWRP to discharge treated wastewater (effluent) into a tributary to the Santa Clara River, a Water of the United States under the Clean Water Act. The concrete channel of Outfall 001 has experienced significant vertical and horizontal movements that a portion of the concrete channel is broken. Underneath the compromised section, a scoured void is observed, leaving the structure vulnerable to collapse. While a second outfall (Outfall 002) exists at the VWRP, it is designated to handle stormwater overflows. It also has a lesser capacity and cannot handle the peak flow from the VWRP. Therefore, the purpose of the project is to repair the Outfall 001 concrete channel to ensure continuous operations at the VWRP.

ceqa-c7083dadeb995945d6.name: Valencia Water Reclamation Plant Scour Emergency Repair/Riprap Installation
ceqa-c7083dadeb995945d6.projectTitle: Valencia Water Reclamation Plant Scour Emergency Repair/Riprap Installation
ceqa-c7083dadeb995945d6.description: The middle section of the retaining wall that separates the Valencia Water Reclamation Plant (VWRP) from the Santa Clara River (SCR) consists of a mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) wall and large rock riprap. The large rock riprap was installed under the California Regional Water Quality Control Board, Los Angeles Region, File No. 05-140, to repair the damaged retaining wall resulting from the January 2005 flood. Since the riprap installation, scour and erosion have advanced the riverbank northward, exposing the MSE wall beyond the riprap for approximately 50 feet in length and 14 feet in height. With the expected El Niño conditions during the 2026-2027 wet weather season, heavy flows in the SCR could extend erosion and scour farther north, undermining and destabilizing the MSE wall, interrupting wastewater treatment service for over 200,000 residents, and ultimately sending untreated wastewater down the SCR. The emergency project was originally part of the VWRP Middle Section Retaining Wall Ground Improvement Project under the California Regional Water Quality Control Board, Los Angeles Region, Clean Water Act Section 401 Certification File No. 26-113, with an expected construction start date of April 2027. However, due to the expected El Niño conditions during the 2026-2027 wet-weather season, the Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District advanced the riprap installation as an emergency project.

The Project encompasses sidewalk reconstruction, cross-slope adjustments, curb and gutter repairs, and installation of accessible curb ramps across 160 addresses CD 8. ceqa-9fa9b4454f03205f68.name: Landscape and Site Design Ordinance
ceqa-9fa9b4454f03205f68.description: The Proposed Project involves the adoption of a new ordinance known as the “Landscape and Site Design Ordinance” (Proposed Ordinance) that will amend the City's current Landscape Ordinance (No. 170,978), Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC) Sections 12.40 through 12.43, previously adopted in May 1996 and amended in April 2005. The proposed amendment to LAMC Sections 12.40 through 12.43 will create new landscape and site design objective standards (Landscape and Site Design Point System) using a dynamic and flexible performance-based point system, in order to implement healthy building design and climate-adapted site design. Through established point targets dependent on project types, the Point System will establish a more efficient and effective implementation process. The objective design standards represent a more comprehensive approach to site design that aligns with broader Citywide policy goals of climate resilience, designing for health and the protection and enhancement of the City’s urban forest and biodiversity. Related amendments to LAMC Sections 12.03, 12.10.5, 12.11.5, 12.12.2, 12.13, 12.21, 12.21.1, 12.40, 12.41, 12.42, 12.43, 13.08, 13.09, 14.00, 19.04, 62.177 and 91.7012 are necessary in order to effectuate the Landscape and Site Design Ordinance and Point System. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Ordinance will apply Citywide and will address pressing sustainability and health-related needs, building upon The Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles, the General Plan’s Health and Wellness Element, and the Citywide Design Guidelines that are in effect today. Policy 2.2 of The Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles (Chapter 2.2) addresses healthy building design and construction and the relationship of health to the built environment. This policy encourages the design and rehabilitation of buildings and sites for healthy living and working conditions, promoting enhanced pedestrian-oriented circulation, lighting, attractive and open stairs, healthy building materials and universal accessibility. Secondly, a future Implementation Program identified in the Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles (Program 36) speaks to streamlining and updating the 1996 City of Los Angeles Landscape Guidelines and Ordinance to better respond to climate change and healthy communities. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Point System implements Policy 2.2 of the Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles through a set of objective standards that are organized into the following three design approaches: (1) Pedestrian-First Design, (2) 360 Degree Design and (3) Climate Adapted Landscape and Site Design, similar to the Citywide Design Guidelines. Under each design approach, the standards are further organized under topical categories accompanied by corresponding strategies that are identified as either Mandatory or Elective, each with an assigned point value. The Ordinance will apply to residential and non-residential projects that may employ any of the standards in each category to obtain a required total of points, some of which will be mandatory, with a minimum of three points in each category and at least eight Designing for Health standards. To encourage the protection and expansion of tree canopy and heat island reduction in climate-vulnerable communities, projects that are in a mapped “Health and Urban Forest Equity Priority” area, per the draft Zoning Information file that accompanies the Proposed Ordinance, will be required to meet two additional health-related standards in the Landscape and Site Design Point System. These projects will also be eligible for up to five additional bonus points if certain standards related to tree canopy conservation, tree planting, and reduction of climate impacts are selected. Industrial or hybrid-Industrial projects and surface parking lot projects must meet a total of 15 points, through a combination of Mandatory and Elective standards. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Ordinance also includes a new definition for Outdoor Amenity Areas to support the integration of indoor and outdoor spaces. Outdoor Amenity Areas are outdoor spaces that are covered with overhead structures like patios, terraces, and courtyards and/or outdoor spaces that are only partially enclosed. This new definition and set of standards, allows for creative design solutions for outdoor areas that provide shade and comfort without counting these outdoor spaces toward the building’s floor area and height.
