ceqa-3a83d9479a480fef26.name: Lakewood Plaza Removal Action Workplan
ceqa-3a83d9479a480fef26.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-3a83d9479a480fef26.description: Project Description: The project consists of implementing the Lakewood Plaza Removal Action Workplan (RAW) to address the presence of tetrachloroethylene (PCE) and trichloroethylene (TCE) in groundwater beneath approximately 7.3 acres of land located in Long Beach, CA (Site). The project activities entail performing on-Site treatment of groundwater using enhanced reductive dichlorination (ERD, a process that consists of injecting microbes capable of converting contaminants to inert substances) to achieve groundwater remedial action objectives and eliminate future concerns of vapor intrusion due to off-gassing from groundwater. Background: The Site is a commercial retail property comprised of four parcels (Los Angeles County APNs 719-1027-25, -27, -28, and -29) situated at the northwest corner of East Spring Street and Palo Verde Avenue in the city of Long Beach. The Site was initially used for agricultural purposes and was developed as a shopping center in the 1950s. Additional buildings were constructed in the 1960s, and the number and footprint of the buildings have not changed since that time. Two dry cleaning businesses previously operated on the Site, one of which (Happy Hanger Cleaners) historically used PCE until approximately 2003. Other businesses on site include a dental clinic, a gym, a bakery, a nail salon, and a grocery store. The Site also contains asphalt-paved parking areas, concrete walkways, and palm trees and other minor landscaping. Residential properties are located immediately north and west of the site, and commercial retail properties are located east of the site across Palo Verde Avenue and south of the site across East Spring Street. There are five groundwater monitoring wells currently at the site. Groundwater monitoring is currently conducted on a semi-annual frequency. The project applicant and DTSC entered into a Standard Voluntary Agreement on November 26, 2019 (Docket No. HAS-FY19/20-037). Previous Investigations: In April 2019, a Phase I Environmental Assessment was conducted on Site. As part of the assessment, soil vapor probes were installed at 5 feet below ground surface (bgs) either inside the tenant space adjacent to the Happy Hanger Cleaners building, or in the parking lot immediately behind the dry-cleaning businesses. PCE was detected in each of the soil vapor samples at elevated concentrations. In May 2019, indoor air, soil, groundwater, and additional soil vapor samples were collected to evaluate the potential for vapor intrusion into the tenant spaces and to delineate the lateral and vertical extent of PCE concentrations in the subsurface. Elevated concentrations of PCE were found in soil vapor and groundwater in the immediate area surrounding the source area on Site, with the highest concentrations present at the former source area adjacent to the dry-cleaning machine in the Happy Hangers Cleaners business. In February 2022, additional sampling of soil, soil vapor, indoor air and groundwater were conducted as part of the Supplemental Site Investigation. Elevated concentrations of PCE were found in soil vapor and groundwater in the immediate area surrounding the source area on Site, with the highest concentrations adjacent to the former dry-cleaning machine in the Happy Hangers business. From July 2023 to October 2024, a Soil Vapor Extraction (SVE) Pilot Study was conducted on Site. The SVE system was turned off for rebound evaluation, then restarted November 2024 until December 2024. During November 2024 rebound evaluation, vapor samples were collected from the individual SVE wells, the highest concentrations were found in the wells located within the former Happy Hanger Cleaners tenant space, but remained well below the target cleanup goals. In February 2025, SVE system was removed from Site. Project Activities: Implementation of the RAW involves a process known as enhanced reductive dichlorination (“ERD”) which will be used to reduce concentrations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the area of the source plume core area and beneath the former dry cleaning facilities. ERD works by injecting a solution containing microbes into the ground, which then reacts with contaminants and converts them to inert end products. ERD will be implemented in an area measuring approximately 10,000 square feet in the area of the core plume source area around existing monitoring wells MW 1 and MW 3 and beneath the former dry-cleaning facilities. Implementation will consist of a single injection in up to 17 injection points. The injection wells will be installed using a drill rig, with boring widths measuring approximately 2 to 3 inches in diameter. The target depth of the injection is approximately 15 to 35 feet bgs at the core plume source area around existing monitoring wells MW 1 and MW 3 and approximately 15 to 55 feet bgs and beneath the dry cleaning facilities utilizing angle borings. The estimated time/duration of the injection is six to eight working days. Monitoring of groundwater will be performed to evaluate baseline conditions, performance and for compliance with applicable permits. It is noted that additional rounds of injections may be necessary depending on the VOC concentrations in the wells post injection. Limited monitoring of indoor air is proposed until cleanup goals are confirmed to be achieved for soil vapor and groundwater. The RAW estimates it will take 1 to 3 years to achieve the reduction goals. Sampling and analysis will be performed as required by Waste Discharge Requirements (WDR) to be issued by the Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB). Compliance monitoring is typically performed on a quarterly basis. The results of compliance testing will be reported in the required WDR monitoring reports. Although not anticipated, in the event biological, cultural or historical resources are discovered in the course of project activities, work will be suspended while a qualified biologist, cultural or historical specialist makes an assessment of the area and arrangements are made to protect or preserve any resources that are discovered. If human remains are discovered, no further disturbance will occur in the location where the remains are found, and the County Coroner will be notified pursuant to the Health and Safety Code, Chapter 2, Section 7050.5.

ceqa-22fc8518ebe8c9e344.name: Former Crocker Plating Works Facility – West Lot Removal Action Workplan for Soil
ceqa-22fc8518ebe8c9e344.projectTitle: Former Crocker Plating Works Facility – West Lot Removal Action Workplan for Soil
ceqa-22fc8518ebe8c9e344.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-22fc8518ebe8c9e344.description: The project consists of the excavation and off-site disposal of soils that have been impacted by total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH) characterized as oil range organics (ORO), hexavalent chromium (Cr6+), and lead at the Former Crocker Plating Works Facility - West Lot property located at 5879 and 5887 Crocker Street in Los Angeles California (Site). The Site encompasses an area of approximately 0.24 acres. The estimated volume of soil proposed for removal, minus any additional soil removed for excavation sloping (sidewall stability) purposes, will be approximately 370 bank cubic yards (bcy). The project is estimated to take approximately 3 months. Background: The Site consists of two City-owned parcels identified by the Los Angeles County Assessor’s Office by Assessor Identification Numbers 6006-029-900 (5879 Crocker Street) and 6006-029-901 (5887 Crocker Street). The Site is currently vacant but was previously used as a parking lot with outdoor storage in connection with the former Crocker Plating Works business that operated immediately east of the Site at 5888 and 5910 Crocker Street. The Site and surrounding parcels are zoned “RD - Restricted Density Multiple Dwelling Zone”. The Site is located within a mixed residential, commercial, and manufacturing area of south-central Los Angeles, with a long history of offsite businesses and industries (both historical and active) that include uses such as metal plating, furniture manufacturing and motor vehicle repair. The City of Los Angeles plans to redevelop the Site for high density residential housing. Previous Investigations: Multiple Phase I and Phase II Environmental Site Assessments (ESAs) have been conducted at the Site under the oversight of the Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC); these ESAs have involved the assessment of Site soil, groundwater, and soil vapor. Soil at the Site has been analyzed for various analytical suites including petroleum hydrocarbons, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs), Cr6+, Title 22 metals polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), and cyanide. Assessed Site soils appear to be sporadically impacted by ORO, arsenic (one sample location at a depth of 90 feet below ground surface), Cr6+, and lead at concentrations exceeding screening levels for a residential land use scenario. Results indicate that shallow Site soil impacts warrant remediation, while identified groundwater and soil vapor impacts either do not represent a complete or potentially complete exposure pathway, or can be adequately mitigated through the implementation of engineering controls emplaced during Site redevelopment. Accordingly, the RAW is intended to solely address impacts to Site soil via soil excavation in preparation for subsequent Site redevelopment activities. Project Activities: The proposed soil remedy project activities include the following: • Excavation at five 20-foot by 20-foot areas (totaling approximately 370 bcy) located across the Site to a maximum total depth of approximately 8 feet below ground surface (bgs) to remove ORO, Cr6+, and lead-impacted soil. Off-site disposal will require approximately 25-30 truck trips to one or more of the following facilities: California, Simi Valley Regional Landfill in eastern Ventura County, California, La Paz Landfill in southwest Arizona, South Yuma Landfill in southwest Arizona, Kettleman Hills Landfill in Kings County, California. • The evaluation of underlying and sidewall soils for visual or olfactory indications of previously unidentified impacts. • Post-excavation confirmation soil sampling activities. • Preparation of a Soil Management Plan (SMP) to ensure that any residual impacted soil (if encountered) will be managed in accordance with pre-established processes and procedures that will be protective of human health and the environment. Because geotechnical assessments conducted at the Site in preparation for Site redevelopment have resulted in the conclusion that the uppermost five feet of Site soil beneath proposed building footprints will need to be removed and replaced prior to construction, the RAW proposes leaving the completed excavations open, with all excavation sidewalls sloped to mitigate the potential for fall-related injuries to Site visitors or trespassers, and to preclude stormwater runoff from the excavated areas. The Site will be left in compliance with stormwater best management practices (BMPs) adopted to prevent soil runoff post-RAW implementation. A grading permit and clearances will be required from the City of Los Angeles. The project is also subject to: • South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD) Rule 1166 – Volatile Organic Compound Emissions from Decontamination of Soil - which requires owners or operators excavating, grading, handling, or treating VOC-contaminated soil to implement an approved VOC mitigation plan and provide notification to control emissions during decontamination activities • SCAQMD Rule 1466 – Control of Particulate Emissions from Soils with Toxic Air Contaminants. Mandates that any earth-moving activity disturbing soil contaminated with specified toxic air contaminants at designated cleanup sites must employ dust-control measures, implement PM10 monitoring, and adhere to notification, signage, and recordkeeping requirements to minimize off-site particulate emissions. • SCAQMD Rule 403 – Dust Control, to minimize emission of fugitive dust. Monitoring will be conducted during all soil disturbance activities by qualified technicians under the supervision of a Certified Industrial Hygienist. The following additional permits may be required: • California Department of Public Health Abatement of Lead Hazards Evaluation Notification Form 8551 and Lead Hazard Evaluation Report Form 8552 or latest versions. • Los Angeles Departments of Transportation and Bureau of Engineering: Traffic control and encroachment permits for work activities that require encroachment and/or traffic control or pedestrian control measures, and implementation of the transportation plan. • Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board: Stormwater Pollution and Prevention Plan. • Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety (LADBS) and Los Angeles Department of Water and Power: Temporary water connection (fire hydrant) installation and meter permits, if necessary. In addition, planning documents have been prepared for the following: Health and Safety, Soil Management, Remedial Design Implementation, Community Air Monitoring, and Traffic and Transportation. Although not anticipated, in the event biological, cultural or historical resources are discovered in the course of project activities, work will be suspended while a qualified biologist, cultural or historical specialist makes an assessment of the area and arrangements are made to protect or preserve any resources that are discovered. If human remains are discovered, no further disturbance will occur in the location where the remains are found, and the County Coroner will be notified pursuant to the Health and Safety Code, Chapter 2, Section 7050.5.

The single-family residence located on Lot 16 is not operating as a school, however; the project requests a rear yard setback adjustment on Lot 16 to connect the school yard and elementary school to the pre-school and middle school via a pedestrian walkway. The campus has approximately 482.92 feet of street frontage along Burlington Avenue to the east and 150.09 feet of frontage along Wilshire Boulevard to the north. The project site is limited to four R4 zoned lots on a rectangular-shaped parcel of land covering approximately 30,750 square-feet of net lot area. The subject site is improved with a school yard, parking lot, and single-family residence. The project site has approximately 205 feet of street frontage along Burlington Avenue to the east. The project consists of the construction of new fences, walls, and a covered pedestrian walkway. The applicant is requesting a Director’s Adjustment to allow the construction, use, and maintenance of a 10-foot-wide covered pedestrian walkway with a maximum height of 13 feet and 8 inches in the rear yard setback, and eleven (11) over-in-height fences/walls with a maximum height of 10 to 13 feet within the front, side, and rear yard setbacks. The project does not propose demolition of existing buildings or tree removal. All buildings and trees will remain. Since the project is for the construction of new fences, walls, a covered pedestrian walkway and no physical changes to the existing buildings are proposed, this project qualifies for the Class 3 (New Construction or Conversion of Small Structures) Categorical Exemption.

ceqa-ebbaf03c88f7c571d6.name: CVWD Groundwater Wells PFAS and Nitrate Water Treatment Facility Project
ceqa-ebbaf03c88f7c571d6.projectTitle: CVWD Groundwater Wells PFAS and Nitrate Water Treatment Facility Project
ceqa-ebbaf03c88f7c571d6.description: The CVWD Groundwater Wells PFAS and Nitrate Water Treatment Facility Project consists of the installation, operation, and maintenance of water treatment facilities at eleven existing groundwater well sites operated by Crescenta Valley Water District. The Project includes pre-engineered ion exchange (IX) treatment systems, associated piping, valves, instrumentation, electrical improvements, and appurtenant facilities necessary to remove PFAS and nitrate from groundwater produced by the District's existing wells. The Project is intended to ensure compliance with applicable state and federal drinking water regulations and maintain a safe and reliable drinking water supply. All improvements will occur entirely within the existing operational footprints of the District's groundwater well facilities. The Project will not increase groundwater production capacity, alter extraction rates, expand facility boundaries, or increase the overall service capacity of the District's water system. The beneficiaries of the Project are the customers and residents served by Crescenta Valley Water District, who will receive a safer and more reliable drinking water supply.

ceqa-1b4a0dd9750e8b192e.name: Landscape and Site Design Ordinance
ceqa-1b4a0dd9750e8b192e.description: ENV-2022-4857-ND The Proposed Project involves the adoption of a new ordinance known as the “Landscape and Site Design Ordinance” (Proposed Ordinance) that will amend the City's current Landscape Ordinance (No. 170,978), Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC) Sections 12.40 through 12.43, previously adopted in May 1996 and amended in April 2005. The proposed amendment to LAMC Sections 12.40 through 12.43 will create new landscape and site design objective standards (Landscape and Site Design Point System) using a dynamic and flexible performance-based point system, in order to implement healthy building design and climate-adapted site design. Through established point targets dependent on project types, the Point System will establish a more efficient and effective implementation process. The objective design standards represent a more comprehensive approach to site design that aligns with broader Citywide policy goals of climate resilience, designing for health and the protection and enhancement of the City’s urban forest and biodiversity. Related amendments to LAMC Sections 12.03, 12.10.5, 12.11.5, 12.12.2, 12.13, 12.21, 12.21.1, 12.40, 12.41, 12.42, 12.43, 13.08, 13.09, 14.00, 19.04, 62.177 and 91.7012 are necessary in order to effectuate the Landscape and Site Design Ordinance and Point System. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Ordinance will apply Citywide and will address pressing sustainability and health-related needs, building upon The Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles, the General Plan’s Health and Wellness Element, and the Citywide Design Guidelines that are in effect today. Policy 2.2 of The Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles (Chapter 2.2) addresses healthy building design and construction and the relationship of health to the built environment. This policy encourages the design and rehabilitation of buildings and sites for healthy living and working conditions, promoting enhanced pedestrian-oriented circulation, lighting, attractive and open stairs, healthy building materials and universal accessibility. Secondly, a future Implementation Program identified in the Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles (Program 36) speaks to streamlining and updating the 1996 City of Los Angeles Landscape Guidelines and Ordinance to better respond to climate change and healthy communities. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Point System implements Policy 2.2 of the Plan for a Healthy Los Angeles through a set of objective standards that are organized into the following three design approaches: (1) Pedestrian-First Design, (2) 360 Degree Design and (3) Climate Adapted Landscape and Site Design, similar to the Citywide Design Guidelines. Under each design approach, the standards are further organized under topical categories accompanied by corresponding strategies that are identified as either Mandatory or Elective, each with an assigned point value. The Ordinance will apply to residential and non-residential projects that may employ any of the standards in each category to obtain a required total of points, some of which will be mandatory, with a minimum of three points in each category and at least eight Designing for Health standards. To encourage the protection and expansion of tree canopy and heat island reduction in climate-vulnerable communities, projects that are in a mapped “Health and Urban Forest Equity Priority” area, per the draft Zoning Information file that accompanies the Proposed Ordinance, will be required to meet two additional health-related standards in the Landscape and Site Design Point System. These projects will also be eligible for up to five additional bonus points if certain standards related to tree canopy conservation, tree planting, and reduction of climate impacts are selected. Industrial or hybrid-Industrial projects and surface parking lot projects must meet a total of 15 points, through a combination of Mandatory and Elective standards. The proposed Landscape and Site Design Ordinance also includes a new definition for Outdoor Amenity Areas to support the integration of indoor and outdoor spaces. Outdoor Amenity Areas are outdoor spaces that are covered with overhead structures like patios, terraces, and courtyards and/or outdoor spaces that are only partially enclosed. This new definition and set of standards, allows for creative design solutions for outdoor areas that provide shade and comfort without counting these outdoor spaces toward the building’s floor area and height.

ceqa-ed3eba0a50e43b49a4.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-ed3eba0a50e43b49a4.description: This project consists of defensible space vegetation management on approximately 35 acres of California State Park Land directly adjacent to residences in Topanga Canyon, California. The work includes mechanical thinning of dense vegetation and removal of flashy fuels and non-native annual grasses to reduce fuel continuity, ladder fuels, and potential wildfire intensity. Work will be performed by qualified and licensed vegetation management contractors. Residents adjacent to the project area will obtain Right of Entry permits from California State Parks prior to conducting work within the project area, including individual site reviews from California State Park Staff.

ceqa-f425346976860893a0.name: Bayramian Hall 5th Floor University Counseling Services Renovation
ceqa-f425346976860893a0.projectTitle: Bayramian Hall 5th Floor University Counseling Services Renovation
ceqa-f425346976860893a0.description: The proposed project will expand the UCS suite on the 5th floor of Bayramian Hall. Following the completion of the Matador Success and Inclusion Center (MSIC) in summer 2027, the Matador Achievement Center (MAC), which currently occupies the 5th floor of Bayramian Hall, will relocate to MSIC. UCS will then renovate the former MAC space to create eight new counseling offices, a reception area, a sensory room, and a training space with storage. This expansion will allow UCS to be fully staffed on campus and better meet student counseling needs. This project is an interior tenant improvement project that will renovate portions of Bayramian Hall to support the expansion of UCS. The scope includes renovation of the former MAC space on the 5th floor, expanding the existing 7,200-square-foot UCS suite by approximately 2,070 square feet and increasing counseling offices from 22 to 34 offices. The project also includes conversion of approximately 570 square feet on the first floor to create a gender-inclusive, multi-stall restroom and lactation room, along with minor accessibility upgrades to the 5th floor restrooms, safety upgrades to the UCS reception service window and suite, upgrades to the existing group counseling and observation rooms, provision of a new conference room with audio-visual equipment, and renovation of the existing UCS suite’s storage room and open office space.

ceqa-a49981f799d159ea58.name: Soil Vapor Extraction System Upgrade Project
ceqa-a49981f799d159ea58.projectTitle: Soil Vapor Extraction System Upgrade Project
ceqa-a49981f799d159ea58.description: This environmental document supplements the Proposed Lockheed Soil Vapor Extraction System Focused EIR (State Clearinghouse No. 1995061010). The Project constitutes a source area removal action that is a continuation of past remediation efforts (including the operation of a soil vapor extraction [SVE] treatment system), referred to in this document as the Approved Project, at a portion of the former Lockheed Martin Plant B-1 Site, focusing on reducing concentrations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) within two source areas, per Cleanup and Abatement Order (Order) No. 87-161 by the Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board. Proposed remediation efforts would be contained within the Project Site. Although the legacy SVE treatment system installed for the Approved Project removed a substantial amount of VOCs from impacted areas within the former Plant B-1 Site, elevated concentrations of VOCs remain in the subsurface soils at and around two smaller, more localized source areas, Vapor Monitoring Points (VMP) VMP-3 and VMP-5, within the Project Site. Therefore, the legacy SVE treatment system is no longer capable of meeting the Order requirements and must be upgraded. The Proposed Project would replace the legacy SVE treatment system with a smaller, more efficient system capable of handling the lower flowrates and higher VOC concentrations anticipated during source area removal. Although the entire former Plant B-1 Site is over 100 acres, the Project Site for the Proposed Project comprises a smaller portion of the former Plant B-1 Site associated with the proposed remediation of source areas VMP-3 and VMP-5.

ceqa-a3f93314b568be1595.name: Hi-Grade Materials Co (Western Joshua Tree Conservation Act (WJTCA) Incidental Take Permit No. 1927-ITP-2025-012-05 (ITP))
ceqa-a3f93314b568be1595.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has issued an ITP (No. 1927 ITP-2025-012-05), pursuant to Section 1927.3 of the Fish and Game Code to HiGrade Materials Co. The project consists of surface mining and excavation activities on an approximately 70- acre portion of an overall 386-acre property. Project activities include vegetation grubbing and clearing, fencing, and mining material using loaders and bulldozers, and a material conveyance system. The project also includes relocation of western Joshua tree (Yucca brevifolia) into a 25-foot-wide setback area. The Project will result in incidental take of 511 western Joshua trees, which are protected under the WJTCA and the California Endangered Species Act. The WJTCA ITP referenced above as issued by CDFW authorizes incidental take of western Joshua tree that may occur as a result of Project implementation.

Commercial/retail, hospitality, community benefits, educational facilities, warehouse, general office, medical office, hospital, and industrial uses would also be developed across the Campus. Implementation of the Master Plan would include adaptive reuse of the 1.2-million-square-foot General Hospital to accommodate a range of uses, as listed previously. Parking, open spaces, and infrastructure improvements would be implemented across the Project Site. Demolition of existing buildings is proposed. The new Master Plan would serve as a regulatory document with central concepts for design and connectivity in the Campus that would serve as a guide for future redevelopment of the Project Site.

ceqa-c1c17cff38b2550d54.projectTitle: Scattergood Generating Station - Water Tank Art Panel Removal
ceqa-c1c17cff38b2550d54.agency: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
ceqa-c1c17cff38b2550d54.agencyName: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
ceqa-c1c17cff38b2550d54.description: The Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP) plans to remove a series of artistic panels currently installed on the exterior surface of an existing water tank in the southern portion of the Scattergood Generating Station located at 12700 Vista Del Mar, Los Angeles, CA 90293. Since its installation in 2018, the panels have experienced sun-related deterioration, including fading and material degradation. In 2023, LADWP initiated efforts to repair and replace affected panels. LADWP will remove all artistic panels from the water tank. Following removal of the panels, LADWP will conduct surface restoration activities to preserve the structural integrity and appearance of the water tank. Restoration activities may include rust removal, surface cleaning, spot repairs, application of protective coatings, paint, and/or new panel installations. The activities are limited to maintenance, repair, and minor alteration of an existing facility and will not involve ground disturbance, expansion of use, or any changes to facility operations.

ceqa-088f6ee2200d46f1e1.projectTitle: San Pedro Street Elementary School Green Schoolyard Improvement
ceqa-088f6ee2200d46f1e1.description: The proposed Project (Project) replaces approximately 33,000 square feet of paving in two main playgrounds with green/natural surfaces that includes native/drought tolerant planting, natural grass playfields, trees and other shade elements, outdoor learning elements. landscaping with irrigation, decomposed granite and pavers, planting areas, restriping of sport courts. and accessibility improvements (Exhibit A). On December l2, 2023, the Board of Education approved an initial $75,000.000 of Green Schoolyard Upgrade projects on 15 sites including San Pedro Street ES. Approximately $5.4 million is budgeted for the Project. The Project will be implemented per all applicable local and State regulations. as well as all District Standards and Specifications, such as those provided in LA Unified‘s Subsequent Program Environmental Impact Report for the School Upgrade Program (Subsequent PEIR). The purpose of the Project is to facilitate removal of portable classrooms pursuant to State and District policies and to provide outdoor learning experiences. The Project will not cause an increase in student capacity or enrollment and would not result in an increase in the intensity of use. The beneficiaries of the Project include students and staff at each of the respective schools and the community at large who may request access to the facilities and grounds of the Campuses pursuant to the Civic Center Act (CA Ed. Code Sections 38 130 - 38139).

ceqa-de4779b3070726b896.name: Lincoln Park Neighborhood Green Street Network
ceqa-de4779b3070726b896.projectTitle: Lincoln Park Neighborhood Green Street Network
ceqa-de4779b3070726b896.description: The Project includes three components: Lincoln Park Lake Improvements; installation of approximately 37 to 50 drywells with associated storm drain infrastructure; and installation of approximately 172 street trees along selected public streets in Lincoln Heights. Lake improvements would include sediment removal, shoreline stabilization, pump house and circulation and aeration system upgrades, passive bioswales, and associated landscape and hardscape modifications. The drywells would capture, treat, and infiltrate runoff from an approximately 125-acre drainage area and would be sized to achieve an 80 percent long-term pollutant load reduction. The Project would provide short-term water quality improvement in Lincoln Park Lake, reduce pollutant loads to the Los Angeles River, enhance lake, park, and streetscape infrastructure, reduce localized flooding, increase groundwater recharge, and improve the neighborhood’s visual quality through landscaping. These objectives would support the Safe Clean Water Program and broader water quality goals for the Upper Los Angeles River watershed.
ceqa-de4779b3070726b896.developmentType: Other (Stormwater infrastructure, parkland, lake, landscape improvement)

ceqa-c9b54e8e00fb725228.name: Coca-Cola Bottling Plant Dock Expansion and Quad Generation Project
ceqa-c9b54e8e00fb725228.projectTitle: Coca-Cola Bottling Plant Dock Expansion and Quad Generation Project
ceqa-c9b54e8e00fb725228.description: The Project proposes the construction of a new 89,889-square-foot industrial tilt-up building (i.e., dock expansion building); installation of a new 3,275-square-foot ingredients cooler to be located to the west immediately adjacent to the existing warehouse (i.e., Building 6); construction of a quad generation facility; and implementation of circulation, parking, and landscaping improvements within the existing Coca-Cola facility in Downey, CA. The proposed dock expansion building would have a maximum height of 42 feet and 7 inches and would be rectangular in shape. While the new structure would include a new production line, there would not be an increase in the number of employee vehicles or trucks accessing the facility or in the quantity of production at the facility. The proposed 3,275-square-foot ingredients cooler would be located within an existing, open truck yard on the west side of the Project Site. North of existing Building 6, the Project proposes to construct a quad generation facility, which would include installation of new combined heat and power (CHP) units that would supply electricity and chilled water to the Coca-Cola facility. The quad generation system would capture and recover exhaust carbon dioxide (CO2) from the CHP units, converting it to beverage-grade CO2 for use in the bottling plant operations. The Project would include site pavement, drainage, and landscaping improvements and would include off-site improvements, including resurfacing (grinding and overlaying) the full width of Cleta Street between Patton Road and Lakewood Boulevard, resurfacing half-width of Patton Road from Cleta Street to the northern extent of the Project Site, and undergrounding the overhead utility lines along the Project Site’s Patton Avenue frontage. The Project requires approval of a variance to consider a reduction in required parking and site plan review.

ceqa-46e29a4aca6f0b50f0.name: NOD - El Segundo Surf Club Project (EA 1411)
ceqa-46e29a4aca6f0b50f0.projectTitle: Professional Sports Headquarters and Training Facility Project
ceqa-46e29a4aca6f0b50f0.description: The El Segundo Surf Club Project (Project) proposes construction and operation of a private commercial/recreational surf club on an approximately 9.3-acre site located at 100–200 South Nash Street in the City of El Segundo (Project site). The Project site is primarily undeveloped but previously improved with limited improvements (i.e., paved areas, a former helicopter pad, surface parking, access roads, and limited ornamental landscaping). The Project would remove existing onsite improvements and construct four three-story buildings totaling approximately 50,236 gross square feet (44,853 net square feet), including member-only recreational and hospitality uses, a public restaurant and meeting space, wellness, retail, office, administrative, and support uses, along with a large surf wave pool, standing wave pool, two recreational pools, outdoor amenities, landscaping, padel courts, surface parking, bicycle parking, and associated utility and circulation improvements. The Project would provide vehicular access from East El Segundo Boulevard and South Nash Street, and would include frontage and circulation improvements consistent with the El Segundo South Campus Specific Plan and Development Agreement (i.e., widening and improving East El Segundo Boulevard adjacent to the Project site), except that the Project requests to amend the El Segundo South Campus Specific Plan, the Development Agreement, and associated prior approvals to remove a requirement to provide a pedestrian easement and walkway connection to the LA Metro El Segundo Station. The Project has been found consistent with the density planned for the Project site by the El Segundo South Campus Specific Plan (i.e., zoning action). Environmental impacts were previously considered and mitigated through the El Segundo South Campus Specific Plan Environmental Impact Report, which was certified in December 2015 (State Clearinghouse (SCH) No. 2012101081) (Certified EIR). No environmental effects were found to be peculiar to the Project or the parcel on which the Project is located; the Project would not cause any environmental effects that were not analyzed as significant in the Certified EIR; cumulative and off-site impacts associated with Project development, as proposed, were fully addressed in the Certified EIR and because the Project is consistent with the ESSCSP development density analyzed in the Certified EIR, Project implementation would not result in any new or altered cumulative impacts or off-site impacts beyond those addressed in the Certified EIR; and there is no substantial new information which was not known at the time the Certified EIR and which indicates that any previously identified significant effects would be more severe. Therefore, the Project has been found to be consistent with the analysis contained in the Certified EIR and no further analysis is necessary.
ceqa-46e29a4aca6f0b50f0.crossStreets: Nash Street and El Segundo Boulevard

ceqa-e73292f6ea732581b1.projectTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, Honeywell Aerospace US, LLC. (Honeywell), Torrance, California
ceqa-e73292f6ea732581b1.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-e73292f6ea732581b1.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to Honeywell, (EPA ID# CAD071896336) to treat hazardous waste through a controlled reaction with chemical solutions. Specifically, one (1) 100-gram container of Picric Acid must be stabilized prior to transport to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. This chemical is currently being stored at Honeywell located at 2525 West 190th Street Torrance, California 90504. DTSC has determined as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued to chemically stabilize the hazardous waste prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site by Clean Harbors Environmental Services (Clean Harbors). Background: Shock and/or temperature sensitive materials can decompose or detonate with external energy when dry or concentrated. If the material is improperly handled, there is a potential for a reaction, which includes fire, deflagration, or detonation. Due to the presence of shock-sensitive materials, DTSC considers these chemicals to be an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment. Chemical stabilization is recommended prior to transport to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility. Project Activities: The treatment of this hazardous waste involves the addition of solutions to the containers in a controlled manner to reduce the reactive or ignitable characteristics of the chemicals. Treatment will take place within a designated exclusion zone. Only technicians from Clean Harbors will be allowed in the exclusion zone. Movement, preparation, and treatment of the containers will be in accordance with established standards. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, Honeywell will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning October 6, 2026 and shall expire on December 6, 2026.

LAUSD’s SCs, design guidelines, and best management practices are designed to be incorporated into the Project design in order to avoid or limit potential adverse impacts associated with the District’s projects. The beneficiaries of the Project include Cochran MS students, faculty, staff, families, school supporters, and the community at large who may request access to the playground pursuant to the Civic Center Act (CA Ed. Code Sections 38130 -38139).

ceqa-6e41ddbbe04345990b.name: Proposed Amended Rule 1143 – Consumer Paint Thinners and Multipurpose Solvents
ceqa-6e41ddbbe04345990b.projectTitle: Proposed Amended Rule 1143 – Consumer Paint Thinners and Multipurpose Solvents
ceqa-6e41ddbbe04345990b.agency: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-6e41ddbbe04345990b.agencyName: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-6e41ddbbe04345990b.description: Rule 1143 is designed to reduce volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions from the use, storage, and disposal of consumer paint thinners and multipurpose solvents that are not regulated by the California Air Resources Board (CARB). Proposed Amended Rule (PAR) 1143 partially implements Control Measure CTS-01: Further Emission Reductions from Coatings, Solvents, Adhesives, and Lubricants of the 2022 Air Quality Management Plan to phase out the use of para-Chlorobenzotrifluoride (pCBtF) and tert-Butyl Acetate (t-BAc) due to toxicity and public health concerns. PAR 1143 includes: 1) a prohibition pertaining to the manufacture, sale, and use of consumer paint thinners and multipurpose solvents with pCBtF, t-BAc, or cyclic, branched, or linear, completely methylated siloxanes (VMS) at future effective dates; 2) sell-through provisions to ensure that manufacturers, distributors, and end users are provided with adequate time to transition to products without pCBtF, t-BAc, or VMS, if needed; 3) an alternative compliance pathway based on Product-Weighted Maximum Incremental Reactivity (PW-MIR) VOC limits which provides additional reformulation flexibility by allowing substitution of lower-toxicity VOCs with known reactivity characteristics, rather than relying on exempt solvents; and 4) revisions for clarity and consistency with other South Coast AQMD rules, streamlined administrative requirements, minor editorial changes, and removal of outdated rule provisions. While no change to ozone formation potential relative to baseline conditions is expected since compliant formulations of consumer paint thinners and multipurpose solvents that do not contain pCBtF, t-BAc, or VMS are currently available and capable of meeting the established VOC emission limits, implementation of PAR 1143 will reduce the associated risk of exposure to emissions of pCBtF, t-BAc, and VMS for workers, nearby receptors, and the public.

ceqa-27cd10ea50fca13bc3.name: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, Phenomenex, Torrance, California
ceqa-27cd10ea50fca13bc3.projectTitle: Emergency Permit for Management of Hazardous Waste, Phenomenex, Torrance, California
ceqa-27cd10ea50fca13bc3.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-27cd10ea50fca13bc3.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to Phenomenex, (EPA ID# CAD982320574) to treat hazardous waste through a controlled reaction with chemical solutions. Specifically, four (4) 5-gallon containers and ten (10) 1-liter containers of 1,4 Divinyl Benzene must be stabilized prior to transport to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. This chemical is currently being stored at Phenomenex located at 431 Amapola Avenue, Torrance, California 90501. DTSC has determined as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued for Triumvirate Environmental, LLC (TE) to chemically stabilize the hazardous waste prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site. Background: Temperature sensitive materials can decompose or detonate with external energy when dry or concentrated. If the material is improperly handled, there is a potential for a reaction which includes fire, deflagration, or detonation. Due to the presence of temperature sensitive materials, DTSC considers these chemicals to be an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment. Chemical stabilization is recommended prior to transport to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility. Project Activities: The treatment of these hazardous wastes involves the addition of a solution to the containers in a controlled manner to reduce the reactive or ignitable characteristics of the chemicals. Treatment will take place within a designated exclusion zone. Only technicians from TE will be allowed in the exclusion zone. Movement, preparation, and treatment of the containers will be in accordance with established standards. Within 10 business days of the expiration of this permit, Phenomenex will submit a final report, signed in accordance with Title 22, CCR Sec. 66270.11(d). The report shall include certification that the treatment area has been cleared of all residual hazardous waste generated from this emergency treatment and all generated waste has been properly managed. The Emergency Permit is effective beginning October 7, 2026, and shall expire on January 5, 2027.

ceqa-dbe75b80aac7f7a059.description: This research will demonstrate the advanced insulation and air sealing technologies in three single family all-electric manufactured accessory dwelling units built on two different lots and verify their impact on the overall energy performance of the homes. ceqa-0ee29385ef39492fce.name: Proposed Amended Rule 1168 – Adhesive and Sealant Applications
ceqa-0ee29385ef39492fce.projectTitle: Proposed Amended Rule 1168 – Adhesive and Sealant Applications
ceqa-0ee29385ef39492fce.agency: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-0ee29385ef39492fce.agencyName: South Coast Air Quality Management District
ceqa-0ee29385ef39492fce.description: PAR 1168 proposes to: 1) extend the parachlorobenzotrifluoride (pCBtF) prohibition date for Roof Adhesive Primers to allow more time for reformulations; 2) delay the effective dates of volatile organic compound (VOC) emission limits for three categories of adhesives and sealants to allow more time for reformulations; 3) include equivalent alternative reactivity-based limits for Top and Trim Adhesives and Roof Adhesive Primers; 4) delete the exemption that allows facilities to use up to 55-gallons of non-compliant products per year; 5) require manufacturers to provide a list of their distributors annually; 6) transition reporting to a recordkeeping requirement for distributors; 7) include a new category for battery adhesives with an extended pCBtF prohibition date; and 8) provide clarifications, updates to definitions, and cross references to maintain consistency with other South Coast AQMD rules. PAR 1168 is expected to result in delayed VOC emission reductions of 0.115 ton per day (tpd) from Top and Trim Adhesives until January 1, 2030; 0.020 tpd from Rubber Vulcanization Adhesives until January 1, 2029; and 0.011 tpd from Clear, Paintable, Immediately Water-Resistant Sealant until January 1, 2028. Extending the pCBtF prohibition date for Roof Adhesive Primers would also delay the benefit of reducing the use of and exposure to pCBtF, a known carcinogen. The Draft SEA concluded that significant and unavoidable adverse environmental impacts may occur for air quality during operation. No other significant adverse impacts were identified. While products subject to PAR 1168 may be used at facilities and other locations within the South Coast AQMD jurisdiction that may be identified on lists compiled by the California Department of Toxic Substances Control per Government Code Section 65962.5, implementation of PAR 1168 will not alter the status of the facilities and other locations on these lists. Delaying the compliance dates in PAR 1168 for certain adhesives and sealants will benefit manufacturers by providing additional time to reformulate these products in response to the needs highlighted in the technology assessment while avoiding market disruptions and allowing temporary continued access to users of these commercially available products.

ceqa-df21bed4a355d71304.name: 849398_0100006_SoCalGas_UGS
ceqa-df21bed4a355d71304.description: Southern California Gas Company proposes to Rework existing Gas Storage well Porter 69A at Aliso Canyon UGS 0100006. The intent of this project is to inspect the well integrity and remediate identified conditions as part of the Storage Integrity Management Program (SIMP). After reviewing well history, available directional surveys and inspection logs, and current wellbore configuration (casing size, restrictions, perforations, liner, etc.), a plan has been developed to return the well to service. This project includes pulling completion equipment, cleaning to total depth, performing punch and inject, and probable casing expansions as proposed and with approval from CalGEM, performing integrity tests, and running new completion tubing. Temporary equipment such as a mud pump and return bins will be utilized. No permanent facilities will be constructed during the process, and no expansion of associated facilities will be required. All waste material, including brine kill fluid, will be properly disposed of as non-hazardous or hazardous waste, as appropriate, at a facility licensed to accept the waste. The established oil field surrounding the project location consists of graded pads, wells, oilfield equipment and roadways with areas of undisturbed non-native grasses and California sage brush vegetation. The proposed project consists of the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division (CalGEM) approving 1 permit for Southern California Gas Company (S4700) to rework the well listed below, in the Aliso Canyon Gas Field. API # Well Name 0403722051 Porter 69A

ceqa-4c1e08e700060ee9ab.agency: Los Angeles County Department of Parks & Recreation
ceqa-4c1e08e700060ee9ab.description: Eugene A. Obregón Park, located at 4021 E. First Street in unincorporated East Los Angeles, features amenities for children, teens, and adults including a baseball field, basketball courts, children’s play areas, a community center, computer labs, gymnasium, handball courts, and a swimming pool. The park serves a densely populated neighborhood and experiences significant usage year-round. However, Eugene A. Obregón Park lacks sufficient shade and cooling infrastructure, making it difficult to provide a safe and comfortable environment during periods of extreme heat. City Terrace Park, located at 1126 N. Hazard Avenue in unincorporated East Los Angeles, offers a range of amenities for children, teens, and adults, including a baseball field, basketball courts, children’s play areas, a social hall, gymnasium, picnic tables, tennis courts, and computer labs. The park is especially popular during the hot summer months, drawing crowds to the splashpad, swimming pool, and play areas. Like Eugene A. Obregón Park, City Terrace Park lacks adequate shaded areas and updated infrastructure to provide sufficient relief from high temperatures. The proposed projects will replace existing playground equipment including safety surfacing; implement integrated shade within the playground equipment; plant shade trees; install a hydration station, a combination of a drinking fountain and water bottle filler; and make related improvements to help reduce heat-related health risks and increase climate resilience. At City Terrace Park, Measure A funding will be used to resurface and restripe the existing parking lot; install new vehicle entry gates; investigate the social hall acoustics; upgrade the existing park security system; and make related improvements. Measure A funding will also be used at Eugene A. Obregón Park to replace the existing walking path.

ceqa-b19798d4aec71e0cfb.description: The Mission Mile Sepulveda project (Project) would result in the transformation of Sepulveda Boulevard to enhance safety, provide a greener environment, and provide a more active community for all ages by incorporating innovative active transportation treatments along the corridor (specific improvements to each segment are described in further detail below). These treatments include reducing Sepulveda Boulevard to a 4-lane roadway from Rayen Street to Devonshire Street and from Devonshire Street to Chatsworth Street by widening the existing median and constructing a new 2-way Class IV bikeway and meandering pedestrian pathway within the median. The project also includes reducing Sepulveda Boulevard to a 4-lane roadway through the Sepulveda Boulevard Undercrossing from Chatworth Street to the SR-118 westbound ramp intersection and constructing new Class II buffered bicycle lanes. From the SR-118 westbound ramp intersection to Rinaldi Street the project would include the reduction of Sepulveda Boulevard to a 4-lane roadway and construction of new Class IV protected bicycle lanes. The project consists of safety improvements and connections for pedestrians and bicyclists to neighborhood parks, cultural sites, and two major Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority planned transit projects. Project beneficiaries include all corridor users, enhancing safety, increasing use of active modes of transportation, enhancing community spaces, and increasing connectivity. Please see the Project description continuation in the narrative for more details. On June 5, 2026, 95% Project design plans were issued for City review and 100% design plans are anticipated in October 2026. The City's request for funding approval from the California Transportation Commission is anticipated in December 2026.

ceqa-8d810eb80cb42cc82f.description: The proposed Homestead South project is located within and implements a portion of the approved Newhall Ranch Specific Plan (Specific Plan). The approximately 1,752-acre area (Project Site) is located in unincorporated Los Angeles County south of State Route 126 (SR-126) and the Santa Clara River and west of the developing community of Mission Village. ceqa-da957af2f14882d3f5.name: Conditional Use Permit No. 26-009: Pronghorn Solar and BESS
ceqa-da957af2f14882d3f5.projectTitle: Conditional Use Permit No. 26-009: Pronghorn Solar and BESS
ceqa-da957af2f14882d3f5.description: Pronghorn Solar Plus, LLC (“Applicant”) proposes to entitle, construct, operate, maintain and decommission a utility-scale solar photovoltaic (PV) electrical generating and storage facility that would generate and deliver renewable energy to the statewide electricity transmission grid. As shown on Figure 2, Proposed Project, the project would include the construction and operation of up to 50 megawatts (MW) of PV solar generation, a BESS with a capacity of up to 50 MW, installation of 34.5 kilovolt (kV) collection lines and a 66 kV generation transmission (gen-tie) line, and a project Substation that would step up the voltage from 34.5 kV to 66 kV. A gen-tie line would directly connect the project substation to the existing SCE Piute substation. Per Sections 17.08.290 and 17.08.050 of the City of Lancaster Municipal Code, utility scale solar facilities and utility scale BESS are allowable uses subject to a conditional use permit (CUP) within the RR-2.5 zone. The Applicant is seeking a CUP (CUP No. 26-009) for construction and operation of the project. The project would sell the renewable energy it produces under the terms of a long-term Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with a load serving entity or other power off-taker. For purposes of the CEQA analysis, it is assumed the project would operate for 30 years. Upon completion of the PPA term, the project operator may, at its discretion, continue to generate and sell power from the project, or decommission and remove the system and its components. Upon decommissioning, project structures not needed for subsequent use would be removed from the project site and the site could be converted to other uses in accordance with applicable land use regulations in effect at that time.

ceqa-44b1ac559f6112b811.name: Sierra Gateway Neighborhood Plan
ceqa-44b1ac559f6112b811.description: The Sierra Gateway Neighborhood Plan (also referred to as the “Specific Plan”) implements Program H-5.2 of the City’s Housing Element. Program H-5.2 involves an to update the Lancaster Transit-Oriented Development Zones (adopted in 2015) to promote high-quality, walkable, mixed-use, and transit-oriented neighborhoods surrounding the Lancaster Boulevard core and the Metrolink station, as further detailed in Section 1.5, Relationship to the Lancaster Municipal Code, of the Specific Plan. The Housing Element also identifies several vacant parcels within the Specific Plan Area (“Plan Area”) as additional residential capacity for 193 very-low and low-income units, as defined by the Department of Housing and Community Development (Table H-5.22 and H-5.25). The Plan Area includes several sites identified in the Housing Element as Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA) sites. This includes 89 parcels totaling 7.56 acres that comprise the drainage basin located at the southwest corner of Division Street and Milling Street. As part of the Specific Plan preparation, it was determined that while these are designated RHNA sites, future development of these sites is unlikely given the high cost and engineering that would be required to accommodate and re-route the drainage that the basin currently supports for the area. Therefore, given that these sites would be highly unlikely to be developed as housing, as part of the Specific Plan, these sites would be rezoned from Neighborhood Medium (NM) to Public (P) with a future vision to utilize the area as open space. To ensure there is no net loss of Housing Element sites, the Housing Element includes a surplus sites inventory. There are several surplus sites in the Plan Area on vacant lots that would be suitable and feasible for future development. Per the Housing Element, the surplus sites in the Plan Area could accommodate 193 units. The rezone of the basin sites would remove an estimated potential of 129 units. This would represent a net of 64 units. Therefore, there would be no net loss of Housing Element sites designated for the Plan Area.
ceqa-44b1ac559f6112b811.crossStreets: 10th Street, Avenue I, Division Street, and Avenue J

ceqa-4f27fccfc9fc32007a.description: This project consists of rehabilitation and reconstruction of existing public streets in the northeast portion of Lomita (Zone G), and portions of Doria Avenue, 254th Street, and 255th Street. The streets were identified in the City’s 2024 Pavement Management Program Update based on existing pavement conditions. Depending on the existing pavement condition, rehabilitation will range from asphalt overlay to full-depth reconstruction of the existing roadway use and function. The project will retain the existing roadway use and function. The project also includes repair or replacement of existing sidewalks, driveway aprons, cross gutters, curbs and gutters, and restriping of existing roadways to provide bicycle lanes. These improvements are intended to address existing pavement and infrastructure conditions and improve accessibility, multimodal circulation, and traffic safety. Additionally, the project includes an intersection redesign and installation of curb extensions and ADA curb ramps. The project will not construct additional automobile travel lanes, materially widen the existing roadway system, extend streets into undeveloped areas, or increase the vehicular capacity of the roadway network. The project further includes installation of a fire hydrant and associated lateral within the existing public right-of-way. The hydrant will connect to the existing water distribution system and is a minor utility and public safety improvement intended to improve fire protection for the existing developed neighborhood. It will not extend service into unserved areas, expand the geographic service area of the existing water system, or provide infrastructure necessary to accommodate new development.

ceqa-f4dfa84a58398ce181.name: Palace Cleaners Interim Removal Action Workplan for Soil Vapor Extraction
ceqa-f4dfa84a58398ce181.projectTitle: Palace Cleaners Interim Removal Action Workplan for Soil Vapor Extraction
ceqa-f4dfa84a58398ce181.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-f4dfa84a58398ce181.description: Project Description: The project consists of installation and operation of a soil vapor extraction (SVE) system to address soil vapor releases from Palace Cleaners located at 201 South Glendale Avenue in the city of Glendale (Site). The project activities consist of constructing nine new extraction wells as part of the overall SVE system. The SVE will be implemented to address elevated volatile organic compounds (VOCs) concentrations in soil vapor at the Site and adjacent properties while a final comprehensive remedial approach is developed to address the VOCs. Background: The Site is located in a mixed commercial and residential area and consists of two adjoining buildings and a parking lot. It consists of two adjoining buildings and a parking lot Palace Cleaners occupies one of the buildings (201 South Glendale Avenue) and Best Liquor Meat and Deli occupies the second building (205 South Glendale Avenue) covers approximately 0.1 acres. The Site is bound to the south by Shiraz Restaurant and Banquet Hall, to the west by an alley and parking lot, to the north by commercial and residential apartment buildings across East Harvard Street, and to the east by commercial buildings across South Glendale Avenue. Dry-cleaning operations began at the Site in approximately 1955 which included Palace Cleaners from 1955 to the present, and Norge Coin Operated Laundry & Dry-Cleaning Village that operated at 205 South Glendale Avenue between approximately 1961 and 1972. The dry-cleaning solvent tetrachloroethene (PCE) was used at Palace Cleaners between 1955 and March 2017, after which the PCE machine was replaced by a dry-cleaning machine using a petroleum hydrocarbon solvent. Previous Investigations: Based on previous investigations the contaminants concern include PCE and trichloroethene (TCE) in soil vapor because these exceeded applicable regulatory screening criteria. Soil vapor releases of VOCs have been identified at and in the vicinity of the Site through multiple environmental investigations conducted since 2016. A total of 33 soil samples have been collected at depths ranging from 5 feet to 130 feet below ground surface (bgs) and PCE was detected at 5 feet bgs in 3 soil samples. A total of 74 soil vapor probes have been installed at depths ranging from 5 feet 130 feet bgs and PCE has been detected in all soil vapor samples. In addition, sub-slab soil vapor probes have been installed and sampled repeatedly since 2015 at 201 South Glendale Avenue, 205 South Glendale Avenue, 211 South Glendale Avenue. Data from a December 2024 sampling event showed the highest PCE concentrations located beneath and directly west of Site. PCE concentrations decrease radially with distance from the Site with the exception of elevated concentrations to the north that may be associated with an off-Site source yet to be identified. Project Activities: The project is intended to address elevated VOCs in soil vapor and to prevent accumulation of residual soil vapor at the Site and adjacent properties thereby reducing the potential for vapor intrusion. An SVE system will be implemented to remove soil vapor at the Site and the vapor stream will be treated to prevent VOC emissions to the atmosphere. The SVE system will consist of: Vapor extraction wells and associated piping connecting the wells to the vapor treatment system; A water knockout tank with transfer pump; A soil vapor extraction and carbon adsorption unit to extract and treat soil gas from the vapor extraction wells; Required valves, gauges, hoses, and sample ports for the SVE systems; On-Site power to the system; and Meters and gauges as required to obtain system operation data. Three new extraction wells (screened from 5 to 30 feet below ground surface (bgs)) will be located at the following locations in the upper 30 feet of the subsurface: EX-2 – immediately to the north of the Site on the south side of East Harvard Street (approximately 20 feet north of the Site) EX-3 – immediately to the south of the Site in the northeast corner of the 211 South Glendale Avenue (approximately 30 feet south of the Site) EX-4 –on the northern boundary of the 217 South Glendale Avenue (approximately 80 feet south of the Site) Six new deep extraction wells (screened from 65 to 85 feet bgs) will be located at the following locations: EX-5 – on the southern corner of the East Harvard Street before the intersection of South Glendale Avenue (approximately 75 feet northeast of the Site) EX-6 – on the western side of South Glendale Avenue (approximately 90 feet south of the Site) EX-7 – in the parking lot immediately east (approximately 5 feet east of the Site) EX-8 – in the parking lot (approximately 170 feet west of the Site) EX-9 – on the western side of South Isabel Street (approximately 150 feet north of the Site) EX-10 – on the in the parking lot (approximately 200 feet southwest of the Site) All extraction wells will be constructed of 2-inch diameter casing and screen. Piping trenches will be installed to connect each vapor extraction well to a manifold in the SVE system enclosure. Each extraction well will have a dedicated pipe connecting the well to the manifold. At the manifold, the dedicated pipe from each well will be fitted with a valve and sampling port so that each well can be individually controlled and sampled. A single 4-inch diameter pipe will convey vapor exiting the manifold into the knockout pot and activated carbon tanks. The vapor treatment system will consist of three, 2,000-pound carbon adsorption canisters plumbed in series. Ports will be installed to sample vapors at the inlet to the first canister, between each canister, and the exhaust stack to the atmosphere. Once installed, the system will operate continuously for 2 years except for as needed for maintenance and brief shutdowns to collect soil vapor samples to evaluate remedial progress. Once SVE operations cease DTSC will evaluate the risk to human health and the SVE’s effectiveness in removing and treating VOCs in the subsurface. This evaluation along with any additional sampling will be used in preparation for the development of a final remedy to address releases in all media. A Permit to Operate the SVE system will be obtained from the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD). Requisite permits/releases from the City of Glendale Building, Planning, and Fire Departments will also be obtained as necessary. The Site is in a previously developed area and does not provide habitat value. The project is consistent with applicable state and local environmental permitting requirements including, but not limited to, air quality rules such as those governing VOC emissions and approved by the regulatory body with jurisdiction over the Site (e.g., SCAQMD, City of Glendale). In addition, a Permit to Operate will be obtained from SCAQMD for the SVE system. For these reasons, the project would not have the potential to negatively impact any nearby receptors, which include industrial and commercial land uses. Although not anticipated, in the event biological, cultural or historical resources are discovered in the course of project activities, work will be suspended while a qualified biologist, cultural or historical specialist makes an assessment of the area and arrangements are made to protect or preserve any resources that are discovered. If human remains are discovered, no further disturbance will occur in the location where the remains are found, and the County Coroner will be notified pursuant to the Health and Safety Code, Chapter 2, Section 7050.5.

ceqa-2c924f71cbe6669b8c.projectTitle: Professional Sports Headquarters and Training Facility Project
ceqa-2c924f71cbe6669b8c.description: The El Segundo Surf Club Project (Project) proposes construction and operation of a private commercial/recreational surf club on an approximately 9.3-acre site located at 100–200 South Nash Street in the City of El Segundo (Project site). The Project site is primarily undeveloped but previously improved with limited improvements (i.e., paved areas, a former helicopter pad, surface parking, access roads, and limited ornamental landscaping). The Project would remove existing onsite improvements and construct four three-story buildings totaling approximately 50,236 gross square feet, including member-only recreational and hospitality uses, a public restaurant and meeting space, wellness, retail, office, administrative, and support uses, along with a large surf wave pool, standing wave pool, two recreational pools, outdoor amenities, landscaping, padel courts, surface parking, bicycle parking, and associated utility and circulation improvements. The Project would provide vehicular access from East El Segundo Boulevard and South Nash Street, and would include frontage and circulation improvements consistent with the El Segundo South Campus Specific Plan and Development Agreement (i.e., widening and improving East El Segundo Boulevard adjacent to the Project site and providing a pedestrian easement and walkway connection to the LA Metro El Segundo Station). The Project has been found consistent with the density planned for the Project site by the El Segundo South Campus Specific Plan (i.e., zoning action). Environmental impacts were previously considered and mitigated through the El Segundo South Campus Specific Plan Environmental Impact Report, which was certified in December 2015 (State Clearinghouse (SCH) No. 2012101081) (Certified EIR). No environmental effects were found to be peculiar to the Project or the parcel on which the Project is located; the Project would not cause any environmental effects that were not analyzed as significant in the Certified EIR; cumulative and off-site impacts associated with Project development, as proposed, were fully addressed in the Certified EIR and because the Project is consistent with the ESSCSP development density analyzed in the Certified EIR, Project implementation would not result in any new or altered cumulative impacts or off-site impacts beyond those addressed in the Certified EIR; and there is no substantial new information which was not known at the time the Certified EIR and which indicates that any previously identified significant effects would be more severe. Therefore, the Project has been found to be consistent with the analysis contained in the Certified EIR and no further analysis is necessary.

ceqa-961f59b6619fdc6ef7.description: The proposed UCLA Research Park East Core and Shell Improvements (Core and Shell) Project is the first in a series of phased projects at UCLA Research Park. UCLA Research Park consists of two connected buildings totaling approximately 1,308,000 gross square feet (gsf) on 9.2 acres. The Core and Shell Project would retrofit the East building (10800 West Pico Boulevard), a 706,000-gsf, three-story facility with two underground levels, for multi-tenant use, including biomedical research and quantum physics laboratories, which would be developed in subsequent tenant improvement projects. An Advanced Work Phase of the Core and Shell Project would involve interior and roof demolition, site and utilities preparation, and procurement of long lead-time equipment. In accordance with CEQA, an Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (IS/MND) (State Clearinghouse No. 2026050140) has been prepared for full buildout of the UCLA Research Park project, including future phases.

ceqa-1f5e05118bed3f2722.name: Compton 60
ceqa-1f5e05118bed3f2722.description: The Project includes development of the Project Site with 60 single-family residential homes, including 48 market-rate homes and 12 affordable homes. Each home would be two stories with a maximum building height of 30 feet. The Project is proposed as an all-electric community. Landscaping amenities include decorative paving at the entrance of the Project, open space with a shade swings, bench, and game table. Trees and other landscaping vegetation are proposed throughout the site and along the Project Site frontage where applicable. Each home would have a private side and rear yard. A Project site plan is included in Figure 3. Forty-eight homes would have a two-car garage, and twelve homes would have a one-car garage. Twenty-one guest parking spaces would also be provided at the site. Vehicular access to the Project Site would be provided via a gated ingress/egress driveway near the northeast corner of the site on Parmelee Avenue. A gated emergency-access-only ingress/egress driveway would be located near the southwest corner of the site on Parmelee Avenue. Access to the individual homes would be provided via private roadway. Site improvements include grading; sewer, storm water, water, and dry utilities; and street improvements. Sewer conveyance improvements include a connection to an existing Los Angeles County Sanitation District sewer line within the project’s boundaries, a main line located in the internal streets, and individual sewer laterals to each unit. Storm water conveyance improvements include a main line located in the internal streets, on-site catch basins, on-site biofiltrations vaults, and an on-site parkway culvert to allow for storm water sheet-flow to an existing storm drain at Parmelee Avenue. Water conveyance improvements include a main line located in the internal streets, laterals to each unit, three fire hydrants, and two offsite connections to an existing water main located within the adjacent Parmelee Avenue right-of-way. Internal street improvements include rolled curb, zero-inch curb, and paved streets. In addition to the utility connections within Parmalee Avenue, sidewalk, curb and gutter, and street improvements would be installed along the Project Site frontage along Parmelee Avenue. The Applicant is seeking the following discretionary approvals from the City: • Conditional Use Permit (Case No. 24-007); • Tentative Tract Map No. 84563 (Case No. 24-002); and • Design Review (Case No. 24-00136) Other approvals and permits from the Department of Building and Safety and other municipal agencies would be required for Project construction actions including, but not limited to demolition, excavation, shoring, grading, foundation, and building.

ceqa-058852f87dce893a03.name: Mitigated Negative Declaration No. MND 21-01 for the 2021-2029 Housing Element, Downtown Bellflower Transit Oriented Development Specific Plan Amendment, and Re
ceqa-058852f87dce893a03.projectTitle: 2021-2029 Housing Element, Downtown Bellflower Transit Oriented Development Specific Plan Amendment, and Required Zone Changes to the Mixed Use Overlay Zone
ceqa-058852f87dce893a03.description: In 2022, MND 21-01 evaluated potential environmental impacts resulting with the Bellflower 2021-2029 Housing Element, Downtown Bellflower Transit Oriented Development Specific Plan (TOD SP) Amendment, and Future Zone Changes. The Housing Element, TOD SP Amendment, and Zone Changes provided programs and regulations to ensure that the City’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation for residential units could be met, as required by State law. In early 2025, the City then approved a General Plan Amendment, Zone Change, Amendment to the TOD Specific Plan, and Zoning Ordinance Text Amendments to specifically implement goals and policies identified by the various housing programs, including ensuring adequate sites to accommodate the RHNA. In 2026, HCD required further amendment to the City’s Zoning Ordinance to further ensure compliance with Government Code Section 65583.2 (h) and (i) by requiring: (1) 50% of total gross floor area for Mixed-Use development be allocated to residential uses, (2) owner-occupied and rental multifamily uses would be permitted-by-right for developments when at least 20% of the units are affordable to lower-income households, and (3) future sites being rezoned to satisfy the City’s lower-income RHNA have a minimum density of 20 dwelling units per acre. With approval of the 2026 Zoning Ordinance Text Amendments, the City determined that MND 21-01 provided the necessary environmental evaluations and clearance for the 2026 Zoning Ordinance Text Amendments. This NOD notices the City’s CEQA determination.

The redesigned parking layout would accommodate 66 spaces, including 18 standard spaces for customers, 18 tandem parking spaces designated for vehicle service, and 30 tandem parking spaces for vehicle display. Due to the site's proximity of less than half a mile from the Glendale Transportation Center and its designation as part of a High-Quality Transit Corridor, the applicant is seeking parking requirement relief under Assembly Bill 2097.

ceqa-ac23837677fd30213a.description: The Department of Fish and Wildlife is issuing a permit to the California State University, Long Beach pursuant to Fish and Game Code Section 2081(a) for educational purposes. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to take steelhead trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) during the course of sampling, subject to terms and conditions set forth in the permit. The purpose of this sampling is to support California State University, Long Beach’s permanent educational collections. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to potentially capture steelhead trout during surveys. The applicant will conduct year-round permanent collection sampling of nearshore marine species using hook & line – baited dropper loop, bottom trawl, midwater trawl, and beach seines through December 31, 2029.

ceqa-d7f7c70a28ffc59f2e.name: Harpoons and Flying Gaffs for Recreational Tuna Fishery and Gear Marking in Commercial Harpoon Swordfish Fishery
ceqa-d7f7c70a28ffc59f2e.projectTitle: Harpoons and Flying Gaffs for Recreational Tuna Fishery and Gear Marking in Commercial Harpoon Swordfish Fishery
ceqa-d7f7c70a28ffc59f2e.description: The California Fish and Game Commission (Commission) proposes to use regular rulemaking authority to amend the recreational fishing regulations for tuna, marlin, and swordfish and the commercial fishing regulations for swordfish as set forth in Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations (Project). The amendments will allow recreational anglers to use harpoons and flying gaffs to help land tuna that have been legally taken. The amendment will also make a variety of minor, nonsubstantive, changes to update the species common name from “broadbill” or “broadbill swordfish” to “swordfish,” and “fin fish” to “finfish” and to clarify existing prohibitions on the use of spears and bow and arrow fishing gear to take marlin. The amendment will add gear marking requirements for commercial harpoon gear to clearly differentiate that gear from federally authorized deep-set buoy gear.
