ceqa-a1c4d5d561a4e46f26.name: Mill Creek Defensible Space and Roadside Fuel Reduction (EPP Project No.: d87d0796-3deb-4464-8a09- e9cfae7f6f2b)
ceqa-a1c4d5d561a4e46f26.projectTitle: Mill Creek Defensible Space and Roadside Fuel Reduction (EPP Project No.: d87d0796-3deb-4464-8a09- e9cfae7f6f2b)
ceqa-a1c4d5d561a4e46f26.description: The District will conduct manual understory thinning on approximately 37 acres within the Mill Creek Redwood Preserve to reduce hazardous fuel loading in areas of dense ladder fuels and brush adjacent to Preserve infrastructure and ingress/egress routes. Work is limited to manual treatment. Brush and ladder fuels 8 inches DBH and under will be thinned, and trees over 8 inches DBH will be retained and will be limbed or pruned to create up to 8 feet of vertical separation from the crown. Dead/dying oaks infected with SOD may be thinned regardless of size. Work will follow established SOD hygiene BMPs, and no woody material will be removed from site. Treatment will prioritize dead, diseased, and invasive material. Brush outside the tree canopy will be thinned to a functional mosaic with horizontal spacing of roughly twice the height of the brush layer in order to retain habitat and prevent type conversion. Low-growing herbaceous understory an average of 18 inches and under will be retained for erosion control and habitat. Rare and sensitive species will not be treated, and prescriptions may be reduced in sensitive habitats, including seasonal stream, areas of slide potential, culturally sensitive areas, and areas identified to support sensitive species. Timing of treatment of areas of invasive French broom (Genista monspessulana) may be modified to limit seed cast potential. Cut material will be chipped in place or lopped and scattered to a depth not exceeding 4 inches in sensitive areas and not to exceed 8 inches elsewhere; large downed logs over 10 inches DBH will be laid flat and retained as habitat. Biomass left on site will be placed where it cannot enter water bodies. Equipment is limited to hand and light powered tools, 4x4 trucks, UTVs, and trailered chippers, which will remain on established roads and service road/trails. No new roads will be constructed and no significant ground disturbance will occur. The purpose of the Project is to reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Preserve, to improve emergency ingress and egress along arterial evacuation routes, and to reduce roadside ignition risk. Beneficiaries are the residents of the Palo Colorado community and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Preserve itself.
ceqa-a1c4d5d561a4e46f26.crossStreets: Palo Colorado Road at Mill Creek Redwood Preserve

ceqa-1da55376b915e8cff3.name: La Mesa Prescribed Burn Project (EPP Project No.: 1081f8a6-30d9-41aa-8cal-7eb99f2afba6)
ceqa-1da55376b915e8cff3.projectTitle: La Mesa Prescribed Burn Project (EPP Project No.: 1081f8a6-30d9-41aa-8cal-7eb99f2afba6)
ceqa-1da55376b915e8cff3.description: The District will conduct prescribed burning (broadcast burning) on approximately 39.9 acres within Garland Ranch Regional Park (GRRP) to reduce horizontal and vertical wildfire fuel continuity, facilitate nutrient cycling, improve soil health and water infiltration, promote recruitment of fire tolerant native perennial grass species, reduce dominance and seed bank of non-native annual graces, reduce encroachment of brush species which threaten type conversion of grasslands, and protect and restore habitat for native wildlife species. Within the project boundary, approximately 2.5 acres have been identified for manual understory thinning, and 4.9 acres have been identified for mechanical mowing to establish and improve control lines prior to burning. MPRPD will reduce hazardous fuels through limited mechanical treatment and low intensity broadcast burns in grassland/oak savannas using light-impact methods to protect natural resources. The existing network of service roads and trails will be used to establish control lines. Horizontal fuels (fine grasses, shrubs and surface debris) will be mowed and/or hand cut to improve control lines around broadcast burn plots before burning operations. Prior to burning, vertical brush and tree understory will be reduced by manually thinning small stems (<Bin DBH). Trees greater than 8 inch DBH will be limbed up to 8 feet in height, while preserving approximately 60-80% of the canopy and retaining legacy trees. Work will follow established SOD hygiene BMPs, and no woody material will be removed from site. Treatment will prioritize dead, diseased, and invasive material. Cut material will be either chipped in place or lopped and scattered within the project area prior to burning. Rare and sensitive species will not be treated, and prescriptions may be reduced in sensitive habitats. Equipment is limited to hand and light powered tools, 4x4 trucks, UTVs, and trailered chippers, which will remain on established roads and service road/trails. No new roads will be constructed and no significant ground disturbance will occur. The purpose of the Project is to promote grassland and oak savanna health, reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Park, improve firefighter access within the park's backcountry, and to provide increased protection between the backcountry and the community. Beneficiaries are the residents and businesses of the Carmel Valley community and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Park itself.
ceqa-1da55376b915e8cff3.crossStreets: Carmel Valley Road (G16) at Garland Ranch Regional Park

ceqa-bfa698928a1ecd1a28.name: JSMPP Roadside Fuels Reduction Project (EPP Project No.: bfeb9f39-65f3-4fd6-8a48-f2a030f4d9be)
ceqa-bfa698928a1ecd1a28.projectTitle: JSMPP Roadside Fuels Reduction Project (EPP Project No.: bfeb9f39-65f3-4fd6-8a48-f2a030f4d9be)
ceqa-bfa698928a1ecd1a28.description: The District will conduct manual understory thinning on approximately 45.6 acres within the Joyce-Stevens Monterey Pine Preserve (JSMPP) to reduce hazardous fuel loading in areas of dense ladder fuels and brush adjacent to residential and commercial development and along Aquajito Road, Monhollan Road, Olmsted Road, Jacks Peak Road, and Loma Alta Road. Work is limited to manual treatment. Brush and ladder fuels 8 inches DBH and under will be thinned, and trees over 8 inches DBH will be retained and may be limbed or pruned to create up to 8 feet of vertical separation from the crown. Standing dead trees will be removed from the buffer area to reduce fuel loading and ember cast potential. Removal will prioritize dead, diseased, and invasive material. Brush outside the tree canopy will be thinned to a functional mosaic with horizontal spacing of roughly twice the height of the brush layer in order to retain habitat and prevent type conversion. Low-growing herbaceous understory will be retained at an average height of 18 inches for erosion control and habitat. Rare and sensitive species will not be treated, and prescriptions may be reduced in sensitive habitats, including seasonal streams and areas identified to support sensitive species. Cut material will be chipped in place or lopped and scattered to a depth not exceeding 4 inches in sensitive areas and not to exceed 6 inches elsewhere; large downed logs over 10 inches DBH will be laid flat and retained as habitat. Biomass left on site will be placed where it cannot enter water bodies. Equipment is limited to hand and light powered tools, 4x4 trucks, UTVs, and trailered chippers, which will remain on established roads and service road/trails. No new roads will be constructed and no significant ground disturbance will occur. The purpose of the Project is to reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Preserve, to improve emergency ingress and egress along arterial evacuation routes, and to reduce roadside ignition risk. Beneficiaries are the residents and businesses of Monterey and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Preserve itself.
ceqa-bfa698928a1ecd1a28.crossStreets: Aquajito Road, Monhollan Road, Olmsted Road, Jacks Peak Road, and Loma Alta Roads

ceqa-e5702308ddbed52390.name: Guerrin's Ranch Fuels Reduction Project (EPP Project No.: 461fa164-fcea-403a-87be-249a668d92db)
ceqa-e5702308ddbed52390.projectTitle: Guerrin's Ranch Fuels Reduction Project (EPP Project No.: 461fa164-fcea-403a-87be-249a668d92db)
ceqa-e5702308ddbed52390.description: The District will conduct mechanical fuels treatment on approximately 13.2 acres of enclosed pastural paddock within the backcountry of Palo Corona Regional Park to reduce hazardous fuel loading, reduce encroachment of highly flammable invasive French Broom (Genista monspessulana), promote grassland ecosystem health and recruitment of fire tolerant native perennial grasses, and improve fire fighter access. Mechanical treatment is limited to surface level mastication and repetitive mowing, with a target height of 6 inches, preferentially targeting Genista during its growing season to reduce fuel load and limit reseeding potential. Encroaching coyote brush may also be targeted, but with emphasis on creating and maintaining a functional mosaic of habit with gaps of at least twice the shrub height (i.e. ~2oft between shrubs or groups). Mowing will be conducted using a combination of light tractors, masticators, and trailered wood-chippers. Touch-up mowing may also be conducted using a combination of weed-trimers, chainsaws, pole-saws, loppers, brush-cutters, etc. In strategic cases, around sensitive sites, genista may be removed by the root using weed wrenches. A minimal amount of manual thinning may occur around individual native trees to create vertical separation of fuels up to 8ft. Mowed woody debris will be either masticated, chipped, or lopped and scattered in place. Woody debris will be treated within the season to reduce fuel loading. Slash/chip depth is not to exceed 4 inches. The purpose of the Project is to reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Park, to improve emergency ingress and egress along a previously identified fire road, to reduce roadside ignition risk, and to promote grassland health. Beneficiaries are the residents and businesses of Carmel and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Park itself.
ceqa-e5702308ddbed52390.crossStreets: Corona Road and Highlands Road (Highlands Trail)

ceqa-f37a666c41ce03cc59.name: GRRP Roadside Fuels Reduction Project: Snively's Ridge to Sleepy Hollow (EPP Project No.: 7145900f- 98db-48df-8e53-62cf981fe51d)
ceqa-f37a666c41ce03cc59.projectTitle: GRRP Roadside Fuels Reduction Project: Snively's Ridge to Sleepy Hollow (EPP Project No.: 7145900f- 98db-48df-8e53-62cf981fe51d)
ceqa-f37a666c41ce03cc59.description: The District will conduct manual understory thinning on approximately 165.7 acres within Garland Ranch Regional Park (GRRP) to reduce hazardous fuel loading in areas of dense ladder fuels and brush adjacent to strategic ridge top section of the existing service roads and trails network and associated ingress/egress. Work is limited to manual treatment within the SO feet of existing roads/trails. Brush and ladder fuels 8 inches DBH and under will be thinned, and trees over 8 inches DBH will be retained and will be limbed or pruned to create up to 8 feet of vertical separation from the crown. Dead/dying oaks infected with SOD may be thinned regardless of size. Work will follow established SOD hygiene BMPs, and no woody material will be removed from site. Treatment will prioritize dead, diseased, and invasive material. Brush outside the tree canopy will be thinned to a functional mosaic with horizontal spacing of roughly twice the height of the brush layer in order to retain habitat and prevent type conversion. Steep slopes may require greater horizontal distance. Low-growing herbaceous understory may be retained at an average height of 18 inches for erosion control and habitat. Rare and sensitive species will not be treated, and prescriptions may be reduced in sensitive habitats, including seasonal stream, areas of slide potential, culturally sensitive areas, and areas identified to support sensitive species. Timing of treatment of areas of invasive French broom (Genista monspessulana) may be modified to limit seed cast potential. Cut material will be chipped in place or lopped and scattered to a depth not exceeding 4 inches in sensitive areas and not to exceed 8 inches elsewhere; large downed logs over 10 inches DBH will be laid flat and retained as habitat. Biomass left on site will be placed where it cannot enter water bodies. Equipment is limited to hand and light powered tools, 4x4 trucks, UTVs, and trailered chippers, which will remain on established roads and service road/trails. No new roads will be constructed and no significant ground disturbance will occur. The purpose of the Project is to reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Park, to improve emergency ingress/egress, to improve firefighter access within the park's backcountry, and to serve as a fuel break providing protection between the backcountry and the community. Beneficiaries are the residents and businesses of the Carmel Valley community and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Park itself.
ceqa-f37a666c41ce03cc59.crossStreets: Carmel Valley Road (G16) at Garland Ranch Regional Park

ceqa-d749c93bfdccfcce98.name: Garland Meadow Prescribed Burn Project (EPP Project No.: cd69cd86-85e3-4a28-80ef-465047576544)
ceqa-d749c93bfdccfcce98.projectTitle: Garland Meadow Prescribed Burn Project (EPP Project No.: cd69cd86-85e3-4a28-80ef-465047576544)
ceqa-d749c93bfdccfcce98.description: The District will conduct prescribed burning on approximately 102 acres (90 acres broadcast burning and 12 acres pile burning) within Garland Ranch Regional Park (GRRP) to reduce horizontal and vertical wildfire fuel continuity, facilitate nutrient cycling, improve soil health and water infiltration, promote recruitment of fire tolerant native perennial grass species, reduce dominance and seed bank of non-native annual grasses, reduce encroachment of brush species which threaten type conversion of grasslands, and protect and restore habitat for native wildlife species. Within the project boundary, approximately 41.5 acres have been identified for manual understory thinning and 11.5 acres have been identified for mechanical mowing to establish and improve control lines prior to burning. MPRPD will reduce hazardous fuels through limited mechanical treatment and low intensity broadcast burns in grassland/oak savannas (which are being heavily impacted by brush encroachment) using light-impact methods to protect natural and cultural resources. The existing network of service roads and trails will be used to establish control lines around designated burn units. Horizontal fuels (fine grasses, shrubs and surface debris} will be mowed and/or hand cut to improve control lines around broadcast burn plots before burning operations. Prior to burning, vertical brush and tree understory will be reduced by manually thinning small stems (<8in DBH). Trees greater than 8 inches DBH will be limbed up to 8 feet in height, while preserving approximately 60-80% of the canopy and retaining legacy trees. Work will follow established SOD hygiene BMPs, and no woody material will be removed from site. Treatment will prioritize dead, diseased, and invasive material. Within Broadcast burn units, cut material will be either chipped in place or lopped and scattered within the project area prior to burning. Within the pile burning unit, slash will be hand piled (6ft x 6ft x 4ft), cured through the dry season, and burned in the wet season. If the piles are not able to be burned due to weather or permitting issues, then piles may be chipped in place or lopped and scattered at a later date. Larger logs will be laid flat to the ground be retained for habitat and to promote nutrient recycling. Rare and sensitive species will not be treated, and prescriptions may be reduced in sensitive habitats. Equipment is limited to hand and light powered tools, 4x4 trucks, UTVs, and trailered chippers, which will remain on established roads and service road/trails. No new roads will be constructed and no significant ground disturbance will occur. The purpose of the Project is to promote grassland and oak savanna health, reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Park, improve firefighter access within the park's backcountry, and to provide increased protection between the backcountry and the community. Beneficiaries are the residents and businesses of the Carmel Valley community and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Park itself.

ceqa-806b725f99e33093be.projectTitle: Frog Pond Understory Thinning Project (EPP Project No.: a9ffa93d-0d5c-44ae-8c92-8670c64d18af)
ceqa-806b725f99e33093be.description: The District will conduct manual understory thinning on approximately 28.6 acres within the Frog Pond Wetland Preserve to reduce hazardous fuel loading in areas of dense ladder fuels and brush adjacent to residential and commercial development and along Canyon del Rey Boulevard and General Jim Moore Boulevard. Work is limited to manual treatment. Brush and ladder fuels 6 inches DBH and under will be thinned, and trees over 6 inches DBH will be retained and may be limbed or pruned to create up to 8 feet of vertical separation from the crown. Removal will prioritize dead, diseased, and invasive material. Brush outside the tree canopy will be thinned to a functional mosaic with horizontal spacing of roughly twice the height of the brush layer in order to retain habitat and prevent type conversion. Low-growing herbaceous understory will be retained at an average height of 18 inches for erosion control and habitat. Rare and sensitive species will not be treated, and prescriptions may be reduced in sensitive habitats, including wetlands, where manual work will occur only during dry periods. Cut material will be chipped in place or lopped and scattered to a depth not exceeding 3 inches in sensitive areas and 6 inches elsewhere; large downed logs over 10 inches DBH will be laid flat and retained as habitat. Biomass left on site will be placed where it cannot enter water bodies. Equipment is limited to hand and light powered tools, 4x4 trucks, UTVs, and trailered chippers, which will remain on established roads and service road-trails. No new roads will be constructed and no significant ground disturbance will occur. The purpose of the Project is to reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Preserve, to improve emergency ingress and egress along two arterial evacuation routes, and to reduce roadside ignition risk. Beneficiaries are the residents and businesses of Del Rey Oaks and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Preserve itself.

ceqa-132ba6bcc39942060d.projectTitle: East Garzas Fuel Break Maintenance and Expansion Project (EPP Project No.: 0f84a9da-ddeb-4c7e-81de- 09871cld21a0)
ceqa-132ba6bcc39942060d.description: The District will conduct manual understory thinning on approximately 17.8 acres within Garland Ranch Regional Park (GRRP) to reduce hazardous fuel loading in areas of dense ladder fuels and brush adjacent to residential communities in Carmel Valley. Within this project area, 7.5 acres have been identified for prescribed pile burning. Work will primarily be limited to manual treatment, though follow-up treatment with prescribed herbivory (goats) and limited herbicide application have also been approved, as necessary. Brush and ladder fuels 8 inches DBH and under will be thinned, and trees over 8 inches DBH will be retained and will be limbed or pruned to create up to 8 feet of vertical separation from the crown. Standing dead trees will be removed to reduce fuel loading and ember cast protentional. Work will follow established SOD hygiene BMPs, and no woody material will be removed from site. Treatment will prioritize dead, diseased, and invasive material. Brush outside the tree canopy will be thinned to a functional mosaic with horizontal spacing of roughly twice the height of the brush layer in order to retain habitat and prevent type conversion. Rare and sensitive species will not be treated, and prescriptions may be reduced in sensitive habitats, including seasonal streams, culturally sensitive areas, and areas identified to support sensitive species. Cut material will be hand piled on location (6 ft x 6ftx x 4ft) and left to cure through the dry season. Hand piles will be burned in the wet season. If pile burning is not possible due to weather or permitting issues, then woody residue (piles) may be chipped in place or lopped and scattered (no greater than 3-inch fuel bed thickness in sensitive areas). Large downed logs over 10 inches DBH will be laid flat and retained as habitat. Biomass left on site will be placed where it cannot enter water bodies. Equipment is limited to hand and light powered tools, 4x4 trucks, UTVs, and trailered chippers, which will remain on established roads and service road/trails. No new roads will be constructed, and no significant ground disturbance will occur. The purpose of the Project is to reduce the risk of a catastrophic wildfire originating in or spreading through the Park, to improve emergency ingress/egress, to improve firefighter access to the park, and to serve as a fuel break providing protection between the backcountry and the community. Beneficiaries are the residents and businesses of the Carmel Valley community and the surrounding Monterey Peninsula communities, emergency responders, users of District lands, and the habitat resources of the Park itself.

ceqa-f48a41e162e012a84c.name: Shifting Ocean Predator Ecology in the California Current
ceqa-f48a41e162e012a84c.projectTitle: Shifting Ocean Predator Ecology in the California Current
ceqa-f48a41e162e012a84c.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Marine Region 7
ceqa-f48a41e162e012a84c.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 7 - Marine, Monterey
ceqa-f48a41e162e012a84c.description: The Department of Fish and Wildlife is issuing a permit to the California State University, Monterey Bay pursuant to Fish and Game Code Section 2081(a) for scientific purposes. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to take coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch), Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), steelhead trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss), and white sturgeon (Acipenser transmontanus) during the course of sampling, subject to terms and conditions set forth in the permit. The purpose of this sampling is for the California State University, Monterey Bay’s research studies. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to potentially capture coho salmon, Chinook salmon, steelhead trout, and white sturgeon during surveys. The applicant will conduct yearround research sampling of various shark species using hook & line – surface, hook & line – baited dropper loop, and beach seines through December 31, 2029.

ceqa-21881296e9e7f69c83.description: Ordinance No. 2026-845 is a zoning text amendment to Title 17, Chapter 17.79 (Seasonal Employee Housing) of the King City Municipal Code. The amendment removes local discretionary barriers and aligns the City’s local development standards with the California Employee Housing Act (Health and Safety Code Section 17000 et seq.) and the Fair Employee and Housing Act. It standardizes review processes to match state-mandated allowances for seasonal employee housing. The amendment does not change the applicable zoning designations or zoning densities for seasonal employee housing. The amendment is intended to align the City's regulations with State law and does not authorize a change in land use or density beyond what is already permitted under the City's existing General Plan and Zoning Code.

ceqa-982dde567ca59ac317.name: Point of Use/Point of Entry Ordinance Amendments
ceqa-982dde567ca59ac317.description: The project consists of adoption and implementation of an amended Ordinance by the County of Monterey that would allow the use of point of use (POU) and point of entry (POE) drinking water treatment devices for lots on private wells and in non-compliant local small, State small, and public water systems in unincorporated Monterey County. These systems currently exceed one or more primary drinking water maximum contaminant levels for constituents such as nitrate, arsenic, fluoride, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, and/or 1,2,3-Trichloropropane. The Ordinance would amend Chapter 15.06 of the Monterey County Code to authorize POU and POE treatment as an alternative compliance pathway to centralized treatment, well replacement, or system consolidation. The amended Ordinance would allow POU and POE treatment to serve vacant legal lots of record, and to support accessory dwelling units, within non-compliant water systems and on private wells, subject to specified requirements. The Ordinance is intended to provide a feasible compliance option to protect public health where existing centralized solutions are impractical or infeasible.

ceqa-257845712eb00c212f.name: Shale Point RSP Revetment 05-1R190 MON-001-7.2/7.9
ceqa-257845712eb00c212f.agencyName: Caltrans, District 5 - San Luis Obispo/Santa Barbara
ceqa-257845712eb00c212f.description: Large swells and high tides hit the Central Coast during the week of December 24th, 2023. Wave erosion from the high seas damaged slopes supporting Highway 1 along the Big Sur Coast, causing significant damage to existing rock slope protection (RSP) revetments and gabion wall shoreline protection at Shale Point, located between Ragged Point and Gorda. In addition, Mud Creek Landslide loss approximately 6 tons of rock protection. The shoreline north and south of Shale Point is armored from the Pacific Ocean with RSP designed to prevent wave action from eroding the slopes that support Highway 1. Two gabion basket walls at the north end of the northern beach also provide armoring along with naturally occurring rock that accumulates along the northern shoreline. The combined high tides and very large waves in late 2023 evacuated RSP from the revetments and caused rotation of the South Gabion Wall, allowing wave runup and splash to scour and undermine the now unprotected slopes. Evidence of slope failures advancing toward the Highway is apparent and worsening as continued winter swells and high tides persist into January 2024. Mud Creek Landslide revetment experienced large wave events and hightides at the end of 2023, which caused damage to several areas where wave energy concentrates, again requiring replenishment of evacuated rock. Protection of the slopes by re-armoring the toe at the ocean elevation is required to prevent slope retreat into the roadway prism. Replacement of the evacuated RSP at Mud Creek and at Shale Point South and North Revetments, including armoring the failed South Gabion Wall with RSP were recommended to halt the current damage and protect the Highway from continued slope failures caused by wave action.

ceqa-27824fcc09982a2b52.name: Lake El Estero Aquatic Vegetation Removal
ceqa-27824fcc09982a2b52.projectTitle: Lake El Estero Aquatic Vegetation Removal
ceqa-27824fcc09982a2b52.description: The project consists of mechanical removal of wigeon grass from Lake El Estero, an existing managed urban lake owned and maintained by the City of Monterey. Vegetation would be removed using specialized aquatic harvesting equipment designed to cut and collect vegetation above the sediment surface without disturbing the underlying lakebed. Harvested vegetation would be temporarily staged in designated upland areas for vegetation dry-out before being transported to an approved off-site disposal facility. The purpose of the project is to restore and maintain safe recreational use of the lake, including paddle boat operations, improve water circulation, support operation of existing lake infrastructure, and maintain the lake's ecological and hydraulic function. The project would benefit the City of Monterey, residents, and visitors by maintaining an existing public recreational facility while minimizing environmental impacts through implementation of best management practices and resource protection measures.

ceqa-015a5dcef38fef5b9a.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 7 - Marine, Monterey
ceqa-015a5dcef38fef5b9a.description: The Department of Fish and Wildlife is issuing a permit to the Monterey Abalone Company pursuant to Fish and Game Code Section 2081(a) for educational purposes. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to take coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) and Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) during the course of sampling, subject to terms and conditions set forth in the permit. The purpose of this sampling is for the Monterey Abalone Company’s collections of marine fishes, invertebrates, and algae to serve as a marine biological supply house for various public aquariums, research centers, and universities throughout the United States. The Section 2081(a) permit authorizes the applicant to potentially capture coho salmon and Chinook salmon during surveys. The applicant will conduct year-round collection sampling of nearshore fishes, invertebrates, and algae using hook & line – surface, hook & line – baited dropper loop, hook & line – baited shrimp fly, and fish traps through December 31, 2027.

ceqa-898ca75589705d06bd.name: 8th Street Re-Opening and Improvements Project
ceqa-898ca75589705d06bd.agency: California State University Board of Trustees
ceqa-898ca75589705d06bd.agencyName: California State University Board of Trustees
ceqa-898ca75589705d06bd.description: The proposed project consists of roadway improvements along 8th Street between 3rd Avenue and 5th Avenue in the City of Marina, Monterey County. The project includes reconstruction and rehabilitation of the existing roadway; construction and replacement of curb, gutter, sidewalk, ADA-compliant curb ramps, bicycle lanes, and a multi-use path; installation of new pavement, pavement markings, traffic signage, and striping; and improvements to intersections, including curb returns and pedestrian crossings. The project also includes installation of a new storm drainage system consisting of pipelines, catch basins, manholes, infiltration chambers, and associated drainage facilities; grading; utility adjustments and relocations as necessary; demolition and replacement of existing pavement and other roadway improvements; and restoration of disturbed areas. Construction would occur within the existing roadway corridor on California State University, Monterey Bay-owned property and existing public rights-of-way. The purpose of the project is to rehabilitate existing transportation infrastructure, improve pedestrian, bicycle, and vehicular circulation, enhance accessibility in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), improve stormwater drainage, and maintain the long-term functionality of the roadway. The primary beneficiaries of the project include California State University, Monterey Bay; the City of Marina; campus students, faculty, staff, and visitors; adjacent property owners; and the traveling public.

ceqa-9df765dda03ce214ec.name: Aera San Ardo Two (2) Wells Administrative Grouping
ceqa-9df765dda03ce214ec.projectTitle: Aera San Ardo Two (2) Wells Administrative Grouping
ceqa-9df765dda03ce214ec.description: The primary work objective is to sidetrack two (2) existing wells. This work is designed to support continuation of oil and gas resource development in the area. The wells are not being sidetracked (i) for abandonment purposes only or (ii) in connection with an enforcement order to mitigate or prevent environmental damage or surface expression. Sidetracking is the process of drilling a new wellbore from an existing wellbore. This is typically done when the original wellbore encounters a problem, when accessing remaining hydrocarbons within portions of the same reservoir, or when obstructions in the wellbore need to be bypassed. This process allows drilling a new section in an existing wellbore in the same rock formation restoring the well’s original functionality. The potential disturbance footprint would encompass an existing 20,000 square foot (100 ft x 200 ft) well pad per well. The entirety of this work would be located in an area of existing disturbance and no change in the surface topography (such as drainage patterns) would result. There will be no expansion of the existing well pads, roads, staging areas, or pipelines. No new grading would occur in any undisturbed areas. No new road construction or expansions would be required for the proposed project. Routine maintenance activities at the site would include removal of weeds and other ruderal vegetation for fire control and road maintenance. For a single well, it is expected to take approximately 17 operational days to complete all construction phases. The proposed project consists of the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division (CalGEM) approving 2 permit(s) for Aera Energy LLC to sidetrack the well(s) listed below, in the San Ardo Oil Field. (0405322272: Orradre 1614-12 & 0405322013: Orradre 1528H-12)

ceqa-057f2cc5934e6fed93.name: County of Monterey Sixth Cycle (2023-2031) Housing Element Project
ceqa-057f2cc5934e6fed93.projectTitle: County of Monterey Sixth Cycle (2023-2031) Housing Element Project
ceqa-057f2cc5934e6fed93.description: The County of Monterey has prepared this Draft Program Environmental Impact Report (DPEIR) to inform the public, local community, organizations, responsible agencies, trustee agencies, and other interested public agencies about potential significant environmental effects resulting from implementation of the draft County of Monterey Sixth Cycle (2023–2031) Housing Element Update (HEU6), as well as amending other components of the General Plan and other approvals as necessary to implement the draft HEU6 and comply with state law (project), and possible measures to mitigate those significant effects and alternatives to the project. The draft HEU6 is required to identify sites and zoning designations that can accommodate housing developments capable of satisfying the County’s assigned Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) of 3,326 housing units distributed across four income categories (1,070 extremely low/very low-income, 700 low-income, 420 moderate-income, and 1,136 above moderate-income housing units). Pursuant to legal requirements for the Housing Element, the draft HEU6 identifies sites in the UMC that are suitable for the development of all housing types, with the capacity to satisfy the housing needs for the current Sixth Cycle. The Sites Inventory has the capacity for at least 4,434 housing units from opportunity sites, 1,117 housing units from pipeline sites under the proposed or existing zoning, and 346 accessory dwelling units (ADUs) without specific sites, for a combined total capacity of 5,897 housing units. Additional information on the project can be found in Chapter 3: Project Description of the DPEIR. The project is located in Unincorporated Monterey County and one site within the City of Marina. The precise location and boundaries of the project, as shown on a detailed project site map and a regional map are provided in the DPEIR (refer to Figures 2-1, Regional Location, and Figures 2-2a through 2-2i, Project Location).
ceqa-057f2cc5934e6fed93.action: General Plan Amendment, General Plan Element, General Plan Update, Rezone

ceqa-ed5b80d1b9fdd9078d.name: San Ardo 2024 Wells Project, Aera Energy, LLC
ceqa-ed5b80d1b9fdd9078d.projectTitle: San Ardo 2024 Wells Project, Aera Energy, LLC
ceqa-ed5b80d1b9fdd9078d.description: Aera Energy LLC (Aera) has applied to the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division’s (CalGEM) for permits to drill six new cyclic steam injection wells and two new steamflood injection wells within the San Ardo Oil Field in Monterey County, California. The project includes the drilling of 6 new cyclic steam injection wells and 2 new steamflood injection wells, some potential grading on existing well pads, and the installation of new pumping units and flowlines. The impacts of this project are addressed in the Final Recirculated Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (Final Recirculated IS/MND).

An Initial Study found all environmental impacts to be less than significant or mitigated, except for VMT. A Focused EIR concluded the project's VMT impact would remain significant and unavoidable because no feasible mitigation measures are available to reduce it below the significance threshold.

ceqa-f282bfa42dc920e7f1.name: Olivier Street Stormwater Diversion Project
ceqa-f282bfa42dc920e7f1.description: The Proposed Project would modify the existing storm drain system to divert urban drainage from the existing storm drain utility collection system on Olivier Street to the City’s sanitary sewer system. Modifications to the existing underground storm drain system would include construction of a wet well, pump, and ancillary improvements which would include a new electrical panel, trash capture device, and SmartCover monitoring system. By capturing and removing dry-weather flows that are currently discharged to Monterey Bay, the Proposed Project would reduce dry-weather urban runoff discharges to Monterey Bay by diverting nuisance and low-flow urban runoff to the sanitary sewer system for treatment and indirect potable reuse. Additionally, water diverted through the Proposed Project would provide ancillary benefits to the community by contributing to regional recycled water production through the Pure Water Monterey Program. The Proposed Project would provide approximately 10-12 acre-feet per year (“AFY”) of recycled water.

ceqa-b9e39fa971fe19e3cc.name: Fremont Peak State Park Vault Restroom Relocation
ceqa-b9e39fa971fe19e3cc.projectTitle: Fremont Peak State Park Vault Restroom Relocation
ceqa-b9e39fa971fe19e3cc.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-b9e39fa971fe19e3cc.description: The project proposes relocating an existing non-compliant precast vault restroom from the day-use area to Doe Flat Group Campground in Fremont Peak State Park to address accessibility compliance and equal facilitation for visitors with disabilities. One (1) accessible sized portable chemical toilet will be permanently located on a concrete pad adjacent to the precast vault restroom and one (1) concrete “Van Accessible” parking stall will be constructed to facilitate a level surface for parking and approach to the restrooms with a concrete route of travel constructed to connect the buildings to parking. In the group campground work will: To Install the Precast Vault Restroom Use equipment to excavate a 11 foot long by 11 foot wide by 6 foot deep area; Install a layer of road base or similar aggregate at the bottom of the excavation to create a level installation surface; and Use a crane truck to remove the vault restroom from the current location in the day use area and place the vault restroom into the excavated area within the group campground. For the Accessible Sized Portable Chemical Toilet Use equipment to excavate a 10 feet by 10 feet by approximately 12 inches deep area and pour concrete to create a level surface; and Use equipment to install a 7 foot by 7 foot accessible sized portable chemical toilet on the concrete pad For the Parking and Travel Path Use equipment to excavate an approx. 20 foot by 22 foot by 12 inch deep area and install 6 inches of base rock followed by 6 inches of reinforced concrete to create a level parking surface; Use equipment to excavate an approx. 7 foot wide by 26 foot long by 12 inch deep area to create a path from the parking to the restrooms; Use equipment to install 6 inches of base rock followed by 6 inches of reinforced concrete and create a level path of travel; Install truncated domes between the travel route and the parking area; and Installed boulders between the travel route and the parking area to act as dividers.

ceqa-e00b14148138289df4.description: The proposed project consists of unifying Greenfield Union Elementary School District and Greenfield High School into a new Greenfield Unified School District, and unifying King City Elementary School District, King City High School, Pinnacle Coastal Valley High School, and Portola-Butler Continuation High School into a new King City Unified School District Greenfield High School, King City High School, Pinnacle Coastal Valley High School, and Portola-Butler Continuation High School are currently part of the South Monterey County Joint Union High School District. The South Monterey County Joint Union High School District would be dissolved. The proposed project would not result in physical changes or change student enrollment and the new unified school district would continue to accommodate current programs. Purpose: In the State of California, the goals for school district reorganization (e.g., unification) include promoting a high•quality education, fiscal responsibility, equitable access to educational resources and programs, and aligning boundaries with changing community needs. Beneficiaries: Students within the unification boundary areas and taxpayers.

The amended ITP referenced above as issued by CDFW adds two additional activities as Covered Activities in order to minimize and fully mitigate impacts of the authorized take.

ceqa-9c7351482eac3fbfd6.name: Underground Storage Tank (UST) Closure and UST Removal
ceqa-9c7351482eac3fbfd6.projectTitle: Underground Storage Tank (UST) Closure and UST Removal
ceqa-9c7351482eac3fbfd6.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-9c7351482eac3fbfd6.description: The purpose of this project is to close down or remove two (2) Underground Storage Tanks (UST) at Asilomar State Beach and Conference Grounds to eliminate the possibility of contamination from the tanks and/or their contents. The tank in the courtyard of the Stuck-up Inn will be closed and abandoned in place and a second UST located adjacent to the Chapel will be removed, along with any associated piping. Work at each tank will include the following: For the Closure of the UST at Stuck-up Inn: A licensed contractor will use a non-sparking hand tool to core through the top of the tank and assess for the presence of liquid. If liquid is present, work will use a vacuum truck to remove the liquid and fill the tank with concrete slurry to render the tank inert and then cap the tank with a layer of native soil. A hand auger will be used to take soil samples around the tank for sampling. If liquids are not present, an excavator will be used to excavate the tank, associated piping, and any stained or visibly contaminated soil and properly dispose of all materials. For the Removal of the UST at the Chapel: Work will use a vacuum truck to remove any liquids remaining in the tank and a backhoe to excavate an approx. 12-ft long x 4-ft wide x 5-ft deep area for the tank removal. Stained or visibly contaminated soils will be removed and stockpiled in lined roll-off bins or drums and sampled for proper disposal. Any associated piping will be removed as well and disposed of properly.

ceqa-a6faf8d04320d4143f.name: 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy and 2050 Regional Transportation Plans for San Benito, Santa Cruz, and Monterey Counties
ceqa-a6faf8d04320d4143f.projectTitle: 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy and 2050 Regional Transportation Plans for San Benito, Santa Cruz, and Monterey Counties
ceqa-a6faf8d04320d4143f.agency: Association of Monterey Bay Area Governments
ceqa-a6faf8d04320d4143f.agencyName: Association of Monterey Bay Area Governments
ceqa-a6faf8d04320d4143f.description: As the metropolitan planning organization for the tri-county region of Monterey, San Benito, and Santa Cruz counties, the Association of Monterey Bay Area Governments (AMBAG) is charged with developing a 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy (MTP/SCS). The 2050 MTP/SCS is both a long-range transportation plan and Sustainable Communities Strategy for Monterey, San Benito, and Santa Cruz counties. The Council of San Benito County Governments, the Santa Cruz County Regional Transportation Commission, and the Transportation Agency for Monterey County are the state-designated Regional Transportation Planning Agencies for San Benito, Santa Cruz, and Monterey counties, respectively. Each prepares a county-level long-range Regional Transportation Plan, which is evaluated in the EIR. The 2050 MTP/SCS is used to guide the development of the Regional and Federal Transportation Improvement Programs, as well as other transportation programming documents and plans. The MTP/SCS outlines the region's goals and policies for meeting current and future mobility needs, providing a foundation for transportation decisions by local, regional, and state officials that are ultimately aimed at achieving a coordinated and balanced transportation system. The 2050 MTP/SCS sets forth actions, programs, and projects to address these needs consistent with adopted policies and goals. The 2050 MTP/SCS also documents the financial resources needed to implement the plan. Additionally, pursuant to SB 375, AMBAG (as the regional MPO) must prepare an SCS that demonstrates, and the MTP/SCS does demonstrate, how the region will meet its greenhouse gas reduction target (6% reduction by 2035) through integrated land use, housing, and transportation planning.

ceqa-95775f92d4892507bd.name: Crespi Pond Vegetation Management Project (Request No. 1652-2026-090-001-R4)
ceqa-95775f92d4892507bd.projectTitle: Crespi Pond Vegetation Management Project (Request No. 1652-2026-090-001-R4)
ceqa-95775f92d4892507bd.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Central Region 4
ceqa-95775f92d4892507bd.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 4 - Central, Fresno
ceqa-95775f92d4892507bd.description: Pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1652, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife has approved the Crespi Pond Vegetation Management Project submitted by the City of Pacific Grove. Avian utilization of habitat at Crespi Pond is limited by the overgrowth of emergent vegetation. The Project is intended to restore the historic balance of 70% open water and 30% emergent vegetation at Crespi Pond to provide habitat diversity suitable for avian species such as waterbirds and passerine birds. The Project consists of an initial vegetation removal event and two subsequent vegetation removal events. Each event will include the launch of a barge from the bank of Crespi Pond and operation of that barge from the open water. Emergent vegetation will be removed down to the root mass using a clam bucket attachment. Removed vegetation will be temporarily stockpiled along the edge of Crespi Pond and left to dry. Once that vegetation dries, it will be loaded into dump trucks by an excavator for disposal offsite. Subsequent vegetation removal events will occur no more than once every two years and will not remove more than 50% of the emergent vegetation present at that time.

ceqa-da1eeb97302e4af794.projectTitle: Carmel Woods and Pescadero Road Sewer Main Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-da1eeb97302e4af794.description: The Carmel Woods and Pescadero Road Sewer Main Rehabilitation Project (Project) is located on two sites in a residential area located primarily within unincorporated Monterey County, with a small portion of the Project occurring within the northern limits of the City of Carmel-by-the-Sea. The Pescadero Road component of the Project would consist of constructing a new sewer main in Pescadero Road and abandoning a portion of the existing sewer main in the hillside located behind nearby residential connections. The Carmel Woods component of the Project consists of the replacement and/or rehabilitation of approximately 14,850 LF of existing deteriorated 6-inch diameter vitrified clay pipe gravity sewer main with new polyvinyl chloride or high-density polyethylene sewer mains or installation of a lining system. The majority of the sewer mains would be replaced and/or rehabilitated along the existing alignments where feasible. However, several sewer segments would be realigned to improve ease of maintenance. Replacing and rehabilitating the damaged sewer mains at the Pescadero Road and Carmel Woods sites is necessary to continue to provide reliable service to the District’s customers and minimize the potential for sewer spills in the future. The rehabilitated sewer main would continue to be used to convey wastewater for District customers located along Pescadero Road, whose service laterals directly connect to the sewer main to be replaced, while the majority of existing flows to this sewer main would be redirected to the new sewer main.

ceqa-bd4b94685437804983.name: Aromas Shaded Fuel Break EPP
ceqa-bd4b94685437804983.agency: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
ceqa-bd4b94685437804983.agencyName: Forestry and Fire Protection, Department of
ceqa-bd4b94685437804983.description: This project aims to create a shaded fuel break to reduce heavy fuel loading to mitigate the threat of a large catastrophic fire within the Aromas Community. The fuel break will serve as a strategic control line for pre-suppression efforts and increase the likelihood of successful wildfire containment by lowering fire intensity, severity and slowing the rate of spread. These conditions facilitate safer and more effective engagement by both ground and aerial suppression resources. Ultimately, the project will help protect nearby communities, critical infrastructure, and natural resources. Treatment objectives include reducing ladder fuels and dense understory vegetation in oak woodlands to disrupt vertical fuel continuity and support effective shaded fuel break function. In eucalyptus-dominated stands, trees will be mechanically or manually removed to reduce extreme flammability and high ember-cast potential. Removing eucalyptus will also allow native species to reestablish, creating a more fire-resilient landscape. Herbicide treatments will be applied to cut stumps and targeted regrowth under the direction of licensed professionals to maintain long-term hazard reduction.

ceqa-1be6bfc3860fa7ff4d.name: California State University Monterey Bay Stadium Expanded Use Project
ceqa-1be6bfc3860fa7ff4d.projectTitle: California State University Monterey Bay Stadium Expanded Use Project
ceqa-1be6bfc3860fa7ff4d.description: The CSUMB Stadium Expanded Use Project proposes an expansion of existing programming at the CSUMB Stadium by CSUMB and the Monterey Bay Football Club (MBFC) and the construction and operation of two (2) new locker room facilities, two (2) new restroom buildings, and a gated event staging area just north of the stadium. The underlying purpose of the proposed project is to modernize and enhance the existing stadium to function as a flexible, multipurpose venue that better supports CSUMB's academic and athletic programs while accommodating expanded use, including partnerships with external organizations such as professional athletic entities (e.g., United Soccer League). The expanded programming of CSUMB Stadium would allow CSUMB to host the men's and women's California Collegiate Athletic Association (CCAA) Championship tournaments and the NCAA Division II National Championships. CSUMB would also host the following non-athletic events: Latinx Affinity Ceremonies for graduating students; Monte's 5k and post-race event; new student fall convocation; Otter Cross Cultural Center (OC3) affinity celebration; fall welcome concert; a spring concert; the Relay for Life; and up to 25 other university-related events. Additionally, the project would allow the CSUMB Stadium to host three (3) new teams under the oversight of the MBFC (the existing professional team that is engaged in a 14-year Facilities Shared-Use Agreement with CSUMB): one (1) USL League Two (Men's Amateur), one (1) USL Super League (Women's Pro), and one (1) USL W League (Women's Amateur). The project would accommodate games associated with these teams, totaling 18 events over 18 days for the USL Super League and 12 events over 10 days each for the USL League Two and USL W League. The CSUMB Stadium would also host other MBFC events, including a 28-day Winter Festival and up to 20 weekend concerts annually, with a maximum of 6,000 attendees. Proposed new facilities include the following: 1. Men's & Women's Locker Room and Shower Facility. Two (2) permanent 1,400-sf locker room facilities would be constructed. One (1) facility would replace the existing portable showers utilized by the men's teams and would be built at the stadium entrance northwest of the field house. Another facility would be constructed to accommodate the women's teams southwest of the field house. 2. Permanent Restroom Facilities. Two (2) permanent restroom buildings, each approximately 1,000 sf, would be constructed within the existing beer garden area to replace the existing 36 portable facilities. 3. Storage and Staging Area. A new 1.25-acre dedicated storage and staging area would be established north of the stadium to support event operations, equipment storage, and logistical needs. No permanent construction of any structures besides fencing is planned for this site.

ceqa-c3c18719896db4d4a1.projectTitle: San Lucas County Water District Treatment Plant Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-c3c18719896db4d4a1.description: San Lucas County Water District (SLCWD) provides water service to approximately 315 people through 87 residential metered connections and seven commercial metered connections in San Lucas, an unincorporated community in Monterey County. SLCWD proposes to rehabilitate the existing water treatment facility to comply with iron and manganese secondary maximum contaminant levels until a permanent solution is feasible. The proposed project consists entirely of above-ground construction activities to include replacement or filter control panel solenoids, filter media, multiple appurtenances, fittings, pressure gauges, and some of the external piping to restore filtration and backwash capacity of the facility. The internal filter vessel coating would also be inspected, and if necessary, re-coated.

ceqa-7121d7e0f0461c6ff9.name: Del Rey Park ADA Sidewalk Improvements Project
ceqa-7121d7e0f0461c6ff9.projectTitle: Del Rey Park ADA Sidewalk Improvements Project
ceqa-7121d7e0f0461c6ff9.description: The Project is designed to improve accessibility and ensure compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Del Rey Park is an approximately 10-acre developed public park that contains recreational facilities and includes playgrounds, a basketball court, a volleyball pit, a softball field, restrooms, picnic tables, and barbecue pits (Attachment 1). The Del Rey Park ADA Sidewalk Improvements Project (Project) consists of new accessible ADA sidewalks, landing areas, and related park features. Specifically, the Project includes installation of ADA-accessible walkways, sidewalks, curb ramps, safety components, and surfacing improvements within the existing footprint of Del Rey Park. Project details are shown in the Plans for “Del Rey Park ADA Sidewalk Improvements,” prepared by Neill Engineers Corp., dated February 2026 (See Attachment 2). The Project is funded through a Community Development Block Grant administered by the County of Monterey.
ceqa-7121d7e0f0461c6ff9.crossStreets: Angelus Way and Canyon Del Rey Blvd.

ceqa-e3be2b68a2497b7f6f.name: Sidetrack Administrative Grouping
ceqa-e3be2b68a2497b7f6f.description: The primary work objective is to sidetrack two (2) existing wells. This work is designed to support continuation of oil and gas resource development in the area. The wells are not being sidetracked (i) for abandonment purposes only or (ii) in connection with an enforcement order to mitigate or prevent environmental damage or surface expression. Sidetracking is the process of drilling a new wellbore from an existing wellbore. This is typically done when the original wellbore encounters a problem, when accessing remaining hydrocarbons within portions of the same reservoir, or when obstructions in the wellbore need to be bypassed. This process allows drilling a new section in an existing wellbore in the same rock formation restoring the well’s original functionality. The potential disturbance footprint would encompass an existing 20,000 square foot (100 ft x 200 ft) well pad per well. The entirety of this work would be located in an area of existing disturbance and no change in the surface topography (such as drainage patterns) would result. There will be no expansion of the existing well pads, roads, staging areas, or pipelines. No new grading would occur in any undisturbed areas. No new road construction or expansions would be required for the proposed project. Routine maintenance activities at the site would include removal of weeds and other ruderal vegetation for fire control and road maintenance. For a single well, it is expected to take approximately 17 operational days to complete all construction phases. The proposed project consists of the California Department of Conservation, Geologic Energy Management Division (CalGEM) approving 2 permit(s) for Aera Energy LLC to sidetrack the well(s) listed below, in the San Ardo Oil Field.

ceqa-e63061050781b6705b.name: Amendment to the Water Quality Control Plan for the Central Coastal Basin to Establish TMDLS for Organophosphate Pesticides and Toxicity in the Salinas
ceqa-e63061050781b6705b.projectTitle: Amendment to the Water Quality Control Plan for the Central Coastal Basin to Establish TMDLS for Organophosphate Pesticides and Toxicity in the Salinas
ceqa-e63061050781b6705b.agency: California Regional Water Quality Control Board, Central Coast Region 3
ceqa-e63061050781b6705b.agencyName: Regional Water Quality Control Board, Region 3 - Central Coast, San Luis Obispo
ceqa-e63061050781b6705b.description: The Central Coast Regional Water Quality Control Board (Central Coast Water Board) adopted this amendment to the Water Quality Control Plan for the Central Coastal Basin (Basin Plan amendment). The Basin Plan amendment incorporates Total Maximum Daily Loads (TMDLs) with an associated implementation strategy for reducing organophosphate pesticide loading to surface waters in the lower Salinas River watershed in Monterey County, California for the following: three organophosphate pesticides (chlorpyrifos, diazinon, and malathion), additive toxicity of those pesticides, and individual toxicity. TMDLs are a requirement of the federal Clean Water Act, and waterbodies assigned TMDLs in this Basin Plan amendment include segments of the lower Salinas River, the Salinas Reclamation Canal, and their respective tributaries including Chualar Creek, Esperanza Creek, Quail Creek, Toro Creek, Blanco Drain, Tembladero Slough, Merritt Ditch, Alisal Slough, Espinosa Slough, and Santa Rita Creek. The Central Coast Water Board is relying on existing regulatory measures (i.e., the Agricultural Order and stormwater NPDES permits), voluntary actions, and grant funding to ensure implementation actions to reduce organophosphate pesticides to the watershed are carried out and maintained by the responsible parties.

ceqa-40a89a51f0df1e4f26.description: The project consists of the installation of Flock Safety automated license plate reading (ALPR) cameras to be installed on behalf of the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office. ceqa-1bab67733e9a3bf8f5.name: Jack's Peak CAPM
ceqa-1bab67733e9a3bf8f5.agencyName: Caltrans, District 5 - San Luis Obispo/Santa Barbara
ceqa-1bab67733e9a3bf8f5.description: The purpose of this project is to preserve and extend the service life of the existing pavement and facilities on State Route 1 (SR-1) in Monterey County, CA. Deteriorating pavement conditions within the project limits requires pavement rehabilitation to maintain road integrity and driver safety. Additionally, guardrail and median thrie-beam barrier within the project limits will be upgraded to meet the current Manual for Assessing Safety Hardware (MASH) standards. One overhead sign structure and 16 sign panels are in poor condition, requiring replacement to enhance roadside safety. Gore areas that have been identified as showing signs of deterioration will be re-paved. The project proposes to use polyurethane injections at one location to improve sub-surface conditions and stabilize a deteriorating embankment. The pavement rehabilitation project will overlay the existing pavement and will not alter existing roadway geometric features. Construction activities will occur within State Right of Way (ROW), primarily limited to the roadway matrix, center median, and previously disturbed areas. Night work is anticipated due to the potential traffic impacts of lane closures during the daytime. Vegetation trimming and/or tree removal are not anticipated. Temporary traffic control can be utilized during drilling/injection operations, allowing both lanes to be reopened after each shift to accommodate the traffic demand in this busy area.
ceqa-1bab67733e9a3bf8f5.crossStreets: SR-1, between South San Luis Ave and Sloat Ave

ceqa-e0a37b8c90953f16b9.agency: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
ceqa-e0a37b8c90953f16b9.agencyName: Forestry and Fire Protection, Department of
ceqa-e0a37b8c90953f16b9.description: This project involves recurring maintenance and repair of the Thompson Valley Truck trail which travels generally north to south through the Gabilan Mountain Range starting in the north from San Juan Canyon Road to the southern end of the route which ends at Limekiln Road. The Thompson Truck Trail is 16 miles long and the project will cover approximately 78 acres. The purpose of the project is to maintain and improve emergency vehicle access in the area in the event of a wildfire or other emergency. Road maintenance activities will include grading the existing road surface as well as manual and mechanical vegetation removal within 20 feet of the road. Manual vegetation removal will include the use of hand tools and chainsaws to prune limbs, bushes and trees to accommodate fire engine access. Mechanical treatments will include the use of an excavator with a masticating head as well as a tow-behind or tracked chipper. Heavy equipment will be limited to the existing road surface. Trees greater than 12” dbh will not be removed unless they are clearly dead or dying all remaining trees near the road will be pruned up to 16 feet or 50% of the live crown.

ceqa-b9372069470c8f53c5.projectTitle: Increase Testing of Longlining Traditional Gear for Dungeness crab (Pacific Coast Federation of Fishermen’s Associations and California Coast Crab Association;
ceqa-b9372069470c8f53c5.description: An approved experimental fishing permit (commission tracking #2023-01) tests traditional longline fishing systems in the California commercial Dungeness crab fishery. The EFP tests the use and efficacy of using longline gear to help fill critical information gaps for alternative gear usage in the Dungeness crab fishery. ceqa-4ec89a601c23208c29.name: Expansion of Pop-Up Gear Testing in the California Dungeness and Rock Crab Fisheries and Addition of Commercial Spot Prawn Testing (Greg Wells/National Marine S

ceqa-4ec89a601c23208c29.description: An approved experimental fishing permit (commission tracking #2023-02) tests commercial use of several popup gear systems in the California Dungeness crab and rock crab fisheries. The EFP is used to inform future alternative gear certification under the Risk Assessment and Mitigation Program in California Code of Regulations (CCR; Title 14, Section 132.8). ceqa-56d61975aa6831afb5.name: Brothers Ranch Hydrologic Restoration Project
ceqa-56d61975aa6831afb5.agency: Santa Cruz County Resource Conservation District
ceqa-56d61975aa6831afb5.agencyName: Santa Cruz County Resource Conservation District
ceqa-56d61975aa6831afb5.description: The Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz County, Elkhorn Slough Foundation and UCSC Hydrogeology are partnering to restore hydrologic processes at the Brothers Ranch. The project area consists of 4 acres of farmland and 1 acre of an ephemeral creek corridor. The creek corridor has been greatly impacted by farming over many decades. Impacts include the channeling of water flow into ditches and excavated channels and the creation of berms and levees to hasten the flow of water off the landscape. Additionally there is much plastic sheeting, abandoned culverts, plastic bags, pipe remnants and other agricultural waste distributed throughout the corridor. Our project will remove the ditches and berms created by past agricultural users to re-create a broad, low floodplain similar to what was believed to have been there in the past and re-vegetate that area with a sedge/rush dominant wet meadow mix that is thought to be very rare in the area now. This treatment will provide needed habitat complexity to a site currently dominated by willows with very little/low additional plant species diversity. Additionally, in the farmland, the project will build two (2) infiltration basins that will receive excedent stormwater runoff resulting from current farming operations and infiltrate that water into the critically overdrafted aquifer below. In restoring hydrologic processes of improved water infiltration, restored floodplain dynamics and reduced and slowed runoff, the project will result in a myriad of benefits to on and off site water resources including attenuation of flooding and decreases in sediment load to downstream resources and on-site, specifically, improved habitat diversity, agricultural refuse remediation and a strong demonstration of how farming and environmental goals can be achieved side by side.
ceqa-56d61975aa6831afb5.crossStreets: Hall Road and Valley View Road

ceqa-8583aa0a9b9efaa19a.projectTitle: Garland Ranch Regional Park Defensible Space Maintenance Project
ceqa-8583aa0a9b9efaa19a.description: Defensible space maintenance around the Garland Ranch Ranger Station, Cooper Barn complex, and the Kahn Ranch complex and all their associated outbuildings. ceqa-63910dc516c9cef7cd.name: Salinas River Disposal Site Restoration Project (Request No. 1652-2025-085-001-R4)
ceqa-63910dc516c9cef7cd.projectTitle: Salinas River Disposal Site Restoration Project (Request No. 1652-2025-085-001-R4)
ceqa-63910dc516c9cef7cd.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Central Region 4
ceqa-63910dc516c9cef7cd.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 4 - Central, Fresno
ceqa-63910dc516c9cef7cd.description: Pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1652, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife has approved the Salinas River Disposal Site Restoration Project submitted by the City of Marina. The primary purpose of the Project is to improve the quality of 0.45-acres of riparian habitat along the Salinas River. The Project includes initial restoration activities and subsequent monitoring and maintenance activities. Initial restoration activities include: removal and disposal of 1,000 cubic yards of debris within a 0.24-acre area; smoothing and scarification of soil; installation of biodegradable erosion control materials; removal of invasive nonnative plants with manual and chemical methods; installation of locally-native container plants; installation of willow (Salix spp.) and cottonwood (Populus spp.) hardwood stakes; application of wood chip mulch; hydroseeding with a locally native seed mix; installation of a temporary at-grade drip irrigation system; and installation of browse protection cages. Monitoring and maintenance activities include: monthly inspections of the Project site; adaptive management of invasive non-native plants; adjustment and removal of browse protection cages; adjustment and removal of the temporary at-grade drip irrigation system; application of additional wood chip mulch; application of supplemental water; installation of additional locally-native container plants or hardwood stakes; and reseeding. Supplemental water for the temporary on-grade drip irrigation system will be sourced from a water truck or temporary water tank. The Project does not include the diversion of water from the Salinas River.

ceqa-e8727b14e78e0f529a.name: Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project California Endangered Species Act Incidental Take Permit No. 2081-2018-027-04 (ITP) Minor Amendment No. 2
ceqa-e8727b14e78e0f529a.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has issued an ITP (No. 2081-2018-027-04 (ITP) Minor Amendment No. 2), pursuant to Section 2081(b) of the Fish and Game Code to California American Water. The Project involves the installation of a desalination plant, associated pipelines, including the Transmission Main Pipeline, Castroville Pipeline, Desalinated Water Pipeline, and the Source Water Pipeline along with the installation of two Aquifer Storage and Recovery (ASR) Wells. Project activities encompass a total of 54.57 acres. The Project will permanently remove 14.746 acres and temporarily impact 34.681 acres of California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense) (CTS) upland habitat. The Project is expected to result in incidental take of CTS, which is designated as a threatened species under the California Endangered Species Act. The ITP referenced above as issued by CDFW authorizes incidental take of species listed under CESA that may occur as a result of Project implementation. Minor Amendment No. 2, as referenced above and issued by CDFW revises the Project description to include specific construction phases, revises the compensatory mitigation language to allow for the phased purchase of Covered Species credits by Project phase, adds language to allow for establishing security funding by Project phase, revises the Permittee’s Principal Officer and Contact Person, revises the CDFW contact, and other non-substantial changes. Minor Amendment No. 2 does not increase the Project’s impact.

ceqa-b798c7cabff7622e08.name: D Booster Station Monitoring Wells Project
ceqa-b798c7cabff7622e08.projectTitle: D Booster Station Monitoring Wells Project
ceqa-b798c7cabff7622e08.description: The proposed project involves the construction of two new groundwater monitoring wells at the MCWD D Booster Pump Station site, where MCWD holds an exclusive permit. Work will include site preparation, mobilization of drilling equipment, drilling, and installation of well casings and screened intervals at depths appropriate to site-specific hydrogeologic conditions. Each well will be completed for long-term groundwater level and water quality monitoring. Portable sound walls will be installed around drilling equipment to reduce noise transmission toward nearby residential areas and office buildings across the street. The purpose of the proposed project is to improve groundwater monitoring coverage within the MCWD service area in support of Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) requirements. Installation of the proposed monitoring wells will provide additional groundwater level and water quality data needed for basin evaluation, regulatory reporting, and long-term groundwater management within the Monterey Subbasin. The proposed project is needed to address identified groundwater monitoring data gaps and to support MCWD’s responsibilities as a Groundwater Sustainability Agency (GSA) under SGMA. Accurate and reliable groundwater level and water quality data are required for informed basin management, compliance with SGMA reporting requirements, and evaluation of long-term groundwater sustainability. There are no long-term safety concerns associated with the proposed action. Temporary construction-related effects will be minimized through standard best management practices.

Buildout of the specific plan is expected to result in an approximate population increase of 8,971 and approximately 307 new employment opportunities. The existing on-site structures would be demolished. The specific plan is proposed to be developed in seven phases over a currently undetermined period of time.

ceqa-5cfe03cbebe7f0aa14.name: Monterey County Regional Bicycle and Pedestrian Wayfinding Plan
ceqa-5cfe03cbebe7f0aa14.projectTitle: Monterey County Regional Bicycle and Pedestrian Wayfinding Plan
ceqa-5cfe03cbebe7f0aa14.description: TAMC’s Monterey County Regional Bicycle and Pedestrian Wayfinding Plan provides standard design guidelines for uniform wayfinding signage throughout Monterey County. The Plan identifies regional bicycle and pedestrian routes, sign locations and provides standard design guidelines for uniform wayfinding signage throughout Monterey County. Wayfinding signs will be placed within existing streets and public right-of-way throughout the jurisdictions and unincorporated areas of Monterey County, including within California State University, Monterey Bay (CSUMB). Within CSUMB specifically, 15 new signs will be installed within developed and previously disturbed areas around campus. The Regional Bicycle and Pedestrian Wayfinding Plan includes implementation strategies. Implementation includes a Memorandum of Understanding between the Transportation Agency for Monterey County and the jurisdictions in Monterey County, such as CSUMB, to manufacture and install the wayfinding signage in the locations identified in the Plan. The Regional Bicycle and Pedestrian Wayfinding Plan will encourage bicycling and walking, improve access to regional destinations, and improve regional connections between communities in Monterey County. The project's beneficiaries include the jurisdictions and unincorporated areas of Monterey County, including CSUMB.

ceqa-9ea21c56c63949c700.name: D’Arrigo Brothers and General Farm Investments Well Replacement Project
ceqa-9ea21c56c63949c700.projectTitle: D’Arrigo Brothers and General Farm Investments Well Replacement Project
ceqa-9ea21c56c63949c700.description: The Proposed Project would install two new replacement wells for existing agricultural production wells experiencing issues with water quality. Specifically, D’Arrigo Brothers of USA would install a new replacement well with a maximum capacity of 2,000 gallons per minute (GPM), and General Farm Investments would install a new 1,500 GPM replacement well. Both wells would be drilled to a depth of approximately 1710 feet and be screened in the Deep Aquifer of the Salinas Valley Groundwater Basin (Deep Aquifer). The proposed wells would have about 800 feet of conductor casing and seal to isolate the production zone from the overlying sediments of the aquitard and the 180/400 Foot Aquifer of the Salinas Valley Groundwater Basin. The Proposed Project would not result in an increase in irrigated land, and new replacement wells in the Deep Aquifer would replace existing wells in the shallow zones of the 180/400 Foot Aquifer. The Proposed Project would include destruction of the existing shallow wells by state and county approved methods.

ceqa-4ff4fd1dae443f4db2.name: Building 201 Gavilan Hall Housing Renovation Project
ceqa-4ff4fd1dae443f4db2.projectTitle: Building 201 Gavilan Hall Housing Renovation Project
ceqa-4ff4fd1dae443f4db2.description: The proposed project involves the renovation of Gavilan Hall, a three-story, 39,000 GSF building originally constructed in the 1970s, to convert existing office and program space into a modern student residence hall. The project will provide 246 student beds within the existing building footprint and square footage. Improvements will include upgrades to seismic safety, accessibility (ADA), HVAC, plumbing, fire/life safety, lighting, and other essential building systems. Interior reconfiguration will incorporate restrooms, shared kitchens, social/study lounges, and other community and support spaces. The project also includes minor improvements to the adjacent one-story annex building to accommodate shared amenities such as a multipurpose room and kitchen. Limited site improvements to the existing courtyard and pathways will be made to enhance student life and outdoor use. The project expands housing within existing facilities and does not change the building footprint. By addressing seismic, ADA, and infrastructure deficiencies, this renovation supports campus housing needs, reduces deferred maintenance, and provides additional affordable on-campus housing in response to limited off-campus rental availability and high local housing costs
ceqa-4ff4fd1dae443f4db2.crossStreets: Southeast corner of Inter Garrison Road and 6th Avenue.

ceqa-f19cd1d2c99512d1ca.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-f19cd1d2c99512d1ca.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20, Sec. 66270.61, has issued an Emergency Permit to the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI), (EPA ID# CAD982401283) to treat hazardous waste through a controlled reaction with chemical solutions. Specifically, one (1) 1-liter container of Diethyl ether, one (1) 500 mL container of Collodion solution 4-8% ethanol/diethyl ether, one (1) 2.5-liter container of tert-butyl methyl, one (1) 1-liter bottle of Tetrahydrofuran must be stabilized prior to transporting off-site to an authorized hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facility. These chemicals are currently being stored at MBARI located at 7700 Sandholdt Road, Moss Landing, CA 95039. DTSC has determined, as a safety precaution to prevent an accident or severe injury, an Emergency Permit should be issued for treatment of chemicals to chemically stabilize the hazardous waste prior to storage and eventual transportation off-site by Veolia.
