ceqa-665261f916f1076daa.name: Sage Valley Reserve CUP190046
ceqa-665261f916f1076daa.description: Glen Aery (Applicant) is requesting the approval of a Development Agreement (DA190037) and a Conditional Use Permit (CUP190046) allowing for the development and operation of a Cannabis Cultivation and Distribution facility. The Project Site is located at 38455 East Benton Road in unincorporated Riverside County. The Project Site is identified as Assessor’s Parcel Number (APN) 915-330-040 and is approximately 9.85 gross acres in size. The Project Site has an existing one-story, 2,086-square-foot residence. A septic system, domestic well, and water storage tank to serve the residence. There is an existing concrete driveway along Benton Road for access to the residence. No change to the existing residence is proposed as part of the Proposed Project. The Proposed Project includes a TPM to subdivide the property into two parcels: Parcel 1 is 5.0 acres and comprises the proposed commercial facility, and Parcel 2 is 4.88 acres and comprises the existing residential area. A 5.33-acre portion of the eastern portion of the Project Site would be incorporated into the Multiple Species Habitat Conservation Plan Reserve Assembly as Additional Reserve Land. A fence is proposed along the perimeter of this area. The proposed development would occur on the remaining 4.52 acres. The Proposed Project includes 15,864 square-feet of building coverage, and four (4) 5,000-gallon water tanks. A new septic system with a 1,000-gallon septic tank with a 50-foot setback from certain structures and features to help ensure public safety and proper functioning of the system would also be included. Two retention basins are proposed. There would be a new well near the northern property line to serve the commercial facility. Development of the Proposed Project involves construction of three (3) 3,472-square-foot (SF) buildings each with grow rooms and storage (Buildings 1A, 2, & 3); and a 1,542-square-foot (SF) building with grow room, storage, and area for logistics (Building 1B). Buildings 2 and 3 each have an additional 1,853-SF covered patio with two 348-SF storage containers. Security fencing would fully enclose the portion of the Project Site to be developed. Back-up generators would be located adjacent to the proposed buildings 1A, 2 and 3. A solar array with 91 solar panels is proposed near the new water well. Trash disposal areas shall be fully enclosed, shown at the Northeast corner of the site. Cannabis vegetation waste would be disposed of in a separate locked bin within the enclosure. It would be removed by a certified hauler for cannabis waste. A 24-foot-wide access driveway with secure access gates is proposed along Benton Road. The Proposed Project would provide 11 parking spaces, two of which are handicap accessible and 1 as electric vehicle parking. The Proposed Project would require a maximum of seven (7) employees. Operations would consist of 2 shifts: 6:00 AM to 2:00 PM and 2:00 PM to 10:00 PM. Growing season would be year-round with harvesting occurring four times a year. The Project Site is designated Rural Residential in the Riverside County General Plan and occurs within the Light Agriculture (A-1-10) Zoning district. This zoning classification permits greenhouses, orchards, and herbs gathering in a commercial scale. The Proposed Project is a cannabis cultivation facility that would be consistent with the A-1-10 zoning. The Proposed Project would harvest all water collected from HVAC cooling coils and dehumidifiers. In addition, the facility would implement an automated load-shifting system during peak hours (4PM to 9PM). During peak hours, lights would be turned off and HVAC use would be minimized.

ceqa-0c176c7d8ce17af049.name: Temecula Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility Plant 3 Electrical Modifications
ceqa-0c176c7d8ce17af049.projectTitle: Temecula Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility Plant 3 Electrical Modifications
ceqa-0c176c7d8ce17af049.description: Temecula Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility (TVRWRF) Plant 3 is currently experiencing intermittent failures in the membrane bioreactor mixers (MBM). This was found to be a result of sever mixer corrosions from a faulty grounding system. Electrical issues at Plant 3 were also found, including potential bonding issues with the aluminum handrailing around the MBR basins, tripping of ground fault circuit interrupters (GFCI) which damaged onsite wastewater samplers, and return activated sludge SCADA hardware failure. The scope of work would include installation of sump pumps to discharge drainage and groundwater infiltration and the upgrade to existing electrical panel with isolation transformer and GFCI protection for wet location application. These upgrades would eliminate potential safety hazards within six electrical vaults and stop infiltration from entering the interconnected conduits and below grade electrical panels. Beneficiaries of the project are Eastern Municipal Water District TVRWRF staff and ratepayers.

ceqa-37b2fb9647813a400e.name: Perris Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility Secondary Clarifier 5, 6 and 8 Rehabilitation
ceqa-37b2fb9647813a400e.projectTitle: Perris Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility Secondary Clarifier 5, 6 and 8 Rehabilitation
ceqa-37b2fb9647813a400e.description: Eastern Municipal Water District's (EMWD) Perris Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility (PVRWRF) provides the Perris Valley region with wastewater treatment services. As a result of rehabilitation PVRWRF is currently undergoing, EMWD staff observed that Secondary Clarifier (SC) 6 and SC 8 were experiencing severe deterioration and required immediate repairs. SC 5 was also inspected and the gate, plugged drain lines, and steel structure are in need of repairs. The scope of work includes the removal and replacement of existing clarifier mechanism components, bridge and scum hopper, weirs and scum baffles, and drive unit. Beneficiaries of this project are EMWD ratepayers.

ceqa-b3c6dfec8e74e8d59b.name: 2026 Water Storage Tanks Rehabilitation Construction Projects
ceqa-b3c6dfec8e74e8d59b.projectTitle: 2026 Water Storage Tanks Rehabilitation Construction Projects
ceqa-b3c6dfec8e74e8d59b.description: Water tanks are key assets in Eastern Municipal Water District’s (EMWD) ongoing mission to provide reliable water service. Exterior inspections and interior dive inspections revealed several water tanks operating at sub-optimal conditions, including deteriorated coating and corroded structural members in several tanks. Proper maintenance is required to ensure optimal protection of district assets and extension of the tank’s service life. The purpose of this project is to rehabilitate the following tanks: Sun City Tank, Cajalco Tank, and Riparian Tank. The project includes recoating the tank exterior and interior, installation of new roof vents, perimeter safety railing, replacement of the cathodic protection system, and repair or replacement of corroded structural members. Beneficiaries of the project are EMWD ratepayers.

ceqa-61bba904a99f8e91db.name: Hillside Ordinance Updates (DCA-2021-2396), Ordinance No. 638-26
ceqa-61bba904a99f8e91db.projectTitle: City of Murrietta General Plan Update 2035
ceqa-61bba904a99f8e91db.description: The “Project” is an ordinance amendment to revise Chapters 8.20 and 15.52 of the Municipal Code, and amend the City’s Development Code for the purpose of revising and updating Chapters 16.08, 16.14, 16.18, 16.22, 16.24, 16.28, and to add a new Sections 16.24.080, entitled “Exceptions”, 16.24.090, entitled “Reserved”, and 16.24.100, entitled “Hillside Overlay Map”. The main objective for bringing forward these updates is that when the hillside development standards were originally adopted in conjunction with the Comprehensive Development Code in 1997, these standards may have been over time misapplied and misinterpreted by project proponents and City staff as it relates to project review. The proposed updates will clarify and assist project proponents and City staff in the implementation of existing hillside criteria within an objective framework. This would be consistent with recent State housing legislation. Also, it should be noted that individual projects will still be subject to subsequent environmental review and site-specific analysis. Additionally, the updates being considered under Chapters 8.20 “Nuisances Generally” and 15.52, “Grading, Erosion and Sediment Control”, are proposed to be modified for consistency and referencing with the proposed modifications under Title 16. The proposed action was reviewed for consistency with the adopted Negative Declaration for implementation of the Comprehensive Development Code on October 28, 1997, and the more recently benchmarked against the certified Murrieta General Plan Final FEIR in 2011 and Subsequent SEIR in 2021. These updates have been evaluated for consistency for the current “Project” proposal utilizing this Negative Declaration and the Murrieta General Plan Final FEIR and Subsequent SEIR in 2021 (SCH No. 2010111084), by the City of Murrieta. Pursuant to Public Resources Code Section 21166 and CEQA guidelines 15162, the City has determined that: (1) there is substantial evidence that none of the conditions requiring preparation of a subsequent Negative Declaration exist, and (2) the City will rely on the previous environmental document, which adequately addresses this Project. The proposed project would not introduce additional impacts or increase the severity of impacts beyond those already analyzed in the 1997 Comprehensive Development Code Negative Declaration. On September 15, 2026, the City of Murrieta City Council determined that the Project qualified for a Consistency Determination pursuant to Public Resources Code Section 21166 and Section 15162 of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines, pertaining to Subsequent Environmental Impact Reports and Negative Declarations. The City Council subsequently conducted the second reading and adopted the Ordinance on October 6, 2026. The Ordinance will become effective 30 days following its adoption, which will occur on November 6, 2026.

ceqa-3fab46012ce63c83e3.name: Winchester Community Plan (GPA No. 1207)
ceqa-3fab46012ce63c83e3.description: The Winchester Community Plan (GPA No. 1207) project (project area) is located within the southwestern portion of the County of Riverside (County). The project area is surrounded by unincorporated County land and the city of Hemet to the north and east, unincorporated County land and the cities of Murrieta and Temecula to the south, and the cities of Murrieta and Menifee to the west. The project area is almost entirely within the General Plan’s Highway 79 Policy Area (49,275 acres) boundary. The Draft EIR for the Winchester Community Plan (GPA No. 1207) project was circulated for a 45-day public review period that began on July 5, 2022 and concluded on August 19, 2022. It is noted that the County of Riverside extended the Draft EIR public review period from August 19, 2022 to September 23, 2022. Following the end of the public review period for the Draft EIR, the County prepared a Final EIR and published the Final EIR on August 16, 2024 with the State Clearinghouse. The County also published the Final EIR on the Winchester Community Plan project website and distributed a link to the document to commenters on the Draft EIR. In addition to addressing public comments, the Final EIR included minor revisions to the Draft EIR resulting from minor corrections or updates to Draft EIR information, including minor revisions made in response to several public comments submitted on the Draft EIR. Following publication of the Final EIR on August 16, 2024, the County placed the project on hold to address regional transportation concerns raised by neighboring jurisdictions and communities. To address these concerns, the County prepared the Transportation Analysis for the Winchester Community Plan (Fehr & Peers, July 24, 2026). The Transportation Analysis evaluates the capacity of future transportation infrastructure within the cities of Menifee, Murrieta, and Temecula, as well as unincorporated areas of southwestern Riverside County. The analysis is intended to serve as a regional planning tool to help the County and neighboring jurisdictions identify and coordinate future transportation improvements needed to address cumulative traffic impacts associated with regional growth. The County has also revised the Proposed Land Use Plan by modifying certain land use designations and adding/removing select parcels from the project area. These changes are a result of the public review process and would not result in population or employment levels that exceed those evaluated in the Draft EIR. In accordance with Public Resources Code Section 21092.1 and California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15088.5, the County has elected to recirculate specific portions of the Winchester Community Plan Draft EIR (SCH No. 2019049114) to incorporate the Transportation Analysis and revisions to the Land Use Plan. The information added to the Draft EIR, specifically in the Project Description and Transportation sections, does not identify a new significant environmental impact or a substantial increase in the severity of a previously identified environmental impact. Rather, the new information clarifies and refines the Draft EIR and provides additional information to the County’s decision-makers and the public. Although CEQA does not require recirculation based on these changes, the County has elected to recirculate specific portions of the Draft EIR to promote full disclosure and transparency and to obtain additional public input.

ceqa-60f853df271a151f07.projectTitle: Hemet-Ryan Air Attack Base Replacement Project
ceqa-60f853df271a151f07.agency: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
ceqa-60f853df271a151f07.agencyName: Forestry and Fire Protection, Department of
ceqa-60f853df271a151f07.description: CAL FIRE is proposing to replace the existing Hemet-Ryan Air Attack Base with a new facility. The Project includes a two-story air operations building with a control room; landing pads and retardant loading pits; a 32-bed barracks/mess hall; a combination helicopter/OV-10 hangar; two aircraft storage canopies; a helicopter training tower with a hoist system for repelling training; a fire retardant mixing station; a vehicle storage building; and a generator yard/electrical building. Site work would include demolition of an existing RCSD helipad, barracks, pilot’s building, office, Quonset hut, tanks, gas shed, canopies, maintenance and storage buildings; the replacement of existing structures with new facilities, and the installation of sewer connections, fencing, paving, landscaping, utilities, and other related site work. The facility lease would be extended to 50 years.

ceqa-2751feb902de464395.name: I-15 Nicholas Road Interchange Project
ceqa-2751feb902de464395.description: The City of Lake Elsinore, in cooperation with the Caltrans District 8, is proposing to improve the Interstate 15 (I-15)/Nichols Road interchange located within the city of Lake Elsinore, from postmile 22.8 (0.5 mile north of Central Avenue) to postmile 24.5 (2.2 miles south of Lake Street) in Riverside County. The Project proposes to widen the Nichols Road Overcrossing and ramps to improve storage capacity and increase shoulder widths to standard; add a segment of auxiliary lane on I-15 in the northbound direction; add complete streets elements such as sidewalks, crosswalks, Americans with Disabilities Act--compliant curb ramps, and bicycle lanes; and add or upgrade intersection traffic control devices. The Project would be implemented primarily along Nichols Road within and adjacent to the I-15 interchange area, with associated improvements on portions of Collier Avenue. Other Project improvements include realigning Nichols Road and providing a new bridge over Temescal Creek, west of the interchange.

ceqa-609a4ccd81c139e77a.projectTitle: Utility Potholing for the San Timoteo Canyon Road Signal Project

The potholing will be performed to obtain information regarding existing utilities located within the project footprint. There are 26 utility potholes located in predetermined locations within the project’s footprint in the County right-of-way. Potholing locations will be back filled upon completion, and sites will be restored to pre-project conditions. No significant ground disturbing activities or construction will take place as part of these utility potholing activities. The proposed utility potholing will take place within the County right-of-way and will not occur within jurisdictional areas.

ceqa-d456a1939c288aefb3.name: Mission Creek Groundwater Replenishment Facility
ceqa-d456a1939c288aefb3.description: The proposed Project consists of Desert Water Agency’s (DWA’s) approval of an amended exchange agreement to facilitate the continued operation and maintenance of the Mission Creek Groundwater Replenishment Facility (MCGRF), including a potential increase in quantities of water delivered to the MCGRF for replenishment of groundwater in the Mission Creek Subbasin (MCSB). The amended exchange agreement would increase the annual State Water Project (SWP) Table A allocation, shared between DWA and Coachella Valley Water District (CVWD), from a total of 194,100 AF to a proposed 244,100 AF per year. The SWP Table A water is exchanged for a like amount of water from the Colorado River Aqueduct (CRA). The increased allocation will potentially result in an increase in CRA water deliveries to the MCGRF of up to a theoretical maximum of 5,000 AF per year over a long-term average. The actual quantity of water delivered to the MCGRF in any given year will continue to vary depending on available SWP water and CRA water supplies and the applicable terms of the amended exchange agreement and be proportional to groundwater pumping in the MCSB per the DWA and CVWD water management agreement. The proposed Project will provide for ongoing management of the MCSB as a sustainable source of water supply for the Coachella Valley region. All Project activities would occur within the existing operational framework and physical footprint of the MCGRF and its existing facilities. The Project does not include any construction or installation of new facilities. A more detailed description of the Project is included in the Project Initial Study.
ceqa-d456a1939c288aefb3.crossStreets: Worsley Road and Mission Creek Road
ceqa-d456a1939c288aefb3.developmentType: Water Facilities (Mission Creek Groundwater Replenishment Facility)(Type Water, MGD 68)

ceqa-d7d5cacceadccb3f89.description: The Loan Agreement for the Use of PLHA Program Funds for $4,000,000 will be used to pay a portion of the construction costs for Palm Villas at State Apartments located on an approximately 7 .76 acres of Housing Authority-owned real property located at 761 & 785 North State Street and 160,260 & 320 West Menlo Avenue in the City of Hemet, CA 92543, identified as Assessor's Parcel Numbers (APNs) 439-060-009, 010, 011, 014, 015 and 439-281-035. The Project consists of 108 rental units within four, three-story residential buildings, including 75 two-bedroom units, 33 three-bedroom units, and one three-bedroom manager's unit. Except for the manager's unit, all rental units will be restricted for households earning between 30% and 60% of the Riverside County Area Median Income (AMI). Site amenities will include a community center, computer lab, kitchen, flexible community rooms, playground, picnic areas, and sports courts. Under the County's PLHA program, 52 units will be restricted to low and very low income households. Those will be restricted fora period of atleast55 years from the recordation of the Notice of Completion.

ceqa-79ac3aa572dba49bbe.description: The Public Safety Campus Project (Project) consists of three primary components: (1) development of a Public Safety Campus (PSC); (2) construction of a Corporate Yard Fueling Station (CYFS); and (3) tenant improvements at existing civic center facilities throughout the City. These improvements would accommodate a range of civic uses identified in the City's Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) and are intended to enhance emergency response capabilities, improve operational efficiency, and support the City's growing public safety and municipal service needs as the City continues to grow. The Project also includes improvements to a drainage culvert and roadway improvements on nearby streets. The Project would encompass approximately 60.37 acres at various locations throughout the City.

ceqa-6a8b31996114f995a4.name: Mesa Verde Specific Plan Area 2 Amendment 2
ceqa-6a8b31996114f995a4.projectTitle: Mesa Verde Specific Plan Area 2 Amendment 2
ceqa-6a8b31996114f995a4.description: The Mesa Verde Specific Plan Area 2 Amendment 2 Project (Project) site consists of approximately 1,463 acres of undeveloped land located in the northwestern portion of the City, in the County of Riverside, California. The Project site is generally located in the northwestern portion of the City, adjacent to and south of the border of San Bernardino County. The Project is an amendment to the approved Mesa Verde Specific Plan Area 2 Amendment 1, and would permit a maximum of 3,650 residential units. The projected number of units within each of the residential zones include: 790 units of High Residential, 594 units of Medium High, 1,450 units of Medium, 677 units of Low Medium, and 139 units of Low. The Project would permit up to 4.44 million square feet of building area with the Business Park zone (allowing for industrial, logistics, office, and/or educational uses), up to 300,000 square feet of commercial building area within the Commercial and Mixed-Use zones, two school sites, open space and public/private parks, utility infrastructure, and roadways. An internal network of trails would connect the Project’s land uses and parks. Off-site improvements for roadway infrastructure, utility connections, and fuel modification would be required. County Line Road improvements would require redeveloping and widening the roadway within the existing 60-foot to 80-foot right-of-way. This NOD is filed related to the second reading of Ordinances 424 and 425.

ceqa-13d05001f1e90f53de.name: Florence Street Road Construction Project
ceqa-13d05001f1e90f53de.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department is proposing a new asphalt roadway on Florence Street between the limits of about 250 feet north of Cajalco Road to Dawes Street, approximately 0.25 miles, in Mead Valley, Riverside County. Florence Street is a local, predominantly unpaved roadway with a current width of approximately 60 feet wide and a proposed road width of 26 feet, the right-of-way is 60 feet. The proposed project will remove and replace about 50 feet of existing asphalt concrete and pave the remaining dirt portion of Florence Street. In addition, it will include grading and moisture conditioning the roadway width and paving with Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA). Additional improvements include: • Asphalt Concrete Pavement • Safety edge and shoulder backing • Removing and replacing asphalt dike • Remove existing asphalt concrete • Pavement delineation of roadway • Trimming and/or removing trees and vegetation as needed • Removing rocks as necessary All proposed improvements are within the County’s right of way. No additional right-of-way or temporary construction easements are required to construct the proposed improvements.

The project includes a 4,456 square foot drive through restaurant, a 4,000 square foot convenience store, a gas station with eight Multiple Product Dispensers (MPDs), and a 4,150 square foot express car wash facility. ceqa-3b15739f458a7d5d7a.name: Extra-Territorial Wastewater Service to the Islamic Center
ceqa-3b15739f458a7d5d7a.projectTitle: Extra-Territorial Wastewater Service to the Islamic Center
ceqa-3b15739f458a7d5d7a.description: The purpose of this Project is to provide wastewater service to the Islamic Center of Jurupa Valley, a mosque located immediately adjacent to, but outside Jurupa Community Services District service area. The mosque currently relies on septic system for wastewater service because although the mosque is located within the Santa Ana River Water Company (SARWC) service area, the SARWC does not provide wastewater service. The proposed Project would install a new sewer main line to facilitate wastewater services to the mosque, eliminating its reliance of the existing septic system. The Project includes the installation of a new 8-inch diameter PVC sewer main line from an existing manhole, within the intersection of Etiwanda Avenue and 50th Street, to approximately 490 linear feet (LF) west, along 50th Street. The Project consists of trenching, backfill and compaction work to facilitate the installation of the sewer pipeline connection to JCSD’s existing sewer system. Restoration of surfaces to their original condition will be performed as well as protection of existing above and below grade facilities and utilities. Beneficiaries of the Project are the Islamic Center of Jurupa Valley a Jurupa Community Service District customer, and the mosque congregants.

ceqa-c7edf17ebe08b93883.projectTitle: Long Range Application No. LR26-0401, (PW25-07) Meadows Parkway Pavement Rehabilitation
ceqa-c7edf17ebe08b93883.description: The Meadows Parkway Pavement Rehabilitation proposes roadway maintenance and rehabilitation project to address pavement deficiencies on existing roadways. The roadway rehabilitation shall generally consist of grinding existing pavement followed by the installation of asphalt concrete leveling course,. a chip seal with asphalt rubber and aggregate membrane (ARAM), and asphalt concrete cap. ceqa-1fe5e689ea1e395ffc.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department will be conducting emergency repairs on Strawberry Creek Bridge (Bridge No. 56C0225, County Bridge No. M8113) which sustained damage to the barrier segment at the northeast corner of the bridge. The reinforced concrete post support detached from its base resulting in failure of the barrier system at the northeast corner. The scope of work includes the removal and disposal of debris, including removing damaged Hot Mix Asphalt surrounding the damaged post, the reconstruction of a reinforced concrete barrier post and the compaction of fill in the undermined and eroded cavity, the placement of new Hot Mix Asphalt over an aggregate base and the installation of a object marker sign. All repairs will occur at the northeast end of the bridge, which is a County maintained and located within the County Right-of-Way. ceqa-09ec5f52ac24c48511.name: Hexavalent Chromium-6 Mitigation Project
ceqa-09ec5f52ac24c48511.description: The Coachella Water Authority (CWA) is required to comply with state requirements to lower Cr-6 levels in drinking water by October 2027. The CWA proposed to implement a remediation program to reduce the levels of Chromium-6 (Hexavalent Chromium) in the City’s drinking water to 10 micrograms per liter (ug/l) as required by the State of California. The project will include retrofitting seven domestic water wells and the installation of wastewater discharge lines and three sewer line upgrades. The Project sites are located throughout the city with two sites located adjacent to city parks, while other sites are located within existing residential subdivisions and open lands. Well improvements will include filter and reduction vessels, additional chemical injection systems and electrical systems, on-site backwash tanks and discharge lines. preliminary design of each of the well sites’ treatment measures using reduction/coagulation/filtration (RCF) treatment technology. The RCF treatment process includes ferrous iron chemical injection to reduce Cr-6 to less soluble trivalent chromium (Cr(III) or Cr-3) through reduction contact vessels.

ceqa-f7c94f3af798f328ba.name: Hydropneumatic Tank Replacement Phase 3
ceqa-f7c94f3af798f328ba.description: The Coachella Valley Water District (CVWD) will replace two (2) existing steel hydropneumatic tanks at CVWD Booster Station 05505 (BS 05505) and 06730 (BS 06730) and rehabilitate one (1) hydropneumatic tank at CVWD Booster Station 06504 (BS 06504). BS 05505 (3,200 gallons) and BS 06730 (5,000 gallons) will be replaced with two (2) new 5,000-gallon tanks. The rehabilitation of BS 06504 will retain its 5,000-galon capacity. CVWD’s domestic water system relies on pressurized tank(s) to maintain domestic water pressure allows for booster pump(s) to cycle at appropriate intervals and reduces unnecessary over pumping during high demand. These three (3) tanks are in need of rehabilitation and replacement because the current tanks are deteriorating and corroding and run the risk of failure that can cause disruptions within the domestic water system. This project includes the manufacturing to fabrication of two new (2) hydropneumatic tanks (BS 05505 and 06730) and rehabilitation of one (1) hydropneumatics tank (BS 06504) using CVWD’s current system sizing parameters and coating specifications. Construction is anticipated for the duration of up to 280 calendar days and will start in September 2026. This project will require minimal excavation for the placement of structures and equipment. There will be no disruptions to water services during construction. BS 05505 is within the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto Mountains Conservation Areas and is subject to the CVMSHCP Conservation Measures and the CVWD established Operations and Maintenance manual. BS 05505 and 06730 are within the conservation areas of the Coachella Valley Multiple Species Habitat Conservation Plan (CVMSHCP); however, the sites are not subject to the CVMSHCP development mitigation fee because the sites are previously developed.
ceqa-f7c94f3af798f328ba.crossStreets: Jefferson St, La Quinta; Tepin Wy, Palm Desert, Falcon Pt, Rancho Mirage

ceqa-79644a3d1bea03d3df.name: Murrieta Creek Master Drainage Plan Line-E (MDP Line-E)
ceqa-79644a3d1bea03d3df.projectTitle: Murrieta Creek Master Drainage Plan Line-E (MDP Line-E)
ceqa-79644a3d1bea03d3df.description: This Project is divided into two distinct areas; the main channel area and the conservation area located at the northeastern corner of the channel (Figure 3). Area 1 – Main Channel The main channel area starts at Washington Avenue where a closed underground storm drain converts into an approximately 1,415 foot long unlined earthen channel. The earthen channel flows into a reinforced concrete box culvert underneath New Clay Street before discharging into Murrieta Creek. The box culvert is lined with a riprap armored apron for energy dissipation and erosion control. When the earthen channel was originally constructed, the design plans intended for the channel to be revegetated with native grassland species. A four foot swath of native grass was to be planted along the channel invert, while the remainder of the channel bed and banks were to be maintained free of vegetation to preserve hydrologic capacity. Current conditions differ substantially from the original design intent. The channel now supports emergent wetland vegetation buffered by a mature riparian forest and scrub community. Dominant riparian species include willow (Salix spp.), cottonwood (Populus fremontii), and mulefat (Baccharis salicifolia). Of particular concern, dense stands of cattails have become established in the channel invert and are expanding toward the banks. These stands are reducing conveyance capacity and causing water to pond during the dry season, leading to stagnant conditions. Routine maintenance is required to manage the spread of cattails and maintain intended channel function. Cattail population control will primarily involve selective application of aquatic approved herbicides. In addition, periodic vegetation management may also be needed to limit overgrowth of mature willows and cottonwoods along the banks to ensure adequate flood conveyance and reduce fuel loads. Area 2 – Conservation Area The conservation area consists of 400 feet long by 119 feet wide unmaintained earthen channel that was revegetated with native riparian species. This portion of the channel was designed to be a low-flow meandering drainage course adjacent to the main channel. Although the conservation area does not have an official conservation easement, vegetation within this area will be protected in place and no vegetation removal, trimming, or thinning is proposed. The only maintenance activity planned for this area is the selective application of herbicides to manage and control the expansion of cattail populations and non-native/invasive species.
ceqa-79644a3d1bea03d3df.crossStreets: Washington Avenue and New Clay Street

ceqa-2aa31734e4edf8a012.name: Change of Zone No. 2600012. Ordinance No. 348.5056 - Riverside County Land Use Ordinance. Additional Residential Accommodations Ordinance Update
ceqa-2aa31734e4edf8a012.projectTitle: Change of Zone No. 2600012. Ordinance No. 348.5056 - Riverside County Land Use Ordinance. Additional Residential Accommodations Ordinance Update
ceqa-2aa31734e4edf8a012.description: Change of Zone No. 2600012 - ORDINANCE NO. 348.5056 is a proposed text amendment to Ordinance No. 348, the Riverside County Land Use Ordinance, that would update regulations for Additional Residential Accommodations, update mobile home and manufactured home regulations and establish procedures allowing certain applications to be referred from the Director's Hearing to the Planning Commission. The amendment would reorganize Article XIXj (Additional Residential Accommodations), add Senate Bill (SB) 9 Units as a new housing type, and update development standards and procedures. The updated list of housing types would include: (1) Accessory Dwelling Units. (2) Junior Accessory Dwelling Units. (3) SB 9 Units, (4) Second Units, (5) Guest Quarters, (6) Ranchets, and (7) Multiple Owner Group Units. The amendment would remove mobile home-specific development standards and apply the same development standards as other one-family residences, consistent with State law. This amendment also amends administrative provisions in Article I to allow the Planning Director to elevate projects from a Director's Hearing to the Planning Commission as warranted. The proposed ordinance amendments would apply to all unincorporated areas of Riverside County.

ceqa-3fe7405adea6f125a4.description: On April 8, 2014, the Board of Supervisors approved Minute Order 3.11, a ten-year lease for office space consisting of approximately 40,353 square feet for the Riverside University Health System-Department of Public Health (RUHS-PH), for the leased premises located at 4210 Riverwalk Parkway Suites 110, 300, and 400, in Riverside (Lease). On August 6, 2019, the Board of Supervisors approved Minute Order 3.14 that reduced the premises to 29,341 square feet and extended the term of the Lease through July 31, 2026. The Second Amendment to Lease dated June 7, 2022 expanded the leased premises by an additional 18,227 square feet (Expanded Premises) to accommodate RUHS-PH program administration offices, increasing the total leased space to 47,568 square feet. This Third Amendment to the Lease (Third Amendment) reduces the total leased premises of 47,568 square feet by removing Suite 400, which consists of 22,117 square feet, excluding Suite 410, a 1,280-square-foot space located within Suite 400. As a result, the overall leased square footage is reduced to 26,731 square feet. The Third Amendment to the Lease Agreement with SchoolsFirst Credit Union, Riverside is identified as the proposed project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The proposed project would not result in an increase in capacity or physical expansion. No significant physical changes would occur as a result of the Third Amendment to the Lease Agreement.

The Green River Ranch Business Park Industrial Project (Project) includes a total of 78.87 acres of impacts, permanent and temporary, to undeveloped land. The Project includes the onsite construction of 50.53 acres associated with the Green River Ranch Business Park Industrial area which includes five proposed buildings, parking, and landscaping; grading of 2.57 acres of land that, after construction, will be established into an oak woodland mitigation area and protected by a conservation easement; and approximately 14.15 acres of grading associated with the creation of manufactured slopes for stabilization purposes and potential future residential development. If developed in the future, the 14.15-acre Estate Residential area is planned to accommodate a maximum of 32 residential lots. Offsite impacts, including both permanent and temporary, consist of 11.62 acres of improvements to roads and utilities and additional Business Park- Industrial uses. The Project will result in impacts to 78.87 acres of Crotch’s bumble bee (Bombus crotchii) habitat including temporary impacts to 2.57 acres; the Project will permanently remove 76.04 acres of Crotch’s bumble bee habitat. The project is expected to result in incidental take of Crotch’s bumble bee, which is designated as a candidate species under the California Endangered Species Act (CESA). The ITP referenced above as issued by CDFW authorizes incidental take of species listed under CESA that may occur as a result of Project implementation.

ceqa-bbf8c26d796784dd18.name: Adoption of Ordinance No. 861.3, an Ordinance of the County of Riverside Amending Ordinance 861 Establishing Procedures and Limited Delegation of Authority for
ceqa-bbf8c26d796784dd18.projectTitle: Adoption of Ordinance No. 861.3, an Ordinance of the County of Riverside Amending Ordinance 861 Establishing Procedures and Limited Delegation of Authority for
ceqa-bbf8c26d796784dd18.description: [title continued]: Leases and Licenses of Real Property, and Introduction of Ordinance 598.9, an Ordinance of the County of Riverside Amending Ordinance 598 Establishing Procedures and Delegating Authority for Disposition or Acquisition of Real Property Riverside County Ordinances 861 and 598 (Ordinances) were originally adopted by the Board of Supervisors (Board) in 1997 and later modified on April 13, 2021 (M.O. 3-10) and on April 27, 2021 (M.O. 3-10). These Ordinances granted delegated authority and provided efficiencies to the Department of Facilities Management and Transportation and Land Management Agency to execute certain real estate agreements pertaining to the acquisition, disposition, leasing, and licensing of real property. The Board adopted an order to initiate minor amendments to Ordinances 598 and 861 on July 28, 2026, and introduced the reading of Ordinances 598 and 861 on August 25, 2026. Since the last adoption of this ordinance, market conditions and the general increase in property values have raised the working threshold of smaller real estate transactions. The ordinances also require extension of expiration dates on certain purchase authority. The primary purpose of this Form 11 is to adopt Ordinances 861.3 and 598.9, incorporating these and related modifications into each of the Ordinances. These modifications are as follows: Ordinance 861.3 1. Authority is delegated to designated county officers, including the Assistant County Executive Officer over the Department of Facilities Management; Director and Assistant Director of the Department of Facilities Management, the TLMA Agency Director, the Director and Assistant Director of the TLMA, Transportation Department, and the Director of Airports of TLMA, Aviation Division to execute certain real estate documents including leases and licenses of real property. 2. Modifies the maximum monthly rental to $100,000 per month for leases or licenses of county owned real property subject to delegated authority. Ordinance 598.9 1. Authority is delegated to designated county officers, including the Assistant County Executive Officer over the Department of Facilities Management; Director and Assistant Director of the Department of Facilities Management, Director of Transportation, Assistant County Executive Officer/TLMA, the Director and Assistant Director of Transportation, TLMA, and the Airport Manager of TLMA, Aviation Division to execute certain acquisition and disposition agreements pertaining to real property. 2. Requires a Notice of Intention approved by the Board of Supervisors in the event County desires to acquire real property in which the acquisition price exceeds $750,000. 3. Authorizes the delegate to execute real estate agreements pertaining to acquisition of real property in which the acquisition price is $750,000 or less for the purpose of acquiring a public structure, facility, or a project. 4. Authorizes the delegate to execute real estate agreements pertaining to acquisition of real property pertaining specifically to a highway project in which the acquisition price is $750,000 or less. The adoption of the amendments to Riverside County Ordinances 861.3 and 598.9 were reviewed and determined to be not a project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to 15378. The Ordinances include the modification of procedures to the execution of real estate agreements pertaining to the acquisition, disposition, leasing, and licensing of real property which would result in the continuation of existing County operations and would not result in a significant effect on the environment.

ceqa-8fed6ca5da14d140c2.name: Office of Economic Development, Community Facilities District (CFD) No. 26-2M (Summit Ridge) of the County of Riverside; Adoption of Ordinance No. 1012, an Ordi
ceqa-8fed6ca5da14d140c2.projectTitle: Office of Economic Development, Community Facilities District (CFD) No. 26-2M (Summit Ridge) of the County of Riverside; Adoption of Ordinance No. 1012, an Ordi
ceqa-8fed6ca5da14d140c2.description: [title continued]: Ordinance of the County of Riverside Authorizing the Levy of a Special Tax Within the Summit Ridge CFD On January 27, 2015, the Board of Supervisors revised Board Policy B-12 entitled “Land Secured Financing Districts” to include “Service and Maintenance CFDs” to fund the ongoing maintenance of landscape, storm water Best Management Practices (BMP), street lighting, or other similar improvements and set goals and policies concerning Community Facilities Districts (CFD). As approved by voters, a special tax is to be levied on each individual parcel located within the boundary of the CFD to fund the costs associated with ongoing maintenance of landscape, storm water Best Management Practices (BMP), street lighting, or other similar improvements located within the designated boundaries of the CFD. SSP-HS Lot Option A Pool 02, L.P., and SSP-HS Lot Option A Pool 03, L.P., are the Owners of Tract Map 36504 and have petitioned that the County of Riverside Office of Economic Development assist them in forming a CFD to cover the costs associated with the maintenance of public improvements within the district. The boundaries of CFD No. 26-2M (Summit Ridge) will encompass the entire Tract Map No. 36504, which is projected to include 527 single-family residential units, none of which are currently occupied. On June 23, 2026, the County of Riverside Board of Supervisors approved Resolution No. 2026-063, a Resolution of Intention as the initial step for forming the CFD and declared the intention of the Board of Supervisors as required by the Mello-Roos Act of 1982 to levy a special tax to fund the service and maintenance functions requested by the Developer. On July 28, 2026, the County of Riverside Board of Supervisors held a public hearing to receive public comments and conduct a majority protest hearing concerning the establishment of the CFD and the levy of the special tax. At the conclusion of the public hearing, the Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution No. 2026-064, the Resolution of Formation of the CFD, which also authorized the levy of a special tax within the CFD subject to voter approval during a duly called election held that same day. On August 25, 2026, the Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution No. 2026-065 declaring the results of the election regarding the proposed special tax and finding that 100% of the votes cast were in favor of the levy of the special tax. Riverside County Ordinance No. 1012, which authorizes the levy of a special tax within the Summit Ridge CFD to fund services for maintenance and service activities, was reviewed and determined to be not a project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to 15378. The Ordinance includes the creation of a funding mechanism to provide maintenance and service activities within the CFD. No additional direct or indirect physical environmental impacts are anticipated from the provision of maintenance services identified in Riverside County Ordinance No. 1012.

ceqa-5c3a242fd246b37eef.name: Meadowbrook Market Commercial Project
ceqa-5c3a242fd246b37eef.description: The project proposes construction and operation of a neighborhood-serving commercial center totaling approximately 21,872 square feet of building area plus a 4,850 square foot fueling canopy. Five primary commercial components are included, consisting of a full-service market, a fueling station and convenience store with canopy; a quick-service drive-through restaurant, an automated carwash, and a multi-tenant retail building. Access will be provided from both State Route 74 and Greenwald Avenue. Street frontage improvements along Highway 74 and Greenwald Avenue will include curb, gutter, sidewalk, and landscaped parkways, designed to be consistent with the Highway 74 Multimodal Corridor Plan.

ceqa-9e0467f50e4b64e470.name: Disposition, Development and Loan Agreement for Camino Terrace (DDLA)
ceqa-9e0467f50e4b64e470.projectTitle: Disposition, Development and Loan Agreement for Camino Terrace (DDLA)
ceqa-9e0467f50e4b64e470.description: The Housing Authority of the County of Rivers ide (HACR) is the legal owner of a parcel of real property consisting of approximately 15.5 acres of residentially zoned real property located at the east side of Camino Real south of Lakeside Drive and north of Limonite Avenue in the City of Jurupa Valley, State of California, 92509 and referred to as APNs 185-460-001, 185-470-001 and 185-470-002 (HACR Parcel). Pursuant to applicable provisions of the Dissolution Law, the CRL and the "Housing Authorities Law" (California Health and Safety Code, Sections 34200, et seq.), notwithstanding any other provision of law, whenever the Board of Commissioners determines that any real property owned by the HACR can be used to provide housing affordable to low income families, and this use is in the HACR's best interest, the HACR may sell, convey or otherwise dispose of the real property to provide that affordable housing without complying with other provisions of Title 3, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 5, Article 8 of the California Government Code. The HACR is committed to providing affordable housing and services to the residents of the County of Riverside. Developer desires to acquire the HACR Parcel from the HACR to develop and construct approximately 79 units reserved for low-income families and individuals and one unrestricted on-site manager's unit, for a combined total of an eighty (80)-unit affordable housing project restricted for persons earning 80% or less of the area median income for the County of Riverside. Under the terms of the proposed Disposition, Development and Loan Agreement for the HACR Parcel, approximately forty-nine percent (49%) or thirty-nine (39) of the housing units developed and operated as part of the Project shall be rented to and occupied by low-income households earning 80 percent or less of the area median income for the County of Riverside. There is an unmet need for affordable housing within the County of Riverside. Consistent with applicable provisions of the Health and Safety Code and subject to the satisfaction of certain conditions precedent, the Property will be sold at fair market value. Developer shall be responsible for all (i) entitlements, land use approvals, permits and CEQA compliance, (ii) construction and development costs, (iii), securing financing, construction, on-site and off-site improvements, and (iv) property maintenance obligations. Developer intends to build an affordable housing project and proposes to transfer the parcel to a limited partnership entity in accordance with the Disposition, Development and Loan Agreement when sufficient financing has been secured. All land use and development entitlements, including compliance with CEQA must be obtained from the City of Jurupa Valley.

ceqa-30dc377b75359a28f9.name: Approval of Resolution 2026-165 - Authorization to Apply for Grants Funds through the Urban Greening Program at the Indio Fairgrounds Facility, Indio
ceqa-30dc377b75359a28f9.projectTitle: Approval of Resolution 2026-165 - Authorization to Apply for Grants Funds through the Urban Greening Program at the Indio Fairgrounds Facility, Indio
ceqa-30dc377b75359a28f9.description: In 2024, California voters approved Climate Bond Act, which will invest $10 billion in local projects that strengthen communities -- protecting drinking water, reducing wildfire and flood risks, restoring natural places, supporting healthy working lands, and expanding access to parks and outdoor spaces. Approximately $100 million has been allocated for Urban Greening Grants. Funding will be awarded in two competitive cycles, with $46,125,000 available for the first round commencing in 2026. Urban Greening projects use nature-based solutions—planting trees that provide strategic shade, expanding green spaces that serve as places of refuge during heat waves, and creating green streets and alleyways that capture and clean stormwater—to help communities become more climate resilient. The Urban Greening Grant Program will fund projects using nature-based solutions to mitigate climate change impacts such as the urban heat island effect, rising temperatures, and extreme heat. Grant funding priorities have been established and used as screening criteria for award. Projects providing meaningful benefits to vulnerable populations, disadvantaged communities and have the potential to successfully mitigate extreme heat are then invited to submit full proposals. The Department of Facilities Management submitted a concept proposal requesting $1,500,000 for urban greening enhancements to the Indio Fairgrounds. The proposal has advanced through the screening process and the County has been invited to submit a full proposal for consideration of grant funds. Projects that include local funding are awarded additional points through the competitive evaluation process, so the County is proposing a ten percent contribution of $166,667 to the enhancements for a total project cost of $1,666,667. As part of the proposal requirements, the Board is required to adopt Resolution 2026-165 which certifies that the County understands the assurances and certification in the application, certifies that the applicant or title holder will have sufficient funds to develop, operate and maintain the project consistent with the land tenure requirements; or will secure the resources to do so, and certifies that it will comply with the prevailing wage provisions of the California Labor Code. The approval of the resolution to apply for grant funds is defined as the proposed project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The project is the approval to apply for grant funds through the Urban Greening Program; no expansion of an existing facility or change in land use will occur. No additional direct or indirect physical environmental impacts are anticipated.

ceqa-e138c3c2e7a62050bc.name: Riverside University Health System Behavioral Health (RUHS-BH) Rustin Wall and Structural Analysis Project
ceqa-e138c3c2e7a62050bc.projectTitle: Riverside University Health System Behavioral Health (RUHS-BH) Rustin Wall and Structural Analysis Project
ceqa-e138c3c2e7a62050bc.description: The Riverside University Health System – Behavioral Health Rustin Office is located at 2085 Rustin Avenue in Riverside, California, and provides a multitude of essential services to the County, residents, and businesses. The proposed scope of work for the RUHS-BH Rustin Wall and Structural Analysis Project includes, but is not limited to, the selective demolition and modification of interior partitions to combine two existing meeting rooms (Rooms 101 and 139) into a single functional space by removing the existing full-height demising wall between the rooms, removing two existing single-leaf exit doors, and installing a new pair of double-leaf exit doors in place of the current single-leaf configuration. Additional improvements will include modifications to the existing ceiling system and lighting layout, as necessary, to accommodate the revised floor plan and maintain compliance with applicable building codes and standards. In addition, Bureau Veritas North America, Inc. will perform a structural evaluation of the building primary structural systems, including both gravity and seismic load-resisting components, and develop repair/retrofit measures where structural deficiencies are identified. Structural analysis and evaluation will be performed in accordance with California Existing Building Code (CEBC 2026) and ASCE 41-23 Seismic Evaluation and Retrofit of Existing Buildings, as applicable. The structural evaluation will be performed at the ASCE 41 Tier 1 / Tier 2 screening level unless additional analysis is authorized. The evaluation will primarily focus on the primary structural framing systems including roof framing, floor framing, diaphragms, and primary lateral force-resisting elements. The improvements to the Rustin facility is defined as the proposed project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The operation of the site will continue to provide public services at the existing facility and will not result in a significant expansion of existing use. No additional direct or indirect physical environmental impacts are anticipated.
ceqa-e138c3c2e7a62050bc.crossStreets: 2085 Rustin Avenue, north of Spruce Street

CZ2400019 is a proposal to modify and establish the Planning Area boundaries of Planning Areas 36 and 55 to be consistent with SP00286A09, and to modify the permitted uses and development standards for Planning Areas 36 and 55 in the Specific Plan Zoning Ordinance. TTM38917 is a Schedule "A" subdivision that would subdivide proposed Planning Areas 36 and 55 of SP286A9 to establish individual lots implementing the land uses proposed as part of SP286A9, including 66 single-family residential lots on 5.0 acres, 82 residential lots on 5.33 acres, a 0.44-acre water quality basin, a 0.86-acre park, on-site private streets on approximately 5.45 acres, and 2.43 acres of public right-of-way (ROW) dedications along the site's frontages with Moser Road, Benton Road, and Washington Street. ceqa-e6fe8b2c8f886f95c8.name: San Jacinto Commerce Center Specific Plan
ceqa-e6fe8b2c8f886f95c8.projectTitle: San Jacinto Commerce Center Specific Plan
ceqa-e6fe8b2c8f886f95c8.description: The proposed Project is located south of Ramona Boulevard (Record Road), east of Odell Street, west of Sanderson Avenue, and north of Cottonwood Avenue in the City of San Jacinto, Riverside County, California and is within Sections 17, 18, 19, 20, 29, and 30, Township 4 South and Range 1 West of the San Bernardino Baseline and Meridian. The Project Study Area is comprised of 660 acres consisting of a 514-acre On-Site Study Area encompassing Assessor’s Parcel Numbers (APNs): 432-030-006, 432-030-010, 432-030-011 and 432-030-012. The 146-acre Off-Site Study Areas are located within unimproved and partially improved rights-of-ways (ROWs). The proposed Project would replace the Villages of San Jacinto Specific Plan with the proposed San Jacinto Commerce Center Specific Plan (SJCCSP), amend the General Plan Land Use Map and Change the Zoning designations, provide an updated Zoning Ordinance, subdivide the On-Site Study Area into 19 parcels and propose a Development Agreement (DA). Approval of the proposed Project would provide a plan and pathway for future implementing development projects. The proposed Project includes the entitlements necessary for the planning of future industrial warehouse buildings along with associated parking, landscaping, amenity spaces, trails, bike paths; and infrastructure necessary to support future development on the approximately 514-acre On-Site Study Area. A portion of the approximately 146-acre Off-Site Study Area would be planned for future utilities and roadway improvements, necessary to support future implementing development. The intent of the SJCCSP is to provide high quality industrial land uses to serve existing and future residents, employees, and businesses of the City of San Jacinto and Riverside County. The land use plan has been designed to ensure economic viability, functional integrity, and a positive aesthetic impact on the surrounding community. The proposed SJCCSP would guide the buildout of the On-Site Study Area through two Development Scenarios consisting of eight or seven planning areas (PAs). The SJCCSP would provide for land uses with interrelated opportunities and consist of Industrial (I) , Public (P), and Flex-Use land use designations as well as two overlay areas as defined below. Industrial The Industrial land use designation would allow for a variety of industrial and manufacturing activities. Activities that do not generate significant amounts of pollution, including limited regional and sub-regional commercial activities that co-exist with surrounding land uses in a compatible manner would also be allowable, subject to the approval of a Conditional Use Permit. The SJCCSP also proposes “Good Neighbor” policies intended to provide the City and future implementing development projects with ways to ensure compatibility issues associated with warehouse, logistics and distribution facilities. These policies are designed to promote economic vitality and sustainability of businesses, while protecting the general health, safety, and welfare of the public that may be located within properties near or adjacent to the SJCCSP. A portion of industrial tenant space and Overlay areas as described below, may also be utilized for office, retail space, or ancillary support services. Other supporting uses that are determined to be compatible with the primary Industrial use may be allowed by the SJCCSP. The average overall intensity of development would provide a floor area ratio (FAR) of up to 0.55. Public The Public land use designation would allow for publicly-owned facilities and properties, including regional and subregional drainages, basins, and other public facilities. The SJCCSP would permit uses in these PAs that are determined to be compatible with the primary Public land use, including but not limited to open space areas, hiking, biking, or recreational spaces. Flex-Use The Flex-Use land use designation would offer flexibility in permitted land uses, providing for a range of uses based on evolving market conditions, technological changes, and community needs. The purpose of this designation is to support economic resilience by reducing commute distances, fostering mixed-use environments, optimizing land use, and reducing development barriers. This designation encourages integrated development that supports employment, housing, and services within a short distance to create a vibrant, self-sustaining community. It also incorporates design standards and guidelines to ensure compatibility among uses. Allowable land uses within the Flex-Use Zone include industrial and manufacturing uses, service retail trade, warehousing, education, business/professional uses, research/technology, and residential uses. The residential units allowable within the Flex-Use land use designation were already considered by the approved VSJ SP, Tentative Tract Map No. 38107, and 2040 General Plan, all anticipated residential development based on existing approvals and/or current land use designations within the Project Study Area so the residential uses permitted within the Flex-Use land use designation are no different than the residential land uses previously contemplated. The SJCCSP also includes two Overlays which would allow for additional uses as permitted by the SJCCSP to certain PA’s or additional design requirements as defined below: - Industrial Support Overlay (ISO). This overlay would allow for industrial/business support services, including, but not limited to food service, gas stations, and limited retail uses within the SJCCSP without affecting the integrity of areas available for industrial uses. - Sanderson Avenue Restricted Overlay (SO). This overlay is intended to provide additional design guidance to support the corridor along Sanderson Avenue. The SO would restrict certain heavier industrial and outdoor uses by establishing a maximum building height of 60 feet from within the first 300 feet of Sanderson Avenue. If a portion of a building falls within the Sanderson Overlay area, the restrictions would apply to any outdoor component of the use within the 300 foot-buffer along the eastern boundary of the On-Site Study Area along Sanderson Avenue since this stretch has the potential for significant visual impacts. Drainage infrastructure within the SO would require landscape screening. The SJCCSP would also include open space areas, amenity areas, requirements for pedestrian connections, and a proposed 12-foot-wide trail along Sanderson Avenue. The proposed Project could be implemented under two different future development scenarios. Depending upon market conditions and availability of specific tenants, the Specific Plan would accommodate varying industrial intensities. Scenario 1 land uses assume no cold storage uses. Scenario 2 land uses assume up to 1.2 million square feet of cold storage uses. Development Scenario 1 Under Development Scenario 1, PA’s 1 through 4 would be designated Industrial (I) allowing up to 7,500,000 square feet of industrial land uses, as well as related supporting land uses as permitted by the SJCCSP. PA’s 5, 6A, and 6B would be designated Public (P) and provide for flood control and open space land uses. Planning Area 7 would be designated Flex-Use (F) allowing up to 1,500,000 square feet of industrial land uses as well as related supporting land uses as permitted by the SJCCSP or a maximum of 532 residential dwelling units (which were already contemplated), and/or a mix of retail trade and services as permitted by the SJCCSP. Planning Areas 2 through 4 and 7 are also part of the Sanderson Avenue Restricted Use Overlay (SO) while PA 4 is also part of the Industrial Support Overlay (ISO). Under Development Scenario 1, a maximum of 9 million square feet of industrial land uses and related supporting land uses are permitted by the SJCCSP. Development Scenario 2 Under Development Scenario 2, PA’s 1 through 4 would be designated Industrial (I) and PA 7 would be designated Flex-Use (F) allowing for a maximum of approximately 6.9 million square feet of industrial land uses that include cold storage, as well as related supporting land uses as permitted by the SJCCSP. The cold storage use would be an allowable use within PA's 1 through 4 under Development Scenario 2 and is anticipated to occur primarily within PA3. However, cold storage uses may develop within any of the PA’s designated Industrial within Development Scenario 2 provided the overall maximum cold storage square footage does not exceed 1.2 million square feet. Planning Area 7 would be designated Flex-Use (F) allowing up to 1,500,000 square feet of industrial land uses as well as related supporting land uses as permitted by the SJCCSP or a maximum of 532 residential dwelling units (which were already contemplated), and/or a mix of retail trade and services as permitted by the SJCCSP. PA’s 5, 6A, and 6B would be designated Public (P) and provide for flood control and open space land uses. Planning Areas 2 through 4 are also part of the Sanderson Avenue Restricted Use Overlay (SO) while PA 4 is also part of the Industrial Support Overlay (ISO). Infrastructure The proposed Project would require on- and off-site infrastructure improvements related to roadways and utilities. On-Site infrastructure improvements that may be required from future implementing development projects would include utility alignments/connections and roadway improvements within the On-Site Study Area. Off-site improvements include those necessary for roadway improvements and connections/alignments for utilities. Vehicular Access Primary vehicular access would be provided from Sanderson Avenue along the proposed Project’s eastern boundary, and Ramona Boulevard/Record Road along the northern boundary. De Anza Drive and Bridge Street would provide east and west access through the proposed Project. Additional access would be provided by Cawston Avenue, which traverses the center of the proposed Project, linking Ramona Boulevard/Record Road to the north with De Anza Drive and Bridge Street to the south. Under Development Scenario 2, segments of Cawston Avenue and Bridge Street would be removed from the General Plan Circulation Element. A segment of Cawston Avenue between De Anza Drive and Bridge Street and a segment of Bridge Street between Sanderson and Cawston Avenues, would be removed as General Plan roadways. These two streets would instead, terminate within the On-Site Study Area. Water The proposed Project is located within the service area of Eastern Municipal Water District (EMWD) for potable, recycled water, and wastewater treatment. Eastern Municipal Water District (EMWD) would provide potable water service to the proposed Project from the existing 12-inch diameter waterline located in Sanderson Avenue. New 12-inch to 18-inch diameter facilities are proposed in Cawston Avenue, De Anza Drive, Ramona Boulevard/Record Road, and Bridge Street. All existing groundwater wells within the On-Site Study Area would be properly abandoned with the development of the proposed Project. All new water lines located in new or existing public rights-of-way would be maintained by EMWD. Not related to providing potable water service directly to the proposed Project, but an adjacent source of important potable water supplies to southern California is the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California’s (MWD) Colorado River Aqueduct, Casa Loma Barrel 1 (or Siphon) and San Diego Pipeline 1 and Pipeline 2. Areas of off-site improvements may intersection with MWD fee land. Any improvements or construction within MWD’s right of way or fee areas, will require MWD approvals. The proposed Project would receive recycled water service from EMWD for outdoor irrigation purposes. The nearest point of connection is an existing 42-inch diameter EMWD recycled water pipeline located approximately 30-feet from the southern boundary of the On-Site Study Area. The on-site recycled water plan to serve the proposed Project’s land uses has pipelines of diameters ranging from 2-inches to 8-inches totaling approximately 20,337 linear feet. The maximum irrigation peak recycled water demand for buildout of the proposed Project is 308 acre-feet per year (AFY). EMWD produces and distributes recycled water at the San Jacinto Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility. Sewer The City of San Jacinto Public Utilities Department is responsible for overseeing the City’s Sewer Collection System consisting of main sewer lines. All City sewage is transferred to EMWD’s treatment plant. EMWD would provide sewer treatment service to the proposed Project from the existing 30-inch diameter sewer trunk line located in Ramona Boulevard/Record Road. Installation of10-inch to 18-inch diameter sewer lines throughout the On-Site Study Area would be connected to existing sewer lines. All sewer lines located in new or existing public rights-of-way would be maintained by the City. Storm Drain The proposed Project would construct a new back-bone system of storm drain pipelines with laterals in Cawston Avenue, De Anza Road, and Bridge Street that are collectively referred to as “Line V,” which would range in size from 18-inch to 126-inch diameter for a total length of approximately 14,200 LF. Line V would drain up to 369 cubic feet per second (cfs) on-site stormwater runoff to the proposed Hydrologic Conditions of Concern (HCOC) Basin to be constructed within Planning Area 5. The unlined HCOC Basin provides storage capacity instead of direct stormwater quality treatment. Each future implementing project of the SJCCSP would provide stormwater treatment for its proportion of runoff generated prior to flowing to the HCOC Basin. To regulate the rate of flow out of the HCOC Basin, a pump station would be constructed, and flows would go to the reinforced concrete box (RCB) culvert that would cross Ramona Boulevard/Record Rd. The culvert would be sized for 536 cfcs to accommodate the developed flows of the proposed Project. To convey off-site flows that come onto the proposed Project during a regional flooding event from the area that is southeast of Sanderson Avenue, the proposed Project would also construct Line 2, a segment of a future MDP facility (SJV MDP Line E) and an unlined Confluence Basin. Line 2 would be a concrete-lined flood control channel and culverts to collect and convey the FEMA-established 100-year storm event flood flows from the San Jacinto Reservoir through the proposed Project and outlet into the proposed Confluence Basin located on-site and directly adjacent to the HCOC Basin. Line 2 and the Confluence Basin would be the on-site component of a future MDP facility that extends out from the Project and constructed by others. The Confluence Basin is the terminus of Line 2. The Confluence Basin provides storage capacity and would also be drained at a controlled rate using the proposed pump station. ceqa-952b1190d8e2419a6f.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department (County) is proposing to construct a parking shade structure at its Thermal Maintenance Yard in Thermal, Riverside County. The maintenance yard is located at 86199 Airport Boulevard, approximately 720 feet east of the intersection of Tyler Street and Higgins Drive. The proposed parking shade structure will involve a cantilever structure and will replace the existing pavement surface with reinforced concrete placement. All work will occur within previously disturbed or developed portions of the facility. Additional improvements include: • Removal of asphalt concrete pavement and construction of concrete pavement • Reconstruction of asphalt concrete pavement • Dewatering of ground water as needed • Stripping of parking stalls • Clearing and grubbing of any vegetation (including trees) • Utility potholing • Any additional work required to complete the activity, which may include minor construction-related tasks such as installing traffic control, implementing dust-prevention measures, compacting base and asphalt during reconstruction, performing inspector-directed miscellaneous work, or saw-cutting pavement. All improvements are proposed within the existing County right of way; therefore, no additional right of way or temporary construction easements or permits will be required to construct the proposed improvements.

ceqa-d939264da56e9c16ca.name: Van Buren Blvd. Resurfacing Project
ceqa-d939264da56e9c16ca.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department is proposing to resurface approximately 3,300 feet (0.62 miles) of Van Buren Blvd. from Opportunity Way to 440 feet south of the I-215 Northbound Off Ramp located in the community of Arnold Heights, Riverside County. The County of Riverside General Plan classifies Van Buren Blvd in the project area. as an Urban Arterial Road (152’ ROW), Major Road (118’ ROW), Secondary Road (100’ ROW). Van Buren at Opportunity Way is a ten-lane road and transitions to a Major Road, then a Secondary Road and ranges from 100 to 152 feet wide with a mix of curb and gutter, asphalt dike and edge of pavement. The proposed project will include removing the existing roadway followed by paving back with hot mix asphalt (HMA). The proposed project will also include: • Construct concrete sidewalk • Remove and replace asphalt dike • Remove turf and install rock blanket • Utility adjustments • Striping of roadway, including pavement markers and reflectors • Removal and installation of road signs • Removal and installation of Inductive Loop Detectors • Upgrading existing signal backplates to include yellow reflective border at the intersection of Van Buren Boulevard and Opportunity Way. All improvements are proposed within the existing right of way. No additional right of way or Temporary Construction Easements will be required to construct the proposed improvement. A Permit to Enter and Construct will be required from the Riverside National Cemetery to modify the existing landscaping and irrigation affected by the new concrete sidewalk installation within a small portion of the cemetery.

ceqa-6ce0219dd4b281c637.name: Approval of Lease Agreement with Canyon Springs Plaza Limited Partnership, and the Riverside University Health System (RUHS) at 12125 Day Street, Moreno Valley

ceqa-6ce0219dd4b281c637.description: On August 1, 2023, the Board of Supervisors approved Minute Order 3.80 authorizing Facilities Management Real Estate (FM-RE) to locate suitable office space for RUHS throughout the County. Facilities Management - Real Estate (FM-RE) has searched for suitable medical and or behavioral health clinic space. FM-RE issued a Request for Proposal (RFP) and received submittals from various landlords. Canyon Springs Plaza Limited Partnership, a California limited partnership (Landlord), was selected for its existing building known as the Canyon Springs Plaza located at 12125 Day Street, Suite U205A, Moreno Valley. The 10,656 square foot suite will accommodate RUHS's program needs by providing improved and more efficient employee workspace to deliver services to this region and community. A new lease agreement (Lease) for a 5-year term will commence upon completion of tenant improvements and issuance of the Certificate of Occupancy. The improvements requested include a new lobby and reception area to accommodate staff and the public, exam rooms, offices, conference room, breakroom, large supply room, restrooms, two vital rooms and an open space for workstations. The work will be contracted and paid for by the Landlord and the County will reimburse the Landlord monthly. The occupancy of the facility by RUHS is anticipated to commence October 2026. The Lease Agreement is defined as the proposed project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The project is limited to the Lease of an existing building, with minor interior improvements, and no expansion of the existing facility will occur. The operation of the facility will continue to provide public health services. No additional direct or indirect physical environmental impacts are anticipated.

ceqa-60ca04df93dc28571f.description: Anza Electric Cooperative's Anza Rural Resilience Microgrid Initiative project will expand the capacity of the pre-existing BESS supporting AEC’s 3.4 MW solar PV microgrid. It will provide additional stored energy to support critical community and tribal facilities during extended outages and improve service reliability for members located in the Anza region of Riverside County, including the Cahuilla Band of Indians. By increasing available storage capacity, the project will reduce the frequency and duration of service interruptions and improve system performance during periods of high electric demand. The added BESS will also help manage peak load by storing solar generation and discharging during times of elevated system stress.
