ceqa-7bde0cb46a95aa4fc2.projectTitle: Approval of Fifth Amendment to Master License and Operating Agreement with Family Services Association at Norton Younglove Community Center, James A. Venable Co
ceqa-7bde0cb46a95aa4fc2.description: [PROJECT TITLE CONTINUED]: Venable Community Center and Lakeland Village Community Center, and Lakeland Village Sports Park On May 9, 2017, the Board of Supervisors approved Minute Order 3.10, the Master License and Operating Agreement by and between the County of Riverside (County) and Family Service Association (FSA) for operations of the Norton Younglove Community Center, James A. Venable Community Center/Cabazon Child Development Center and Eddie Dee Smith Senior Center (Agreement). The Agreement was for a term of approximately three years expiring June 30, 2020. During the term of this Agreement, FSA is required to provide community center services which include youth, adult, and senior programs as outlined and further described within the Agreement. The scope of those services includes community, recreational, healthcare, child development, and food programs. On July 2, 2019, the Board of Supervisors approved Minute Order 3.6, the First Amendment to the Agreement. This First Amendment served to refine and improve the Agreement and to formally address the necessity for background checks and confidentiality with all Community Center Operators. On June 30, 2020, the Board of Supervisors approved Minute Order 3.16, the Second Amendment to the Agreement. A Second Amendment extended the term for three years and transferred the Eddie Dee Smith Senior Center to the City of Jurupa Valley on June 30, 2020, removing this facility from the scope of the Agreement through the Second Amendment. On June 27, 2023, a Third Amendment, extended the term an additional three years and reduced the square footage of the James A. Venable space, by excluding the Board of Supervisors 5th District space. On December 16, 2025, a Fourth Amendment was adopted, adding the Lakeland Village Community Center and Library to the Agreement, increasing compensation to account for the new Center. Facilities Management-Real Estate (FM-RE) now proposes to update the Agreement through a Fifth Amendment which would expand services at the Lakeland Village Community Center to include the Lakeland Village Sports Park to provide community, senior, childcare and recreations programs and increase the compensation to account for the addition of the Lakeland Village Sports Park. The Fifth Amendment to the Agreement is defined as the proposed project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The project is for the use of existing facilities and no expansion of the existing facility will occur. The operation of the facilities will continue to provide community services. No additional direct or indirect physical environmental impacts are anticipated.

ceqa-99adac2d664f1e1ed4.name: Introduction of Ordinance No. 861.3, an Ordinance of the County of Riverside Amending Ordinance 861 Establishing Procedures and Limited Delegation of Authority
ceqa-99adac2d664f1e1ed4.projectTitle: Introduction of Ordinance No. 861.3, an Ordinance of the County of Riverside Amending Ordinance 861 Establishing Procedures and Limited Delegation of Authority
ceqa-99adac2d664f1e1ed4.description: [PROJECT TITLE CONTINUED]: for Leases and Licenses of Real Property, and Introduction of Ordinance 598.9, an Ordinance of the County of Riverside Amending Ordinance 598 Establishing Procedures and Delegating Authority for Disposition or Acquisition of Real Property Riverside County Ordinances 861 and 598 (Ordinances) were originally adopted by the Board of Supervisors (Board) in 1997 and later modified on April 13, 2021 (M.O. 3-10) and on April 27, 2021 (M.O. 3-10). These Ordinances granted delegated authority and provided efficiencies to the Department of Facilities Management and Transportation and Land Management Agency to execute certain real estate agreements pertaining to the acquisition, disposition, leasing, and licensing of real property. The Board adopted an order to initiate minor amendments to Ordinances 598 and 861 on July 28, 2026, and introduced the reading of Ordinances 598 and 861 on August 25, 2026. Since the last adoption of this ordinance, market conditions and the general increase in property values have raised the working threshold of smaller real estate transactions. The ordinances also require extension of expiration dates on certain purchase authority. The primary purpose of this Form 11 is to introduce Ordinance 861.3 and 598.9, incorporating these and related modifications into each of the Ordinances. These modifications are as follows: Ordinance 861.3 1. Authority is delegated to designated county officers, including the Assistant County Executive Officer over the Department of Facilities Management; Director and Assistant Director of the Department of Facilities Management, the TLMA Agency Director, the Director and Assistant Director of the TLMA, Transportation Department, and the Director of Airports of TLMA, Aviation Division to execute certain real estate documents including leases and licenses of real property. 2. Modifies the maximum monthly rental to $100,000 per month for leases or licenses of county owned real property subject to delegated authority. Ordinance 598.9 1. Authority is delegated to designated county officers, including the Assistant County Executive Officer over the Department of Facilities Management; Director and Assistant Director of the Department of Facilities Management, Director of Transportation, Assistant County Executive Officer/TLMA, the Director and Assistant Director of Transportation, TLMA, and the Airport Manager of TLMA, Aviation Division to execute certain acquisition and disposition agreements pertaining to real property. 2. Requires a Notice of Intention approved by the Board of Supervisors in the event County desires to acquire real property in which the acquisition price exceeds $750,000. 3. Authorizes the delegate to execute real estate agreements pertaining to acquisition of real property in which the acquisition price is $750,000 or less for the purpose of acquiring a public structure, facility, or a project. 4. Authorizes the delegate to execute real estate agreements pertaining to acquisition of real property pertaining specifically to a highway project in which the acquisition price is $750,000 or less. The introduction of the Amendments to Riverside County Ordinances 861.3 and 598.9 were reviewed and determined to be not a project under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to 15378. The Ordinances include the modification of procedures to the execution of real estate agreements pertaining to the acquisition, disposition, leasing, and licensing of real property which would result in the continuation of existing County operations and would not result in a significant effect on the environment.

ceqa-a5f2cf4866ac2b500f.name: County of Riverside Roadway Safety Action Plan
ceqa-a5f2cf4866ac2b500f.projectTitle: County of Riverside Roadway Safety Action Plan
ceqa-a5f2cf4866ac2b500f.description: The County of Riverside Safety Plan (RivCo SAP) is a planning study for possible future action. The Plan has three (3) main goals: analyze the existing safety conditions or roadway network in unincorporated Riverside County, identify potential transportation safety improvements, and reduce and eventually eliminate severe injuries and fatalities on roads in unincorporated Riverside County. Additionally, the Plan is meant to be a roadmap that improves transportation safety throughout the County. This Plan does not impose any requirements on others or the County but serves to provide information and guidance for any possible future transportation improvements to the transportation network and infrastructure in the unincorporated Riverside County region. Such transportation improvements have been considered and evaluated in the County of Riverside's Environmental Impact Report No. 521 for its General Plan Amendment No. 960 which was certified by adoption of Resolution No. 2015-259 on December 8, 2015, M.O. 3-54 by the Riverside County Board of Supervisors. The Plan was reviewed to ensure consistency with the County's General Plan. This Plan does not commit funding or approve any implementing safety-oriented infrastructure improvements but merely adopts a safety plan to aid in efforts to achieve the goals described in the Plan.

Accordingly, DEH desires to temporarily extend the Lease for an additional two-year term through a Third Amendment to Lease (Third Amendment) to ensure continuity of operations while the County completes the solicitation process and secures a suitable replacement location. The Third Amendment to the Lease Agreement is identified as the proposed Project under California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The leased premise consists of approximately 13,482 square feet and the proposed Project is the letting of property involving existing facilities; no expansion of an existing use will occur. ceqa-fadf75513b9069d938.name: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Moreno Valley for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle.
ceqa-fadf75513b9069d938.projectTitle: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Moreno Valley for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle.
ceqa-fadf75513b9069d938.description: The California Energy Commission (CEC) adopts and regularly updates regulations that define a process for local governments to apply to the CEC to make certain findings regarding locally adopted energy conservation or energy insulation standards (California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 and section 10-110; Public Resources Code (PRC) section 25402.1(h)(2)). The local government’s proposed standards are often referred to as the Local Reach Codes and require local governments to submit an application to the CEC consistent with the requirements listed in section 10-106(b). Before the local standards may be enforced, the CEC must make the following findings pursuant to PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and as listed in section 10-106(a): 1) The proposed local standards will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Energy Code, and 2) The local government has filed the basis of its cost-effectiveness determination with the CEC. On September 4, 2025, the City of Moreno Valley (the City) submitted an application to the CEC that included: 1) the basis of its determination that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 1030 are cost-effective; and (2) documentation that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 1030 will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Energy Code), as required by PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and by CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106. Based on the information submitted, staff analysis, and the Executive Director's recommendation, the CEC approved findings of City of Moreno Valley’s section 10-106 application at the CEC’s August 17, 2026, Business Meeting.

ceqa-1f0403f2fe3a2a3aaf.name: Lake Skinner Regional Water Transmission System Project
ceqa-1f0403f2fe3a2a3aaf.projectTitle: Lake Skinner Regional Water Transmission System (formerly EM-11)
ceqa-1f0403f2fe3a2a3aaf.description: The Project includes construction and operation of three main components: (1) a new water service connection (also referred to as a turnout) to transfer treated water deliveries from Metropolitan’s Skinner Water Treatment Plant (WTP) to the District; (2) a new booster pump station that would connect to the turnout to pump water to the EMWD’s service area; and (3) 14 miles of new and relined transmission pipelines to deliver water from Skinner WTP to EMWD's service area. Collectively, these components comprise the Project and would be sized to meet build out demand of 140 cubic feet per second of additional treated water supplies. The four-phased project would be fully online by 2045.

ceqa-697368f285898e8e68.name: ZTA2026-0001 Landscape and Fencing Ordinance Update

ceqa-697368f285898e8e68.description: ZTA2026-0001 amends Chapter 17.70 of the Corona Municipal Code to update the City of Corona's water-efficient landscape requirements and Landscape Design Guidelines to ensure consistency with 2015 and 2025 changes to the State of California Model Water Efficient Landscape Ordinance (MWELO). The amendment also updates fence and wall standards in Chapter 17.70 to reflect advancements in fencing materials and design, providing greater flexibility for property owners. ceqa-ec5c8cd2f34b7f2382.name: City of Riverside Adaptive Re-Use Ordinance
ceqa-ec5c8cd2f34b7f2382.projectTitle: City of Riverside Adaptive Re-Use Ordinance
ceqa-ec5c8cd2f34b7f2382.description: The project consists of adoption of an Adaptive Reuse Ordinance establishing regulations and incentives to facilitate the conversion of existing nonresidential buildings to residential uses within designated areas of the City. The Ordinance implements housing goals and policies in the General Plan and applies to existing buildings and establishes objective standards under which qualifying adaptive reuse projects may be permitted, subject to applicable limitations. The Ordinance facilitates the reuse and reconfiguration of existing building envelopes and includes limited provisions for modest and incidental building additions consistent with existing zoning regulations. The Ordinance does not approve or authorize any specific development project.

ceqa-044b3943b0de7ae389.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department is proposing to construct approximately 420 feet of Willsie Drive from Borchard Road to the end of Willsie Dr. Willsie Drive is currently classified in the County of Riverside’s General Plan as a local road. Willsie Drive is an approximately 26-foot-wi de dirt road and the proposed improvements will maintain the same width. The proposed project will include grading and moisture conditioning the roadway width and paving with Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA). Additional improvements include: • Asphalt Concrete Pavement • Pavement Delineation, pavement markings, and reflectors • Removal and installation of signs • Vegetation (trees and bushes) trimming and/or stump removal Additional right-of-way or temporary construction easements (TCE) will not be required to construct the proposed improvements.

ceqa-18d8303d9a88e181a0.name: William Collier Elementary School Modular Classrooms Project
ceqa-18d8303d9a88e181a0.projectTitle: William Collier Elementary School Modular Classrooms Project
ceqa-18d8303d9a88e181a0.description: The proposed project includes the installation of four modular classrooms on the southeast portion of the campus, north of the existing modular classrooms. The four modular classrooms would be relocated from Terra Cotta Middle School (MS). The modular classrooms would meet the current needs of the campus and would not increase the student enrollment of William Collier ES. The proposed project would require the removal, relocation, and reinstallation of existing playground equipment. The proposed project would disturb less than one acre of the project site. The proposed project would be constructed in two phases over approximately one month during Summer 2026. Phase 1 would consist of the removal, relocation, and reinstallation of existing playground equipment; grading, trenching, construction of concrete and asphalt pavement; hydroseeding the turf to match existing species; modifying or adding irrigation pipes and heads as necessary; and constructing redwood headers and truncated domes. The proposed project would include utility trenching that would connect to existing utility lines at the existing campus. Phase 2 would consist of the construction of the asphalt landing transition, installation of a landing and ramp, the construction of the condensate drywell and installation of the modular classrooms from Terra Cotta MS. No trees will need to be removed during construction.

ceqa-788e396416823b2441.name: Lester Water Treatment Plant Backwash Tank Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-788e396416823b2441.projectTitle: Lester Water Treatment Plant Backwash Tank Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-788e396416823b2441.description: The Lester Water Treatment Plant (WTP) Backwash Tank Rehabilitation Project consists of rehabilitation of the existing backwash tank to restore structural integrity and improve long-term operational reliability. The project includes demolition and replacement of the existing welded steel roof with a new press-brake steel roof system, structural steel improvements, interior and exterior tank coating rehabilitation, piping modifications, structural repairs, testing, startup, and commissioning. The rehabilitation will extend the service life of the existing facility, improve treatment plant reliability, and ensure continued delivery of safe and reliable drinking water for the residents of the City of Corona.

ceqa-92495eebf56c009512.name: Running Deer Estates Flood Control Channel Maintenance (Streambed Alteration Agreement No. EPIMS-RIV-62145-R6)
ceqa-92495eebf56c009512.projectTitle: Tentative Map Tract No. 31957; Lake Elsinore Highlands; MND 2005-06
ceqa-92495eebf56c009512.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed and issued Lake and Streambed Alteration Agreement (EPIMS-RIV-62145-R6), pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1602, to the project Applicant, Larry Liebel. The Project is limited to the routine maintenance, as needed, of the existing soil-cement armored flood control embankments on the southwest bank of Rice Canyon Wash to preserve the hydraulic capacity and structural integrity of the flood control embankment to convey a 100- year storm event past the Project site. Routine maintenance activities include: Hand and limited mechanical clearing of vegetation and debris within the hydraulic and structural envelope, removal of localized sediment bars that reduce capacity or redirect flow toward the bank, repair of localized soil-cement damage by cleaning, pre-moistening, and replacing with soil-cement or approved patch to match the existing profile, re-establishment toe-down to the design scour depth where undermining is observed, abatement and backfilling of animal burrows in the face or toe, and routine upkeep of inlets, outlets, and transitions. Routine maintenance will be conducted using both hand tools and larger machinery. The hand tools that will be used include chain saws and larger machinery that will include rubber-tired or low-ground-pressure mini-excavator or skid-steer, and water truck. Equipment will primarily be operated from the existing developed or disturbed areas outside of CDFW jurisdiction; however, work on the slope revetment may require equipment to access and operate within the channel at the toe of the slope within the District's easement. In addition, a standard dump truck will be used to dispose of any debris and trash in the Project site

ceqa-c809fdd5b7f68ef6d8.name: City of Norco 2050 General Plan Update Project
ceqa-c809fdd5b7f68ef6d8.projectTitle: City of Norco 2050 General Plan Update Project
ceqa-c809fdd5b7f68ef6d8.description: The City is preparing a comprehensive update of the Norco General Plan. The proposed 2050 General Plan includes updates of the following elements required by State Planning and Zoning Law: (1) Land Use and Community Character, including the Land Use Map; (2) Circulation; (3) Infrastructure and Facilities; (4) Open Space and Conservation; (5) Safety; and (6) Noise. The 2050 General Plan will include Goals, Policies, and implementation actions developed based on community outreach to advance the City’s vision and community priorities. The City is largely developed at this time with residential agricultural, animal-keeping neighborhoods with a rural, equestrian-oriented atmosphere. Commercial uses in the City are primarily located along Sixth Street, Hamner Avenue, and River Road. The 2050 General Plan includes Goals, Policies, and implementation actions developed through community outreach to advance the City's vision and community priorities. The General Plan is intended to preserve the rural, equestrian-oriented atmosphere of Norco's residential agricultural, animal-keeping neighborhoods; support local businesses; establish a more prominent downtown consistent with the community's identity; maintain and enhance parks, public facilities, and open space; improve transportation and public safety; and strengthen Norco as a destination for equestrian, agricultural, and recreational experiences while addressing current planning needs and State planning requirements.

ceqa-424193cda5fa4145d3.name: 36-Inch Recycled Line Emergency Repair
ceqa-424193cda5fa4145d3.description: Eastern Municipal Water District's(EMWD) 36-inch transmission recycled water pipeline was recently discovered to be leaking near the Murrieta Creek. This transmission pipeline is an essential part of Temecula Valley Regional Water Reclamation Facility's (TVRWRF) recycled water. The purpose of the proposed project is to identify the section of the pipeline that has experienced failure and conduct repairs. If the transmission line is left unrepaired, there is a potential for rupture which could result in the release of significant quantities of recycled water into the Murrieta Creek, potentially leading to significant erosion. It may also damage other recycled water lines that convey water from the TVRWRF. Overall, the potential for pipe rupture poses an imminent threat to life and property. To identify and repair the section of failing pipeline, the pipeline needs to be isolated, excavation needs to occur, and restoration of the excavated area would happen once repaired. The location of the damaged section of pipeline is located near Murrieta Creek. Excavation would happen on the south levee outside Murrieta Creek channel and would be restored. Due to the imminent threat to life and property posed by the potential rupture of the pipeline, EMWD has been working with regulatory agencies to notify of the emergency action. These agencies include California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Regional Water Quality Control Board, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and Riverside County Flood Control.

ceqa-02bf5850ad7622b318.name: Copper Basin Valve Replacement and Access Road Improvements Project (California Endangered Species Act Incidental Take Permit No. 2081(b)-2025-066-06 (ITP))

ceqa-02bf5850ad7622b318.agency: Metropolitan Water District of Southern California
ceqa-02bf5850ad7622b318.agencyName: Metropolitan Water District of Southern California
ceqa-02bf5850ad7622b318.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has issued an ITP (No. 2081(b)- 2025-066-06), pursuant to Section 2081(b) of the Fish and Game Code to The Metropolitan Water District of Southern California. The Project will rehabilitate the emergency slide gate valve and replace the discharge valve within the Copper Basin Dam valve house; install new conduit and electrical components; install new concrete pads; replace the ladder on the dam face; install a new catwalk and stairs; remove and reconstruct two concrete weirs. The Project will also improve the existing 1.66-mile, existing dirt access road that runs around the perimeter of Copper Basin Reservoir. The Project will result in temporary, indirect impacts to 2.38 square kilometers of Desert bighorn sheep (Ovis canadensis nelsonii) habitat. The project is expected to result in incidental take of Desert bighorn sheep, which is/are designated as a fully protected species in Fish and Game Code section 4700, subdivision (b). Section 4700 of the Fish and Game Code prohibits the take of fully protected mammals specified in Fish and Game Code section 4700, subdivision (b). However, for qualifying projects, CDFW may authorize the take of any such species by permit pursuant to the conditions set forth in Fish and Game Code section 2081.15, subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (d)The California Endangered Species Act (CESA) ITP referenced above is issued by CDFW pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 2081.15. and authorizes incidental take of Desert bighorn sheep that may occur as a result of Project implementation.

ceqa-271f9d134fb8485200.name: Skyline Heights Project (SP2025-0001 and Resubmitted TTM36544)
ceqa-271f9d134fb8485200.description: The Skyline Heights Project is a proposal to revise a previously approved tentative tract map (TIM 36544) from 2017, which was originally for the subdivision of 271 acres into 292 lots for single family development. The project site is located southwest of Foothill Parkway and north of Skyline Heights Drive in the City of Corona. The proposed project includes a revised TTM 36544, which would subdivide 249.39 acres into 144 lots for residential development and 47 lettered lots which are being designated for open space, public and private parks, slopes, and infrastructure associated with the plan. The revised project proposes several key revisions to the previous proposal, including a reduction of 16 dwelling units, the introduction of detached condominium homes as part of the project's housing mix, the addition of 11.42 acres of parks, trailheads, and the introduction of the Skyline Heights Specific Plan (SP25-0001), which was not part of the original approval. Also, since approval of the original project, the project site has reduced from 271 acres to 249.39 acres. The Skyline Heights Specific Plan proposes two residential zoning designations that would replace the site's existing RI-7.2 zoning in addition to development standards, community design guidelines, an infrastructure plan, construction phasing, and a financing plan to implement the development. The specific plan provides for up to 276 residential dwelling units on a total of 65.41 acres across three planning areas within the project site; 11.42 acres of combined parkland, trails and trailheads, and supporting infrastructure. The proposed project's overall density is 1.1 dwelling units per acre, which complies with the site's General Plan land use designation of Low Density Residential designation, which permits a density range of 3 to 6 dwelling units per acre.
ceqa-271f9d134fb8485200.crossStreets: West of Foothill Parkway, North of Skyline Drive

ceqa-ffbd1b4e268f7be0ce.name: California Stream Gage Improvement Program (CalSIP) - City of Beaumont Stream Gage Installation
ceqa-ffbd1b4e268f7be0ce.projectTitle: City of Beaumont Stream Gage Installation Project
ceqa-ffbd1b4e268f7be0ce.description: As part of the California Stream Gage Improvement Program, the California Department of Water Resources has executed a contract with the City of Beaumont to install a total of four stream gages. One stream gage will be installed on Cooper's Creek at W. 4th Street (33.929545, -117.021603), one on San Timoteo Creek at Potrero Blvd. (33.941267, -117.017003), and two on San Timoteo Wash at San Timoteo Canyon Road crossing (33.986681, -117.134239) and Eastside Ranch road crossing (33.972931, -117.085200). Each gaging station will include a staff plate, 2-inch diameter PVC stilling well with flexible conduit, a conductivity and water level probe, data logger with integrated telemetry, and antenna. The staff plate will be installed in the channel attached to a T-post. The stilling well will be installed on the streambank and extend to the channel invert, where the water level and conductivity probe will be installed near the channel bottom. Flexible conduit will connect the stilling well to a ~2" diameter PVC pipe that will house the instrumentation outside the channel. The stilling well will be secured to a T-post driven into the streambank, while the data collection equipment and antenna will be secured to a T-post outside the channel or on the bridge structure at the San Timoteo Wash at San Timoteo Canyon Road. Installation will be limited to the use of hand tools with no use of heavy equipment.
ceqa-ffbd1b4e268f7be0ce.crossStreets: San Timoteo Canyon Road, Potrero Blvd.

ceqa-6f5632848674519ca6.name: Desert Pupfish Conservation on Torres Martinez Desert Cahuilla Indians (TMDCI) Land
ceqa-6f5632848674519ca6.projectTitle: Desert Pupfish Conservation on Torres Martinez Desert Cahuilla Indians (TMDCI) Land
ceqa-6f5632848674519ca6.description: The proposed Project includes the creation of two new ponds for the endangered desert pupfish on Torres Martinez Desert Cahuilla Indians land, adjacent to the Whitewater Channel which connects to the Salton Sea. The ponds would provide breeding habitat and serve as a refugia for the desert pupfish to help ensure sustainable population genetic diversity, be a backup for desert pupfish populations, and would be available for release back into natural watercourses in the Salton Sink basin. These ponds will also serve as high-quality freshwater drinking and feeding resources that will be available for many species (migratory birds and local wildlife) to use as they are traversing the area.

ceqa-4dc07135d9d609034f.name: Keller Crossing
ceqa-4dc07135d9d609034f.description: The proposed Project consists of applications for a General Plan Amendment (GPA210004), an amendment to the Keller Crossing Specific Plan No. 380 (SP00380A01), a Change of Zone (CZ2100012), and a Tentative Tract Map (TTM38163) to allow for the future development of the approximately 196.1-acre Project site with a mix of residential, recreational, and open space land uses. ceqa-7f5d256e8dd0d62098.name: HM2 RIV 15; EA 08-1P911/PN 0825000074
ceqa-7f5d256e8dd0d62098.description: Caltrans proposes to rehabilitate an existing 72-inch Corrugated Steel Pipe (CSP) culvert at Postmile (PM) 29.6 on Interstate 15 (I-15), near Temescal Valley in Riverside County. The proposed rehabilitation method is concrete invert paving. Construction activities will primarily be performed from the inlet located on De Palma Road, where a Traffic Control System with Reversible Control will be implemented. No temporary access roads are required. All equipment and vehicles will be parked on the shoulder. Vehicles and equipment will not be traveling to and from the culvert work area. This project is funded by State-only funding. The purpose of this project is to perform preventive maintenance on the existing culvert to preserve the drainage system and extend its service life. The need of this project is to delay or prevent further deterioration of the culvert and to postpone the need for more extensive rehabilitation or replacement in the future. Limited work will occur in the channel near the outlet to implement best management practices (BMPs), including installing a temporary gravel bag berm and removing sediment from the last 50 feet inside the culvert. Additional limited work will occur in the channel near the inlet to establish a ~6-foot-wide walkway for the construction crew to access the work site. To establish this walkway, plants and bushes will be cut while leaving the roots in the soil. Minor clearing and grubbing will also occur in front of the inlet and outlet for fire prevention related to welding operations. On I-15 Northbound and Southbound, shoulder closures will be implemented to replace the culvert markers and install Temporary Drainage Inlet Protection. Traffic Management Plan (TMP) Elements include “Traffic Management Plan-Public Information” and “Construction Zone Enhanced Enforcement Program (COZEEP)”. Per Right-of-Way Engineering, there are impacted areas on this culvert project along De Palma Road that were purchased by the State and subsequently relinquished to the County of Riverside. As a result, a request for an encroachment permit will be submitted to the County of Riverside. The Encroachment Permit will be temporary and valid only during the construction period. The estimated construction duration is 50 working days, and the total culvert length is approximately 440 feet.
ceqa-7f5d256e8dd0d62098.crossStreets: De Palma Rd and Glen Eden Rd

ceqa-36a5f554929c5e327e.name: General Plan Update, Zoning Code and Map Amendment, and Climate Action and Adaptation Plan (CAAP)
ceqa-36a5f554929c5e327e.projectTitle: General Plan Update, Zoning Code and Map Amendment, and Climate Action and Adaptation Plan (CAAP)
ceqa-36a5f554929c5e327e.description: The General Plan Update (GPU) succeeds the last comprehensive general plan adopted in 2011, with the Housing Element updated in 2022. The GPU incorporates statutory requirements for general plans and guidance provided in the 2023 General Plan Guidelines; coordinates future development and policies with regional planning efforts and serves as the city’s fundamental guide in developing strategies to address greenhouse gas reduction, climate change, and climate planning. The PEIR addresses each of the seven elements’ goals, policies, and programs of the General Plan Update. The Zoning Code and Map Amendment (ZCA) is a revision to the City’s zoning regulations and zoning map to implement the proposed General Plan. The Zoning Code and Map Amendment implements the General Plan. The Climate Action Adaptation Plan (CAAP) is a strategic policy framework that outlines how the City will address climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and prepare for climate change impacts. The CAAP implements the General Plan and will include a baseline assessment of GHG emissions as well as the climate change hazards experienced in the city. Emissions will be forecasted for future years based on anticipated growth to assess trends and establish GHG reduction targets and strategies. Additionally, climate adaptation strategies have been developed to address climate hazards in the city.
ceqa-36a5f554929c5e327e.crossStreets: S. Main Street / East Graham Avenue

ceqa-1641b6bcdeeb2a5236.name: Coachella Valley Water District - System Conservation Implementation Agreement - Lower Colorado Conservation and Efficiency Program 2027-2028
ceqa-1641b6bcdeeb2a5236.projectTitle: Coachella Valley Water District - System Conservation Implementation Agreement - Lower Colorado Conservation and Efficiency Program 2027-2028
ceqa-1641b6bcdeeb2a5236.description: The proposed action consists of CVWD extending a fallowing program for the System Conservation Implementation Agreement- Lower Colorado Conservation and Efficiency Program under which CVWD will enter into agreements with participating growers and the Bureau of Reclamation. CVWD’s conservation participation will take place within the CVWD service area for Colorado River Water irrigation service area, which is located in the Eastern Coachella Valley, Eastern Riverside County. Under the program CVWD will compensate the participating growers in consideration for water that is conserved by the fallowing of the agricultural farmland with a history of irrigation. CVWD or other Colorado River contractors will not consumptively use the water conserved and will instead be made available by forbearance to assist in the management of reservoir levels in the Colorado River in the Lower Basin during current drought conditions. The program is intended to operate temporarily, conserving up to 10,000 acre-feet per year (AFY) in CVWD contributions in 2027 and 2028. CVWD on average provides approximately 245,000 AFY of Colorado River Water for agricultural irrigation. The program is not a long-term program intended to permanently change agricultural land use designations. The program initially began as a two-and-half year effort in 2024 through 2026. The extended program is anticipated to begin in January 2027 and end in December 2028. Participating growers will be responsible for any required weed control and dust control on the fallowed land and will agree not to change land maintenance and crop cultivation practices on other lands within CVWD to result in an increased consumptive use of water on those lands. Participants in the program will be prohibited from shifting water use to pumped groundwater while in the fallowing program.

ceqa-cea7482228de08b5fa.name: CVWD Replenishment Facilities Curtailment Program
ceqa-cea7482228de08b5fa.description: The Coachella Valley Water District (CVWD) Replenishment Facilities Curtailment Program consists of CVWD entering an agreement with the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation), acting through the Department of Interior (DOI), for conservation of Colorado River water through replenishment curtailment in calendar years (CYs) 2027 and 2028; conserve water of up to 35,000 acre-ft/year (af/yr) at a fixed price of $325/af. This program is temporary and an extension of the Thomas E. Levy (Levy) Facility replenishment curtailment program established in 2022. The temporary and compensated Colorado River water conservation proposals cover the two calendar years of 2027 and 2028. CVWD operates the Thomas E. Levy Groundwater Replenishment Facility, Whitewater River Groundwater Replenishment Facility, Mission Creek Groundwater Replenishment Facility, and Palm Desert Groundwater Replenishment Facility, which are key to groundwater management in the Coachella Valley. The Levy Facility benefits the East Whitewater River Subbasin Area of Benefit (East AOB) and has averaged annual recharge of over 37 taf in recent years. Although delivering water to the recharge facilities is important for CVWD’s groundwater management, it was decided that temporarily suspending delivery to the Levy Facility would allow CVWD to achieve the goal of contributing materially to the River with minimal impacts to the region. Under the Agreement, CVWD will achieve the up to 35,000 af/yr of conservation by limiting the maximum groundwater replenishment at the CVWD replenishment facilities in the Coachella Valley while enrolled in the Lower Colorado Conservation program. The Replenishment Facilities Curtailment Program shall conserve a total of up to 70,000 af of Colorado River water for the two-year term of the agreement. This program will not result in expansion of use of CVWD’s existing irrigation distribution system or its irrigation drainage system. Accordingly, the proposed program involves operation and implementation of CVWD’s existing irrigation distribution facilities and irrigation drainage for Lower Basin Shortages and Coordinated Operations for Lake Powell and Lake Mead. The proposed action of using conserved water from the proposed Conservation Program to assist in managing reservoir elevations is within the scope of analysis of actions that were previously analyzed in that EIS and in the SEIS currently underway. Thus, to the extent the proposed actions involve or may affect areas outside of California, such as at Lake Mead or on the portions of the Colorado River in Nevada or Arizona, they are exempt from CEQA under a Statutory Exemption State CEQA Guidelines Section 15277. The proposed action of adopting and extending the Coachella Valley Water District Replenishment Facilities Curtailment Program for 2027 and 2028 is exempt under the provisions of State CEQA Guidelines.

ceqa-c54b3e064dd18f8a2e.name: Tract 38832 Outfall Structure (Lake or Streambed Alteration Agreement No. EPIMS-RIV-58320-R6)
ceqa-c54b3e064dd18f8a2e.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed and issued Lake and Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification No. EPIMS-RIV-58320-R6, pursuant to Fish and Game Code section1602, to Mark Hayden. The Project is limited to the construction of a residential subdivision with one new storm drain outfall structure on the north bank of Salt Creek Flood Control Channel, as well as roadway improvements on Olive Avenue from Leon Road to Beeler Road and Leon Road from Salt Creek to Olive Avenue. Approximately 970 cubic yards of one-half-ton riprap will be placed onsite and 1,050 cubic yards of soil will be excavated from the Project site. The proposed outfall structure will convey outlet flows from future Storm Drain Line A-9 as part of the local Winchester Hills Community Facilities District (CFD) to drain both offsite and Tract 38832 onsite flows. The storm drain outfall will consist of a concrete pipe within a square, at-grade concrete apron that outlets into ungrouted riprap.

Approximately 215 cubic yards of one-half-ton riprap will be placed onsite and 520 cubic yards of soil will be excavated from the Project site. The outfall will contain a concrete pipe within a square, at-grade concrete apron that outlets into ungrouted riprap.

ceqa-58e37abcf77692347f.name: MARD2026-0002 (City Park Revitalization Project)
ceqa-58e37abcf77692347f.description: The project (MAR.D2026-0002) is for the review of proposed alterations to City Park, which is listed on the City of Corona Register of Historic Resources as a historic district (HD-005). The alterations to the park are proposed as part of the City Park Revitalization Project, which includes the construction of a new community center, aquatic center, new landscaping, pedestrian pathways, parking lots, large open-air event area ("Community Canvas"), playgrounds, fitness and sports courts, and other improvements including updated supporting infrastructure. The project also includes the preservation, relocation, and replacement of several existing trees within the park, as well as the preservation of four historic resources within the park. Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15164, an Addendum to the certified 2020-2040 General Plan Environmental Impact Report was prepared to analyze the potential environmental impacts of the proposed alterations and improvements to City Park. Based on the analysis in the Addendum, the City determined that the proposed City Park alterations and improvements would not result in any new significant environmental impacts or substantially increase the severity of impacts previously identified in the previously certified EIR.

ceqa-c76a1e1c85f07c45f3.name: Heacock Street South Extension Project
ceqa-c76a1e1c85f07c45f3.description: The proposed project would widen and realign Heacock Street in Moreno Valley between San Michele Road and the Perris Valley Storm Drainage Lateral “B” (channel) to a total width of 76 feet. The project proposes to extend Heacock Street’s Arterial classification south from San Michele to the Ccity limits. The project site is a total of 15 acres. Under the proposed project, 11.91 acres of the total 15-acre project site would be disturbed under the proposed project, this would include permanent new roadway and infrastructure improvements. The remaining 2.89 acres of the existing roadway would be temporarily disturbed. Heacock Street improvements would terminate in a cul-de-sac adjacent to and north of the channel. Storm drain improvements are also proposed in the project impact area and are included in the 11.91 acres of disturbance.

ceqa-9c1c90ff6123e68963.name: Boulders II Project
ceqa-9c1c90ff6123e68963.description: The Boulders II Project proposes the development of 240 multi-family units on 10.15 acres. The Project proposes a (gross) density of 23.7 dwelling units per acre. A total of 378 parking spaces are proposed (269 carports/garages and 109 non-covered). In addition, the Project proposes a 795-square-foot maintenance building and recreational amenities, including a community center, a 5,025-square-foot clubhouse, pool, fitness center, business center, tot lot, multiple barbeque areas, dog park, and pickleball court. Within the southerly and southwesterly portions of the site the Project would conserve the existing hillsides. The Boulders II development consists of an approximately 10.15-acre parcel with a proposed developed area of roughly 9.6-acres. The proposed multi-family residential development includes 240 total units within five (5) four-story buildings, ten (10) two-story buildings, and two (2) one-story recreational and maintenance buildings totaling 126,028 square feet of development (“Proposed Project” or “Project”). The Proposed Project also includes 378 parking stalls to accompany residents and guests visiting the Project Site. As part of the approval process, the Applicant is requesting approval of a Zone Change, General Plan Amendment, and Minor Plot Plan (MPP# 24-0251)

ceqa-cd4749d91f56b88bf7.name: Lake Perris Lift Station Lot 7
ceqa-cd4749d91f56b88bf7.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-cd4749d91f56b88bf7.description: Eastern Municipal Water District (EMWD) identified an existing lift station within Lake Perris State Recreation Area (LPSRA) in need of repair. The station is located in Parking Lot 7, approximately 70’ northwest of the existing restroom within that lot. In addition, EMWD will install a security gate, five removable guard posts, and replace the existing block wall building with a sunshade structure in the vicinity of the lift station. The packaged lift station will be installed at a maximum of 36.18’, in accordance with existing structures. The security gate will be installed at a depth of 4’, and the removable guard post shall be installed to a maximum of 10”, with an additional 8” concrete footing below. All excavation activities will occur within already developed areas, causing little to no natural habitat disturbance.

ceqa-462670d1ae26ff97c9.name: Winchester Ranch CFD Line A Channel Outfall Structure Project (Streambed Alteration Agreement No. EPIMS-RIV-62220-R6)
ceqa-462670d1ae26ff97c9.projectTitle: Winchester Ranch Infrastructure Community Facilities District
ceqa-462670d1ae26ff97c9.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed and issued Lake and Streambed Alteration Agreement (EPIMS-RIV-62220-R6), pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1602, to the project Applicant, Mark Hayden. The Project is limited to the construction of the Line A storm drain and a storm drain outlet structure as part of the SP 293 Winchester Hills development. The channel will extend 0.5 miles with a storm drain outfall structure that will be constructed on the north bank of Salt Creek. Approximately 5,508 cubic yards (CY) of soil will be excavated; 838 CY will occur in the temporary impact area, and 4,670 CY will occur in the permanent impact area. Permanent impacts will total 0.71-acre and temporary construction impacts total 0.52-acre and consist of the 30-foot-wide buffer around the permanent impact area. Fill will only be placed in the permanent impact area and consist of 2,321 CY of Class V riprap, 561 CY of concrete for the headwall, wingwall, parapet wall, and cutoff wall, and 318 linear feet of cable railing. Construction equipment to be used during Project activities include but are not limited to: Excavator, Backhoe, Box Grader, D6 Bulldozer, and hand tools. No water will not be diverted or extracted during Project activities.

ceqa-dba30dc34ed34a4b79.name: City Park Revitalization Project
ceqa-dba30dc34ed34a4b79.description: The approximately 19.6-acre project site and currently operates as Corona City Park. The proposed project would redevelop Corona City Park with a new aquatics center, a new parking lot, a community lawn (“Community Canvas”) with a community center building, a new playground structure replacing the existing playground, a new splash pad, replacement restrooms, parking areas and relocated basketball courts with a new pump track surrounding them.

ceqa-fee235580878b17729.name: Savira Solar Project
ceqa-fee235580878b17729.description: Savira Renewables, LLC proposes to construct the Savira Solar Project, a utility-scale solar photovoltaic (PV) electrical generating and storage facility and associated infrastructure to generate and deliver renewable electricity to the statewide electricity transmission grid. The Project would generate up to approximately 150 megawatts (MW) of renewable energy via arrays of solar PV panels. Project facilities include an Operations and Maintenance (O&M) building, a Project substation, and up to approximately 250 MW Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), and access driveways. The Savira Solar Project would include a 230 kilovolt (kV) substation. From there, the solar energy generated by the Project would be transmitted via the new approximately 1.8-mile-long, 230 kV gen-tie line.

ceqa-f34594b0c45fa223d6.description: The Housing Authority of the County of Riverside (Housing Authority) is authorized to administer 10,187 Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) units, a form of tenant-based rental assistance funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). ceqa-70fd2aaf1651f530e3.name: Gibson Ave. & Contour Ave. Resurfacing Project
ceqa-70fd2aaf1651f530e3.projectTitle: Gibson Ave. & Contour Ave. Resurfacing Project
ceqa-70fd2aaf1651f530e3.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department proposes to resurface approximately 3,070 feet of Gibson Avenue from Nuevo Road to 11th Street and resurface approximately 1,860 feet of Contour Avenue from 11th Street to Hansen Avenue, in the Nuevo area of Riverside County. Gibson Avenue is a two-lane road with width varying from 28 to 29-feet and Contour Avenue is a two-lane road with width varying from 24 to 25 feet. The proposed work will consist of pulverizing in place the existing Asphalt Concrete (AC) pavement on Gibson Avenue and excavating the existing AC pavement on Contour Avenue, performing moisture conditioning and recompacting of existing material, and paving with Hot Mix Asphalt Concrete. The proposed project will also include: • Reconstruction of AC dike. • Reconstruction of AC driveways. • Extension of a culvert pipe to avoid erosion around a power pole. • Placement of safety edge and shoulder backing. • Utility valve can adjustments. • Re-striping of roadway, including pavement markers/reflectors. • Salvage/removal of existing signs and installation of new signs. No additional right-of-way will be required to construct the proposed improvements. The project improvements will remain within the existing footprint of the roadway and within County limits.

ceqa-3726d040fbf9b08915.name: 10th Street Reconstruction Project
ceqa-3726d040fbf9b08915.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department is proposing to replace approximately 0.74 miles of existing asphalt concrete pavement on 10th Street from Reservoir Avenue to Wolfskill Avenue in the community of Lakeview. The County of Riverside General Plan classifies 10th Street as a Secondary Highway. This road is currently a two-lane road with a road width of 24 feet. The proposed work will consist of grinding in place (pulverize) the existing concrete asphalt pavement on 10th Street, perform moisture conditioning, mixing and recompacting grindings with existing native material, and paving back the new base with Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA). The project will include the following: • Reconstruction asphalt concreate dikes. • Reconstruction of asphalt concreate driveways • Construction of energy dissipator (rip rap installation and cutoff walls). • Placement of safety edge and shoulder backing. • Adjustment of valve can • Application of hydroseeding. • Restriping of roadway, including pavement markers and reflectors. • Salvage/removal and installation of new signs. • Utility adjustments

ceqa-4225e3ee039208c43d.name: Gilman Springs Rd Reconstruction
ceqa-4225e3ee039208c43d.description: The County of Riverside Transportation Department is proposing to reconstruct approximately 4,100 feet of Gilman Springs Road from approximately 300 feet west of Kevin Road to approximately 100 feet east of Alessandro Blvd. in the Community of Badlands. Gilman Springs Rd is a two-lane road with a width that varies between 28’ to 48’ and is classified as an Arterial Highway in the County of Riverside’s General Plan. The proposed work will consist of removing existing Asphalt Concrete (AC), scarifying underlying material, perform moisture conditioning and recompacting of existing material, and paving back with new Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA). The proposed project will also include: • Placement of safety edge • Re-striping of roadway, including pavement markers, rumble stripes and centerline channelizer • Salvage/removal of existing signs and installation of new signs The proposed project will remain within the existing County right-of-way (ROW) and will not require any additional ROW. Temporary construction easements may be required for the proposed improvements.

ceqa-5bb139b2c70d342f40.name: Second Amendment to the Riverside County Information Technology Department (RCIT) Chicago Lease Agreement with JS MCA Hunter Park, LLC, Riverside
ceqa-5bb139b2c70d342f40.projectTitle: Second Amendment to the Riverside County Information Technology Department (RCIT) Chicago Lease Agreement with JS MCA Hunter Park, LLC, Riverside

ceqa-7a3d496074b9389e74.name: Approval of the Plans and Specifications and Authorization to Advertise for Bids for the Installation of Primary Apron Mast Lighting and Control Access Gate Pha
ceqa-7a3d496074b9389e74.projectTitle: Approval of the Plans and Specifications and Authorization to Advertise for Bids for the Installation of Primary Apron Mast Lighting and Control Access Gate Pha
ceqa-7a3d496074b9389e74.description: [PROJECT TITLE CONTINUED]: se II Construction Project at Blythe Airport (BLH); District 4 On February 25, 2025, the Board of Supervisors approved the five-year design and engineering services agreement with Mead and Hunt for airport engineering, architectural, planning and environmental services which includes the design, construction administration, construction inspection of projects, planning and environmental services for the County’s five airports. The design services for the Blythe Airport’s Installation of Primary Apron Mast Lighting and Control Access Gate Project are now complete, and staff request approval to solicit bids for construction of the project. The Blythe Airport has Runway 8-26 and 17-35, with partial parallel taxiways serving each runway. On the southeast corner of the Runway intersection is the Airport’s only apron, so all transient or parked Aircraft must come to this location. There is no Airport perimeter road with public street access, so vehicles entering or using the Airport must pass through the apron as well. Currently, to access the airport is through two pad-locked swinging gates along the southwest and southeast edges of the apron. The purpose of this project is to enhance safety by replacing both gates with a digital keypad, add low-mast lighting at select locations along the perimeter of the apron, and at the fueling facility to approve visibility issues during transient nighttime operations. The proposed Project is categorically exempt from the provisions of CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act) according to the State CEQA Guidelines Section 15301, Class 1 Existing Facilities Exemption: Section 15302 Replacement or Reconstruction; and Section 15061 (b)(3) “Common Sense” Exemption, and categorically excluded from NEPA US Department of Transportation Federal Aviation Administration Order 1050.1E, Categorical Exclusion 5-6.4e Facility Siting, Construction, and Maintenance. The Project will not have any impact on an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern, nor will the Project include unusual circumstances which would have a potentially significant effect on the environment.

ceqa-793750a34520996dc0.name: Geotechnical Investigation for Point 1 ADA Fishing Pier (Extension)
ceqa-793750a34520996dc0.projectTitle: Geotechnical Investigation for Point 1 ADA Fishing Pier (Extension)
ceqa-793750a34520996dc0.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-793750a34520996dc0.description: The purpose of the Inland Empire District ADA Fishing Pier Extension Project is to maintain reliable, year-round ADA-compliant fishing access at the lake despite significant seasonal and long-term water level fluctuations. The project is intended to ensure continued recreational access for visitors with disabilities, protect public safety, and uphold the park’s commitment to equitable outdoor recreation opportunities. To support design development for the pier extension and to ensure adequate structural and foundation recommendations, the project will include a geotechnical field investigation consisting of one engineering boring and one Cone Penetration Test (CPT) sounding within the area of the proposed pier extension. This investigation will occur upland near the shoreline and will not involve work within the submerged lakebed.

ceqa-95aca6420042adc3e5.description: Addendum No. 1 to Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) No.2351 (SCH No. 2020020363)– The proposal is a revision to the southern portion of the Perris Valley Storm Drain Channel Trail – Phase 2 (approved by the City on April 20, 2020). The two key changes in design are 1) to the drainage crossings of the 7th Street Channel (formerly referred to as G Street) and the San Jacinto River Channel after its confluence with the Perris Valley Storm Drain Channel and 2) a realignment of the trail from the west side to the east side of the San Jacinto River Channel south of the I-215 freeway. Instead of spanning these two drainages, the Revised Project proposes a low-flow Arizona crossing at-grade at the confluence of the 7th Street Channel and the San Jacinto River Channel immediately downstream of I-215 freeway, with the trail then extending out of the channel to the eastern side of the river.

ceqa-99f108d04664c2a73a.name: Grace Solar Energy Center
ceqa-99f108d04664c2a73a.description: CUP03684R01 proposes to revise the previous approval of a 463.5 megawatt (MW) photovoltaic solar power plant, referred to as the Palo Verde Mesa Solar Project. The revision expands site acreage from 3,250 to 3,310 acres (60-acre increase), increases total energy production from 463.5 MW to 500 MW (37 MW increase), includes a new 500 MW battery storage system (BESS), and replaces a proposed full transmission line with connections to an existing transmission line. The new route would add approximately 1.9 miles of transmission line and connect the site to an approximately 8.6-mile existing transmission line that connects to the Southern California Edison (SCE) 230-kV Colorado River Substation, for a total approximately 10 .5-mile transmission line. The Project also includes an expansion of Bureau of Land Management-managed land from 28 to 395 acres, outside the scope of this approval. PUP00916R01 proposes a revision to the previous approval of approximately 11 .8 miles (out of 14.5 miles) of new transmission lines proposed on lands in County of Riverside rights-of-way. These transmission lines connect the solar power plant to the Colorado River Substation, which crosses certain County public rights-of-way. The modified Project includes primarily proposed transmissions lines on private land (covered under the CUP revision above) or federal land outside County of Riverside jurisdiction. However, proposed transmission line to the SCE 230-kV Colorado River Substation extends over a 158-foot portion of the County Right-of-Way and is subject to review under a public use perm it. DA0086A01 proposes a revision of the previously approved development agreement (DA No. 86) under the previously approved conditional use permit (CUP No. 3684). Board of Supervisors Policy No. B-29 regarding solar power plants states, "No approval required by Ordinance No. 348 shall be given for a solar power plant unless the Board first approves a development agreement with the solar power plant owner and the development agreement is effective."

ceqa-0b4424bb7979643f69.name: City of Calimesa Annexation Project
ceqa-0b4424bb7979643f69.description: The Project consists of the proposed annexation of approximately 313.4 acres (herein, “Annexation Area”) from the County of Riverside into the City of Calimesa. No new development is proposed as part of the Project, as the Project would consist of an administrative adjustment to the boundary between the City of Calimesa and unincorporated Riverside County. Discretionary applications associated with the Project include Annexation No. ANNX-25-1, General Plan Amendment No. GPA-25-2, Zone Change/Prezone No. ZC-25-2, Zone Text Amendment No. ZTA-25-4, and two proposed Conditional Use Permits (CUP-25-4 and CUP 25-5). The Project is a preliminary step in the annexation application process with the Riverside Local Agency Formation Commission (LAFCO). The Project’s discretionary applications are described below: • Annexation No. ANNX-25-1 would allow for the annexation of +/- 234.0 acres of land located north of and abutting Cherry Valley Boulevard and east of and abutting the existing City of Calimesa City limits (herein, “Northern Annexation Area”), and approximately 79.4 acres of land located south of and abutting Cherry Valley Boulevard and south and east of and abutting the existing City of Calimesa City limits (herein, “Southern Annexation Area”). • General Plan Amendment No. GPA-25-2 would accommodate the proposed annexation of the 313.4-acre Annexation Area into the jurisdictional limits of the City of Calimesa, and would amend the City of Calimesa’s General Plan Land Use Map in a manner generally consistent with the existing adopted Riverside County land use designations for the Annexation Area. • Pre-Zoning application No. ZC-25-2 would amend the City of Calimesa’s Zoning Map to apply prezoning designations to the 313.4-acre Annexation Area. Zoning classifications would include “Light Industrial (L-I) Zone” on approximately 138.7 acres and “O-S-R (Open Space Residential)” on approximately 87.0 acres for the Northern Annexation Area, and “C-C (Community Commercial, FAR 50:1)” on approximately 19.8 acres and “R-E (Residential Estate)” on approximately 58.5 acres within the Southern Annexation Area. In addition, proposed ZC-25-2 would apply a “Warehouse Overlay Zone (WOZ)” over the 138.7 acres of the Northern Annexation Area that currently are developed with two warehouse buildings. • Zone Text Amendment No. ZTA-25-4 is required to amend Table 18.30.030 (Uses Permitted Within Industrial Districts) of Chapter 18.30 (Industrial Zone Districts) of Title 18 (Zoning, Land Use and Development Regulations) of the City of Calimesa Municipal Code to identify warehouse buildings that up to 1,100,000 s.f. in size as a conditionally-permitted use within the L-I zone for properties located within an adopted “Warehouse Overlay Zone (WOZ).” • Conditional Use Permit No. CUP25-4 is required to fulfill the requirements of (amended) Municipal Code Table 18.30.030 for Building 1, which is the existing warehouse building in the western portions of the Northern Annexation Area. • Conditional Use Permit No. CUP-25-5 is required to fulfill the requirements of (amended) Municipal Code Table 18.30.030 for Building 2, which is the existing warehouse building in the eastern portions of the Northern Annexation Area.

ceqa-67b1bb9c01f1ea1774.name: Colorado River Indian Tribe Californian Broadband Network
ceqa-67b1bb9c01f1ea1774.projectTitle: Colorado River Indian Tribe Californian Broadband Network
ceqa-67b1bb9c01f1ea1774.description: The proposed Project is funded in part through the CPUC Federal Funding Account (FFA), and would enhance broadband connectivity across tribal lands by combining aerial and underground installations of fiber optic cables. The Project would provide high-speed fiber optic broadband service to unserved Tribal households across two routes: Blythe, and Parker Dam. The Project includes two principal components: (1) attachment of new broadband fiber to existing utility poles across the majority of the alignment, and (2) installation of underground fiber optic conduit within CalTrans right-of-way (ROW) corridors along key road segments. The Project is divided into two distinct sites the Blythe Route and the Parker Dam Route. Blythe Route extends from Palo Verde Dam, extending southwest to Defrain Blvd before proceeding southward and intersecting with 6th Avenue. From this point, it turns eastward, traversing 6th Avenue and leading to Lovekin Boulevard. Continuing southward, it eventually reaches Hobsonway and terminates at the Hobsonway and Interstate 10 intersection at the Arizona-California border. This route would include interconnections with Palo Verde Valley High School, the Mesa Bluff Village Development including four other developed areas along W Wells Road, and Palo Verde College. The Parker Dam Route interconnects with the existing Big River Segment along Aqueduct Road at approximately 34° 9'47.92"N, 114°18'28.65"W. The line primarily follows Parker Dam Road terminating at 34°11'46.10"N, 114°13'34.11"W. This route includes offshoots into six existing developments along Parker Dam Road including a mobile home development near the intersection of Parker Dam Road and SR 62, Bermuda Palms RV Resort mobile home development, Bluewater Drive W, Bluewater Dr, River Reflections Estates and nearby development, and Riverland Resorts. This route would provide potential interconnection for 744 residences, 15 businesses, and 4 anchor institutions.

ceqa-9998199ded75dfba00.name: Inland Empire Utilities Agency (IEUA) Chino Basin Program Recirculated Final PEIR
ceqa-9998199ded75dfba00.projectTitle: Inland Empire Utilities Agency Chino Basin Program
ceqa-9998199ded75dfba00.description: The Chino Basin Program (CBP) was submitted for Proposition 1 – Water Storage Investment Program funding and was awarded $269M in conditional funding as of August 2025. Under the WSIP, the CBP is proposed to be a conjunctive use project that proposes to use advanced water purification to treat and store up to 15,000 acre-feet-per-year (AFY) of “new” water supply for a period of 25-years to provide for the State exchange, to be used in blocks of up to 50,000 AFY in hydrologically drier years when pulse flows in the Feather River would provide the most ecosystem benefit and other State Water Project (SWP) operations would not be affected. The exchange would be administered through agreements with the California Department of Water Resources (DWR), the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW), MWD, and other project partners. During the first 25 years of the Project life cycle (while the Proposition 1 WSIP water exchange commitment is fulfilled) locally produced CBP water supplies will directly replace a portion of imported supplies when an SWP water transfer is implemented by MWD and DWR and a pulse flow occurs in Northern California. After fulfillment of the Proposition 1 WSIP exchange commitment, the facilities developed under the CBP by IEUA would continue to be operationally viable as part of the overall project life cycle, and during this period the new water supply will be available for local use annually contributing to IEUA’s available supply. The CBP would increase additional available groundwater supplies in the adjudicated Chino Basin through increased water recycling that would result from operation of a new AWPF and through groundwater storage by operation of new injection wells. The CBP would thereby enable IEUA to exchange a commensurate amount of this “new” water locally generated by the proposed facilities to be used locally in order to enable State Water Project water to remain in Lake Oroville in Northern California that would otherwise be delivered to Southern California. The additional Lake Oroville water would subsequently be released in the form of pulse flows in the Feather River to improve habitat conditions for native salmonids and achieve environmental benefits. The CBP’s proposed AWPF, new injection and extraction facilities, conveyance facilities, and water system interconnections will allow more optimal management of local water supplies, including meeting water quality requirements for the continued use of recycled water within the Chino Basin, improved storage and recovery operations, as well as redundancies in water delivery infrastructure that will facilitate future rehabilitation and replacement of existing infrastructure. Furthermore, the data contained in the CBP RDPEIR is augmented by the analysis contained in the Final Pulse Flows Component of the Water Storage Investment Program Groundwater Projects Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (2024 DWR Pulse Flow FSEIR; SCH No. 2022080216) dated July 2024 prepared for the California Department of Water Resources (DWR) and prepared by ICF/ESA. This SEIR was circulated from February 16, 2024 to April 1, 2024, and the final document including responses to comments was completed in July 2024. The Pulse Flows Component is defined by the following DWR actions: (1) Release of the pulse flows from Lake Oroville into the Low Flow Channel of the Feather River, with the goal of improving habitat conditions for listed salmonids, as well as improving spawning and migration conditions for other listed and non-listed native fish species. (2) Implementation of the WSIP Operational Exchange Process that develops water used for pulse flow releases. (3) Diversion and conveyance of water to Kern Fan and Willow Springs that would be stored, in part, for ecosystem benefit. Implementation of the Pulse Flows Component would not require construction of any new facilities in addition to those previously analyzed in the three WSIP Groundwater Projects’ EIRs (including the 2022 CBP FPEIR and now the RDPEIR). Existing facilities would be used, with operations modified to support the pulse flow releases. The Pulse Flows Component study area analyzed in the FSEIR extends approximately 575 miles from Lake Oroville in Northern California to the WSIP Groundwater Projects in the San Joaquin Valley and Southern California. The 2024 DWR Pulse Flow FSEIR is presented as Subchapter 8.3 to the RDPEIR, and the information and analysis contained therein is incorporated by reference as part of the RDPEIR.

ceqa-120cfa079652ef58ba.description: On July 8, 2026, the City of Palm Springs approved a resolution to adopt a palm tree trimming policy, superseding all previous palm tree trimming procedures and policies. The Policy permits minor trimming (fruit pod removal, trunk skinning, and/or shearing) of palm trees within the public right of way to promote public safety. The City is home to one of the largest compositions of heritage quality California Fan Palms. Recent storm events demonstrated that palm trees in their natural state posed a public safety risk. The policy does not permit tree removal of any sort.

ceqa-8f41e6df37005810dd.name: Interstate 215 Garbani Road Interchange Project
ceqa-8f41e6df37005810dd.description: The City, in cooperation with Caltrans, proposes to construct a new interchange at I-215 and Garbani Road. The project site is located in the City of Menifee between PM R15.5 and PM R17.5. The new interchange would be located approximately 1 mile north of the Scott Road Interchange and approximately 2 miles south of the Newport Road Interchange. Garbani Road currently features discontinuous connectivity in the east-west direction due to I-215, which bisects Menifee. The proposed project would improve transportation circulation and connectivity in the area by reconstructing Garbani Road to provide continuous multimodal travel across I-215 and constructing a new I-215 interchange at Garbani Road. The following three alternatives are being studied in the EIR for this project: Alternative 1 – No-Build Alternative Alternative 2 – Compact Diamond Interchange Alternative 3 – Spread Diamond Interchange Alternative 4 – Diverging Diamond Interchange Alternative 1: No-Build Alternative Under the No-Build Alternative, the existing transportation facilities within the project area would remain unchanged, except for planned and programmed improvements being implemented as separate projects by other entities. This alternative does not address the purpose and need of the project. The No-Build Alternative represents the baseline alternative and offers a basis for the analysis and evaluation of the Build Alternatives. Alternative 2: Compact Diamond Interchange Build Alternative 2 includes construction of a new diamond configured interchange along I-215 at Garbani Road, and improvements to Garbani and Antelope Roads. Build Alternative 2 includes four diagonal northbound and southbound on- and off-ramps. The ramp terminal intersections would be signal controlled four-way stop intersections, or unsignalized roundabouts. Auxiliary lanes from the Scott Road interchange directly south of the project would be extended to the Garbani Road interchange northbound off-ramp and southbound on-ramp. The proposed improvements on Garbani Road include reconstruction to a continuous Major (4-Lane) roadway between the Haun Road intersection west of I-215 and the Champagne Drive intersection east of I-215, consistent with the City’s General Plan designation for Garbani Road. The roadway characteristics would be consistent with the City’s roadway standards to include four 12-foot-wide travel lanes, a 12-foot-wide raised median/left-turn lane, two 8-foot-wide Class II bicycle lanes, and two 6-foot-wide sidewalks. In addition, a 10-foot-wide regional trail is proposed along the north side of Garbani Road consistent with the City’s Community/Regional Trail standards. Under Alternative 2 the portion of reconstructed Garbani Road that would be a bridge over the I-215 is approximately 108 feet wide and 204 feet long. The Garbani Road bridge over I-215 would include four 12-foot-wide lanes, 24-foot-wide median/double left-turn lane pocket, two 8-foot-wide bike lanes, a 12-foot-wide sidewalk on the north side, and a 6-foot-wide sidewalk on the south side. The proposed improvements along Antelope Road include upgrade of the road to a Major (4-Lane) Road with four 12-foot-wide lanes, a 12-foot-wide median/left-turn lane, two 8-foot-wide bike lanes, and two 6-foot-wide sidewalks. Antelope Road would be realigned approximately 3,840 feet to the east. The relocated Garbani/Antelope Roads intersection would be a signal controlled intersection or an un-signaled roundabout. Alternative 3: Spread Diamond Interchange Build Alternative 3 includes construction of a new spread diamond interchange along I-215 at Garbani Road. The configuration includes four diagonal northbound and southbound on- and off-ramps that would be signal controlled or roundabouts, similar to Build Alternative 2. Auxiliary lanes from the Scott Road interchange directly south of the project would be extended to the Garbani Road interchange northbound off-ramp and southbound on-ramp. The primary difference between the designs is that the spread diamond configuration is a larger footprint that at a future time could accommodate the addition of a loop on-ramp if traffic conditions past the 20-year horizon year would require it. The proposed Garbani Road bridge over I-215 under Build Alternative 3 is approximately 88 feet wide and 204 feet long. The bridge includes four 12-foot-wide lanes, a 4-foot-wide median, two 8-foot-wide bike lanes, a 12-foot-wide sidewalk on the north side, and a 6-foot-wide sidewalk on the south side. Build Alternative 3 would share the same proposed improvements to Garbani and Antelope Roads as under all build alternatives, which are described above under Build Alternative 2. Alternative 4: Diverging Diamond Interchange Build Alternative 4 includes construction of a new diverging diamond interchange (DDI) along I-215 at Garbani Road. The DDI configuration would include two signalized ramp intersections and a configuration that allows for direct left turns to freeway on-ramps. Auxiliary lanes from the Scott?Road interchange directly south of the project would be extended to the Garbani Road interchange northbound off-ramp and southbound on-ramp. The Garbani Road bridge over I-215 proposed under Alternative 2 is approximately 92 feet wide and 204 feet long. The bridge includes four 12-foot-wide lanes, two 8-foot-wide bike lanes, two 4-foot-wide shoulders, and a barrier-protected 16-foot-wide regional trail and sidewalk path, which converges along the center of the interchange. Build Alternative 4 would share the same proposed improvements to Garbani and Antelope Roads as under all build alternatives, which are described above under Build Alternative 2.

ceqa-69ea1463f476cfe466.name: Goldspotted Oak Borer Management, Removals, and Treatments in San Bernardino Mountain Communities
ceqa-69ea1463f476cfe466.projectTitle: Goldspotted Oak Borer Management, Removals, and Treatments in San Bernardino Mountain Communities
ceqa-69ea1463f476cfe466.description: Goldspotted Oak Borer (GSOB) is an invasive pest to Southern California that has been decimating oak populations in many communities. GSOB infestations have been confirmed in the Cities of Big Bear, Calimesa and Yucaipa and the communities of Crestline, Forest Falls, Oak Glen, and Wrightwood. The project is anticipated to cover 21,971 acres, remove approximately 244 high infested trees, and treat an additional 62 trees with low infestations or high value trees. The purpose of this project is to remove infested oak trees in the Cities of Big Bear, Calimesa and Yucaipa and the communities of Crestline, Silverwood, Forest Falls, Oak Glen, and Wrightwood to prevent larvae living within the infested oak trees from flying during spring/summer and potentially infesting additional oak trees. Additionally, the removal of dead or highly infested trees will reduce the wildfire risk by reducing fuels. Highly infested trees will be fully removed and the infested wood will be either chipped and moved off site using best management practices or tarped on site if access is a challenge. Trees classified as "high-value" or with low infestations will be treated using insecticide. All trees removed during nesting season will be surveyed by a biologist prior to removal to ensure that no nests are observed. If any nest is found, removal of that tree will occur only once the biologist has confirmed that the birds have fledged the nest.
