ceqa-1c1ca4eff28f49ddee.name: NOTICE OF DETERMINATION FOR AN ADDENDUM TO THE ENVISION SAN JOSE 2040 GENERAL PLAN FINAL PROGRAM ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT AS SUPPLEMENTED (SCH# 200972096)
ceqa-1c1ca4eff28f49ddee.projectTitle: PP15-060 Envision San Jose General Plan Supplemental
ceqa-1c1ca4eff28f49ddee.description: NOTICE OF DETERMINATION FOR AN ADDENDUM TO THE ENVISION SAN JOSE 2040 GENERAL PLAN FINAL PROGRAM ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT AS SUPPLEMENTED (SCH# 200972096), DOWNTOWN STRATEGY 2040 FINAL ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT (SCH# 2003042127) AND ADDENDA THERETO The City of San Jose prepared an Addendum pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15164, to the Envision San Jose 2040 General Plan Final Program Environmental Impact Report (General Plan EIR) as supplemented and the Downtown Strategy 2040 Final Environmental Impact Report for amendments to San Jose Municipal Code (SJMC) Chapter 13.48 (Historic Preservation Ordinance). The Historic Preservation Ordinance Amendments revise Section 13.48.020 (Definitions) to update the definition of .. historic district" and "landmark" and add definitions for "detrimental," "historic integrity," and "substantial alteration." Updates clarify that a Historic Preservation Pennit (HP Permit) is required only for exterior changes to properties officially designated by the City Council. New definitions specify what constitutes a detriment and guide evaluation of project compatibility in the HP Permit process. Additionally, Section 13.48.240 is amended to allow the City Council to recognize that a project's detrimental effects on a landmark or historic district property may be outweighed by economic, legal, social, technological, or other benefits. The San Jose City Council certified the General Plan EJR on November 1, 2011 (Resolution No. 76041) for the Envision San Jose 2040 General Plan, a comprehensive update to the San Jose 2020 General Plan. The General Plan provides the long-term policy framework guiding land use, development, and City capital decisions to support San Jose's social, economic, and environmental goals. The EJR analyzed environmental impacts and program-level mitigation measures, including effects on cultural resources under federal and state regulations such as the National Historic Preservation Act, Secretary of the Interior's Standards, CEQA, SB 18 tribal consultation, the California Historical Building Code, the Mills Act, and the City's Historic Preservation Ordinance. A Supplemental Program EIR, certified on December 15, 2015 (Resolution No. 77617), further evaluated greenhouse gas emissions and climate-related impacts associated with ongoing implementation of the General Plan and supported related discretionary actions, including updates and re-adoption of the City's Greenhouse Gas Reduction Strategy. The San Jose City Council certified the Downtown Strategy 2040 Final EIR on December 18, 2018 (Resolution No. 78942)). The Downtown Strategy 2040 updates the 2000 plan by expanding Downtown's development capacity- transferring 4,000 housing units and 10,000 jobs from later General Plan growth areas - and adjusting the.Downtown boundary along North 4th Street between East St. John and East Julian Streets. The Final EIR tiers from the General Plan EIR, provides program-level analysis of overall Downtown growth, and includes project-level review for transportation, air quality, and noise. Future projects must be evaluated for consistency with this EIR, and additional environmental review is required where site-specific issues, including cultural and historic resources, were not previously addressed. The Addendum evaluates whether the Historic Preservation Ordinance Amendments would result in new significant environmental impacts or substantially increase the severity of previously identified impacts disclosed in the General Plan EIR and Downtown Strategy 2040 Final EIR. The analysis concluded implementation of the Historic Preservation Ordinance Amendments would not result in any new significant effects on the environment beyond those already identified in the previously certified General Plan EIR and Downtown Strategy EIR. The General Plan EIR concluded that new development and redevelopment allowed under the General Plan could result in a substantial adverse change in the significance of historic architectural resources; however, implementation of General Plan policies and existing regulations and programs would substantially reduce impacts to historically significant architectural resources to a less than significant level. The Downtown Strategy EIR disclosed significant and unavoidable cumulative impacts to historic resources resulting from the build out of Downtown. The addition of an override provision would not result in new significant impacts or increase the severity of previously identified impacts. Any individual project invoking the override provision would still be subject to CEQA analysis, disclosure of significant and unavoidable impacts, and adoption of a Statement of Overriding Considerations as required.

ceqa-15bb91214e2de8b19c.name: 5853 Rue Ferrari Project
ceqa-15bb91214e2de8b19c.description: A Site Development Permit Amendment to an existing approximately 300,000-square-foot one-story warehouse building that was approved under File No. H2 l-006. This Amendment consists of site modifications due to the change in use to a research and development facility, including the addition of backup generators, transformers, evaporative cooling chillers, and a step-down power transition yard to support research and laboratory uses, and associated site improvements on an approximately 17.4 gross-acre site. To support the project, PG&E will upgrade their infrastructure within their rights-of-way and easements in off-site areas.

ceqa-1484fc08d356acc826.name: Rosewood/Morgan Hill Medical Campus Project
ceqa-1484fc08d356acc826.description: The proposed project consists of a request to amend an adopted PD Master Plan to allow an increase in medical office square footage within the 9.61-acre project site. Through approval of the PD Master Plan Amendment, the proposed project would result in a net increase of 150,500 sf of medical/commercial uses relative to the originally approved project. After accounting for the existing 15,900 sf of medical office use that would be demolished as part of the proposed project, the total net increase would be 134,600 sf. The development would generally include three new medical office buildings, a six-story, 65-foot-tall parking structure with 965 parking spaces, additional surface parking, and installation of utilities.
ceqa-1484fc08d356acc826.crossStreets: Juan Hernandez Drive and Barrett Avenue

ceqa-2418e4e2cdc0175ac7.name: Canna Culture Corporation
ceqa-2418e4e2cdc0175ac7.description: The proposed project will operate a retail license out of an existing facility located at 1101 W. San Carlos Street, San Jose, CA 95126 (APN 261-41-103). The building is 3,680 sq ft on 0.4 acres. The parcel is flat, hosts several trees and provides a parking lot. The building is free standing, constructed in 1980, painted white with a flat black roof. The property is located on the corner of Lincoln Avenue and W. San Carlos Street and north of HWY 280. The City of San Jose Zoning Permit certifies that the property complies with location requirements for a cannabis retail storefront and dispensary site.
ceqa-2418e4e2cdc0175ac7.crossStreets: Lincoln Avenue and W San Carlos Street

ceqa-b9adac3d0445256fad.name: 1207 North Capitol Avenue Residential Project
ceqa-b9adac3d0445256fad.description: As proposed, the project would include demolition of the existing 3,680 square foot single-family residence to construct a five-story, 128-unit affordable housing development. All units would be located within a single U-shaped building with a courtyard and maximum building height of 53 feet and two inches. All units would be low-income units, with the exception of one manager’s unit at market rate. The building would include two lobbies, a fitness room, yoga studio, game room, community kitchen, offices, bike storage, and package room on the ground floor. The courtyard would consist of outdoor common open space and surface parking. Solar panels would be installed on the roof of the building. Access to the project site would be provided via a new 24-foot wide, two-way, right-in, right-out driveway along North Capitol Avenue. The driveway would lead to a surface parking lot located in the courtyard of the proposed building. The parking lot would contain 52 parking spaces.

ceqa-471f30a0f06907e97e.name: Idlewild Townhomes Project
ceqa-471f30a0f06907e97e.description: The approved Idlewild Townhomes Development Project will involve the demolition of the existing commercial building and the construction of 55 townhome units and 10 accessory dwelling units. There are several different townhome types proposed, including two-, three-, and four-bedroom units, ranging from 1,442 to 2,295 square feet. Each townhome will have three stories with a roof deck and will be approximately 43 feet tall at the highest point. Each townhome will include private open space through a porch, roof deck, and balcony, averaging approximately 396 square feet per unit. The approved project includes 110 off-street garage residential parking spaces and 9 guest uncovered parking spaces. Each unit will have an attached private two-car garage. Bicycle storage for residents is provided in the private garages. The approved project will provide 1,140 square feet of common usable open space.

ceqa-426254fdb01b06d686.name: Wildlife Improvements
ceqa-426254fdb01b06d686.description: The purpose of this project is to improve wildlife connectivity by providing a safe passage for wildlife by through the construction of wildlife-vehicle collision reduction devices in Santa Clara County along US 101. These devices are intended to reduce wildlife access to the roadway and decrease maintenance exposure to roadway cleanup. Due to the size and weight of animals accessing the roadway, wildlife-vehicle collisions can result in property damage, personal injury, and wildlife mortality. The proposed devices would direct wildlife away from the roadway traffic and toward safer locations. The project is needed to prevent wildlife-vehicle collisions and reduce maintenance exposure along US 101.

ceqa-06b5040b626c32b02d.name: San Francisco Bay Federal Channels Operation and Maintenance Dredging and Sediment Placement Activities, Dredging Years 2025-2034
ceqa-06b5040b626c32b02d.projectTitle: San Francisco Bay Federal Channels Operation and Maintenance Dredging and Sediment Placement Activities, Dredging Years 2025-2034
ceqa-06b5040b626c32b02d.agency: California Regional Water Quality Control Board, San Francisco Bay Region 2
ceqa-06b5040b626c32b02d.agencyName: Regional Water Quality Control Board, Region 2 - San Francisco Bay, Oakland
ceqa-06b5040b626c32b02d.description: The United States Army Corps of Engineers San Francisco District will continue maintenance dredging of the federal navigation channels in San Francisco Bay to maintain their navigability for dredging years 2025 to 2034. The San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board has issued a Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification and Waste Discharge Requirements pursuant to the State of California’s Porter-Cologne Water Quality Control Act for USACE’s continued maintenance dredging operations in SF Bay. Dredging involves the excavation of accumulated sediment from the channel, as well as the transportation and placement of the sediment at a permitted location, consistent with permit conditions established by applicable regulatory agencies. Sediment must be tested for suitability for placement at any site.

ceqa-81d199a6bb8d9e1dc6.name: Stevens Creek Bank Erosion & Outfall Repairs, Whisman Park Reach
ceqa-81d199a6bb8d9e1dc6.projectTitle: Stevens Creek Bank Erosion & Outfall Repairs, Whisman Park Reach
ceqa-81d199a6bb8d9e1dc6.agency: California Regional Water Quality Control Board, San Francisco Bay Region 2
ceqa-81d199a6bb8d9e1dc6.agencyName: Regional Water Quality Control Board, Region 2 - San Francisco Bay, Oakland
ceqa-81d199a6bb8d9e1dc6.description: The Project is located at Stevens Creek (Creek) near Whisman Park and about 2.5 miles upstream of San Francisco Bay in Mountain View, Santa Clara County (Lat. 37.40095; Long. -122.06939). Project work will involve bank stabilization and outfall repairs from erosion that occurred at three areas along approximately 700 linear feet (LF) of the Creek during the 2022/2023 Winter season. The bank erosion caused a near-vertical 15-ft-high scarp within about 8-10 horizontal feet from the edge of a paved pedestrian pathway along Stevens Creek Trail (Trail), which separates the Creek from State Highway 85 to the west. Additional bank erosion could result in damage and public access closure to both the Trail and/or the Hetch Hetchy Trail pedestrian bridge. The Project will install planted and non-planted log-crib structures, planted biodegradable fabric-covered compacted soil slopes, and two buried storm drain culvert downdrains discharging onto rock-filled log-crib structure faces. Project work will be implemented at three work areas that include four bank erosion areas and two failed storm drain outfall areas. Work Area 1 is experiencing ongoing severe bank erosion (Bank Erosion Area 1) and features an exposed section of existing sakrete slope armor along the Creek bank, which is undermining the structural integrity of an existing cast-in-place steel-reinforced concrete downdrain (Bank Erosion Area 2 and Failed Storm Drain Outfall 1). Work Area 2 has severe bank erosion (Bank Erosion Area 3) that includes retreatment of the Creek top of bank into the existing gravel maintenance access road within the Santa Clara Valley Water District (SCVWD) easement. At Work Area 3, severe bank erosion (Bank Erosion Area 4) has retreated the Creek top of bank to within eight feet from the Trail and four feet from the pedestrian bridge abutment and is undermining a downstream storm drain outfall (Failed Storm Drain Outfall 2).

ceqa-d0f9359f24386f416d.name: Henry W. Coe State Park New Interpretative Panels
ceqa-d0f9359f24386f416d.projectTitle: Henry W. Coe State Park New Interpretative Panels
ceqa-d0f9359f24386f416d.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-d0f9359f24386f416d.description: The purpose of this project is to install new interpretive panels at the Headquarters complex at Henry W. Coe State Park to provide information about the park’s history for visitors. State Parks staff will: Use hand tools to excavate six (6) 24-inch-deep post holes at six (6) locations within the Headquarters complex; Insert one (1) 8-inch diameter wooden post into each hole and backfill to grade with concrete; On a post installed at the Visitor Center, use a bolt/washer assembly to attach one (1) 54-inch x 32-inch interpretive panel to the post; On the remaining five (5) posts, use a bolt/washer assembly to attach one (1) 22.5-inch x 16-inch interpretive panel to each post, and Spread excavated soils on-site.

ceqa-24685c90638995e7cb.name: 15300 and 15330 Los Gatos Boulevard (The Arya Mixed-Use Development)
ceqa-24685c90638995e7cb.projectTitle: 15300 and 15330 Los Gatos Boulevard (The Arya Mixed-Use Development)
ceqa-24685c90638995e7cb.description: The proposal includes the demolition of the existing structure and the construction of a nine-story building, with three levels of underground parking. Uses include a seven-level, 175-unit luxury condominium project (including 20 percent affordable units) constructed over street level commercial space (37,862 square feet) and three levels of underground parking. An 6,988 square foot open plaza would be located at the street level. An additional commercial space on the roof (4,006 square feet) for a prospective eating establishment is also included. The total project is 575,634 square feet and has an overall height of 116 feet and 6 inches from the commercial floor level to the top of the building located at the roof deck. There would be seven stacked residential levels with 25 units per level totaling at 175 units (21 studios, 21 one-bedroom units, 70 two-bedroom units and 63 three-bedroom units). The second floor includes a pool, spa, barbecue areas, and outdoor community space. The roof level would include a private fitness area, a private community room, and a private outdoor rood deck. The private outdoor roof deck would include a community spa, a covered barbecue area, outdoor game area, outdoor seating, outdoor dining, pet area, and raised planting beds for residents’ use only. The public portion of the roof deck would include a restaurant and bar, an outdoor lounge, an outdoor bar, and outdoor seating and dining. Excavation for the garage would result in a net export of 98,000 cubic yards of soil.
ceqa-24685c90638995e7cb.crossStreets: Los Gatos Blvd and Gateway Drive

ceqa-24685c90638995e7cb.developmentType: Other (Mixed Use- 175 Residential Units and 41,868 s.f Commercial )

ceqa-215048b2c70ba47902.name: Metcalf Motorcycle County Park Site Plan
ceqa-215048b2c70ba47902.projectTitle: Metcalf Motorcycle County Park Site Plan
ceqa-215048b2c70ba47902.description: The Metcalf Motorcycle County Park Site Plan Report proposes various improvements within the core-use area of the Park, including installation of a new visitor center, a vehicle wash, a restroom building, an unloading ramp, shade structures; construction of ADA improvements; creation of additional pathways; reconfiguration of parking areas; and improved connectivity between the main visitor area and OHV trails. Specifically, the project would include: • Demolition of the existing administration building and construction of a new, 2,865-square-foot visitor center west of the main park entry and exit driveway, which would include staff offices, a break room, restrooms, showers, lockers, a mud room, a porch, first aid, and storage. • Demolition of the existing restroom building and construction of a new restroom building in the southwest corner of the parking lot. • Installation of one additional pedestrian shade shelter and a solar photovoltaic system shade structure along the perimeter of the parking lot and along the trail and pedestrian paths. • Construction of a vehicle wash southwest of the visitor center for County Parks vehicles only • Installation of a new trash enclosure at the southeast corner of the parking lot • Installation of an unloading ramp at the northwest corner of the parking lot • Reconfiguration of the parking area to improve vehicular circulation and meet ADA requirements • Provision of pedestrian paths throughout the project site, including along the restroom building and visitor center, to provide enhanced access to the proposed buildings, trail entries, and gazebo. Dirt paths that separate pedestrians from OHV would provide access to the Beginner Oval and Novice motocross track. • Installation of a new bioswale between the parking lot and the Beginner Oval to manage stormwater flows on the project site.

ceqa-02b8542ecdf5996c27.name: El Camino Real Specific Plan
ceqa-02b8542ecdf5996c27.description: The City proposes a Specific Plan to transform the El Camino Real Focus Area from a series of automobile-oriented strip malls to a tree-lined, pedestrian and transit-oriented corridor with a mix of residential and retail uses. The purpose of the Specific Plan is to refine and implement the General Plan vision for the area by creating goals, policies, and design standards for future development within the Plan boundary. The Plan provides a comprehensive vision for the Plan area along with goals, policies, strategies and development standards to guide the Plan area’s future growth in an equitable manner than benefits the community. Build out associated with the proposed Specific Plan over the next 20 to 30 years (2055) would include the development of 4,392 housing units, as well as a reduction of approximately 289,000 square feet of commercial space. General Plan land use designations within the Plan area include: Community Mixed-Use; High Density Residential; Medium Density Residential; Very Low Density Residential, Neighborhood Mixed-Use; Parks/Open Space, Public/Quasi Public; and Regional Mixed-Use. The existing zoning districts include Public/Quasi Public; Mixed Use Community Commercial; Mixed Use Regional Commercial; Parks/Open Space; Planned Development; Single Family; and High Density Residential.
ceqa-02b8542ecdf5996c27.crossStreets: El Camino Real between Lafayette Street on the east and the City limits on the west.
ceqa-02b8542ecdf5996c27.developmentType: Residential (Units 4392, Acres 238), Other (Commercial Area would be reduced under the specific plan), Transportation:Other (Modifications to Roadway)

ceqa-2bcc799e399a248b8e.name: Foothill College Tennis Courts Renovations CEQA Exemption
ceqa-2bcc799e399a248b8e.projectTitle: Foothill College Tennis Courts Renovations CEQA Exemption
ceqa-2bcc799e399a248b8e.description: The District will resurface the existing tennis courts and add pickleball lines and lighting. The size of the courts will not change and there will be no change to student enrollment. The addition of pickleball courts will increase available capacity at the courts and provide another sport available to play on campus. The public will continue to have access to the courts.

ceqa-05ef3a430eaafa860c.name: 333-385 Moffett Park Drive (Platform Moffett Park)
ceqa-05ef3a430eaafa860c.description: The project will demolish the two existing office buildings and redevelop the site with two, three-story buildings totaling 293,996 square feet situated above a three-story podium. The buildings will be for office, research & development, and medical clinic uses with 10,376 square feet reserved on the ground floor for "creation space" (defined as "space for production, distribution, repair, businesses, art or crafting, clean manufacturing, construction industries, start-up spaces, or spaces for similar uses"). The podium will provide three levels of above-grade parking and an outdoor amenity area containing a fitness space, outdoor kitchen and dining area, seating, gaming table, and pollinator garden. The project will also include three privately owned and publicly accessible spaces that would include bike service areas, pedestrian paving, and seating. The project buildings will reach a maximum height of 85 feet and result in a floor area ratio of 1.35. The project approval includes a Special Development Permit, Site Master Plan Permit, and Development Agreement.

ceqa-a7dbedeaa793e32279.name: Multifamily Zone and Objective Design Standards Project
ceqa-a7dbedeaa793e32279.projectTitle: Multifamily Zone and Objective Design Standards Project
ceqa-a7dbedeaa793e32279.description: The Project consists of (1) amendments to the Land Use Element of the Los Altos Hills General plan implementing multi-family designation and use; (2) amendments to Title 10 of the Los Altos Hills Municipal Code to rezone parcels from Residential-Agricultural (single family) to Multi-Family zoning districts and adopt development standards; and (3) adoption of Objective Design Standards for Multi-Family Zoning Districts (collectively, "Project"). The Project would implement Programs A-1, A-4, A-5 and B-4 of the 2023-2031 Housing Element, including the rezoning of approximately 19 acres of land and creation of multi-family zones/overlay zones, and would ensure the Town has the appropriate zoning in place to achieve its RHNA requirement and a 15 percent buffer as outlined in the Housing Element. The multifamily zones would be adopted with Objective Design Standards that would provide for the future development of residential housing at a density of 20-24 du/ac. In addition, minor amendments to the General Plan Land Use Element would be made for consistency purposes. The zones would introduce a new housing typology (multifamily) that does not currently exist in the Town of Los Altos Hills. The City Council adopted separate resolutions on October 16, 2025 approving the objective design standards, and introduced an ordinance amending the Municipal Code to effectuate the rezoning. The City Council adopted the Land Use Element and the ordinance on December 9, 2025.

ceqa-d98970a9bc495778bd.name: Amendment to the General Plan 2023-2031 Housing Element
ceqa-d98970a9bc495778bd.projectTitle: Amendment to the General Plan 2023-2031 Housing Element
ceqa-d98970a9bc495778bd.description: The Project consists of an Amendment to the General Plan 2023-2031 Housing Element. The Amendment would specify the proposed maximum densities on sites to be rezoned from the R-A zoning district to multi-family; specify a total multi-family rezoning area of 19 acres; include updates reaffirming property owner interest in redeveloping the multi-family rezoning sites and additional feasibility analysis conducted to demonstrate viability of housing development; and make other non-substantive, clerical revisions. The Housing Element Amendment facilitates the Town's proposal to rezone sites from the single-family R-A district to multi-family and continues to implement the housing strategies, goals and programs of the 2023-2031 Housing Element. It is intended to provide clarity and maintain internal consistency across governing land use and planning documents.

ceqa-55fc0b5a45469f3b11.name: Madera Residential Project Update 4
ceqa-55fc0b5a45469f3b11.description: Special Use Permit Amendment to change the material of the exterior fiber cement board to stucco on the levels above the pedestrian level and to allow Saturday construction hours from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. through August 2027 (referred here as Modified Project). All other project details as previously approved in Planning File No. SP20-019, and subsequent amendments would remain unchanged.

ceqa-e51a2e9a39c952c78e.name: De Anza College Physical Education Complex Renovation Project
ceqa-e51a2e9a39c952c78e.projectTitle: De Anza College Physical Education Complex Renovation Project
ceqa-e51a2e9a39c952c78e.description: This project at De Anza College will renovate the existing Physical Education (PE) Complex to enhance student success by creating modern and code compliant learning environments for kinesiology and physical education programs. The renovation will cover approximately 76,354 gross square feet (GSF), including 1,100 assignable square feet (ASF) of lecture space, 54,360 ASF of PE space, and 3,711 ASF of office space. Renovations will include at minimum a seismic upgrade to all PE Complex buildings along with site improvements that support accessible paths of travel and utility upgrades. The project will not increase or decrease the student enrollment or campus occupant capacity. The project will replace or rehabilitate building systems that have reached the end of their service life. These systems include but are not limited to HVAC systems, water heaters, plumbing and condensate systems, fire protection and detection systems, electrical infrastructure, roofing, exterior wall systems, windows, doors, and elevators. Interior renovations will address restrooms, locker rooms, physical education classrooms including gymnasiums, adapted physical education classrooms, and office spaces. The project will also resolve code compliance and accessibility issues such as the absence of ADA compliant routes and facilities, inadequate locker room layouts, limited gender-neutral facilities, and undersized instructional and storage spaces. Regulatory Compliance: To ensure compliance with the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, FHDA and its contractors will remove vegetation outside of the bird nesting season (February 1 to September 30) when feasible and/or retain a qualified biologist to conduct a preconstruction nesting survey if construction would begin during the nesting season. If this occurs, FHDA and its contractors will ensure that the survey occurs no sooner than 7 days prior to construction and upon the direction of the qualified biologist, construction activities proximate to any active nests are postponed until young have fledged. To ensure compliance with California Fish and Game Code Section 4150 regarding roosting or overwintering bats, FHDA and its contractors will schedule work outside the bat roosting period (generally from March through September) when feasible and/or retain a qualified biologist to conduct a preconstruction bat roosting survey of trees and buildings when site activity would begin during the roosting season. If this occurs, FHDA and its contractors will ensure that the survey occurs no more than 90 days and no less than 30 days prior to the commencement of activities within the project site. If trees or buildings with potential roosting habitat and/or bat sign are identified, the biologist will also conduct an evening visual emergence survey of the roosts from 0.5 hours before to 1-2 hours after sunset for a minimum of two nights, using full-spectrum acoustic detectors to assist in species identification. If evening surveys confirm the presence of an active bat maternity roost, that roost will remain undisturbed with a buffer as determined by the biologist until August 31 or until the biologist has determined that the roost is no longer active.

ceqa-70b62b1ca134e60964.name: Fellows Dike Sampling Investigation
ceqa-70b62b1ca134e60964.description: The Fellows Dike sampling investigation is needed to collect information regarding subsurface materials to support the planning and design for the proposed CDSRP. The investigation would be conducted within Valley Water property by the Fellows Dike area immediately south of Calero Reservoir. Activities would include conducting approximately 19 soil samples at 1 foot below ground surface, and 3 groundwater samples from 25-45 feet below ground surface. The investigation area would be accessed from existing paved or dirt roads. Soil samples would be collected utilizing a direct-push or Standard Penetration Testing (SPT) capable drill rig, which would drill approximately 4-inch diameter holes beneath ground surface. Approximately three temporary groundwater wells would be installed in three of the holes to collect the groundwater samples. Two additional soil samples would be collected from the planned location for the Bailey Fellows House, reaching depths up to 20 feet below ground surface. The house is proposed to be relocated as part of the CDSRP. After work is complete, all excavated areas would be backfilled with the existing soil and samples would be properly sealed and sent to a laboratory to be tested for potential hazardous materials. All excess soil cuttings and purge water would be placed in 55-gallon drums and disposed of off-site. Concurrently with the soil and groundwater sampling, pedestrian surveyors would collect asbestos, lead, and Polychlorinated Biphenyl samples of all on-site structures, except the Bailey Fellows House.

ceqa-ed6cce0f2b89716417.name: MMP-2025-002

ceqa-622fc346f71ef5490c.name: Temporary Additional Point of Delivery of SCVWD’s SWP Supplies and Additional Return Mechanisms to Recover SCVWD's SWP Supplies Stored in Semitropic Water Bank
ceqa-622fc346f71ef5490c.projectTitle: Temporary Additional Point of Delivery of SCVWD’s SWP Supplies and Additional Return Mechanisms to Recover SCVWD's SWP Supplies Stored in Semitropic Water Bank
ceqa-622fc346f71ef5490c.description: Santa Clara Valley Water District (Santa Clara) is a State Water Project (SWP) contractor and a Central Valley Project (CVP) contractor. Santa Clara typically receives its SWP water supplies from DWR through the South Bay Aqueduct and receives its CVP water from Reclamation from Turnout 59 in San Luis Reservoir and subsequently through the CVP’s San Felipe Division facilities. SWP Agreement #25013 provides for the delivery of a portion of Santa Clara’s SWP water supplies to an additional delivery point—specifically Turnout 59 at San Luis Reservoir—for subsequent conveyance to Santa Clara by Reclamation via CVP’s San Felipe Division facilities through December 31, 2029. This agreement aims to enhance operational flexibility during periods when the South Bay Aqueduct is unavailable or operating at reduced capacity. SWP Agreement #25014 similarly seeks to improve delivery flexibility but focuses specifically on the delivery of Santa Clara’s previously banked SWP water stored in Semitropic Water Storage District’s groundwater banking program under SWPAO Agreements #06011 and #10012, which only provide for the recovery of banked water via the South Bay Aqueduct. SWP #25014 provides for additional delivery mechanisms to allow Santa Clara’s banked water under SWPAO #06011 and #10012 to be delivered into 1) San Luis Reservoir for temporary storage and future recovery through the CVP’s San Felipe Division facilities, and/or 2) San Luis Reservoir for temporary storage and future delivery into Santa Clara’s service area through the South Bay Aqueduct, through December 31, 2029.

ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.name: Glencore Recycling LLC, Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Renewal
ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.projectTitle: Glencore Recycling LLC, Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Renewal
ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-22e3117fcbdb48fcea.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to authority granted under California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapter 20 has issued a Standardized Series B Hazardous Waste Facility Permit Renewal (Permit Renewal) for Glencore Recycling LLC (Facility) for ten additional years. This Permit Renewal will allow the Facility to continue to treat and store liquid and solid hazardous waste at the Facility. This Permit Renewal includes the addition of two new miscellaneous units for triple washing containers, and a reduction in the overall volume of hazardous waste the Facility is permitted to treat. The Facility Permit will change from a Series A to Series B Standardized Permit. Pursuant to Health and Safety Code section 25143, DTSC is also granting a variance to the Permittee conditionally exempting Unit 1, Unit 2, and Unit 7a from the setback requirement specified in California Code of Regulations, title 22, section 66264.176.There are no other proposed changes and no physical changes that require construction and/or ground disturbance for the Permit Renewal. Background: The site of the Facility has been used for heavy manufacturing operations since the 1930s. Metal recycling operations were established at this location in the early 1970s and underwent many different names before settling with Glencore Recycling LLC in 2015. The Facility area is approximately 2.2 acres in a developed industrial area. DTSC initially issued a Permit to the Facility on November 1, 1994, and renewed the Permit on May 6, 2012. The Facility area is composed of a warehouse, offices, and treatment and storage areas that are used to process different materials for metals recovery including electronic scraps, components, manufacturing byproducts, wastes, concentrates, and residues. Project Activities: The Facility generates and receives precious metal bearing acid solutions that are stored in designated areas before and after treatment. Treatment of acid solutions includes pH adjustment, precipitation, neutralization, and/or evaporation to convert precious metals into solid form. Tray furnaces are used to bake solids containing combustible organics, dry inorganic sludge, and to evaporate water from neutral and alkaline solutions. Hazardous waste solids, sludge, scrap metal, and excluded recyclable materials are melted in crucible furnaces to recover, refine, or separate metals. Mechanical processing such as grinding, milling, screening, and blending of ash, sludge, and other solids in miscellaneous units to prepare and collect a representative sample of metals for analysis to facilitate further recovery operations. Dry and wet additives may be combined with treated material to improve handling and flow properties. The Permit will authorize the Facility to operate 12 existing hazardous waste management units (HWMU) and install two new miscellaneous units for triple washing containers. The Facility will be authorized to store up to a maximum of 3,300 gallons of liquid hazardous waste and 153 tons of solid hazardous waste, and treat 50,000 gallons per month of liquid hazardous waste and 50 tons per month of solid hazardous waste. The addition of the two miscellaneous units will not require any construction or ground disturbance. The Permit will also authorize a variance from the setback requirement specified in California Code of Regulations, title 22, section 66264.176 for Units 1, 2, and 7a. The variance will not cause any operational changes as containers within these units are currently and will continue to be within 50 feet of the property line. There are no other proposed changes to the Facility, or any of the waste being stored or treated, or to any other operations or units. There will be no operational changes or ground disturbance. All previous Permit requirements will remain in effect. This Permit Renewal will not result in any new or substantially more severe significant impacts on the environment.

ceqa-e526a2ecb2e32b60f7.name: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Sunnyvale for the 2022 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-e526a2ecb2e32b60f7.projectTitle: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Sunnyvale for the 2022 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-e526a2ecb2e32b60f7.description: The California Energy Commission (CEC) adopts and regularly updates regulations that define a process for local governments to apply to the CEC to make certain findings regarding locally adopted energy conservation or energy insulation standards (CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 and section 10-110; Public Resources Code section 25402.1(h)(2)). The local government’s proposed standards are often referred to as the Local Reach Codes and require local governments submit an application to the CEC consistent with the requirements listed in section 10-106(b). Before the local standards may be enforced, the CEC must make two non-discretionary findings pursuant to PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and as listed in section 10-106(a): 1) The proposed local standards will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2022 Energy Code, and 2) The local government has filed the basis of its cost-effectiveness determination with the CEC. On September 04, 2025, the City of Sunnyvale (the City) submitted an application to the CEC that included: 1) the basis of its determination that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 3244-25 are cost-effective; and (2) documentation that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 3244-25 will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2022 Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Energy Code), as required by PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and by CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 (section 10-106). Based on the information submitted, staff analysis, and the Executive Director's recommendation, the CEC approved findings of the City’s section 10-106 application at the CEC’s November 12, 2025, Business Meeting.

ceqa-7f0a8d72c2f5180841.name: 901 N.Rengstorff Avenue Project (project addresses includes 901-987 N.Rengstorff)
ceqa-7f0a8d72c2f5180841.projectTitle: 901 N.Rengstorff Avenue Project (project addresses includes 901-987 N.Rengstorff)
ceqa-7f0a8d72c2f5180841.description: 901 North Rengstorff Avenue Project Project Description – November 2025 The Project Applicant, Mario Ambra, proposes the 901 North Rengstorff Avenue Project (Project), which involves demolition of all existing structures and development of a multi-family residential building on an approximately 1.26-acre (54,782 square-foot) Project site located at 901, 913 and 987 N. Rengstorff Avenue in the City of Mountain View. The project site is located on the east side of N. Rengstorff Avenue between Leghorn Street and Plymouth Street, just south of the U.S. 101 Highway, and is bounded by N. Rengstorff Avenue to the west, a former olive oil factory currently used as a single-family home to the north, existing residential/commercial uses to the east, and Plymouth Street to the south. The Project site contains an approximately 2,253-square-foot multi-family residential building at the southwest corner of the Project site, three accessory buildings at the southeastern portion of the Project site, and an accessory building toward the northern boundary of the Project site. The Project is proposed as a “Builder's Remedy” housing development under the Builder’s Remedy provisions of the Housing Accountability Act (Gov. Code §65589.5). The Project would demolish all existing structures on the Project site and construct an approximately 499,525-square-foot, 15-story multi-family residential building. The proposed building would contain 455 residential units (20% affordable) comprised of 183 studios, 142 one-bedroom units and 130 two-bedroom units. Additionally, the Project would include approximately 15,818 square feet of common open space and 1,313 square feet of private open space. The maximum building height would be approximately 184 feet. The Project would provide 429 garage parking spaces and 356 bicycle parking spaces. Vehicular access to the Project site would be provided via a new 24-foot parking garage entrance on the southern border of the Project site along Plymouth Street. The Project building would connect to existing City infrastructure in N. Rengstorff Avenue and Plymouth Street. The Project would remove 67 on site trees, consisting of 19 Heritage Trees and 48 non-heritage trees. The Project would plant a total of 52 replacement trees. In addition, the Project would relocate 5 Olive trees (4 Heritage) to the northwest corner of 987 N. Rengstorff Avenue immediately adjacent to the former olive oil facility. The project request includes development permits (“Entitlements”) required by the City of Mountain View to construct the building and a Lot Line Adjustment to create the project site and the parcel to the north (for the olive oil factory). Project construction would be developed in a single phase and is anticipated to last up to 30 months beginning in April 2028 and ending by October 2030. The City of Mountain View prepared an AB 130 consistency analysis for the Project that determined the Project meets the criteria for a CEQA exempt housing project under AB 130, including the environmental factors under Public Resources Code Section 21080.66, and the Project is eligible to use the statutory exemption under AB 130. This document is available for review from the City of Mountain View upon request. The City of Mountain View City Council approved the Project, including the above-noted CEQA exemption, on November 18, 2025.

ceqa-66344755e72e36b1d3.name: 1605 South 7th Street
ceqa-66344755e72e36b1d3.description: The Project would construct an approximately 106,752-square-foot new one-story concrete tilt-up warehouse/industrial use building. An approximately 36,613 square-foot prefabricated canopy structure would be installed over the loading zone along the east elevation. The maximum height of the building would be 46 feet. Approximately 8,694 square feet of the total 106,752-square-foot building would be incidental office use. Four access driveways would provide ingress and egress to the Project. The Project would provide approximately 178 employee parking stalls, 10 accessible stalls, 413 van parking stalls, 18 electric vehicle(EV) parking stalls, 72 EV capable stalls with the ability support future EV equipment, 18 bicycle parking stalls, and 5 motorcycle parking stalls. Project implementation would remove existing vegetation on site, including 36 trees. A total of 179 new shade, accent, and street trees would be planted.

ceqa-47ef730d5c2ea47b39.name: Santa Teresa Boulevard/Day Road Intersection Improvement Project

ceqa-47ef730d5c2ea47b39.description: The City of Gilroy, as the CEQA Lead Agency, proposes the Santa Teresa Boulevard/Day Road Intersection Improvement Project (project). The project is located at the intersection of Santa Teresa Boulevard and Day Road in the City of Gilroy. The project would improve safety for pedestrians and cyclists crossing Santa Teresa Boulevard by adding sidewalks, curb and gutter, curb ramps, striped crosswalks, and Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) elements. Pedestrian improvements would meet Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements. The project would cold plane existing Asphalt Concrete (AC) pavement and overlay it with Hot Mix Asphalt Type A. In addition, existing Metal Beam Guard Railing would be replaced with Caltrans standard Midwest Guardrail System and end treatments.

ceqa-4692decd51a20f01a6.name: 4898 El Camino Real – Multi-Family Residential Development
ceqa-4692decd51a20f01a6.projectTitle: 4898 El Camino Real – Multi-Family Residential Development
ceqa-4692decd51a20f01a6.description: The project involves construction of an eight-story multi-family residential building with 85 dwelling units, including 10 very low-income units, on a 0.43-acre vacant site at the southeast corner of El Camino Real and Jordan Avenue. The development includes a fully underground automated parking garage with 95 vehicle spaces, long-term and short-term bicycle parking, and a rooftop deck for resident use. The building would have a maximum height of 109 feet, nine inches to the top of the elevator tower. The project utilizes State Density Bonus Law to request waivers for front setback, interior side setback, exterior side setback, rear setback, building height, upper-story step backs, vertical façade articulation, façade entrances, privacy and line of sight, parapet length and screening, pedestrian-scaled entrance, interior side yard landscaping, rear yard landscaping, driveway landscaping, transformer fence height, and loading space location. Site improvements include new sidewalks, street trees, planters, and curb ramps along both street frontages.

ceqa-bba155f07b37318165.name: 996 Loraine Avenue Mixed-Use Development
ceqa-bba155f07b37318165.description: The project proposes to demolish the existing one-story, approximately 2,240 square foot commercial building, surface parking lot, and landscaping, and construct a new three-story, mixed-use building. The proposed mixed-use building would include approximately 962 square feet of ground floor retail, a total of 12 residential units (totaling 10,230 square feet) on the second and third floors, and an approximately 1,824 square foot landscaped rooftop terrace. The building would have a maximum height of 51 feet, two inches at the top of the elevator tower. The project would utilize the State Density Bonus Law to exceed the allowed maximum building height and requests waivers to the front and side setbacks, third story step-back, building recess guidelines, window and balcony orientation at the side yard, specifications for windows at the side yards, and parking and loading requirements.

ceqa-7282ab56924e50c379.name: Mountain View Public Safety Building
ceqa-7282ab56924e50c379.description: The approved project will remove the existing Mountain View Police Department (MVPD) building and associated parking lot and K-9 training area, and construct a new Public Safety Building, parking garage, indoor shooting range, surface parking, and K-9 training area at the same location. In the eastern corner of the project site, a 0.6-acre area will remain undeveloped for future potential uses by the City. The new Public Safety Building will be approximately 75,000 gross square feet, three stories high, and have a floor area ratio (FAR) of 0.49. Some of the designated areas include an auditorium, offices, sleep quarters, lockers, and a fitness room. ceqa-b3e874df475c0b2430.name: Al Shugart Dog Park
ceqa-b3e874df475c0b2430.description: The Al Shugart Dog Park ("project") is being proposed by the City of Scotts Valley to develop a dog park with additional park amenities. The project site is located on two partially-developed parcels (APNs 023-241-21 and -22) and one undeveloped parcel (023-241-11) at 400 Glenwood Drive in the City of Scotts Valley, Santa Cruz County. Improvements are proposed on approximately 5.64 acres of the property (“project site”). The project site consists of vacant open space and a small parking lot located in the southwest corner of the project site. The City proposes to develop a dog park with additional park amenities. The project would include improvements such as pet-proof fencing and dog park entry corrals; landscaping and irrigation. Pathway lighting along the existing multi-use pathway connecting to the project site and security lighting at the restroom is proposed. Park-user amenities would include the following: a 6,500 square-foot all-weather turf area; 9,000 square-foot area for small dogs; 28,000 square-foot area for large dogs; prefabricated restroom structure with two single use ADA-compliant stalls; park dedication monument; walking paths; benches, picnic areas, and seating areas; metal shade features; outdoor classroom; bike racks; drinking fountains; and, trash and recycling receptacles. The proposed project would require water service for drinking fountains, the restroom, and landscaping, and would connect to existing Scotts Valley Water District water service infrastructure near the project site. The proposed project would require lateral connections and routing to the City’s existing wastewater collection system, and would construct biotreatment planters for stormwater treatment and infiltration. The proposed project would involve the repair of an existing parking lot on Glenwood Road and parking lot expansion, resulting in a total of up to 42 spaces. The project site currently consists of vacant open space and a small parking lot located in the southwest corner of the project site.
ceqa-b3e874df475c0b2430.developmentType: Recreational (Dog park, and repair and expansion of an existing parking lot.)

ceqa-68fd3c89a85edf0ea5.name: Wastewater Energy and Electrical Resiliency Project
ceqa-68fd3c89a85edf0ea5.projectTitle: Wastewater Energy and Electrical Resiliency Project
ceqa-68fd3c89a85edf0ea5.description: The Wastewater Energy and Electrical Resiliency (WEER) Project would modernize and replace aging electrical infrastructure at the City Wastewater Treatment Facility (WWTF) to improve electrical system reliability, resiliency, operational flexibility, worker safety, and emergency preparedness. Most of the electrical distribution systems at the facility were installed in the 1980’s and 1990’s. While well maintained, it has exceeded its useful life and creates operational and maintenance challenges. The project includes replacement of deteriorated underground electrical distribution lines, completion of a redundant facility-wide electrical loop, replacement and consolidation of substations, transformers, and switchgear, construction of a new main electrical building, demolition of the existing maintenance building, installation of a new centralized standby power generation system, and upgrades to electrical equipment serving treatment processes such as interstage pumps and aeration blowers. The project would also replace obsolete medium-voltage equipment with modern electrical systems, incorporate upgraded controls and variable-frequency drives to improve operational efficiency, and provide infrastructure capable of supporting long-term WWTF operations. Replacements and upgrades are needed to improve reliability, safety, maintainability, and alignment with current standards to establish a 30-to-40-year service lifespan.

The Modified Project would involve installing an underground pipeline, an outfall, and an energy dissipation system.

ceqa-3ee59d0f5c3b319d4e.name: New Brighton Middle School Modernization and District Facilities Project
ceqa-3ee59d0f5c3b319d4e.projectTitle: New Brighton Middle School Modernization and District Facilities Project
ceqa-3ee59d0f5c3b319d4e.description: The project scope for Phase I of the modernization at New Brighton Middle School broadly includes the following: renovation of Admin/Student Services Building E including new floor finishes, new casework, new exterior door installation, and minor power and data upgrades; flooring replacement in Room 38 of Classroom Building F; modernization of Buildings K (classrooms), L (classrooms) and M (Library), including new finishes, casework, minor door/window replacement, new exterior awnings, minor structural modifications, plumbing and mechanical upgrades, and electrical (power, data, lighting and fire alarm) upgrades; renovation of Gymnasium Building P, including restroom upgrades (including finishes and plumbing fixtures), backstop replacement (with related structural upgrades), new exterior awnings and minor power, data and lighting upgrades; and site improvements include accessibility upgrades, paving removal and replacement, minor landscaping/irrigation/storm drain and fencing scope. The project scope for Phase II of the modernization broadly includes the following: Classroom modernization of Buildings D, E and F, including new flooring, patch repair and painting of existing wall and ceiling surfaces, new casework and modifications to existing casework to remain, door/window replacement (including window curtain removal), new exterior awnings, minor structural modifications, plumbing upgrades (at classroom sink location), and electrical (power and data) upgrades and bracing of existing light fixtures. Exterior classroom scope to include removal of existing lockers and related exterior finish wall surface repair; modernization of Special Ed Admin Building H to include finish and electrical upgrades (interior doors to remain) and reconfiguration of existing restrooms into gender-neutral, ADA compliant restrooms; restroom (single occupancy and multiple- accommodation) modernization of Buildings D, E and F, including partial removal of finishes at walls, floor and ceiling to stud and related patch/repair/painting of those surfaces. Restroom scope to also include toilet partition replacement and selective plumbing fixture replacement; refinishing of existing MP wood stage flooring; site improvements include accessibility upgrades, paving removal and replacement, landscaping/irrigation/storm drain improvements (primarily in classroom courtyards), two new shade structures, renovation of covered walkway roofs including stucco soffit replacement, replacement of existing roofing (including flashing and gutters) and abandonment/removal of obsolete roof-mounted utilities and a campus-wide fire alarm upgrade. The project also includes a District Office and MOT Department facility component, which broadly includes the following: Renovations/tenant improvements to the existing District Office building including reconfiguration of interior rooms/spaces (with new interior partitions), new interior finishes, exterior wall finishes/roofing improvements, door and window replacement, new casework, new restrooms and utility improvements including power, signal/LV (including lighting and fire alarm), mechanical and plumbing upgrades. Demolition of the existing Board Room/tech offices portable building and replacement with a new pre-engineered Steel Building facility that may include a bus/maintenance shop, offices, restrooms, and storage rooms. Site improvements to include site DWK 4343130v1 paving and landscaping improvements, site security (fencing/gates) and pertinent underground utility (dry and wet) upgrades.

ceqa-073773edcf004c65fe.name: Soquel Elementary School Modernization Project Phases I and II
ceqa-073773edcf004c65fe.projectTitle: Soquel Elementary School Modernization Project Phases I and II
ceqa-073773edcf004c65fe.description: The project scope for Phase I of the modernization at Soquel Elementary School is the DSA review and approval phase and broadly includes the following: Modernization of Building 1A (Administration/Library/Classrooms), including new interior partitions, finishes, casework, doors/windows (including replacement of existing), restroom upgrades, structural modifications, plumbing and mechanical upgrades, and electrical (power, data, signal, lighting and fire alarm) upgrades. Site improvements include accessibility upgrades, paving removal and replacement, and minor storm drain scope. The project scope for Phase II of the modernization is the schematic design phase and broadly includes the following: Modernization of four classrooms (Kindergarten/TKK) in Buildings 2 and 3, including new finishes, casework, door replacement, electrical upgrades (power/data/signal/lighting) and mechanical upgrades. Modernization of two existing restrooms and provision of four new restrooms in Buildings 2 and 3. Two of the new restrooms will include exterior wall/ceiling framing, finishes, doors, MEP, etc. Modernization of the existing MP room and minor modernization of the existing kitchen. Site improvements include accessibility upgrades, AC paving removal and replacement in the Kindergarten/TKK Classroom Buildings 2 and 3 courtyard (and related storm drain system adjustments), new shade structure in the same courtyard, landscaping and irrigation improvements in the two planter/landscaped areas at the school frontage and campus-wide fire alarm upgrade.

ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.name: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project (Notification of Streambed Alteration, No. EPIMS-SCR-62645-R3)
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.projectTitle: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project (Notification of Streambed Alteration, No. EPIMS-SCR-62645-R3)
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.agency: California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Bay Delta Region 3
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.agencyName: Fish and Wildlife, Region 3 - Bay Delta, Fairfield
ceqa-3b2e9b89a6a82c65da.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification No. EPIMS-SCR-62645-R3, pursuant to Section 1602 of the Fish and Game Code to Santa Cruz County - Flood Control and Water Conservation District. The Project is limited to rehabilitating 100 linear feet of an existing 66-inch diameter corrugated metal culvert pipe located below Capitola Road on private property within drainage easements. Temporary diversion dams composed of clean gravel and visqueen sheeting will be installed at 20 and 25 feet from the upstream and downstream ends of the culvert to isolate the work area. Once isolated, the culvert interior will be cleaned, voids will be filled with repair mortar, exterior voids will be compaction grouted with polyurethane geotechnical foam, and fiber-reinforced grout layers will be applied using a centrifugally cast concrete pipe machine. No grading and earthwork will occur, and access to the creek and bank will be limited to foot traffic for diversion dam and pump installation and removal. All work will be conducted through existing manholes with construction staging adjacent to the roadway.

ceqa-d00cacdf9dc3fd48a3.name: San Lorenzo Valley Water District Highland Tank Replacement Project
ceqa-d00cacdf9dc3fd48a3.projectTitle: San Lorenzo Valley Water District Highland Tank Replacement Project

ceqa-d00cacdf9dc3fd48a3.description: Replacement of temporary polyethylene water tanks, installed to replace original leaking redwood tank with larger fire-resistant steel tank that provides increased water supply storage capacity and fire flows for the existing service area, with no expansion of service, to address ongoing drought and fire risk

ceqa-13a86eb44da0833423.name: Groundwater Sustainability Plan Periodic Review - Santa Cruz Mid-County Basin - October 2026
ceqa-13a86eb44da0833423.projectTitle: Groundwater Sustainability Plan Periodic Review - Santa Cruz Mid-County Basin - October 2026
ceqa-13a86eb44da0833423.description: The Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), Water Code 10720 et seq., requires local groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs) to develop and implement groundwater sustainability plans (GSPs). (Water Code 10727) The Department of Water Resources (DWR) is required to evaluate whether GSPs and their local implementation comply with certain provisions of SGMA, are likely to achieve sustainability, and whether they adversely affect the ability of adjacent basins to implement their GSPs. (Water Code 10733) DWR is required to issue an assessment within two years of submission of a GSP and again at least every five years during GSP implementation. (Water Code 10733.4, 10733.8) Accordingly, DWR conducted a 5-year periodic review of the Santa Cruz Mid-County Basin GSP and has issued an assessment that determines the GSP or its implementation is "approved." (23 Cal. Code Regs. 355.2, 355.6)

ceqa-2892ffcaffea72edae.description: Special Use Permit (#PP2026-11259) to allow a new vocational school use for Monsbey College.

ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.name: Natural Bridges Monarch Grove Fuels Reduction
ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.projectTitle: Natural Bridges Monarch Grove Fuels Reduction
ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-723271642c0356bf63.description: Project consists of fuels reduction at Natural Bridges State Beach for the purpose of enhancing monarch overwintering habitat. Work will take place prior to the overwintering season and will consist of using chainsaws to consolidate downed materials and accumulating ladder fuels into approximately 20 burn piles within the Monarch Butterfly Nature Preserve. Pile burning will occur April-May 2027 when conditions are favorable for prescription burning and after all monarchs have migrated away from the overwintering site.

ceqa-a5d518e3e1f618ab92.name: Natural Bridges Boardwalk Accessibility Improvements
ceqa-a5d518e3e1f618ab92.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-a5d518e3e1f618ab92.description: Project proposes replacing the existing Monarch Butterfly Boardwalk at Natural Bridges State Beach for accessibility improvements. Work will: •Improve the paved access route from the visitor center to the boardwalk trailhead; •Install new concrete and asphalt walkways with truncated domes that connect to the existing accessible parking stalls in the main parking lot; •Remove the existing boardwalk and observation platform and utilize existing concrete pier foundations, and install new diamond piers to construct a new elevated boardwalk, with proper grades, clearances and safety rail configurations, that descends to the pond area; and •Remove and replace the bench seating along a portion of the boardwalk and observation platform.

ceqa-f9e4f57ace67df0a52.name: Application 251276 - Mission Drive Subdivision and Planned Unit Development (PUD)
ceqa-f9e4f57ace67df0a52.projectTitle: Application 251276 - Mission Drive Subdivision and Planned Unit Development (PUD)
ceqa-f9e4f57ace67df0a52.description: Proposal for a Subdivision and Planned Unit Development (PUD) to divide three parcels (APNs 025-032-33, 025-032-34, 025-032-35) to create six fee-simple lots with detached single-family dwellings. Five lots and a private street will be developed with access from Thurber Lane, and a sixth corridor access lot will be developed with access from Mission Drive. Project requires adoption of a PUD ordinance by the Board of Supervisors, Administrative Site Development Permit (ASP), a Subdivision Map, a preliminary grading review, and a soils report review.

ceqa-dfadd6c9b3599821d7.name: Atkinson Lane Integrated Flood Management and Watershed Restoration Project - Phase II – Stormwater BMP Bioswale and Wetland Enhancement
ceqa-dfadd6c9b3599821d7.projectTitle: Atkinson Lane Integrated Flood Management and Watershed Restoration Project - Phase II – Stormwater BMP Bioswale and Wetland Enhancement
ceqa-dfadd6c9b3599821d7.description: The proposed project includes construction of a vegetated bioswale and wetland retention basin and revegetation with native plants. The bioswale has been designed to improve water quality within the existing Atkinson Wetland Complex through stormwater capture and infiltration while also providing flood-risk reduction by enhancing the ability of the wetland complex to attenuate floods. The bioswale will tie into the City’s storm drain system at the outfall of an existing 18” storm drain pipe. Work will involve grading to create the new swale and retention basin, revegetation with native wetland and riparian plants, and installation of erosion control. Phase II construction will be implemented in collaboration with the Phase I Habitat Enhancement. All temporarily impacted areas will be restored with native plants upon project completion. Protective measures including worker training, surveys prior to work commencement, and daily monitoring will be implemented to ensure that project activities will not result in adverse impacts on any native wildlife species or their habitats.

ceqa-af1db2736b25be07a9.name: Watsonville General Plan 2050
ceqa-af1db2736b25be07a9.description: The Watsonville General Plan 2050 is a comprehensive update of the Watsonville 2005 General Plan to guide land use, mobility, housing, conservation, safety, public facilities, and other policy decisions through 2050. General Plan 2050 establishes a long-term community vision and planning framework for public and private development while responding to changed conditions and new State requirements including AB 1358 (Complete Streets), SB 99 (Evacuation Analysis), SB 379 (Climate Adaptation), SB 932 (Safe Systems), SB 1241 (Wildfire Hazards), and SB 1000 (Environmental Justice). General Plan 2050 focuses growth within Downtown Watsonville, along the Freedom Boulevard and East Lake Avenue corridors, and in identified new growth areas. It introduces a broader range of housing choices; supports new employment, commercial, regional retail, visitor-serving, and community recreation uses; preserves natural open space and agricultural resources; improves parks and community facilities; implements complete streets improvements; and supports rerouting truck traffic around the City. The plan would also update the City’s land use map, goals, policies, and implementation actions and would serve as a first-tier program-level planning document for future development. The full buildout projections for General Plan 2050 facilitate up to 5,980 new residential units and approximately 2.672 million square feet of nonresidential development. This includes approximately 4,560 residential units within the existing City limits; 1,420 residential units in the Area A (Buena Vista), Area B (Atkinson Lane) and/or Area C growth areas; 513,000 square feet of nonresidential development within the existing City limits; 2.129 million square feet of nonresidential development in the Highway 1 Gateway growth area; and 30,000 square feet of neighborhood-serving retail in the Buena Vista and Area C growth areas.
ceqa-af1db2736b25be07a9.developmentType: Other (5,980 residential units; 2.672 million sqft nonresidential space)

ceqa-e46b88f975a905a812.name: Driftwood Flats
ceqa-e46b88f975a905a812.description: The project consists of a Major Modification to CP25-0156 to request an additional density bonus incentive/concession/waiver and several design modifications for an affordable residential project with ground floor commercial space that was approved in April 2026. The approved project was found to be exempt under CEQA (Public Resources Code [PRC] section 21080.66). One of the project conditions to meet labor standards specified in section 21080.66(d) now cannot be met, which requires modifications to the approved project conditions of approval. As a result, the former environmental documentation is no longer valid as the project no longer meets all of the requirements set forth in PRC section 21080.66. CEQA review was undertaken for the project in conjunction with the new requests, although the project as approved would not change except for the requested modifications.

ceqa-296bac6b724201c6e2.name: Camp Chesebrough Master Plan Amendment
ceqa-296bac6b724201c6e2.description: The project involves an amendment to the approved master plan at an existing organized camp to allow for the construction of a multiple-use building for training purposes, a shower and restroom building, cabins for short term camping, covered teaching pavilions, a climbing and rappelling tower, a replacement water tank, and a recycling and trash receptacles.

ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.name: Waddell Adaptive Management Plan
ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.description: Project consists of creating a vegetated foredune at the mouth of Waddell Creek in the Rancho del Oso subunit of Big Basin Redwoods State Park to guide the creek mouth away from public infrastructure, reduce erosion, restore previous lagoon dynamics and alleviate the need for additional hard armoring. Work will occur as follows: •Biologists will survey and clear the work area of any target animal species; •Biological monitors will guide State Park equipment operators tracking onto the beach from the parking lot and begin lowering the sandbar to the south of the current river mouth; •Generated sand will be stockpiled towards the parking lot; •Operators will create a southerly aligned outlet channel with a similar rise and run to the existing northerly channel; •While being shaped, the southern channel will be hydrologically disconnected from the system by a fill plug left in place at the upstream end; •Upon completion of the channel, the upstream sand plug will be removed, allowing water to flow through the southern outlet channel; •Stockpiled sand will then be moved north to construct a foredune between the embayment and the parking lot; •Woody debris will be buried beneath the dune for added support and will remain lower than the parking lot and will mimic previous foredune; and •Seed and plant dune with native plants and water into the dry season as necessary.
ceqa-92b8ba40313697cbbe.crossStreets: Highway 1 and Skyline to the Sea Trail Rd.

ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.name: Sequoia Group Campground Septic Feasibility Testing
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.projectTitle: Sequoia Group Campground Septic Feasibility Testing
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.description: Project consists of geotechnical testing to evaluate for the installation of new septic restrooms at the Sequoia Group Campground at Big Basin Redwoods State Park to support proposed plans to rebuild the group campground. Within the chosen test location, work will use a rotary auger backhoe attachment and/or manual augers to perform preliminary soil evaluations as follows: •Excavate one (1) 14-ft deep hole for soil profiling; •Excavate four (4) 4-ft to 7-ft deep holes for limited percolation testing; and •Backfill test holes with excavated soils and compact.
ceqa-4bf3f5f9e201254af9.crossStreets: Big Basin Way and North Escape Rd.

ceqa-857b324d3f186c6f43.name: Big Steel Pump Station Fire Hardening
ceqa-857b324d3f186c6f43.projectTitle: Big Steel Pump Station Fire Hardening
ceqa-857b324d3f186c6f43.description: The project will replace the District’s Big Steel booster pump station’s roof and walls with fire-resistant materials. The project involves demolition and removal of the existing wood-framed structure and reconstruction with reinforced concrete masonry unit (CMU) walls, a metal roof, and a perimeter grade beam to support the fire-resistant structure. Fire hardening this booster pump station will mitigate wildfire impacts and improve water supply reliability for the community.
