ceqa-8faac74b0477c068a0.name: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-8faac74b0477c068a0.projectTitle: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-8faac74b0477c068a0.description: In December 2023 and early January 2024, high wave and storm events eroded and collapsed a section of the multiuse pathway across from approximately 800 West Cliff Drive and the Light House Field State Beach. The 800 West Cliff Drive Road Realignment project aims to eliminate the weakest link in the West Cliff Drive roadway system as an eroded scarp at the location has encroached to within 21 feet of the existing roadway, partially damaging an adjacent multiuse pathway. The project would shift an approximately 600-foot section of roadway nearest to the scarp approximately 60 feet inland, out of the 100-year erosion zone. A section of the multiuse pathway would also be shifted inland approximately 30 feet. A right-of-way acquisition from State Parks would be required to realign the road and multiuse pathway, as proposed. Other elements of the project include stormwater drainage improvements, minor utility improvements, minor improvements to an existing parking lot, relocation of existing signage and new signage, new fencing, new and relocated benches, removal of existing asphalt along the existing road and multiuse path, and construction site restoration.

ceqa-94fd757436bf30e6c4.name: Envision Peace Village Housing
ceqa-94fd757436bf30e6c4.description: The project consists of a Major Modification to a previously approved application (CP22-0164), revising the previous density bonus request, increasing the total number of residential units from 40 to 47, altering the unit mix, and modifying the building design/envelope. The revised project includes construction of a five-story residential apartment building on a 2.23-acre site. The project would remove 14 heritage trees to construct the apartment complex and associated site improvements.

ceqa-2ffdbf96881d1e400c.name: UC Santa Cruz Wildfire Vegetation Management Project
ceqa-2ffdbf96881d1e400c.description: The California Department of Forestry and Fire Prevention (CAL FIRE) is providing funding to help implement treatments on State Responsibility Area (SRA) lands on the University of California Santa Cruz (UC Santa Cruz), immediately northwest of the city of Santa Cruz, Santa Cruz County. UC Santa Cruz has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis (PSA) and addendum for the project as a later activity covered by the California Vegetation Treatment Project (CalVTP) Program Environmental Impact Report (PEIR) for the UC Santa Cruz Wildfire Vegetation Management Project, which entails implementation of vegetation treatments on up to 2,017 acres; CAL FIRE is providing funding to the Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz County to implement treatments on up to 165 acres. The proposed treatment types (WUI Fuel Reduction, Fuel Break, and Ecological Restoration) and treatment activities (manual thinning and mastication) are consistent with those evaluated in the CalVTP Program EIR and the writ of mandate issued by the Superior Court of San Diego on November 14, 2025 in California Chaparral Institute and Endangered Habitats League v. Board of Forestry and Fire Protection, and pursuant to PRC § 4483, have been designed to avoid type conversion in areas where chaparral and/or coastal sage scrub plant communities may be present. Maintenance treatments would involve the same vegetation treatment types and activities used in the initial treatments. The purpose of these treatments is to promote forest and watershed health, reduce fuel load, and demonstrate efficacy of climate beneficial prescriptions.

ceqa-3beca53c3b11500eb0.name: San Lorenzo Way Bridge Replacement Project
ceqa-3beca53c3b11500eb0.projectTitle: San Lorenzo Way Bridge Replacement Project
ceqa-3beca53c3b11500eb0.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed Lake and Streambed Alteration Agreement (EPIMS-SCR-64152-R3), pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1602, the project Applicant, County of Santa Cruz, Department of Public Works, as represented by Amber Myer. The Project will replace an aging and historic single lane bridge structure (bridge number 36C-0085) carrying San Lorenzo Way over the San Lorenzo River. In addition to replacing the bridge, the proposed Project includes modifications to the bridge approaches to correct the steep grade and improvements at the SR 9/San Lorenzo Way intersection to facilitate merging on and off the highway. The Project also includes using an existing private gravel road as a temporary access road to land uses on the east side of the bridge during construction. All work for the bridge replacement will be outside the ordinary high-water marks of the San Lorenzo River. Project construction activities will be isolated to the upper banks above the San Lorenzo River channel.

ceqa-975ba8815c3dcda802.name: Forest of Nisene Marks State Park Project
ceqa-975ba8815c3dcda802.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-975ba8815c3dcda802.description: The California Department of Forestry and Fire Prevention (CAL FIRE) is providing funding to help implement treatments on State Responsibility Area (SRA) lands in the Forest of Nisene Marks State Park, north of the city of Aptos, Santa Cruz County. The California Department of Parks and Recreation has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis (PSA) and addendum for the project as a later activity covered by the California Vegetation Treatment Project (CalVTP) Program Environmental Impact Report (PEIR) for the Forest of Nisene Marks State Park Project, which entails implementation of vegetation treatments on up to 9,955 acres; CAL FIRE is providing funding to the Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz County to implement treatments on up to 220 acres. The proposed treatment types (WUI Fuel Reduction and Ecological Restoration) and treatment activities (manual thinning, mastication, and prescribed burning) are consistent with those evaluated in the CalVTP Program EIR and the writ of mandate issued by the Superior Court of San Diego on November 14, 2025 in California Chaparral Institute and Endangered Habitats League v. Board of Forestry and Fire Protection, and pursuant to PRC § 4483, have been designed to avoid type conversion in areas where chaparral and/or coastal sage scrub plant communities may be present. Maintenance treatments would involve the same vegetation treatment types and activities used in the initial treatments. The purpose of these treatments is to promote forest and watershed health, reduce fuel load, and demonstrate efficacy of climate beneficial prescriptions.

ceqa-2a9ad57d05623dbe16.name: Integrated Ecology, LLC Lease
ceqa-2a9ad57d05623dbe16.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-2a9ad57d05623dbe16.description: The District seeks to approve a lease agreement with Integrated Ecology, LLC for the use of 0.3 acres at Wilder Ranch State Park for the purpose having a native plant nursery. There will be temporary fencing and shade structures. Integrated Ecology, LLC will use water from State Parks in exchange for plants.

ceqa-4271af5b811dace987.name: SLVWD Water Storage Tanks Recoating
ceqa-4271af5b811dace987.description: The project consists of the rehabilitation of six above ground water storage tanks ranging from 75,000 to 721,000 gallons capacity in the unincorporated communities of Boulder Creek, Ben Lomond, and Felton. The tanks require recoating to extend their service life. The tank recoating process includes sampling and testing the existing coatings, removal of interior coatings, rewelding damaged metal surfaces, and recoating interior and exterior surfaces. Maintenance, repair, or replacement of tank components or appurtenant structures such as ladders and fences may be needed. Removal of existing tank coatings will follow best management practices and regulatory requirements for any hazardous waste. All work will be limited to existing roads, turnarounds, and within fenced operational areas around tank footprints.

ceqa-1de2c8c6b97bb4e615.name: SLVWD Pasatiempo Wells 7 & 8 Rehabilitation
ceqa-1de2c8c6b97bb4e615.description: The project consists of rehabilitation of two groundwater wells that supply water to over 3,000 residents within portions of the City of Scotts Valley and nearby unincorporated communities. The purpose of the rehabilitation is to restore well efficiency and maintain reliable water production, as Paso 7 is currently under-producing and Paso 8 is inoperable. Rehabilitation activities would include removal of the well pumps, video inspection, mechanical cleaning of the well screens, chemical treatment (acid washing), post-treatment cleaning, disinfection, test pumping, and post-rehabilitation video inspection. Project implementation will require temporary installation of an approximately 2,600-foot-long above-ground pipeline to convey treated water to the nearby Hanson Quarry's drainage pond, where the treated and tested water will be discharged in accordance with regulations.

ceqa-2357fa45abd54533cb.name: 2026 EE36-EE30 Emergency Project
ceqa-2357fa45abd54533cb.description: The project includes repairing an existing failing sewer main after maintenance crews identified structural defects due to age-related deterioration affecting the pipe, joints, and connections that require immediate repair to maintain reliable service

ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.name: Cliff Drive Resiliency Project
ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.description: The City of Capitola Public Works Department (City), is proposing a project to address coastal bluff erosion and associated undermining of the roadway along approximately 800 feet of Cliff Drive in Capitola. The proposed restoration project is intended to remediate current bluff erosion and provide resiliency for projected increased erosion associated with climate change/sea-level rise. Bluff erosion has threatened this route since the 1960s and is expected to worsen due to rising sea levels and more intense storms from climate change. The City of Capitola seeks a strategy to manage access along the portion Cliff Drive adjacent to the coastal bluff. In its current configuration Cliff Drive is a busy corridor serving walkers, bicyclists, motorists, and those parking to enjoy the stunning vistas of the Pacific Ocean. Due to the lack of sidewalks along Cliff Drive, conflicts between pedestrians and motorists are possible. The proposed project would include bluff stabilization via a soil-nail-anchored shotcrete wall, rock protection at the base of the bluff, and a resurfaced roadway with two travel lanes, parking and a bike lane. These improvements would be implemented along the nearly 800-foot stretch of Cliff Drive between Portola Drive and Wharf Road in Capitola. This roadway alignment is classified as a minor arterial roadway, and accommodates nearly 8,000 vehicles daily alongside hundreds of bicyclists and pedestrians. It also serves as the primary evacuation route for Capitola Village.
ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.crossStreets: Cliff Drive between Portola Drive and Wharf Road
ceqa-d52b1a5042d7c6544f.developmentType: Other (Cliff stabilization), Transportation:Other (Roadway stabilization and resurfacing)

The project proposes to operate a Class CA indoor co-location cannabis cultivation facility with up to five cultivators on Commercial Agriculture (CA) zoned property, Class 3 manufacturing (volatile extraction) and Class 2 distribution of cannabis product The project includes approximately 590,922 square feet of cultivation within existing greenhouses, manufacturing, processing, distribution, office and storage within an existing 32,458 square foot processing facility on a site containing existing row crops, greenhouse plant production, cannabis cultivation, shipping and office use. ceqa-8e01bfe28c676e742a.projectTitle: New Single-Family Residence with ADU and JADU

ceqa-1910512c181ae6addf.description: Minor Modification with Environmental Review (PP2026-10831) to Special Use Permit #02-46 to allow the modification of an existing telecommunications facility. ceqa-1910512c181ae6addf.crossStreets: Grove Street and West Front Street

ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.name: SCR 17 PM 7.61 Drainage System Replacement
ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.agencyName: Caltrans, District 5 - San Luis Obispo/Santa Barbara
ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.description: Caltrans Geotechnical Design proposes a geotechnical site investigation for the SCR 17 PM 7.61 Drainage System Replacement. The project proposes abandoning an existing culvert with slurry cement and replacing it with a new reinforced concrete pipe culvert. Recommendations for the improvements requires a subsurface investigation to determine the soil and site conditions by drilling vertical soil borings to perform in-situ soil testing utilizing Standard Penetration Tests, collect soil samples for laboratory testing and classification, and developing a subsurface soil profile. The subsurface investigation is also needed to assess the potential for geotechnical hazards associated with the design and construction of the new culvert. All drilling will occur within pavement limits.
ceqa-3cd430220ac822a773.crossStreets: State Route 17 and Vine Hill Road

ceqa-1ad46a7f84c772c7d0.name: Anna Jean Cummings County Park Water Line Replacement Project
ceqa-1ad46a7f84c772c7d0.projectTitle: Anna Jean Cummings County Park Water Line Replacement Project
ceqa-1ad46a7f84c772c7d0.description: Anna Jean Cummings County Park is located at 461 Soquel San Jose Road in Soquel, California (APN 030-341-09). The park is owned and operated by the County of Santa Cruz and provides a variety of recreational amenities including sports fields, playgrounds, picnic areas, restrooms, trails, open space areas, and supporting infrastructure. The park was developed in accordance with the O'Neill Ranch Master Plan and Environmental Impact Report adopted by the County to guide the long-term recreational use and management of the property. Existing utility infrastructure, including domestic water service, supports park operations and visitor-serving facilities throughout the site. The existing domestic waterline serving park facilities has experienced recurring leaks and requires frequent maintenance and repair. The leaks generally occur at intervals corresponding to individual pipe segments located beneath portions of the park entry drive, requiring excavation within paved areas to access and repair the line. To improve long-term reliability, reduce maintenance costs, reduce waste of potable water, and minimize future disruptions to park operations, the County proposes replacing an approximately 1,300-foot-long portion of the existing waterline and relocating portions of the alignment to adjacent landscaped areas where future access and maintenance can be more readily accomplished. The project consists of replacing a portion of the existing domestic water distribution system serving Anna Jean Cummings County Park with approximately 1,300 linear feet of new waterline and associated components installed within previously disturbed and developed portions of the park. The new waterline will connect to the existing system at the southern side of the athletic fields and extend west toward the restroom facility and east toward the restroom and recreational facilities adjacent to the play area. The proposed alignment relocates portions of the existing waterline from beneath the park entry drive into adjacent landscaped and maintained areas to improve accessibility for future maintenance activities, reduce the likelihood of disruptions to park operations, reduce waste of potable water, and improve the long-term reliability of the water system. Project improvements include trench excavation, installation of new waterline, and related utility infrastructure necessary to maintain water service to existing park facilities. The project also includes abandonment of the existing waterline, limited saw-cutting and restoration of sidewalks and paved surfaces where necessary, reconnection to existing facilities, and restoration of all disturbed areas following construction. All work will occur within the boundaries of Anna Jean Cummings County Park and within areas that have been previously developed, landscaped, or otherwise disturbed. The replacement waterline will serve the same park facilities and provide the same purpose and capacity as the existing system. No expansion of park facilities, recreational amenities, or utility service is proposed. No tree removal is anticipated as part of the project, and all disturbed areas will be restored following completion of construction. The project is limited to replacement of the existing domestic waterline and associated utility infrastructure and constitutes the repair, maintenance, minor alteration, and replacement of an existing public utility system involving negligible or no expansion of existing use. Accordingly, the project is exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15301 (Existing Facilities) and 15302 (Replacement or Reconstruction). The project also includes minor trenching, backfilling, and restoration activities within previously disturbed areas and is therefore exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15304 (Minor Alterations to Land).

ceqa-e8e9ad6dd05da3b252.name: Miller County Park Trails
ceqa-e8e9ad6dd05da3b252.description: Miller County Park is located at 16798 Kings Creek Road near the community of Boulder Creek in unincorporated Santa Cruz County. The park consists of approximately 410 acres across three contiguous parcels (APNs 085-152-05, 085-153-03, and 085-092-08) owned by the County of Santa Cruz and subject to a conservation easement held by Save the Redwoods League. The existing landscape consists of mature redwood forest and riparian habitat adjacent to Kings Creek. The property also includes approximately 2.5 miles of informal trails and an established parking area. The park is currently underutilized, and the existing trail system is in poor condition and in need of maintenance and rehabilitation. The purpose of the project is to improve public access, visitor safety, trail sustainability, and resource protection by formalizing and renovating the existing trail network. The project includes rehabilitation and formalization of the approximately 2.5-mile trail network. Improvements include abandonment and restoration of approximately 1 mile of degraded and unsustainable trail segments. Approximately 1.8 miles of new trail segments will be constructed to replace and bypass the abandoned trail sections while maintaining connectivity within the trail network and improving trail sustainability. The project also includes installation of wayfinding signs, maps, and interpretive displays. Trail improvements may include minor grading (approximately 200 cubic yards), tread improvements, drainage improvements, erosion control measures, revegetation, and related site improvements necessary to support trail construction and restoration activities. The project constitutes minor alterations to existing public facilities involving negligible expansion of use and is therefore exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15301 (Existing Facilities). The project also includes minor alterations to land associated with trail rehabilitation, trail reroutes, restoration activities, drainage improvements, erosion control measures, and revegetation. The project does not involve removal of healthy, mature, or scenic trees and is therefore exempt pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15304 (Minor Alterations to Land). All project activities will be conducted in a manner consistent with the Miller Property Conservation Easement. No healthy, mature redwood trees will be removed as part of the project. The project is limited to trail rehabilitation, trail reroutes, restoration of abandoned trail segments, signage, and associated trail improvements. Future Park improvements not described herein are not included as part of this project. These improvements will enhance trail sustainability, reduce erosion, sedimentation, water quality, and other resource impacts associated with degraded and unsustainable trail segments, and improve public access within an existing county park.

ceqa-66ed4bb9be0104986d.name: Pinto Lake County Park Skatepark
ceqa-66ed4bb9be0104986d.description: The project consists of the construction of a new skatepark and associated site improvements at Pinto Lake County Park, including modification of an existing biofiltration planter along Green Valley Road to comply with County Design Criteria (CDC) stormwater requirements. The skatepark will provide a public recreational facility serving County residents and park visitors. Associated improvements include removal of an existing asphalt path, installation of a cobble-lined swale and area drains to convey runoff to the modified biofiltration planter, and implementation of Low Impact Development (LID) measures and Best Management Practices (BMPs) to minimize hydrologic and pollutant impacts. The total new and replaced impervious area associated with the project is 9,733 square feet, classifying the project as a Large Project under the County Design Criteria and triggering full LID and BMP compliance requirements. The biofiltration planter will be redesigned to provide stormwater treatment and detention consistent with CDC requirements, including detention of runoff from the 10-year, 15-minute storm event at the 5-year pre-development release rate, as required for projects within the Salsipuedes Creek Watershed. To accommodate the proposed skatepark, three (3) mature London Plane trees will be removed as part of site preparation. All remaining on-site trees will be protected in place pursuant to the recommendations of a certified arborist retained for the project. In response to the tree removals, six (6) new trees will be planted on-site, representing a net gain in tree canopy. In addition, all biofiltration planters and associated landscape areas will be planted with 100% native understory species, enhancing habitat value, supporting local pollinators, and reducing long-term landscape maintenance needs. The skatepark footprint will be constructed on areas currently occupied by unused turf grass that required irrigation to maintain. The replacement of non-functional turf with the skatepark hardscape and native plantings will result in overall water savings, consistent with the County's water conservation goals and the State's urban water use reduction objectives. The remainder of the site will be retained in its natural state, further minimizing the project's environmental footprint.

ceqa-534a153317b1c8a3ff.name: Capitola Area Emergency Sewer Project
ceqa-534a153317b1c8a3ff.description: Replace an existing ACP pipe with new PVC pipe in same trench by open-cut and pipe bursting at the following locations; EI5 l-EI54 Capitola Rd, EI51-EK3 38th Ave, and EI4 l-EI43 41 st Ave.

ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.name: Castro Adobe State Historic Park Accessibility Improvements
ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.projectTitle: Castro Adobe State Historic Park Accessibility Improvements
ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-891c375f5e29ee142f.description: Project consists of removing barriers and providing improved access to existing day use facilities at Rancho San Andreas Castro Adobe Park Property to better accommodate visitors with disabilities. Work will: • Construct an accessible concrete parking stall and access ramp to the front entry of the Kimbro House; • Construct an accessible path of travel from the Kimbro House Courtyard to the front of the Castro Adobe with two (2) landings for installation of interpretive signage; • On the front and side exteriors, minimally excavate to construct a timber-edged aggregate paved area for a firm and stable surface for large tour groups to congregate; • Provide an access ramp to the existing wooden deck in front of Adobe; and • Using materials matching the existing deck/boardwalk, construct a new low-profile deck in front of the Cocina entrance to establish a flush entry into the exhibit area.

ceqa-b10b9a885ba27ab4b4.name: Issuance of General Lease – Other – A5413
ceqa-b10b9a885ba27ab4b4.projectTitle: Issuance of General Lease – Other – A5413
ceqa-b10b9a885ba27ab4b4.description: Authorize issuance of a General Lease – Other beginning June 23, 2026, for a term of 10 years, for the reconstruction and use of an existing seawall, removal of debris from prior armoring efforts, and construction of a public access stairway.

ceqa-8a9c723eb16f8e6b49.name: Flock Safety Automated License Plate Reading (ALPR) Camera Installation
ceqa-8a9c723eb16f8e6b49.description: The project consists of the installation of Flock Safety automated license plate reading (ALPR) cameras on behalf of the Watsonville Police Department at multiple locations within public right-of-way. The project includes mounting ALPR camera and solar equipment to existing traffic signal or streetlight poles at certain locations, and installation of new breakaway support poles with small concrete foundations at other locations where existing infrastructure is not available. The purpose of the installation is to assist law enforcement in identifying vehicles associated with criminal activity. The beneficiaries of the project include law enforcement and the public at large, as the installation supports public safety objectives within the City of Watsonville.

ceqa-7840415f9810111930.name: 2026 Annual Code Update
ceqa-7840415f9810111930.description: On June 30, 2026, the County of Santa Cruz approved a project amending various chapters of the Santa Cruz County Code, making minor General Plan Map Amendments, and amending the Zoning Map to streamline provisions to ensure compliance with applicable State and Federal law, and improve clarity, accuracy, and internal consistency. The ordinance also rezoned parcels APN 026-091-54,026-261-17, 029-071-13, 030-121-34, 042-151-23, 070-301-01, and 074-152-30. The County, as Lead Agency, considered an Addendum to the previously certified Environmental Impact Report for the Sustainability Policy and Regulatory Update (SCH No. 2020079005), prepared pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15162 and 15164, and determined that no subsequent or supplemental EIR is required

ceqa-721f73d51c31992f98.name: Reimagining Big Basin Redwoods State Park Facilities Management Plan and General Plan Amendments
ceqa-721f73d51c31992f98.projectTitle: Big Basin Redwoods State Park General Plan Supplemental EIR for the Reimagining Big Basin Redwoods State Park Facilities Management Plan and General Plan
ceqa-721f73d51c31992f98.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-721f73d51c31992f98.description: The approved project includes amendments to the Big Basin Redwoods State Park (BBRSP) General Plan and the adoption of the Reimagining BBRSP Facilities Management Plan. The approved General Plan amendments include text changes to provide clarity consistent with the 2013 General Plan. The Facilities Management Plan is designed to guide stewardship, management, and use of existing and future facilities consistent with the 2013 General Plan. The approved project includes facilities and improvement guidance for 19 identified sites in the five zones in the Focus Area.
ceqa-721f73d51c31992f98.crossStreets: Sky Meadow Road, Big Basin Highway

ceqa-ce3256ba5abef342f3.name: Major Variance for SFD
ceqa-ce3256ba5abef342f3.description: The project proposes a setback that is greater than twenty-five percent of the base build-to-range requirements.

ceqa-53bd7f76fb96f864d7.name: 201 Front Street
ceqa-53bd7f76fb96f864d7.description: Nonresidential Demolition Authorization Permit, Coastal Permit, Design Permit, Administrative Use Permit, Heritage Tree Removal Permit, and Downtown Density Bonus Request to demolish a commercial building and construct an eight-story mixed-use building consisting of approximately 12,000 square feet of ground floor commercial space, live/work units on the ground floor, and 245 rental apartments on a parcel located in the CBD (Central Business District) Subdistrict E – Lower Pacific Avenue/CZ-O (Coastal Zone Overlay)/FP-O (Floodplain Overlay) zone districts and within the South of Laurel Area District of the Downtown Plan.

ceqa-4b29c125343cc2a8b1.name: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-4b29c125343cc2a8b1.projectTitle: 800 West Cliff Drive Roadway Realignment Project
ceqa-4b29c125343cc2a8b1.description: In December 2023 and early January 2024, high wave and storm events eroded and collapsed a section of the multiuse pathway across from approximately 800 West Cliff Drive and the Light House Field State Beach. The 800 West Cliff Drive Road Realignment project aims to eliminate the weakest link in the West Cliff Drive roadway system as an eroded scarp at the location has encroached to within 21 feet of the existing roadway, partially damaging an adjacent multiuse pathway. The project would shift an approximately 600-foot section of roadway nearest to the scarp approximately 60 feet inland, out of the 100-year erosion zone. A section of the multiuse pathway would also be shifted inland approximately 30 feet. A right-of-way acquisition from State Parks would be required to realign the road and multiuse pathway, as proposed.

ceqa-57125d66e38d159b35.name: 307 Chestnut Street Residence
ceqa-57125d66e38d159b35.description: Demolition of an existing single-family dwelling unit and reconstruction of a single-family dwelling unit of similar size and within same footprint and removal of two heritage-sized trees on a parcel located within the Santa Cruz Downtown Historic District.

ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.name: Crestwood Heights Water Association Water System Consolidation Project
ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.projectTitle: Crestwood Heights Water Association Water System Consolidation Project
ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.description: The proposed project involves consolidation of the Crestwood Heights Water Association water system with the City of Watsonville municipal water system. Improvements include installation of new water mains, service laterals, and meters for approximately 45 residences, system interties, and removal of existing water system infrastructure. In total, the proposed project would include 7,000 linear feet (1.33 miles) of new pipelines. The proposed project would install water mains within the right-of-way of Lakeview Road, Cambridge Drive, Kingston Drive, Oxford Drive, Strafford Drive, and Crestwood Drive. The proposed project also involves preparing a Drinking Water State Revolving Fund application to assist in funding construction of the proposed project.
ceqa-440b6242cf61f20782.crossStreets: State Route 129 (Riverside Road) and Lakeview Road

ceqa-b486686c037cb6d243.name: 375 Technology Drive - Hotel Project
ceqa-b486686c037cb6d243.description: The project includes construction of a 72,348-square foot, five-story, 70-foot-tall Holiday Inn Express hotel containing 95 rooms. The project includes 100 parking spaces, 80 of which will utilize mechanical stacking devices. The project also includes a request to amend Watsonville Municipal Code Section 14-16.505(c) - "Other Requirements" to include a 75-foot maximum height limit for hotel uses and a request for a variance for the front yard setbacks.

ceqa-fd624156e1bd88fa02.name: Floral Drive Water Main Replacement
ceqa-fd624156e1bd88fa02.description: The Floral Drive Water Main Replacement Project will replace 1,350 linear feet of existing water main with a new 6” PVC water main between 34th Avenue and 38th Avenue in the Pleasure Point area of unincorporated Santa Cruz County. There will be one new hydrant installed at 35th Ave and Floral Dr. The installation trench will be restored with asphalt, type 2 slurry seal, and thermoplastic striping per County of Santa Cruz standards.
ceqa-fd624156e1bd88fa02.crossStreets: Floral Drive between 34th Avenue and 38th Avenue

ceqa-f144cbcb4b31b5cc5e.name: Ordinances Related to Protections Against On-Shore Support Facilities for Off-Shore Oil and Gas or Deep-Sea Mining or Exploration
ceqa-f144cbcb4b31b5cc5e.projectTitle: Ordinances Related to Protections Against On-Shore Support Facilities for Off-Shore Oil and Gas or Deep-Sea Mining or Exploration
ceqa-f144cbcb4b31b5cc5e.description: The project consists of two ordinances (2026-12 and 2026-13) amending the Santa Cruz Municipal Code (SCMC) and the City's Local Coastal Program. Ordinance 2026-13 would add Section 24.06.093 to Chapter 24.06 - Zoning Map and Text Amendments and amend Sections 24.06.090 and 24.10.1620. These changes would add protections against on-shore facilities supporting off-shore oil and gas drilling and deep-sea mining and exploration. Ordinance 2026-12 would amend SCMC Section 24.10.1525, which is part of the City's Local Coastal Program Implementation Plan, to extend existing land-use prohibitions to on-shore facilities supporting deep-sea mining and exploration. In addition, the ordinances add science-backed findings related to the ecological, public health, economic, and climate impacts related to oil and gas drilling and deep-sea mining and exploration. The two ordinances make the following changes to the SCMC: • Add definitions of related terms for clarity and specificity within the municipal code; • Update the existing requirement that any zoning change to accommodate on-shore support facilities for off-shore oil and gas drilling be subject to a vote of the people to also require that any zoning change to accommodate on-shore support facilities for deep-sea mining and exploration be subject to a vote of the people; and • Add prohibitions against on-shore support facilities for deep-sea mining, in addition to the existing prohibitions against on-shore support facilities for off-shore oil and gas drilling, to the City's General Industrial and General Industrial/Performance Districts.

ceqa-d919397ed0564ad1fc.name: Peavine Water Pipeline Replacement Project
ceqa-d919397ed0564ad1fc.description: The SLVWD watershed and water system were severely impacted and damaged by the CZU Lightning Complex Wildfire in 2020, including the Peavine pipeline. The Peavine Water Pipeline Replacement Project (project) involves replacement of the approximately 1.2-mile-long Peavine pipeline with new HDPE pipe.

ceqa-21465a224f550826d0.name: 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy and 2050 Regional Transportation Plans for San Benito, Santa Cruz, and Monterey Counties
ceqa-21465a224f550826d0.projectTitle: 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy and 2050 Regional Transportation Plans for San Benito, Santa Cruz, and Monterey Counties
ceqa-21465a224f550826d0.agency: Association of Monterey Bay Area Governments
ceqa-21465a224f550826d0.agencyName: Association of Monterey Bay Area Governments
ceqa-21465a224f550826d0.description: The Santa Cruz County Regional Transportation Commission has developed the 2050 Regional Transportation Plan (RTP) for Santa Cruz County which is incorporated into the 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy (MTP/SCS). The 2050 RTP will guide the development of transportation projects and programs throughout Santa Cruz County. The 2050 MTP/SCS EIR serves as the EIR for the 2050 MTP/SCS and for the 2050 RTP for Santa Cruz County.

ceqa-43cbc9eeef687543e7.name: SR-1 Wildlife Crossing
ceqa-43cbc9eeef687543e7.agencyName: Caltrans, District 5 - San Luis Obispo/Santa Barbara
ceqa-43cbc9eeef687543e7.description: Caltrans Geotechnical Design proposes a geotechnical site investigation for the SR-1 Wildlife Crossing, located on State Route 1 (SR-1) at PM 5.11 in Santa Cruz County. Trenchless culvert installation requires a subsurface investigation to evaluate subsurface site conditions by drilling vertical borings, performing in-situ soil testing, and confirming soil and rock conditions for use in design. A total of six borings will be advanced: five through pavement into soil and rock, and one through a dirt road in the median into soil and rock. The proposed borings would be four to six inches in diameter and extend between 30 and 40 feet below the ground surface, depending on the location. Once the borings are completed, each hole will be backfilled following appropriate procedures. Typically, the backfill material is a neat cement and/or bentonite (clay).It may take up to three weeks to complete the investigation. Work is anticipated to occur at night. Drilling activities will occur during dry weather only, June through October. Precautions during drilling will be employed to minimize the potential for equipment leaks or drilling fluid spillage. All borings will be drilled within State Right-of-Way (ROW), accessible from the northbound and southbound travel lanes of SR-1, the median, or in the paved or unvegetated shoulder.

ceqa-e2e74d817d354d9f7c.name: Lower Wilder Ranch Trail Restoration
ceqa-e2e74d817d354d9f7c.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-e2e74d817d354d9f7c.description: Project proposes to improve existing trail alignments within Wilder Ranch State Park to reduce user conflict and improve trail safety. The work is proposed for portions of the Eucalyptus Loop, Old Cabin, and Wild Boar Trails will alleviate erosion, reduce sediment delivery into nearby drainages, and curtail the creation of unofficial trail segments used to bypass trail obstacles. Work will occur as follows: On the Fern Grotto Beach Access • Remove one (1) wood puncheon; • Remove approx. 50 linear feet (LF) of poorly aligned and redundant trail; and • Construct 30 LF of wood cabling steps leading down existing trail to beach. On the Eucalyptus Loop Trail: • Construct an approx. 6,000 LF reroute of the eastern segment of the road and construct a new approx. 4ft wide trail on contour under forest canopy; • Remove approx. 5,000 LF of poorly aligned road in the meadow and topographically Restore approx. 59,510 sq ft of the meadow; • Excavate approx. 300 cu. ft. to install concrete abutments and approaches for five (5) steel I-beam bridges and one (1) wood puncheon. • Construct approx. 170 ft of 6ft wide drainage lens along trail (5 locations); and • Reconstruct sections of the trail with corrected outslope to facilitate proper drainage. On the Old Cabin Trail: • Construct an approx. 3,750 LF reroute to pull the existing trail off the ridge line and away from the water course; • Remove approx. 3,500 LF of poorly aligned trail and topographically restore the area • Excavate approx. 68 cu. ft. for concrete abutments and approaches for one (1) steel I-beam bridge and one (1) wood puncheon; and • Reconstruct sections of the trail with corrected outslope to facilitate proper drainage. On the Wild Boar Trail: • Construct an approx. 2,400 LF reroute to pull existing trail out of the meadow and off of the fall line; • Remove approx. 2,210 LF of poorly aligned road and restore the meadow and forest understory; • Construct a 75ft long x 6ft wide drainage lens along the trail; and • Reconstruct sections of the trail with corrected outslope to facilitate proper drainage.

ceqa-55e6994a3affccc605.name: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle.
ceqa-55e6994a3affccc605.projectTitle: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle.
ceqa-55e6994a3affccc605.description: The California Energy Commission (CEC) adopts and regularly updates regulations that define a process for local governments to apply to the CEC to make certain findings regarding locally adopted energy conservation or energy insulation standards (California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 and section 10-110; Public Resources Code (PRC) section 25402.1(h)(2)). The local government’s proposed standards are often referred to as the Local Reach Codes and require local governments to submit an application to the CEC consistent with the requirements listed in section 10-106(b). Before the local standards may be enforced, the CEC must make the following findings pursuant to PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and as listed in section 10-106(a): 1) The proposed local standards will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Energy Code, and 2) The local government has filed the basis of its cost-effectiveness determination with the CEC. On December 30, 2026, the City of Santa Cruz (the City) submitted an application to the CEC that included: 1) the basis of its determination that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 2025-22 are cost-effective; and (2) documentation that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No.2025-22 will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Energy Code), as required by PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and by CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106. Based on the information submitted, staff analysis, and the Executive Director's recommendation, the CEC approved findings of the City’s section 10-106 application at the CEC’s May 26, 2026, Business Meeting.

ceqa-806c36d7abe6d4871a.name: Ramsay Park Nature and Family Center Educational Exhibits Project
ceqa-806c36d7abe6d4871a.projectTitle: Ramsay Park Nature and Family Center Educational Exhibits Project
ceqa-806c36d7abe6d4871a.description: Watsonville Wetlands Watch and the City of Watsonville are establishing a new Nature Center within the building formerly called the Ramsay Park Family Center located at 1301 Main Street in the City of Watsonville. The proposed project includes design, fabrication, and installation of educational exhibits related to environmental education, nature, cultural history, local wetlands, and related topics within the new Ramsay Park Nature and Family Center. A wall mural highlighting environmental stewardship and California native peoples will be installed on the exterior wall of the Nature and Family Center. All other exhibits will be constructed within the interior of the existing building structure.

ceqa-79d837b3f31dd3c60d.name: Atkinson Lane Integrated Flood Management and Watershed Restoration Project - Phase I - Native Habitat Restoration
ceqa-79d837b3f31dd3c60d.projectTitle: Atkinson Lane Integrated Flood Management and Watershed Restoration Project - Phase I - Native Habitat Restoration
ceqa-79d837b3f31dd3c60d.description: The proposed project includes implementation of approximately 4.0 acres of native habitat restoration around the wetland complex located at 78 Atkinson Lane. Work will involve removal of non-native invasive species, including removal and treatment of approximately 2.0 acres of Himalayan blackberry infestation, planting native plants, and installation of erosion control. Restoration treatment areas for Phase I are outlined in Attachment A. Work will be carried out principally with hand labor. Existing native trees and shrubs will be preserved and protected in place. Protective measures including worker training, surveys prior to work commencement, and daily monitoring will be implemented to ensure that the habitat restoration activities will not result in adverse impacts on any native wildlife species or their habitats.

ceqa-4770cb283ec5e902ec.name: Santa Cruz Metropolitan Transit District Bus Parking Lot
ceqa-4770cb283ec5e902ec.projectTitle: Santa Cruz Metropolitan Transit District Bus Parking Lot
ceqa-4770cb283ec5e902ec.description: The project proposes to establish a local transit use for a bus parking lot. This includes improvements to the lot such as restriping and adding new lighting and cameras.

ceqa-b1c571d25158a47906.name: City of Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Operational Change
ceqa-b1c571d25158a47906.projectTitle: City of Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Operational Change
ceqa-b1c571d25158a47906.description: The project involves a minor operational change at the City of Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility (RRF), located at 605 Dimeo Lane. The RRF is located approximately three miles west of the city limits off Highway 1 and encompasses approximately 100 acres; see Figure 1. The facility serves as the City's primary solid waste management and recycling facility, and currently accepts, processes, and transfers municipal solid waste, recyclables, and organic materials. The RRF currently operates seven days a week, opening at 6:00 AM for City trucks and landfill and ancillary operations, with public access beginning at 7:30 AM, pursuant to terms of its operating permit from the California Department of Resources Recycling and Recovery (CalRecycle) (Solid Waste Facility Permit No. 44-AA-0001). Current permitted hours require ancillary operations, including removing daily cover, to begin at the same time City trucks arrive, causing delays while trucks wait for the site to be prepared. The project would shift the ancillary operations start time from 6:00 AM to 5:00 AM, allowing sufficient time of site preparation before trucks arrive and improving overall coordination and traffic flow at the facility.

ceqa-879b22d2f89b19aa01.name: Graham Hill Water Treatment Plant Concrete Tanks Replacement Project -Water Supply Permit Amendment
ceqa-879b22d2f89b19aa01.description: The State Water Resources Control Board is issuing subsequent discretionary approval for the project (a water supply permit amendment) and no subsequent environmental review under CEQA is necessary because there have been no changes or new information.

ceqa-a46fded97503381f0e.name: SCR-17-Replace Culverts
ceqa-a46fded97503381f0e.agencyName: Caltrans, District 5 - San Luis Obispo/Santa Barbara
ceqa-a46fded97503381f0e.description: The existing drainage system at PM 11.90 is in poor condition. If it is allowed to further deteriorate, roadway failure is possible. This could lead to highway closure to enable repairs, thus inconveniencing area residents and disrupting businesses which depend on this lifeline highway for mobility. The proposed project will replace the existing 99-foot long, 18-inch diameter CSP culvert (Drainage System ID 360174001190) located at PM 11.90 on SR 17 in Santa Cruz County with an 84-foot long, 24-inch diameter reinforced concrete pipe across the highway as well as 400-foot long perforated steel pipe underdrain and 400-foot long slotted corrugated drain along the pavement edge. All work is within operational right-of-way.
ceqa-a46fded97503381f0e.crossStreets: State Route 17 and Santa Cruz Ridge

ceqa-fbde20d8f963110c1d.name: Modification of Waste Management Plan
ceqa-fbde20d8f963110c1d.description: The project proposes an alternative waste management program with new receptacles and temporary receptacles for public events.
ceqa-fbde20d8f963110c1d.crossStreets: Main Street, East Beach Street, Peck Street, Union Street

ceqa-b0b7afb0f4b82b7ae8.name: Heller Student Housing South (formerly known as the Student Housing West Phase 2 – Heller Development project)
ceqa-b0b7afb0f4b82b7ae8.description: The Santa Cruz campus proposes to construct the Heller Student Housing South project, formerly known as the Student Housing West Phase 2 – Heller Development project. The project would demolish the existing Family Student Housing complex and develop approximately 189,000 assignable square feet / 304,000 gross square feet of new residential construction. The project will provide approximately 1,290 beds for upper-division undergraduates, as well as a market, multi-purpose space, mail room, and laundry facilities. The project also includes site utilities, circulation infrastructure, including accessible pedestrian paths, bicycle routes, parking, and vehicular roadways.
ceqa-b0b7afb0f4b82b7ae8.crossStreets: Heller Drive and Empire Grade Road

ceqa-7cc12b91205b500aca.name: Minor Modification to Special Use Permit (#PP2026-10463) 350 Technology Drive - Cell Tower Modification
ceqa-7cc12b91205b500aca.projectTitle: Minor Modification to Special Use Permit (#PP2026-10463) 350 Technology Drive - Cell Tower Modification
ceqa-7cc12b91205b500aca.description: Minor Modification with Environmental Review (#PP2026-10463) to Special Use Permit #PP2015-28 for an existing telecommunications facility located at 350 Technology Drive (APN: 015-111-73). The project consists of minor modifications to an existing telecommunications facility for Verizon that involves swapping and modifying existing telecommunications equipment with no increase in the number of antennas or height.

ceqa-95285ced4a9526f6db.name: San Lorenzo Valley High School Fields
ceqa-95285ced4a9526f6db.projectTitle: San Lorenzo Valley High School Fields
ceqa-95285ced4a9526f6db.agency: San Lorenzo Valley Unified School District
ceqa-95285ced4a9526f6db.agencyName: San Lorenzo Valley Unified School District
ceqa-95285ced4a9526f6db.description: The project would include the installation and operation of field lights and an upgraded PA system at the SLV football, softball, and baseball fields. Additionally, the project would replace the aging bleachers for all three fields, demolish the existing restroom and snack shack to construct a new restroom and snack shack between the softball and baseball fields, and construct two press boxes attached to the softball and baseball bleachers. The field lights would provide safe and flexible nighttime use of the fields for various sporting and marching band activities, including practices and games. ceqa-ca25ecfe1ebe8a6eef.name: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-ca25ecfe1ebe8a6eef.projectTitle: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-ca25ecfe1ebe8a6eef.description: Project Description: The project consists of installation of an enclosed low-nitrogen oxide (Nox) flare to act as the backup landfill gas collection and destruction device for the existing onsite landfill gas collection system and Landfill Gas to Energy (LFGTE) Plant. The purpose of this improvement is to establish a permanent backup flare facility to collect methane gas and burn under regulatory provisions of the Monterey Bay Air Resources District (MBARD) in the event that the LFGTE is temporarily shut down. The facility would be located immediately west of the existing LFGTE Plant. The project includes construction of an approximately 3,600-square-foot flare station, which would house the low NOx flare station equipment, including the enclosed flare stack, an air compressor, three blowers, a condensate management system, and the equipment control panel. The station would be situated on a concrete pad and would be accessed by an existing landfill road. A three-foot tall concrete retaining wait would be installed on the northern boundary of the new station. The project also includes: • Installation of approximately 200 linear feet of landfill gas header pipe to connect the new flare station to the existing LFGTE Plant. • Installation of a line to tie into the air and condensate management lines from the fla re station to the existing LFGTE infrastructure on site. • Trenching and installing new electrical feed to the flare station, wiring, conduits, and associated electrical components. • Installation of the 6-foot-high chain link fence and access gates around the new station. Background. The City of Santa Cruz (City) Resource Recovery Facility (RRF) is required to have a landfill gas (LFG) collection and control system that continuously extracts gas from the landfill and sends it to a control device such as a flare or engine. To meet this requirement, the City has contracted with a third-party vendor for over 20 years to operate the LFGTE Plant to collect and convert landfill gas into electricity which is sent back into the PG&E grid. In early 2024, the LFGTE Plant was shut down, at no fault of the City or its vendor, due to damage to PG&E's electrical infrastructure from a February 2024 storm event, which has since been declared as state and federal natural disasters. Given the uncertainty of PG&E's timeline for repair, the City installed a temporary flare for the landfill to re-start collecting and burning LFG given the potential environmental and health and safety risks associated with uncollected LFG. To ensure safety, the City has been monitoring landfill gas migration since the shutdown, and in May 2024 obtained approval from MBARD to operate the temporary flare as a backup LFG destruction device until a permanent flare could be installed. The temporary flare, which is located next to the LFGTE Plant, was installed and began operating in May 2024 until the LFGTE resumed operation in July 2024. The existing, temporary open flare was meant to be a backup to continue collecting and destroying LFG when the LFGTE Plant is down. It is currently operating under a variance issued by MBARD as the LFGTE plant's backup device and must be removed by July 2026. The new flare would provide a permanent backup to maintain continuous collection and destruction of LFG and prevent the City from violating state law and conditions of the RRF permits. A location for installation of the permanent enclosed flare station was identified near the existing LFGTE Plant. The project location was chosen due to proximity to the LFGTE Plant to reduce the amount of piping required to connect the two systems; proximity to electrical utilities to reduce the amount of trenching and power utility installation; and ability of the flare stack to maintain required clearances.

ceqa-1016a67e6b00966334.name: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-1016a67e6b00966334.projectTitle: Capitola Road at Leona Creek Culvert Rehabilitation Project
ceqa-1016a67e6b00966334.description: The proposed project will rehabilitate the lower 100 lineal feet of a 66-inch corrugated metal culvert pipe. The culvert is located below Capitola Road and on private property within drainage easements. The total length of the culvert is 216 feet. The culvert conveys Leona Creek which drains into Schwan Lagoon. The project will take place between July 1st and September 30th with an expected construction duration of five days, and a maximum dewatered period of fourteen days. Temporary diversion dams composed of clean gravel and visqueen sheeting will be installed at the upstream and downstream ends of the culvert. Creek flow at the upstream dam will be pumped through rigid or flexible pipe to an adjacent sanitary sewer manhole. Nuisance water from the work area that collects upstream of the downstream dam will be pumped through rigid or flexible pipe to a tank and then disposed into the sanitary sewer system. Once the work area is isolated from the creek, the culvert interior will be cleaned, and any voids will be filled with a repair mortar. Exterior voids around the culvert will be compaction grouted from the pipe interior with polyurethane geotechnical foam. A 1.5-inch layer and 1.0-inch layer of fiber reinforced grout will be applied to the pipe interior and lower corroded portion of manholes within the culvert using a centrifugally cast concrete pipe machine. Once the concrete has cured (typically 72 hours) the creek diversion will be removed.

ceqa-ee798a7f41cb0a4d6d.name: UC Santa Cruz Wildfire Vegetation Management Project
ceqa-ee798a7f41cb0a4d6d.description: UC Santa Cruz proposes to implement vegetation treatments on up to 2,017 acres, of which 274 acres are in the California Coastal Zone, on the Main Residential Campus in Santa Cruz County. UC Santa Cruz has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis and Addendum (PSA/Addendum) for the project as a later activity covered by the California Vegetation Treatment Project (CalVTP) Program Environmental Impact Report (EIR). UC Santa Cruz Main Residential Campus and the surrounding area have experienced a legacy of intensive land uses paired with a subsequent period of lack of disturbance. This has resulted in very high forest densities, significant accumulations of live and dead fuels, significant changes to wildlife habitats, shifts in historic pathways of ecological succession, lowered biodiversity, and heightened fire risk to developed communities. The proposed treatment types are ecological restoration, wildland-urban interface (WUI) fuel reduction, and maintenance of existing fuel breaks (shaded and non-shaded). The proposed treatment activities consist of manual vegetation treatments, mechanical vegetation treatments, prescribed burning (broadcast burning, pile burning, and cultural burning), targeted herbicide application, and prescribed herbivory (predominantly with goats or sheep). The objectives of the proposed project broadly are to steward natural resources in a manner that aligns with campus values of biodiversity, resiliency, sustainability, traditional ecological knowledge, unique campus integrity, and the overall academic mission. The specific goals of the proposed project are to establish ecosystem and campus community resilience while promoting biodiversity as well as restore degraded habitats and protect sensitive resources including valuable coastal ecosystems.

ceqa-18f60e9df0da2c4cee.agency: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection
ceqa-18f60e9df0da2c4cee.agencyName: Forestry and Fire Protection, Department of
ceqa-18f60e9df0da2c4cee.description: The proposed project will establish a shaded fuel break along the Mount Hermon Association property adjacent to Graham Hill Road. Approximately 29 acres of roadside understory will be thinned within 500 feet of the Mount Hermon property along Graham Hill Road. Project crews will selectively remove small-diameter trees, shrubs, and ladder fuels to reduce vertical and horizontal fuel continuity and roadside fire hazards. Treatments will focus primarily on conifers and hardwoods less than 12 inches DBH, while also addressing dead or hazardous trees that pose safety risks. Residual trees will be pruned to a height of no more than one-third of their total height. Cut material less than 12 inches in diameter will be chipped on site, piled for later burning, or lopped and scattered. Downed material larger than 12 inches in diameter will be retained on site to maintain habitat and soil health.

ceqa-f55bce188864c9bfe2.description: The proposed project would readopt the emergency regulations which rescinded the commercial 20-fathom depth constraint and extended federal trip limits for non-nearshore groundfish into state waters north of 37° 07' N latitude. The proposed project would also keep in place the prohibition on the commercial take of quillback rockfish, statewide. The proposed project would readopt the emergency regulations which rescinded the commercial 20-fathom depth constraint and extended federal trip limits for non-nearshore groundfish into state waters north of 37° 07' N latitude. The proposed project would also keep in place the prohibition on the commercial take of quillback rockfish, statewide. The purpose of the proposed project is to restore access to fishing grounds based upon updated scientific stock assessment information for the quillback rockfish stock off California. The current unwarranted restrictions constrain commercial fishing efforts to a limited area of the State’s waters. The proposed regulations would remove these unneeded constraints, and be consistent with anticipated federal regulatory actions, thereby distributing effort and pressure on groundfish stocks, in both federal and State waters. Additionally, adoption of scientifically-based seasons, depth constraints, and commercial trip limits provides for the maintenance of sufficient populations of quillback rockfish and other groundfish to ensure their continued existence. Overall, the proposed actions preserves natural resources and is protective of the environment.

ceqa-17c7c4ba778def87f2.name: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-17c7c4ba778def87f2.projectTitle: Approval of Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Standards Application Findings Submitted by the City of Santa Cruz for the 2025 Energy Code Cycle
ceqa-17c7c4ba778def87f2.description: The California Energy Commission (CEC) adopts and regularly updates regulations that define a process for local governments to apply to the CEC to make certain findings regarding locally adopted energy conservation or energy insulation standards (CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 and section 10-110; Public Resources Code section 25402.1(h)(2)). The local government’s proposed standards are often referred to as the Local Reach Codes and require local governments submit an application to the CEC consistent with the requirements listed in section 10-106(b). Before the local standards may be enforced, the CEC must make two non-discretionary findings pursuant to PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and as listed in section 10-106(a): 1) The proposed local standards will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2022 Energy Code, and 2) The local government has filed the basis of its cost-effectiveness determination with the CEC. On 22nd September, 2025, the City of Santa Cruz (the City) submitted an application to the CEC that included: 1) the basis of its determination that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 2025-19 are cost-effective; and (2) documentation that the locally adopted energy efficiency standards contained in Ordinance No. 2025-19 will require the diminution of energy consumption levels compared to the 2025 Building Energy Efficiency Standards (Energy Code), as required by PRC section 25402.1(h)(2) and by CCR, Title 24, Part 1, section 10-106 (section 10-106). Based on the information submitted, staff analysis, and the Executive Director's recommendation, the CEC approved findings of the City’s section 10-106 application at the CEC’s January 21, 2026, Business Meeting.

ceqa-eb081292e37dbfe5de.name: Beltz 10 Aquifer Storage and Recovery & Beltz 11 Well Injection Pilot Tests
ceqa-eb081292e37dbfe5de.projectTitle: Beltz 10 Aquifer Storage and Recovery & Beltz 11 Well Injection Pilot Tests
ceqa-eb081292e37dbfe5de.description: The City of Santa Cruz Water Department is seeking to pilot test aquifer storage and recovery and well injection at its existing Beltz 10 well facility, which has two wells on site, Beltz 10 and Beltz 11, as part of a feasibility study to assess the viability of diverting excess surface water to the Santa Cruz Mid County Groundwater Basin. The Beltz 10 pilot test requires installing a monitoring well at the City's existing Beltz 10 well facility. The pilot testing is expected to last up to 150 days from 2026 to 2027. The City of Santa Cruz Water Department is seeking to pilot test aquifer storage and recovery (ASR) and well injection at its existing Beltz 10 well facility, which has two wells on site, Beltz 10 and Beltz 11 , as part of a feasibility study to assess the viability of diverting excess surface water to the Santa Cruz Mid County Groundwater Basin. The Beltz 10 well facility is shown on figure one. The ASR pilot testing of the Beltz 10 well seeks to field demonstrate the potential application of ASR in the in the A/AA unit Purisima Aquifer system. A new monitoring well will be installed as part of this work. The injection pilot testing of the Beltz 11 well seeks to investigate the potential to raise water levels in the Tu aquifer. The pilot testing results will be used to assess viability of the storage of drinking water underground at the Beltz 10 well facility and will provide the basis for the design and permitting for a long-term full-scale ASR and/or well.injection project. Preparation of Beltz 10 and Beltz 11 wells for pilot testing will include downhole cleaning procedures and modifications to the wells to establish a connection to the distribution system, retain or exchange pumps and add appurtenances. The ASR pilot test at Beltz 10 requires installing a monitoring well at the City's existing Beltz 10 well facility. This new monitoring well will be used to collect water level and water quality data. The monitoring well will be 2.5 inches in diameter. Drilling will be performed using the direct rotary method with bentonite-based fluid, which will be hauled offsite for disposal. Higher turbidity discharges from well development will be routed to the to the Beltz Water Treatment Plant (Beltz WTP) reclaim tank, which drains to the sanitary sewer system. Lower turbidity discharges from well development will be routed via the existing raw water pipeline to the unnamed creek at 30th Ave, a tributary to Moran Lake. A monitoring well vault and manhole will be installed to provide access for instrumentation, monitoring, or sampling. All construction activities will occur during working hours Monday through Friday 8am to 5pm consistent with County noise ordinance requirements. Construction of the monitoring well will require 12 working days. Some tree limbs will be required to be removed to allow the drill rig to access the site. The ASR pilot test at Beltz 10 will involve three repeated injection storage and recovery cycles with increasing quantities of water. Cycle 1 is expected to recover about 0.44 million gallons (mg). Cycle 2 is expected to recover about 3 mg. Water from Cycles 1 and 2 will be routed via the existing raw water pipeline to the unnamed creek at 30th Ave, a tributary to Moran Lake. Cycle 3 injection operations, if water quality pilot testing results from Cycles 1 and 2 are favorable, will result in the recovery of 13 mg that will be treated at the Beltz WTP will go into the distribution system. Water levels will be monitored after recovery. The injection pilot test at Beltz 11 will involve two repeated injection storage and recovery cycles at with increasing quantities of water extracted after injection. Cycle 1 is expected to recover about 0.1 million gallons (mg). Cycle 2 is expected to recover about 1 mg. Cycle 3 injection operations, if water quality pilot testing results from Cycles 1 and 2 are favorable, will result in the storage of 10 mg. Water levels at an existing monitoring well will be monitored to assess the response to injection at Beltz 11. Noise typical of existing operation noise will occur during pilot testing. The pilot testing is expected to last up to 150 days from 2026 to 2027.

The project will allow for up to 657 residential units (consistent with the City’s Housing Element), up to 82,000 square feet of commercial uses, and up to 35,000 square feet of public/civic uses. The project will include adoption of amendments to the City’s General Plan and Zoning Ordinance, changing certain existing land use designations in the Plan Area, creating new zoning districts, and updating existing or establishing new development standards to replace some of the current zoning provisions applicable to the Plan Area.

ceqa-3f85830efde961506f.name: Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health and Resilience Project
ceqa-3f85830efde961506f.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-3f85830efde961506f.description: Coastal Conservancy grant to Sempervirens Fund to conduct the Big Basin Redwood Wildfire Resilience Project consists of vegetation treatments and habitat enhancement on 215 acres in the old-growth coast redwood area of Big Basin Redwood State Park in Santa Cruz County. The Big Basin Redwood Wildfire Resilience Project is addressed in the Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health Project Specific Analysis and Addendum. California Department of Parks and Recreation's Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health Project Specific Analysis and Addendum proposes to implement vegetation treatments and maintenance on up to 9,977.25 acres of land within the eastern and inland portion of Big Basin Redwoods State Park in Santa Cruz and San Mateo Counties. California State Parks prepared a Project Specific Analysis and CEQA Addendum to evaluate if the project is within the scope of the CalVTP PEIR, and consider revisions or changes to the PEIR that would expand its coverage to include all project areas and provide information on the proposed project. Treatment types include ecological restoration. Treatment activities include prescribed burning, manual, mechanical, and targeted herbicide applications. The Inland Big Basin Redwoods State Park Forest Health and Resilience Project PSA/Addendum to the PEIR was prepared for the project as a later activity covered by the CalVTP EIR.

ceqa-a8a23a594d15448723.name: Coastal Santa Cruz Mountains: State Parks Forest Health Initiative
ceqa-a8a23a594d15448723.agency: California Department of Parks and Recreation
ceqa-a8a23a594d15448723.description: The California Department of Parks and Recreation (California State Parks) proposes to implement vegetation treatments and maintenance treatments on up to 11,994.7 acres of land within the project area. The project area consists of the western portion of Big Basin Redwoods State Park, Año Nuevo State Park, the southern extent of Butano State Park, and various adjacent landownerships owned by the Sempervirens Fund (Cougar Ridge, Gazos 320, and Lachenbruch) and Save the Redwoods League (Cascade Creek) located in Santa Cruz and San Mateo Counties and predominately within the coastal zone. California State Parks has prepared a Project-Specific Analysis and CEQA Addendum to evaluate if the proposed project is within the scope of the California Vegetation Treatment Program EIR (CalVTP PEIR), consider revisions or changes to the PEIR that would expand its coverage to include all project areas, and provide environmental information on the proposed project. Treatment types include ecological restoration. Treatment activities include prescribed burning, manual, mechanical, and targeted herbicide application treatments. The goal of the ecologically restorative treatments proposed in this PSA/Addendum is to restore forest and shrubland conditions to exhibit an increase in healthy growth of mature vegetation while allowing for natural regeneration of understory plant species, with alignment to the San Mateo Resource Conservation District and Resource Conservation District of Santa Cruz's Forest health and Fire Resilience Program Public Works Plan goals. The Coastal Santa Cruz Mountains: State Parks Forest Health Initiative PSA/Addendum to the PEIR was prepared for the project as a later activity covered by the CalVTP PEIR.

ceqa-b9c9119174120b2343.name: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-b9c9119174120b2343.projectTitle: Santa Cruz Resource Recovery Facility Enclosed Flare Station Installation Project
ceqa-b9c9119174120b2343.description: The project consists of installation of an enclosed low-nitrogen oxide (Nox) flare to act as the backup landfill gas collection and destruction device for the existing onsite landfill gas collection system and Landfill Gas to Energy {LFGTE) Plant. The purpose of this improvement is to establish a permanent backup flare facility to collect methane gas and burn under regulatory provisions of the Monterey Bay Air Resources District (MBARD) in the event that the LFGTE is temporarily shut down. The facility would be located immediately west of the existing LFGTE Plant. The project includes construction of an approximately 3,600-square-foot flare station, which would house the low NOx flare station equipment, including the enclosed flare stack, an air compressor, three blowers, a condensate management system, and the equipment control panel. The station would be situated on a concrete pad and would be accessed by an existing landfill road. A three-foot tall concrete retaining wall would be installed on the northern boundary of the new station.

ceqa-276d993d23d207e09e.name: 2026 Regional Transportation Plan & Sustainable Communities Strategy
ceqa-276d993d23d207e09e.projectTitle: 2026 Regional Transportation Plan & Sustainable Communities Strategy
ceqa-276d993d23d207e09e.description: The proposed 2026 RTP/SCS is an update to the current 2022 RTP/SCS that was adopted in August 2022. The proposed 2026 RTP/SCS reflects changes in legislative requirements, local land use policies, and resource constraints that have occurred since adoption of the current 2022 RTP/SCS. The 2026 update to the 2022 RTP/SCS is focused on continued implementation of the 2022 RTP/SCS, with updates to ensure consistency with federal, State, and local planning requirements. As have past RTPs, the proposed 2026 RTP/SCS shows how the region can invest limited transportation funds to maintain, operate and improve an integrated, multi-modal transportation system with the purpose of facilitating the efficient movement of people and goods. The updated plan identifies specific strategies, policies, and actions, including a list of programmed and planned transportation projects feasibly within the region’s anticipated transportation funding levels, to meet the current and future needs of the region. The proposed 2026 SCS updates the 2022 SCS, adopted by TCAG in August 2022, and incorporates new strategies to address rapidly the changing regional, national, and global context with the SCS preferred scenario focusing on new development in existing urbanized infill locations and transit corridors, avoiding identified resource areas. The planning horizon of the proposed 2026 RTP/SCS is 2049.

ceqa-194a1c8a9c59d544bc.name: General Plan Amendment No. 2026-01, Change of Zone No. 2026-01 and Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610
ceqa-194a1c8a9c59d544bc.projectTitle: General Plan Amendment No. 2026-01, Change of Zone No. 2026-01 and Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610
ceqa-194a1c8a9c59d544bc.description: General Plan Amendment No. 2026-01 and Change of Zone No. 2026-01 is a request by San Joaquin Valley Homes to change the underlying land use designation of a 7.04-acre portion of an approximately 23.53 acre parcel from the existing Mixed Use Commercial (C-MU) zone and designation to Residential Low Density designation, zoned Single Family Residential (R-1). This land use designation and zoning would match the existing land use designation and zoning of the remainder of the 23.53-acre parcel. The project is supported by the accompanying request for Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610. Blankenship Phase 3 Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5610 is a request by San Joaquin Valley Homes to subdivide a 7.04-acre portion of a 23.53-acre parcel into 36 lots for single-family residential use. This will be a continuation of the existing single-family subdivision which surrounds the proposed site. The residential subdivision will meet the city’s development standards for the zone. Additionally, the project will also include the construction of streets, extension of sewer lines and laterals, future connection to the storm drainage system and extension of utilities and services (electricity, gas, water). Frontage improvements along East Caldwell Avenue including curb, gutter and parkway landscape will also be installed per city standards. Development improvements will also be included along South Santa Fe Street. The proposed site area of 7.04 acres is part of a larger 23.53-acre parcel that was included in a previous approved Annexation No. 2024-05 and Blankenship Tentative Subdivision Map No. 5602. An Initial Study was completed for that project however, at the time, the 7.04-acre commercially zoned area was not included for development and was left as a remainder for the project. Now the applicant is seeking to rezone the commercially zoned area to residential to allow for the continued development of single-family homes expanding the surrounding subdivision to include this area.

ceqa-c817f7a61f404fde59.projectTitle: Woodville Farm Labor Center (WFLC) TCP Mitigation Project
ceqa-c817f7a61f404fde59.description: The proposed Project includes improvements to the existing water system. including a centralized granular activated carbon (GAC) treatment plant to treat both Well 1 and Well 3 and new pipeline. The GAC treatment plant would consist of one pair of 20,000-pound GAC treatment vessels installed on an at—grade mat foundation. A chlorination system would be added to disinfect the water after treatment utilizing a sodium hypochlorite feed system, and a sand separator and cartridge ?ltration system would be used to reduce the concentration of suspended solids reaching the GAC system. In addition to the water system improvements, including improvements to an existing storm water retention basin. a chain link fence enclosure to store sodium hypochlorite and a driveway would be added to the Project site.

ceqa-945242ef544337e16d.name: San Joaquin Cross Valley Loop Transmission Line Project (California Endangered Species Act Incidental Take Permit No. 2081-2013-050-04 Minor Amendment No. 7)
ceqa-945242ef544337e16d.projectTitle: San Joaquin Cross Valley Loop Transmission Project
ceqa-945242ef544337e16d.description: The ITP authorizes the construction, operation, and maintenance of a 23 mile long double-circuit 220 kilovolt (kV) transmission line looping the existing Big Creek 3-Springville transmission line to the existing Rector substation, creating the new Big Creek 3-Rector and Rector-Springville transmission line circuits. Construction was to result in impacts to 98.30 acres of California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense) habitat including temporary impacts to 52.62 acres and the permanent loss of 45.68 acres of California tiger salamander habitat. The activity was expected to result in incidental take of California tiger salamander, which is designated as a threatened species under the California Endangered Species Act. Construction was completed in late 2014 and the Minor Amendment No. 7 (Amendment) includes one change to the ITP as originally issued: an extension of an additional 60 months allowed for the mitigation obligation to be fulfilled.

ceqa-ed1569cf4a098c9f5d.name: Tulare County Roadside Hazardous Fuels Control Project
ceqa-ed1569cf4a098c9f5d.projectTitle: Tulare County Roadside Hazardous Fuels Control Project
ceqa-ed1569cf4a098c9f5d.description: The County proposes a five-year roadside hazardous fuels reduction program. Work will occur along approximately 400 miles of existing County road rights-of-way in High and Very High Fire Hazard Severity areas and will be limited to a 30-foot roadside treatment buffer. Treatments include removal of small vegetation and ladder fuels; selective removal of hazardous woody vegetation, trees, and shrubs up to 18 inches in diameter within or overhanging the rightof-way; weed abatement by pulling, mowing, or lawful herbicide application; and chipping, with chipped material scattered to a depth of less than four inches or removed. Treatment is intended for gentle slopes of less than 20 percent. Work will be performed by County staff and contracted crews. The purpose is to reduce hazardous fuel loads, maintain safer evacuation and emergency-response corridors, protect public infrastructure, and improve ingress and egress for residents and first responders. No roadway widening, new travel lanes, or new roads are proposed. Beneficiaries of the Project are community members and roadway users in mountainous areas of Tulare County.
