ceqa-b8fa7d915f5a939348.name: Oxnard Fire Station No. 2 Project
ceqa-b8fa7d915f5a939348.description: The Project involves the demolition of the existing 4,145-square-foot fire station and adjoining community garden, and the construction of a 12,585-square-foot (gross) new fire station. The fire station would include a separate 312-square-foot trash enclosure, a 180 square-foot earthquake storage enclosure, a 68-square-foot sand storage, and a 54-square-foot hose drying tower. This new fire station would support the daily operation of the OFD in its existing Station 2 location to continue to serve the nearby neighborhoods, upgrading the facility to a larger, more modern space to better suit the OFD's needs. The fire station would include a single-story apparatus bay designed to accommodate two fire engines and one ladder truck. Adjacent to the large apparatus area are support spaces like turnouts where the firefighters would store firefighting equipment, a decontamination (decon) room where they would clean their gear and themselves, a shop space for equipment cleaning and repair of equipment and tools, an EMS storage room for required medical supplies, a restroom, and miscellaneous utility rooms that would support the fire station. The building would also provide living quarters to accommodate up to 10 fire personnel per shift, which would include separate bunk rooms, restrooms, a kitchen, laundry facilities, dining room, day room (living room), an outdoor staff patio, and a fitness room. In addition, an open office space would be included to provide workspaces for fire personnel. The majority of the remainder of the Project Site would be paved to provide parking and circulation, and would include a fueling station for the fire apparatus, earthquake storage building, hose drying tower, and emergency generator located north of the fire station building. A trash enclosure would be provided near the northeastern corner of the Project Site. Landscape would be provided around the perimeter of the site, adjacent to Cloyne Street and East Pleasant Valley Road. The fire station would have a maximum height of 29 feet and 8 inches; and would be designed to include a hose drying tower with a maximum height of 31 feet.
ceqa-b8fa7d915f5a939348.crossStreets: East Pleasant Valley Road and Cloyne Street/Cypress Road

ceqa-7fcc1589afacbaeac9.name: Woodland-Davis Clean Water Agency Long-Term Water Transfer Project
ceqa-7fcc1589afacbaeac9.projectTitle: Woodland-Davis Clean Water Agency Long-Term Water Transfer Project
ceqa-7fcc1589afacbaeac9.description: The Supplemental Environmental Impact Report (SEIR) is a supplement to the Davis Woodland Water Supply Project (DWWSP) Final Environmental Impact Report (EIR) (SCH # 2006042175), which was certified by the City of Davis in November 2007, adopted by the City of Woodland in December 2007, and amended by the Woodland–Davis Clean Water Agency (WDCWA or Agency) through several addenda. The DWWSP Final EIR identified the joint use by the WDCWA and Reclamation District 2035 of a replacement surface water intake as the preferred alternative for diversions of water from the Sacramento River. The DWWSP, which is currently in operation, provides surface water supplies to the cities of Woodland and Davis, and the University of California, Davis. The WDCWA would implement the proposed Project to obtain, divert, and deliver additional water supplies from the Sacramento River through long-term water transfers from the South Sutter Water District (SSWD), Te Velde Farms, The Nature Conservancy, and/or a Sacramento River Settlement Contractor (SRSC) (collectively Sellers and individually a Seller) to meet water demands during dry-year conditions, Term 91 curtailment periods, and Shasta Critical Year conditions, including under a DPP 50-percent reduction scenario. The proposed Project would authorize long-term water transfers over a 25-year period, with transfers of up to 11,000 acre-feet annually, including up to 9,000 acre-feet between April and October and up to 2,000 acre-feet between November and March. The LTWT would allow WDCWA to purchase transfer water supplies on an as-needed basis using one-year contracts with upstream Sellers. Consistent with existing practice for such short-term transfers, Sellers would perform any additional California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and/or National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) analysis required to analyze the impacts of the specific sale and conveyance of water to WDCWA.

ceqa-fc4624010555a569e7.name: Dunnigan 5 Rehab Project
ceqa-fc4624010555a569e7.description: California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) will perform a geotechnical investigation for the planned Changeable Message Sign (CMS) and Closed-Circuit Television Pole (CCTV) located in Dunnigan, California. The purpose of the geotechnical investigation is to explore the existing subsurface conditions and collect subsurface information necessary for foundation analysis of the CMS and CCTV. The borehole will be drilled to maximum depth of 50 feet. The boring will be located within the right of way. Soil samples will be collected for laboratory tests for soil classification and corrosion analysis.

ceqa-a0aa9abcfd0b08a819.name: Pollinator Parkway for Butterflies, Beetles, and Bumble Bees
ceqa-a0aa9abcfd0b08a819.projectTitle: Pollinator Parkway for Butterflies, Beetles, and Bumble Bees
ceqa-a0aa9abcfd0b08a819.agency: Yolo County Habitat Conservation Plan/Natural Community Conservation Plan Joint Powers
ceqa-a0aa9abcfd0b08a819.agencyName: Yolo County Habitat Conservation Plan/Natural Community Conservation Plan Joint Powers
ceqa-a0aa9abcfd0b08a819.description: Restore and enhance floral resources and breeding habitat for pollinators on public lands in Yolo County, California. Project activities include controlling invasive species, preparing and planting areas with native species, and conducting educational workshops and planting events.

ceqa-a2415590f9a383d7f3.name: Bretton Woods Covell Drain (Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification No. YOL-67868-R2)
ceqa-a2415590f9a383d7f3.projectTitle: West Davis Active Adult Community Project
ceqa-a2415590f9a383d7f3.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification Number YOL-67868-R2, pursuant to section 1602 of the Fish and Game Code to the project Applicant, Denova Homes, Inc. The project is limited to the installation of approximately 1,250 cubic feet of rock slope protection (RSP) required to armor Covell Drain under two newly constructed City of Davis required pedestrian bridges, as well as the installation of RSP at the previously permitted and installed weir for erosion control. The project also includes grading repairs to an existing culvert on the Covell Drain that crosses Spirit Street to improve roadside drainage and the installation of a wildlife crossing shelf inside the existing culvert.

ceqa-d9e2e585b897a8b5ea.name: Knights Landing Ridge Cut Erosion Repairs Phase 2 (Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification No. YOL-66031-R2)
ceqa-d9e2e585b897a8b5ea.projectTitle: Knights Landing Ridge Cut Erosion Repair Project
ceqa-d9e2e585b897a8b5ea.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification Number YOL-66031-R2, pursuant to section 1602 of the Fish and Game Code to the project Applicant, Knights Landing Ridge Drainage District as represented by Meegan Nagy. The project is limited to bank repair and levee rehabilitation where needed at erosion sites. The objective of the Project is to repair existing eroded areas along the Knights Landing Ridge Cut (KLRC) levees on the east and west banks to arrest or avoid stream bank erosion that threatens the integrity of the KLRC levee system. Phase 2 will import approximately 7,000 cubic yards of rock slope protection. Revegetation would occur with a KLRDD-approved seed mix and vegetation will only be removed to the extent necessary for the erosion repair.

ceqa-409759d2fda891dbae.name: YOL-5 Bypass Overlay (EA 03-3N020)
ceqa-409759d2fda891dbae.description: California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) proposes to remove existing asphalt cement (AC) and place new hot mix asphalt (HMA) overlay, repair/replace joint headers along the entire bridges, striping, traffic control, and incidental work on Interstate 5 in Yolo County from PM 0.845 to PM 2.479.

ceqa-9672976bc6ba3353dc.name: Putah-Cache Watershed Arundo Eradication (Streambed Alteration Agreement Notification No. 1600-2019-0313-R2) Amendment 1.
ceqa-9672976bc6ba3353dc.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has amended Lake and Streambed Alteration Agreement Notification No. 1600-2019-0313- R2, pursuant to Fish and Game Code section 1602 et. seq, to the project Applicant, Yolo County Resource Conservation District. The amendment to the Agreement includes mechanical treatment through mastication for some Arundo patches smaller than 0.25 acres throughout the extent of the Putah-Cache Watershed Project boundary. The use of mechanical equipment to remove biomass in areas smaller than 0.25 acres will assist in herbicide treatment efficacy and will reduce the amount of herbicide used.

ceqa-e4562a495d55055d11.description: The primary purpose is to restore and maintain the structural integrity and safety of local road infrastructure while improving accessibility and utility functionality by extending pavement life, ensuring ADA compliance for pedestrian accessibility. The primary beneficiaries include residents, property owners, and pedestrians with disabilities who will gain improved accessibility.

ceqa-89e2f29df9c9847ede.projectTitle: Lumen Interstate 80 Middle-Mile Broadband Network Project (Encroachment Permit 03-26-6-BB-1566)
ceqa-89e2f29df9c9847ede.description: Lumen, in coordination with the California Department of Technology and the California Department of Transportation, proposes to install underground broadband infrastructure consisting of conduit on I-80 at PM 11.59 in Yolo County.

ceqa-f16722d5f084593258.projectTitle: Permit No. 20119 – Authorize Existing Access Ramps Project
ceqa-f16722d5f084593258.description: To authorize two existing landside access ramps on the left bank of Elk Slough. The ramps are shown in the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers As-Constructed Drawing No. 06-13-1100, dated January 1933, which signifies that the ramps were constructed with the Flood Control Project.

ceqa-d9398977539bf6e96a.name: Minor Alteration No. WA2026124 – North Ramp Asphalt and Light Pole Removal and Levee Restoration Project
ceqa-d9398977539bf6e96a.projectTitle: Minor Alteration No. WA2026124 – North Ramp Asphalt and Light Pole Removal and Levee Restoration Project
ceqa-d9398977539bf6e96a.description: To authorize corrective action work as a result of Enforcement Case No. 2026-15781, including: (1) saw cutting and removing an approximately 2-foot-wide by 3-inch-thick strip of existing asphalt for approximately 200 linear feet along the edge of the existing north access ramp, as identified in U.S. Army Corps of Engineers As-Built Drawing No. 50-04-2948, dated October 1953, Sheet 2, STA 69+00; (2) removing an unauthorized camera/light pole and its approximately 3-foot-deep concrete footing from the landside levee slope; (3) restoring the disturbed areas along the ramp edge and the excavation resulting from removal of the pole and footing to pre-project conditions in compliance with Title 23 Standards, including soil and density testing to verify compliant compaction; and (4) hauling and properly disposing of all removed debris. The work is intended to restore the levee slope to provide structural stability and proper drainage and is consistent with the Supplement to Standard Operation and Maintenance Manual, Sacramento River Flood Control Project, Unit No. 114, Section 3-01, Repair of Damage.

ceqa-d3e41535cec7da239e.name: ZF# 2026-009 (Davis Waldorf School Major Use Permit)
ceqa-d3e41535cec7da239e.projectTitle: ZF# 2026-009 (Davis Waldorf School Major Use Permit)
ceqa-d3e41535cec7da239e.description: The Davis Waldorf School has operated at its existing 5-acre campus within the City of Davis (APN 035-470-012) since 1992. In early 2026, the Association for Waldorf Education in Davis purchased the adjoining 2-acre property to expand and improve their programs and facilities. The proposed project is a request for Major Use Permit to allow the ±2-acre Agricultural Intensive (A-N) zoned parcel at 25283 County Road l00A to function as part of the Davis Waldorf School campus. The parcel contains a primary dwelling and an ancillary dwelling (cottage), a greenhouse, and swimming pool. The swimming pool will be removed under proper permits for student and staff safety. No expansion of the dwelling or cottage is proposed. The existing residence will be reused for administrative offices, a library, meeting space, staff break area, and handwork programs serving the school's existing student population. Internal renovations to ensure accessibility requirements are met will be required and reviewed through the County's building permit process. The second dwelling on the site (referred to as the cottage) would remain for residential use and may be offered as staff housing. Educational agricultural activities would be conducted outdoors on the parcel, consistent with typical small-scale agricultural uses in Yolo County. Access to the property is off County Road I 00A and is proposed as an administrative staff entrance. Student drop-off and parking operations will remain on the existing campus, which will be connected via a new accessible pathway. Site disturbance would be minimal and largely limited to trenching for potential utility connections and construction of the accessible pathway from the existing campus to the project site.
ceqa-d3e41535cec7da239e.crossStreets: Sycamore Lane and North Davis Farm Road

ceqa-7dcf5cf795a099c0b3.name: Minor Alteration No. WA2026132 – Upper Elkhorn Basin Geotechnical Investigation Project
ceqa-7dcf5cf795a099c0b3.projectTitle: Minor Alteration No. WA2026132 – Upper Elkhorn Basin Geotechnical Investigation Project
ceqa-7dcf5cf795a099c0b3.description: To perform geotechnical explorations within the Upper Elkhorn Basin that will assist in composing the Yolo Bypass Comprehensive Study, a feasibility study assessing the economic justification to widen the Yolo Bypass in the Upper Elkhorn Basin and extend the Fremont Weir to improve flood flow conveyance in the bypass system. will include one test pit, six borings, and ten cone penetration tests (CPTs). The test pit will be approximately three feet wide, eight feet long, and excavated to a depth of approximately eight to ten feet using a track backhoe with a 24-inch bucket and then backfilled by tamping the excavated soil as backfill in approximately 12-inch lifts. The borings will be advanced to depths of approximately 100 feet below the ground surface using truck or track-mounted drill rigs equipped with hollow stem auger and mud rotary (HSA/MR) capabilities. Soil samples will be collected from the borings by driving either a 1.5-inch inner diameter Standard Penetration Test sampler or a 2.5-inch inner diameter California split-spoon sampler 18 inches into undisturbed soil. The CPTs will be conducted by hydraulically advancing an instrumented steel cone into the ground using truck-mounted and/or track-mounted compact CTP rigs. Each CPT will include at least one pore pressure dissipation test to measure the porewater pressure in the aquifer to estimate the groundwater level. The upper five feet of all borings and CPTs will be excavated using hand sampling equipment. Upon completion, all boreholes and CPTs will be backfilled using neat cement grout with bentonite, with the top two feet being backfilled using native material and restoring the project site to pre-project conditions.

ceqa-c4f958612ea52fb0e1.name: Minor Alteration No. WA2025034 – Geotechnical Drilling Exploration for Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area Physical Improvements Project
ceqa-c4f958612ea52fb0e1.projectTitle: Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area Physical Improvements Projects (PIPs) - Geotechnical Exploration
ceqa-c4f958612ea52fb0e1.description: To perform geotechnical investigations activities. The proposed investigations include 24 boreholes and one test pit within the existing roadways and parking areas in the Yolo Bypass Wildlife Area. Construction activities will include clearing and grubbing of existing vegetation or pavement removal in the work areas and ground disturbance by a truck-mounted drill rig and equipment to drill and backfill the boreholes. The exploration activities consist of drilling 8.25-inch diameter geotechnical exploration hollow stem borings drilled to maximum depth of 80 feet, or to refusal, below existing ground, and excavating a 3-feet wide, 5-feet long, and 8-feet deep test pit. Soil samples will be collected using Standard Penetration Tests, Shelby tube sampling, and cuttings from the test pit. The boreholes will be backfilled with grout the same day of drilling, placed to depth by a tremie. The test pit will be backfilled with the excavated spoils. The backfill shall will be in accordance with County Standards and California Code of Regulations, Title 23, Waters, Division 1, (Title 23) standards.

ceqa-21ee780affaf122afa.name: Minor Alteration No. WA2026120 – Sacramento River Erosion Repair Project
ceqa-21ee780affaf122afa.projectTitle: Minor Alteration No. WA2026120 – Sacramento River Erosion Repair Project
ceqa-21ee780affaf122afa.description: To repair an approximately 3,200-square-foot waterside slope slip encompassing approximately 63 linear feet of bank along the Sacramento River, consistent with the Operation and Maintenance Manual, “West Levee of Sacramento River from Sacramento Weir to River Mile 51.2 and South Levee of Sacramento Bypass and East Levee of Yolo Bypass from Sacramento Bypass to South Boundary of Reclamation District No. 900.” The proposed work includes removal of approximately five cubic yards of sloughed material and reconstruction of the levee slope to its existing profile, elevation, and cross-section. Approximately 80 cubic yards of rock slope protection and filter gravel will be placed to stabilize the repaired slope, including a keyed rock toe at the bottom of the slope. The site will be cleared and grubbed as necessary, including removal of trees and vegetation within the construction limits. Construction will include an initial stabilization phase involving placement of rock to establish a working platform, followed by final stabilization of the bank. Willow bundles will be installed at the top of the working platform as part of the final stabilization.

ceqa-4fac6ddaa189a7ca92.name: UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine Project
ceqa-4fac6ddaa189a7ca92.projectTitle: UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine Development Plan
ceqa-4fac6ddaa189a7ca92.description: The UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine (WSVM) Development Project includes approximately 320,000 square feet (sf) of new construction, 188,000 sf of renovations, and 68,000 sf of demolition. The Project would increase the number of graduating veterinarians, expand client services, and advance scientific and clinical discovery. Planned facilities include a Veterinary Education Pavilion and Primary Care Hospital, a Small Animal Hospital, a Large Animal Hospital, a Veterinary Cancer Center, an Equine Reproduction Facility, an Equine Performance Arena, a Raptor Experience, and a surface parking lot with about 250 spaces. Phase 1 projects would include the Education Pavilion and the Small Animal Hospital. Future phase projects are expected to be completed over the next 5 to 10 years.
ceqa-4fac6ddaa189a7ca92.crossStreets: Garrod Drive, La Rue Road, Hutchinson Drive

ceqa-e3f677c68580e485b3.name: The L-119A & L-172A (R-692 & R-1935) Prospect Slough Crossings Replacement Project
ceqa-e3f677c68580e485b3.projectTitle: The L-119A & L-172A (R-692 & R-1935) Prospect Slough Crossings Replacement Project
ceqa-e3f677c68580e485b3.agency: California Regional Water Quality Control Board, Central Valley Sacramento Region 5
ceqa-e3f677c68580e485b3.agencyName: Regional Water Quality Control Board, Region 5 - Sacramento
ceqa-e3f677c68580e485b3.description: PG&E proposes to replace two existing natural gas transmission pipeline crossings beneath Prospect Slough in Yolo County using horizontal directional drilling. The project includes connecting the new segments to the existing system and decommissioning and partially removing the old crossings. The replacement will maintain the safety and reliability of natural gas service without increasing transmission capacity.

ceqa-fb7c8f0b72c0d42daa.name: Yolo Staging Area Project
ceqa-fb7c8f0b72c0d42daa.description: Project improvements include; job site trailer to be installed which will include a concrete pad, ADA parking, a hook up to the septic system, electrical service and upgraded well. A sprinkler system will be installed, along with a panel upgrade, backup power for fire and security, high speed internet, and an EV charging station. A storage tank and pump will be installed, as well an overhead water truck filing station. The existing septic system will be rehabbed. A perimeter fence will be installed, fire suppression will be added to the trailer, and security cameras will be added to the project site.

ceqa-1db544ccac76222e02.projectTitle: Geotechnical Borings for the UPRR Window Closure

ceqa-1db544ccac76222e02.agencyName: West Sacramento Area Flood Control Agency

The borings will assist in the understanding of subsurface soil characteristics and levee erosional susceptibility. The levee project will benefit all West Sacramento residents and property in protecting against the 200-year flood event.

ceqa-ea65bcf0c49c5d46ce.name: Permit No. 20085- I-80 Yolo Causeway Signage and Tolling Improvements Project
ceqa-ea65bcf0c49c5d46ce.description: Approval of Permit No. 20085, under California Code of Regulations, Title 23, Article 3, Section 6, for work within an adopted plan of flood control: To install ten (10) fiber optic conduits, two (2) overhead sign structures, one (1) toll reader, and remove one (1) existing overhead sign structure along Interstate 80 within the Yolo Causeway corridor. Fiber optic conduits consisting of 2-inch and 3-inch diameter polyvinyl chloride (PVC) Schedule 80 pipes will be surface-mounted to existing bridge rails, median barriers, bike path barriers, and concrete barriers, and installed below grade within roadway fill sections where necessary, at depths up to approximately three feet below ground surface. All bridge mounted conduits will be above the bridge low chord. Transverse conduit crossings beneath the roadway and medians are also included and will be installed using directional drilling methods. One (1) overhead sign structure supported on a 60-inch-diameter, 24-foot-long cast in drilled hole (CIDH) pile foundation will be installed within a median barrier located in the Yolo Bypass fill section. The existing overhead sign structure near the Unit No. 02 East Levee will be removed and replaced with a new overhead truss sign structure facing eastbound traffic. The existing piles will be removed to approximately three feet below ground surface, with the remaining pile portions abandoned in place. The new structure will be supported on CDIH pile foundations consisting of one 60-inch-diameter, 42-foot-long pile and one 72-inch-diameter, 29-foot-long pile, within the landside slope of the Unit No. 02 East Levee embankment.

ceqa-534b91453f9afc5557.name: Long Range Development Plan Amendment No. 4
ceqa-534b91453f9afc5557.projectTitle: UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine Development Plan
ceqa-534b91453f9afc5557.description: UC Davis proposes to modify the UC Davis 2018 Long Range Development Plan (2018 LRDP) land use designations to accommodate the proposed California Veterinary Emergency Team Operations Center and Shelter Medicine Clinic Project. The proposed Long Range Development Plan Amendment #4 would redesignate 0.75 acres of Arboretum & Public Garden land use to Academic & Administrative land use in the 2018 LRDP.

ceqa-4f19ba0a7d13faf09c.name: Lower Putah Creek Salmon Habitat Restoration Nishikawa Reach Project
ceqa-4f19ba0a7d13faf09c.projectTitle: Lower Putah Creek Restoration Project, Nishikawa Reach
ceqa-4f19ba0a7d13faf09c.description: The Project will realign a reach of Putah Creek and lower the floodplain to improve habitat for native fish and enhance and re-establish wetland and riparian habitat. Heavy equipment will be used to grade the floodplain, excavate the new channel, and fill the existing channel. Sections of Putah Creek will be dewatered during construction.

ceqa-a509b8edbb3c590c6a.name: Willowgrove (Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification No. YOL- 67737-R2)
ceqa-a509b8edbb3c590c6a.description: The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) has executed Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification Number YOL-67737-R2, pursuant to section 1602 of the Fish and Game Code to the project Applicant, Davis Eastside, LLC. The Project would include the development of a mixed-use community, including a total of 1,250 dwelling units, comprised of both affordable and market-rate single- and multi-family residences across various residential neighborhoods. The Projects covered under the Streambed Alteration Agreement include the installation of two stormwater outfalls, the installation of a clear-span bridge for emergency vehicle access, the removal of an existing road crossing and culvert, and the removal of irrigation infrastructure.

ceqa-e8ccbc5f3913d20be3.projectTitle: Tamano Irrigation Pipe (Streambed Alteration Agreement EPIMS Notification No. YOL-68197-R2)

ceqa-7ec8e4ff85be3cf741.name: Sites Reservoir Project
ceqa-7ec8e4ff85be3cf741.description: The Sites Reservoir Project consists of the construction of an off-stream surface water reservoir located in the Antelope Valley within Glenn and Colusa counties to provide water supply for environmental, municipal, industrial, and agricultural needs throughout the State of California. The Project, in part, consists of: geotechnical investigations; construction of two dams, seven saddle dams, and two saddle dikes; development of two recreation areas; road construction and improvements; and construction of pumping facilities and pipelines. The total construction area for the Project is approximately 27,000 acres and the reservoir has been designed to impound up to 1.5 million acre-feet of water. The Bureau of Reclamation has identified the Sites Reservoir Project need as providing off-stream surface water storage north of the Delta in a manner that is consistent with Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation (WIIN) Act requirements and Reclamation law.

ceqa-6231ecbfc0f331c76f.name: Tide's End Multibenefit Restoration Project
ceqa-6231ecbfc0f331c76f.description: The Tide’s End Multibenefit Restoration Project (Project) is being developed to restore and enhance tidal wetland and floodplain habitat, support multibenefit land uses (including managed wetlands and floodplain agriculture), and maintain or improve flood conveyance in the Yolo Bypass. Tidal inundation would be restored by hydrologically connecting the site to the Toe Drain via a series of berm openings, berm lowering, and channel excavation. The restored habitats would enhance aquatic production and export for food web support and would facilitate volitional fish passage of juvenile salmonids and other native fishes accessing the Project area’s floodplain during high-flow events. The Project’s restoration design elements include tidal wetland, transition zone habitat, floodplain habitat, managed wetlands, managed floodplain agriculture, site revegetation (including riparian communities), access improvements, as well as irrigation and drainage improvements.

ceqa-db2d380863e6f1f2b6.name: Roadside Tree Stand Thinning-Rumsey
ceqa-db2d380863e6f1f2b6.description: This fuels reduction project is part of a series of roadside vegetation reduction projects throughout the Ca pay Valley to protect Highway 16 as an evacuation route and access point during wildfire events. The project consists of mechanical handwork (chainsaws and loppers) and chipping in a roadside section of overgrown vegetation primarily consisting of mature non-native cypress trees. The project footprint is approximately 1.25 acres, or about half a mile along Highway 16 under the PG&E powerlines. Vegetation in the project footprint consists of nonnative cypress trees that have been topped by PG&E to prevent treetops from brushing against powerlines. Topping has caused the trees to degrade or die, making them significant fire hazard risks along Highway 16 and a potential ignition source for wildfire from passing cars. Overgrown vegetation too close to the highway poses a risk to the towns of Guinda/Rumsey and the larger Capay Valley region, as overgrown vegetation can burn and fall into the roadway limiting access or evacuation. Reducing fuels in project footprint along the highway will reduce the likelihood of catastrophic wildfire and protect a vital evacuation route. Thinning and reducing ladder fuels along this section of Highway 16 will be performed by a licensed contractor or conservation corps crews, with biological and botanical monitoring conducted by Yolo County Resource Conservation District. In subsequent years, activities may occur to maintain the fuel break and ensure long-term management objectives are met.(DBH). There are native valley oaks on site that will be left in place. Stumps of cut trees will remain in the ground to minimize soil disturbance. The project entails mechanical thinning of roadside vegetation of non-native highly flammable vegetation. Mechanical treatments can benefit ecosystems by reducing the likelihood of catastrophic wildfires, maintaining and restoring healthy ecosystems, and protecting human communities. An RCD Qualified Biologist conducted biological and botanical surveys at the project site. Based on the results of the biological survey of both units, the project has been designed so it will not cause significant adverse impact to special status species that may occur near the project site. If work commences during nesting bird season (February 1st to September 15th) the project area will be surveyed for nesting birds by a qualified biologist, no more than one week before operations. If nesting birds are located, the RCD will develop measures that avoid impacts and are consistent with the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

ceqa-d7006413650d11f334.name: Prospect Island Tidal Habitat Restoration Project
ceqa-d7006413650d11f334.projectTitle: Prospect Island Tidal Habitat Restoration Project
ceqa-d7006413650d11f334.description: PROJECT DESCRIPTION The fundamental purpose and overarching goal of the Prospect Island Tidal Habitat Restoration Project is to restore tidal action to the interior of Prospect Island. The proposal is intended to partially fulfill the California Department of Water Resources’ (DWR) 8,000-acre tidal habitat restoration obligations contained within Reasonable and Prudent Alternative (RPA) 4 of the 2008 United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) Biological Opinion on the Coordinated Operations of the Central Valley Project and State Water Project (2008 USFWS BiOp) and Condition 7 of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) 2009 Incidental Take Permit for Longfin Smelt (ITP No. 2008-2009-001-03). The 2008 USFWS BiOp RPA 4 restoration obligations were carried forward as baseline conditions in the USFWS Biological Opinion for the Reinitiation of Consultation on the Coordinated Operations of the Central Valley Project and the State Water Project, Service File Number: 08FbTD00-2019-F-0164 (2019 USFWS BiOp) issued on October 21, 2019. In 2021, the United States Bureau of Reclamation requested a reinitiation of consultation on the Biological Opinion. On November 8, 2024, the USFWS issued the 2024 Biological Opinion Reinitiation of Consultation on the Coordinated Long-Term Operation of the Central Valley Project and State Water Project (Reference: 2022-0059509). The 2024 BiOp states that “Reclamation and DWR propose to finish restoring and protecting the remainder of the 8,000 acres and an additional 396.3 acres of intertidal and associated subtidal habitat restoration in the Delta and Suisun Marsh by 2026.” In addition, Section 9.1.1 of the ITP for Long-Term Operation of the State Water Project in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta (2081-2019-066-00) (2020 LTO ITP), issued by CDFW on March 31, 2020, carried forward the 8,000-acre tidal habitat restoration requirement and added 396.3 acres for Delta Smelt, aligning itself with the 8,396.3 acres required in the 2024 BiOp. The 2020 LTO ITP also added an additional 396.3 acres for Longfin Smelt for a new total of 1,196.3 for the species. A new ITP for the Long-Term Operation of the State Water Project in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta (2081-2023-054-00), hereinafter 2024 LTO ITP, was issued to DWR on November 1, 2024, and replaced the 2020 LTO ITP. The restoration acreage requirements for both Delta Smelt and Longfin Smelt were carried forward from the 2020 LTO ITP and remained unchanged. In 2019, a Final Environmental Impact Report for the Prospect Island Tidal Habitat Restoration Project was prepared by DWR in accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act and was certified by DWR in February 2019 (https://ceqanet.opr.ca.gov/2013052056/3). The 2019 FEIR evaluated the impacts and mitigation measures associated with the Prospect Island Tidal Habitat Restoration Project. This third Addendum evaluates a proposed refinement to the site-clearing activities described in the 2019 FEIR. Under the proposed refinement, 220 acres of existing trees and woody vegetation within the shallow subtidal elevation band (0.0 to 2.1 feet NAVD 88) would be retained where located outside the construction footprint and associated buffer areas. This represents a change from the Project described in the 2019 FEIR, which included vegetation-clearing treatments across all subtidal elevations. Under the FEIR, existing trees and woody vegetation within shallow subtidal habitats would be removed, while vegetation within moderate and deep subtidal habitats below 0.0 feet NAVD 88 would be cleared and disked in place. Under the proposed refinement, only trees and woody vegetation located outside the construction footprint and associated buffer areas within the shallow subtidal elevation band would be retained; all other vegetation-clearing activities would remain as described in the 2019 FEIR.

ceqa-6245e229fcdfcd67c1.name: City of Davis Wastewater Treatment Plant and Associated Holding Ponds/Overflow Area –General Plan Amendment, Pre-Zoning, Pre-Annexation
ceqa-6245e229fcdfcd67c1.projectTitle: City of Davis Wastewater Treatment Plant and Associated Holding Ponds/Overflow Area –General Plan Amendment, Pre-Zoning, Pre-Annexation
ceqa-6245e229fcdfcd67c1.description: The proposed project includes an amendment to add the three properties containing the WWTP site and related areas to the City of Davis General Plan Land Use Map and designate them as Public/Semi-Public and a pre-zoning to amend the City’s zoning map to pre-zone the three properties as Public/Semi-Public, in anticipation of their proposed annexation. The properties are currently included within the City’s Sphere of Influence and are designated in the Yolo County General Plan as Public/Quasi-Public with a Yolo County zoning of Public/Quasi-Public. In 2017, the City completed a significant upgrade to the wastewater treatment plant. This $80 million upgrade included replacing aging infrastructure and adding new treatment processes to meet national permit requirements. Currently, the City’s wastewater facility is on land owned by the City, but is not within the City boundaries. Since these improvements significantly increased the value of the property, the property's tax liability will also increase significantly after reappraisal if the property remains in Yolo County. This increase is estimated to be at least five times the existing tax liability of $15,000 per year. This large tax liability is alleviated by annexing the property into the City. While “island annexations” are not typically permitted under Yolo LAFCo and state laws, there are specific exemptions for municipal utility properties, such as this. To be eligible for this exemption, the property must be within the jurisdiction of the City, per Article XIII, Section 11 of the California Constitution. Prior to annexation, the City will need to create a tax share agreement with Yolo County. City and Yolo County staff are working collaboratively to pursue this annexation and understand the mutual benefits. The proposed amendments by the City would retain the public/semi-public designation and zoning of the site and maintain the existing public uses and facilities. No site improvements or physical changes to the site are proposed or anticipated as part of this project.

ceqa-eb392a889613c9b606.name: Agricultural Water Well Ordinance – Extension of Temporary Moratorium (Urgency Ordinance No. 1588)
ceqa-eb392a889613c9b606.projectTitle: Agricultural Water Well Ordinance – Extension of Temporary Moratorium (Urgency Ordinance No. 1588)
ceqa-eb392a889613c9b606.description: On August 26, 2025, the Board of Supervisors adopted an urgency ordinance imposing a temporary 45-day moratorium on the approval or issuance of well permits for new agricultural, non-exempt wells located within the Yolo Subbasin Groundwater Agency’s designated Focus Areas, which has since been extended with the adoption of Urgency Ordinance No. 1577 on October 7, 2025 for an additional 10 months and 15 days (through August 25, 2026) to allow time to better understand, among other things, the impacts of land use changes, particularly the hardening of groundwater demands with increased crop conversions to perennial crops. Domestic wells (wells producing less than two acre-feet per year for individual domestic water use), public supply system wells as defined in Health & Safety Code § 116275, monitoring wells or other wells not intended for extraction of groundwater, and minor alterations to certain existing wells were exempted from the temporary moratorium. On November 4, 2025, the Board of Supervisors adopted Urgency Ordinance No. 1580 amending Urgency Ordinance No. 1577 to also exempt certain replacement wells that may otherwise cause costly delays by allowing for a timelier replacement of existing wells that may fail or need replacement while the moratorium is in effect. Urgency Ordinance No. 1588, adopted by the Board of Supervisors on August 25, 2026, extends the temporary moratorium on the approval or issuance of well permits for new agricultural, non-exempt wells located within the Yolo Subbasin Groundwater Agency’s designated Focus Areas for one additional year through August 25, 2027. The Urgency Ordinance is effective immediately (August 25, 2026).

ceqa-50ca009d44dc82c3cc.name: Cache Creek Rehabilitation Project

This project proposes Resurfacing, Restoration and Rehabilitation (3R) to improve pavement condition and roadway safety. ceqa-0f12d1ac59b9c5a24a.name: Woodland-Davis Clean Water Agency Long-Term Water Transfer Project
ceqa-0f12d1ac59b9c5a24a.projectTitle: Woodland-Davis Clean Water Agency Long-Term Water Transfer Project
ceqa-0f12d1ac59b9c5a24a.description: The Woodland-Davis Clean Water Agency (WDCWA) proposes the Long-Term Water Transfer (LTWT) Project to enhance water supply reliability through long-term transfer agreements with South Sutter Water District, Te Velde Farms, The Nature Conservancy, and/or a Sacramento River Settlement Contractor (SRSC) (collectively referred to as the Sellers). The transferred water would provide an additional source of supply to meet WDCWA's demands during dry-year conditions, Term 91 curtailments, Shasta Critical Year conditions, and potential Drought Preparedness Plan (DPP) scenarios involving a 50 percent reduction in available water supplies. WDCWA provides treated water to the cities of Woodland and Davis and the University of California, Davis (UC Davis). The service area is located in Yolo County, approximately 64 miles northeast of San Francisco and 15 miles west of Sacramento. WDCWA operates under two surface water rights that authorize diversion of Sacramento River water for treatment and distribution within its service area. Existing facilities include the Joint Intake Facility, which is jointly owned with Reclamation District 2035, a raw water transmission pipeline, the Regional Water Treatment Facility (RWTF), and finished water transmission pipelines. Under the proposed LTWT, transfer water would be made available through a Seller’s existing water rights or through an SRSC’s contractual entitlement with the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation. Transferred water would be diverted at WDCWA’s existing Sacramento River intake facility and conveyed through the existing raw water pipeline to the RWTF for treatment. Following treatment, the water would be delivered to municipal and irrigation customers in Woodland, Davis, and UC Davis, serving residential, multifamily residential, commercial, industrial, and institutional uses. WDCWA proposes to implement the LTWT for an initial term of 25 years, with an option to renew subject to future CEQA review. The program would enable WDCWA to acquire transfer water supplies during Term 91 curtailments and/or Shasta Critical Year conditions through agreements with upstream Sellers. The LTWT would be implemented through water agreements for each transfer as required, subject to available water supplies and willing Sellers.

ceqa-88fa9b364c1a05deee.name: Brar Farms Residential Development Project
ceqa-88fa9b364c1a05deee.description: The proposed project involves the subdivision of an approximately 60-acre property to create 259 lots for future single-family homes, comprising approximately 34.78 acres of residential development and 15 open space lots totaling 6.65 acres. The open space lots would include a 0.68-acre Central Park, a 0.14-acre parklet at the corner of Marshall Road and Otis Avenue, and 1.81 acres of landscaped lots, including a roundabout, distributed throughout the proposed development to provide greenspace and buffers. Additionally, the open space areas would include a 4.02-acre detention basin, which would also serve as a recreational field during dry seasons. Of the 259 proposed residential lots, 158 would be 5,000 net square feet, 58 would be 6,000 to 7,000 net square feet, 26 would be 7,200 to 8,400 net square feet. Seventeen of the proposed residential lots would be oversized lots reaching up to 14,800 net square feet. In addition, landscaping, roadway, and utility improvements would be installed within the project site. The proposed project would also require amendments to the City’s existing General Plan, Southport Framework Plan, and the Zoning Map/Zoning Code.

ceqa-e26ab0369979a23dae.name: Ramos Oil Recyclers, Inc. dba Ramos Environmental Services Series C Permit Variance
ceqa-e26ab0369979a23dae.projectTitle: Standardized Permit Reissuance for Ramos Enviromental Services
ceqa-e26ab0369979a23dae.agency: California Department of Toxic Substances Control
ceqa-e26ab0369979a23dae.description: The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC), pursuant to Division 4.5, California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Chapter 20, has prepared an Addendum to consider the approval of a Permit Variance application (Variance) pursuant to California Health and Safety Code section 25200 to the Hazardous Waste Facility Permit submitted by Ramos Environmental Services (Facility). The Variance is required due to the Facility’s request to continue truck to truck transfer of bulk liquid waste oil, waste antifreeze, oily water and oily sludge on and within a secondary containment loading/unloading pad at the hazardous waste storage and transfer facility located at 1515 South River Road, West Sacramento California, 95691. The California Health and Safety Code section 25201.6(i)(3)(A) requires any hazardous waste facility with an effective permit expiring on or after January 1, 2025, to submit a new application at least 2 years before the expiration date of the effective permit (defined as a timely application for the purposes of California Code of Regulations, title 22, section 66270.51) if the facility wishes to continue operating past the permit expiration date. The Facility did not submit their Permit Renewal Application 2 years before the expiration date of April 19, 2026. The Facility submitted their request for a Permit Renewal and DTSC is considering the Renewal separate from this Variance as there are further actions related to DTSC’s Permit Renewal process that have not been completed. The Variance would authorize the Facility to continue to operate while DTSC considers the Permit Renewal Application. The Variance will be effective for 1 year or until a final permit decision is made on their current permit application, whichever comes first. Due to the expired Permit the Facility is not currently permitted to consolidate waste within the onsite above ground storage tank and the Facility is proposing to bulk the waste between small tanker trucks into a large tanker truck before transporting the waste to an authorized Transfer, Storage, and Disposal (TSDF) facility for proper recycling and disposal. The request is to continue to conduct this consolidation activity while DTSC is considering the Renewal. There are no proposed construction nor operational changes and no ground disturbing activities proposed by the Facility.

ceqa-4af00b2354489081f3.name: Clark Pacific Facility Expansion Project (ZF2023-0005)
ceqa-4af00b2354489081f3.description: The Clark Pacific Facility Expansion Project will expand the adjacent existing Clark Pacific facility through the development of up to 500,000 square feet of new industrial buildings and associated internal roadway improvements, utility improvements, parking, and landscaping. The project does not include specific development plans at this time; however, the facilities are anticipated to be similar to the existing facility, with operations consisting of prefabrication of building materials and ancillary outdoor storage of materials. ceqa-98c7f5d7408d925ada.name: Front Country Fire Break- North 1.5 Mile
ceqa-98c7f5d7408d925ada.projectTitle: Front Country Fire Break- North 1.5 Mile
ceqa-98c7f5d7408d925ada.description: The Front Country Fuel Break starts in Rumsey, CA and follows the base of the Inner Coast Range extending the north-south length of Yolo County and ending near west Winters, CA. Historically, the fuel break was implemented during wildfire events, most recently the LNU Complex {2020} and the County Fire (2018} to stop or slow wildfire approaching from the north and east. It serves as an access point for firefighters and a break in fuels to slow the spread of fire that would impact the Capay Valley, Winters, and western Yolo County. Yearly maintenance of the Front Country Fuel Break was proposed by CAL FIRE and included as a project in the Yolo County Community Wildfire Protection Plan (CWPP). The entire N29-mile fuel break crosses through private property, including Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation tribal lands and California Audubon's Bobcat Ranch. To start the fuel break, Yolo County Resource Conservation District (RCD) is partnered with Capay Valley Fire Protection District to map the project, engage landowners, conduct biological and botanical surveys and contract with CAL FIRE or a qualified licensed dozer operator to blade the first mile of the fuel break. The first mile of the fuel break largely follows the path of old Highway 16 and is intermittently paved, but overgrown with invasive grasses and other weeds. Implementation of the fuel break would include 10-15 feet of blading of vegetation by a dozer to remove 100% of groundcover to bare soil/pavement. The fuel break footprint does not contain any shrubs or trees, except for one blue elderberry along a fence line that will have a SO-foot no-disturbance buffer from the dripline. Dozer operations will be overseen by Yolo County RCD and implemented by CAL FIRE's Licensed Dozer Operator or another qualified professional dozer subcontractor to the RCD. An intermittent stream was identified to intersect with the fuel break footprint. The RCD has identified a route for the dozer to travel adjacent to the stream outside of a SO-foot no disturbance buffer towards Highway 16 where the stream crosses beneath the highway. The dozer will then continue the fuel break by using a landowner's driveway to re-access the footprint (see attached map for intermittent stream avoidance route). Yolo County RCD conducted a desktop review of the first one-mile footprint using the California Native Diversity Database (CNDDB), iNaturalist, and Calflora to determine potential biologic and botanical resources. The draft extent of the entire fuel break footprint was submitted via a Native American Heritage Commission Records request and further consultation on the one-mile footprint has occurred withYocha Dehe Wintun Nation's Cultural Department. An RCD California Dept of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) qualified biologist has walked the first mile of the fuel break and found no resources of concern; the project's footprint largely consists of invasive grasses and other non-native species. If work commences during nesting season, an RCD CDFW qualified biologist will survey the entire 1-mile project area for nesting birds or other protected species not less than three (3) days prior to work and will make any necessary adjustments to project implementation plans. After nesting season, surveys will occur a week before work starts. This fire break will be used for emergency access and/or burning-out operations to stop the spread of fires at the base of the foothills to prevent fire from crossing west into adjoining counties, or east into the Ca pay Valley.

ceqa-846aa586720d292f54.name: Rumsey Prescribed Grazing
ceqa-846aa586720d292f54.description: Yolo County Resource Conservation District (RCD) is working with a qualified local grazing professional, a Certified Rangeland Manager, and private landowners to implement prescribed grazing with the purpose of reducing fire danger throughout the community of Rumsey. The project area is in the valley floor of the Capay Valley along Highway 16 in predominantly historical agricultural land. The project sites range from moderate to very high fire severity and were selected for their high biomass, predominantly invasive grasses, and proximity to the community- additional sites in Rumsey may be added in upcoming years, if funding allows. Prescribed grazing will be implemented using goats and sheep to create a buffer of reduced vegetation, and grazing will be controlled and temporary. Grazing will be high-density, short duration grazing and sheep/goats will be rotated through smaller paddocks within the project sites. This grazing project adds to other fuels reduction work spearheaded by the RCD and local partners to create a managed buffers throughout/around Rumsey where fire approaching from the north, east or west would slow to provide better conditions for firefighting and protect evacuation routes. A Rangeland Management Plan was prepared by RCD and certified by a Certified Rangeland Manager. A desktop review for Rumsey was conducted by RCD staff and included queries in the California Natural Diversity Database, iPAC, iNaturalist, and the California Native Plant Society Rare Plant Inventory. Thedesktop review resulted in an extensive list of potential resources that RCD staff have used to guide their on-the-ground surveys. Site surveys identified potential sensitive resources, such as blue elderberry shrubs, wetlands and ephemeral drainages, and a great blue heron rookery. Elderberry shrubs within project footprints will be fenced off to create a 20-foot no disturbance buffer from the dripline. Appropriate buffers around wetlands and riparian areas will also be implemented to exclude sheep and goats from waterways. In regard to the great blue heron rookery, grazing will be timed when great blue herons are no longer on-site. Based on the results of the desktop review and biological surveys, the project has been designed so it will not cause significant adverse impact to special status species with likelihood to occur near the project site. Work may occur during nesting bird season. If work commences during nesting bird season (February 1st to September 15th), the project area will be surveyed for nesting birds by a qualified biologist, no more than one week before operations. If nesting birds are located, the RCD will develop measures to ensure no significant impact to species that are consistent with the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

ceqa-0d03d47ed04516cb70.name: El Macero Country Club General Plan Amendment (ZF2025-003)
ceqa-0d03d47ed04516cb70.projectTitle: El Macero Country Club General Plan Amendment
ceqa-0d03d47ed04516cb70.description: The project is a request from the El Macero Country Club (EMCC) to facilitate the expansion and construction of future residential uses within El Macero, an established community in unincorporated Yolo County, on a portion of Assessor’s Parcel Number (APN) 068-130-010. The property (golf course) is approximately 170 acres and currently designated as Parks and Recreation (PR) within the Yolo County 2030 Countywide General Plan (General Plan) and zoned as Parks and Recreation (P-R). EMCC is seeking to create three new residential parcels from areas of the existing golf course property totaling approximately 0.97 acres. The project included requests for a: General Plan Amendment (GPA) to change the land use of a portion of the 170-acre El Macero golf course parcel from PR to Residential Low (RL); adoption of an Ordinance to change the zoning from P-R to Low Density Residential/Planned Development No. 66 (R-L/PD-66); a Tentative Parcel Map (No. 5267) to create three new parcels; and a Variance request to allow a reduced front yard setback. The remaining approximately 169 acres of the golf course parcel would retain its existing PR General Plan land use designation and P-R zoning. Respectively, the three new parcels would be redesignated to RL and rezoned to R-L/PD-66, consisting of approximately 12,927 square feet (Lot 1), 15,412 square feet (Lot 2), and 13,741 square feet (Lot 3). The Project does not include construction of residences at this time; however, future residential development would be consistent with the applicable development standards, as allowed under the R-L/PD-66 zoning regulations. Additionally, the request for a variance will allow future residential development on the three proposed parcels to match the building envelope of adjacent lots. The project site is located within the City of Davis sphere of influence, approximately 0.6 miles south of I-80. The three proposed parcels are surrounded by recreational use (golf course), single-family residences, and roadways. The El Macero Country Club is a private, member-owned club which features an 18-hole golf course with residential development surrounding the approximately 170-acre course. Lot 1 will be located in the southwest portion of the golf course parcel with access from Clubhouse Drive, while Lots 2 and 3 will be located in the northeastern portion of the golf course parcel with access from Country Club Drive. The three new parcels will connect to the El Macero County Service Area (CSA) which contracts with the City of Davis for water and sewer services. Water and wastewater service for Lots 2 and 3 would be extended from the fronting roadways, whereas Lot 1 would require an approximately 169-foot extension of an existing sewer main from the intersection of El Macero Drive and Clubhouse Drive. Lot 2 also includes a 15-foot access easement to be reserved by EMCC, adjacent to the existing golf course pond for maintenance purposes.

ceqa-d0f59a9f6ea130f4c1.name: City of Woodland General Plan Amendment: Policy 2.A.1
ceqa-d0f59a9f6ea130f4c1.description: The City prepared a Supplemental EIR to supplement the previously certified City 2035 General Plan and Climate Action Plan Environmental Impact Report to amend Policy 2.A.1 in the General Plan (proposed project). The City’s ultimate boundaries are circumscribed by a permanent Urban Limit Line (ULL) established by a vote of the people in 2006, which placed restrictions on the provision of public services outside of the ULL. The ULL provisions of public services outside the ULL may only be modified by another vote of the people. The proposed project would allow the City to provide utilities (i.e., potable water, wastewater, or recycled water) up to one mile beyond the existing ULL to existing commercial facilities in operation on or prior to November 3, 2026. Amendment to Policy 2.A.1 would be subject to voter approval. The City is considering including a measure on the November 2026 ballot that would amend the ULL to allow the expansion of existing City utilities to existing commercial facilities located on parcels with a boundary that falls wholly or partially within one mile of the ULL and in operation on or prior to November 3, 2026. The City received applications to extend utilities beyond the current ULL, and it is anticipated at this time that two existing commercial facilities located within unincorporated Yolo County would make use of the utility extension, if the ballot measure passes. These two existing commercial facilities are Bayer U.S. Crop Science, LLC (located at 37437 CA-16, Woodland, CA 95695) and Clark Pacific (located at 40600 County Road 18C, Woodland, CA 95776). The ballot measure would not require either Bayer or Clark Pacific to extend utility facilities and services.

ceqa-ff6772148399306753.name: Rumsey Buffer Prescribed Burn and Prescribed Grazing
ceqa-ff6772148399306753.description: The Capay Valley Fire Protection District (FPO), in partnership with Yolo County Resource Conservation District, is continuing implementation of the Rumsey Buffer project across multiple properties in northern Rumsey, CA. The project consists of fuels management strategies including prescribed fire, prescribed grazing, pile burning, and mechanical thinning and chipping. In previous years, the project area has been managed with prescribed fire, mechanical thinning, and pile burning. The primary management objective across the project area is hazardous fuels reduction to reduce dead and downed debris and manage invasive grasses and yellow starthistle. In late spring/early summer of 2026, an 11-acre prescribed burn is planned to occur on parcel 060270002 to be implemented by the Ca pay Valley FPO with support from the Yolo County RCD and other local agencies. Burning may occur in subsequent years in the spring or fall with appropriate species monitoring and buffers implemented. Within the burn unit, containment lines (mowed buffers) will be implemented to ensure fire stays within the burn unit. This project continues management of the Rumsey Buffer Project. All burning will be performed or supervised by the Capay Valley Fire Protection District in accordance with the terms and conditions of an air quality burn permit issued by the Yolo-Solano Air Quality Management District. Fuels management and pile burning decreases fuel continuity, which reduces the probability of catastrophic wildfires and promotes a healthy ecosystem. A biological assessment and site visits performed by Yolo County RCD identified two active nests on the parcel next to the prescribed fire footprint: a bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) and a white-tailed kite (Elanus leucurus). Both species are species of concern and subject to the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Yolo County RCD qualified biologists consulted with CDFW to develop a Biological Monitoring Plan and to identify proper buffer measures to ensure work does not impact the nesting species. Bald eagle Buffer and Monitoring An active bald eagle nest was identified in a eucalyptus tree 684 feet from the burn site. This nest does not have a direct line of site with the prescribed burn project site and will not be impacted by prescribed fire smoke. A 660-foot no-disturbance buffer will be implemented between the tree with the active nest and the burn unit. No ignition, vehicles, equipment, or staff will be allowed within the buffer. An on-site biologist will monitor the nest during site preparation, burn operations, and active work for signs of disturbance and work will be halted if the birds show signs of disturbance. White-tailed kite Buffer and Monitoring An active white tailed kite nest was identified in a tree approximately 840 feet from the burn site. This nest does not have a direct line of site with the prescribed burn project site and will not be impacted by prescribed fire smoke. An on-site biologist will monitor the nest during site preparation, burn operations, and active work for signs of disturbance and work will be halted if the birds show signs of disturbance. Burning and site prep is planned for mid to late May which is later in the development season of chicks, especially for the white-tailed kite chicks. For both species, smoke impacts will be minimal or non-existent and implementation of the burn will be halted if smoke drifts towards the nest. Capay Valley Fire Protection District (CVFPD) is the lead implementor for the prescribed burn. CVFPD will obtain CAL FIRE burn permits (if required) and submit a Smoke Management Plan and coordinate with the Yolo-Solano Air Quality Management District. RCD staff, who are Firefighter Type II certified, will be on-site to assist with the burn and survey and monitor (both in the weeks before the burn and during active work) for species. Additional work that may occur in this project area (across all three parcels) includes pile burning, prescribed grazing, mechanical thinning, and chipping but will not occur while occur while nesting birds are on-site without no-disturbance buffers and monitoring (when appropriate).

The proposed work at sites 4.0, 4.1, and 4.2 includes doweling into the existing concrete headwall and concrete slab to form and cast in place headwall/wingwalls up to the height of the levee toe road; backfilling behind headwall assembly and placing 6-inch or less diameter riprap at the ends of the wingwalls; and reseeding all temporarily disturbed areas with typical native erosion control seeds mix. ceqa-7a06b68a5fe37682d0.name: Willowgrove Project
ceqa-7a06b68a5fe37682d0.description: The proposed project would include the development of a mixed-use community, including a total of 1,250 dwelling units, comprised of both affordable and market-rate single- and multifamily residences across various residential neighborhoods. In addition, the proposed project would include neighborhood retail uses; a daycare facility; associated on-site roadway improvements; utility improvements; recreational uses, such as a community park, mini park, and a gym, open space, and greenbelts; and off-site roadway improvements along the project’s East Covell Boulevard frontage and its intersection with Alhambra Drive. The proposed project would also include an Urban Agricultural Transition Area (UATA) located along the northern and eastern boundaries of the site. Primary site access would be provided from East Covell Boulevard. From East Covell Boulevard, Alhambra Drive would be extended into the site from the existing intersection in a north-to-south direction. In addition, a new intersection would be constructed from East Covell Boulevard in the southeastern portion of the project site. Both entry streets would extend into the project site around the proposed community park, and would include traffic circles at the first internal intersections connecting to the modified local street and collector street. The proposed project would also include a multimodal network of bikeways and sidewalks, including six-foot-wide sidewalks along all internal streets; ten-foot-wide shared use pedestrian paths along the entry streets and modified local streets; a pedestrian path within the proposed UATA; a 14-foot-wide shared use path within the proposed North Central Greenbelt; and new pedestrian connections to the adjacent Wildhorse Agricultural Buffer. With respect to transit, the proposed project would include installation of two new transit connections located along the frontage of the project site along East Covell Boulevard, with one new transit station located at the proposed community park and one new transit stop located in the southwestern corner of the project site, closest to the affordable site. The proposed project would require discretionary approvals, including an Amendment of the City’s SOI, Annexation of the 232-acre project site into the City of Davis, a General Plan Amendment, Pre-zoning of the project site to City of Davis zoning designations, Final Planned Development to establish site development standards, Design Review, Large Lot and Small Lot Vesting Tentative Maps, an Affordable Housing Plan, and a Development Agreement.
ceqa-7a06b68a5fe37682d0.crossStreets: East Covell Boulevard and Alhambra Drive

ceqa-c7cda03e976657af05.name: AT&T Yolo 1B (T-17907) Last Mile Infrastructure Project
ceqa-c7cda03e976657af05.projectTitle: AT&T Yolo 1B (T-17907) Last Mile Infrastructure Project
ceqa-c7cda03e976657af05.description: The Yolo 1B Project is located near the Yolo-Colusa County line in and around the unincorporated community of Dunnigan in Yolo County. The project alignment is within an area that is largely rural with some residential and commercial development and is located on eastern and western sides of Interstate 5 (I-5). The terrain is mostly flat. The project alignment includes construction of new aerial cable as well as conduits for installation of fiber optic cable. The project applicant, AT&T, proposes to place approximately 33 miles total of buried, underground, and aerial fiber-optic cable. Some facilities in the project alignment are existing, and new facilities would be installed as part of the project. Aerial fiber would be placed on existing poles, where possible, which would include lashing fiber to existing AT&T strands and attachments. Where new buried (i.e., existing conduit not present) or new underground (i.e., existing conduit present) fiber would be installed, directional boring, micro-trenching, and/or open trenching methods would be used. Most work is planned for the right-of-way, except for some areas that are adjacent to the right-of-way. In some cases, the project mapping slightly deviates from the public rights-of-way (e.g., roads). For the purposes of this analysis, it is assumed that these mapping discrepancies are errors (i.e., that the project alignment mapping was approximate), and that fiber installation would indeed use existing infrastructure (i.e., aerial, underground) and existing rights-of-way in or along roads (i.e., buried). In other cases, segments of the project alignment are located a substantial distance from existing disturbed rights-of-way, and in these cases, the mapping is considered to be accurate. These segments include proposed buried fiber crossings of Buckeye Creek, Dunnigan Creek and a tributary, Bird Creek, and the Tehama–Colusa Canal as well as a freshwater pond, freshwater emergent wetlands, and undisturbed natural vegetation (e.g., annual grassland, blue oak woodland).
ceqa-c7cda03e976657af05.crossStreets: eastern and western sides of Interstate 5

ceqa-93aef5376cb9baba13.name: AT&T Yolo 1 (T-17907) Last Mile Infrastructure Project

ceqa-93aef5376cb9baba13.description: The Yolo 1 Project is composed of approximately 10 sections located in the City of Woodland in Yolo County. The City of Woodland and surrounding areas are largely rural with residential and commercial locations on flat terrain. The project alignment is primarily located throughout the City of Woodland and along Interstate (I)-5, I-505, State Route (SR) 16, and SR 113. I-5 and SR 16 are major connectors throughout the project alignment. The project applicant, AT&T, proposes to install approximately 94 miles of aerial or underground fiber. Aerial fiber would be placed on existing poles, where possible, which would include lashing fiber to existing AT&T strands and attachments. Where buried (i.e., existing conduit not present) or underground (i.e., existing conduit present) fiber would be installed, directional boring, micro-trenching, and/or open trenching methods would be used. The project includes aerial, buried and underground elements. Aerial elements include the addition of new lines to existing utility poles. Buried elements would include ground disturbance to create space for new conduits below grade. Underground elements would use existing conduits below grade and would not include ground disturbance. Project design features for biological resources and historical resources, described below, are project commitments that will be implemented as part of the project.

ceqa-e937b329720222088c.name: Permit No. 19839 – Bees Lakes Habitat Restoration Project
ceqa-e937b329720222088c.projectTitle: Bees Lakes Habitat Restoration Project Initial Study
ceqa-e937b329720222088c.description: Approval of Permit No. 19839, under California Code of Regulations, Title 23, Article 3, Section 6, for work within an adopted plan of flood control: To restore the right (north) bank waterside riparian area of the Sacramento River within Reclamation District 900, Unit 01, between levee miles 3.79 to 4.32 by removing invasive vegetation, installing aeration diffusion devices within two existing ponds, and placing three artificial floating wetlands within the main (larger) pond, Bees Lake. The project also includes construction of foot trails, elevated boardwalks on piles, ADA-compliant ramps, a decomposed granite multi-purpose trail, a ten-stall paved parking area, seasonally installed portable bathrooms, two viewing platforms, and multi-use picnic and recreational areas. Additional features include wayfinding signage, post-and-cable fencing, and information kiosks. In addition, approximately 2.21 acres of mixed riparian woodland habitat will be planted, maintained, and monitored for up to three years. A Class 2 aggregate base maintenance turnaround will be constructed to provide access to the floating wetlands. Electrical power for the aeration system will be supplied from an existing Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) utility pole (authorized under CVFPB Permit No. 19059), with an underground electrical conductor connecting the pole to an aeration pump located south of the multi-purpose trail. Temporarily disturbed areas will be reseeded with a native seed mix once construction is complete, and debris currently in and near the ponds will be removed and disposed of outside the floodway.

ceqa-068d0b1853514bd007.projectTitle: Davis Amtrak Station Fire Damage Repair (CIP ET0048)
ceqa-068d0b1853514bd007.description: The project is to replace/restore existing interior features of the historical ticketing office inside the SP Depot building that were damaged in result of a recent fire. The SP Depot is a nationally registered historical structure. The work entails replacing insulation, drywall, cabinetry, wall paneling and trims as necessary along with the replacement of one exterior wood window with surrounding stucco and the rear entrance door. Any features not significantly damaged will be attempted to be restored and reinstalled. Existing hardwood flooring to be refinished to match previous condition. Some minor electrical interior improvements to be made including the replacement of a light fixture and ceiling fan along with associated switches and outlets. Electrician to also replace several exterior lighting fixtures that melted as a result of the fire and heat damage. For the HVAC system, the thermostat and AC/heat register will be replaced. All interior features replaced will be of like kind material matching grains, texture for the areas altered during the restoration process. Paint/Stain of walls, doors, cabinetry and other wood features to match preexisting color and sheen of the facility. Outdoor benches and outdoor recessed lighting will be replaced. Project also includes pressure washing of the full exterior of the building to remove smoke and soot damage. This repair and restoration project will be performed using the most recent (1995) Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties with Guidelines for Preserving, Rehabilitating, Restoring, and Reconstructing Historic Buildings.

ceqa-87299e84626c32686d.name: El Macero Country Club General Plan Amendment
ceqa-87299e84626c32686d.projectTitle: El Macero Country Club General Plan Amendment
ceqa-87299e84626c32686d.description: The project is a request from the El Macero Country Club (EMCC) to facilitate the expansion and construction of future residential uses within El Macero, an established community in unincorporated Yolo County, on a portion of Assessor’s Parcel Number (APN) 068-130-010. The property is approximately 170 acres and currently designated as Parks and Recreation (PR) within the Yolo County 2030 Countywide General Plan (General Plan) and zoned as Parks and Recreation (P-R). EMCC is seeking to create three new residential parcels from areas of the existing golf course property totaling approximately 0.97 acres. The project requires the following discretionary approvals: • General Plan Amendment (GPA) to redesignate approximately 0.97 acres of the golf course property from PR to Residential Low (RL); • Rezone from P-R to Low Density Residential with Planned Development No. 66 (R-L/PD-66); • Approval of a Tentative Parcel Map (TPM) to create three residential parcels from a portion of the existing golf course parcel; and • A Variance to allow a reduced front yard setback from 35 feet to 30 feet for proposed Lots 2 and 3. The remaining approximately 169 acres of the golf course parcel would retain its existing PR General Plan land use designation and P-R zoning. Respectively, the three new parcels would be redesignated to RL and rezoned to R-L/PD-66, consisting of approximately 12,927 square feet (Lot 1), 15,412 square feet (Lot 2), and 13,741 square feet (Lot 3). The Project does not include construction of residences at this time; however, future residential development would be consistent with the applicable development standards, as allowed under the R-L/PD-66 zoning regulations. Additionally, the request for a variance will allow future residential development on Lot 2 and 3 to match the building envelope of adjacent lots. The project site is located within the City of Davis sphere of influence, approximately 0.6 miles south of I-80. The three proposed parcels are surrounded by recreational use (golf course), single-family residences, and roadways. The El Macero Country Club is a private, member-owned club which features an 18-hole golf course with residential development surrounding the approximately 170-acre course. Lot 1 will be located in the southwest portion of the golf course parcel with access from Clubhouse Drive, while Lots 2 and 3 will be located in the northeastern portion of the golf course parcel with access from Country Club Drive. The three new parcels will connect to the El Macero County Service Area (CSA) which contracts with the City of Davis for water and sewer services. Water and wastewater service for Lots 2 and 3 would be extended from the fronting roadways, whereas Lot 1 would require an approximately 169-foot extension of an existing sewer main from the intersection of El Macero Drive and Clubhouse Drive. Lot 2 also includes a 15-foot access easement to be reserved by EMCC, adjacent to the existing golf course pond for maintenance purposes. Any future development of the project site, including homesite development, will be required to meet the development standards set forth in Article 5 of Title 8, Chapter 2 of the Yolo County Code, and Planned Development No. 66 (Ordinance 1446).

ceqa-5fb6529d5fb44eebbb.name: Upper Swanston Ranch, Inc. Instream Flow Water Purchase Agreement
ceqa-5fb6529d5fb44eebbb.projectTitle: Upper Swanston Ranch, Inc. Instream Flow Water Purchase Agreement
ceqa-5fb6529d5fb44eebbb.description: The Instream Flow Water Purchase Program provides funding for the acquisition of environmentally beneficial instream flows in the Sacramento-San Joaquin watershed to be provided January through June. The water transfers and purchases must measurably enhance streamflow at a time and location necessary to provide fisheries or ecosystem benefits or improve upon existing flow conditions. The Upper Swanston Ranch, Inc. is a family-owned corporation located in the Yolo Bypass just north of the Interstate 80 and adjacent railroad tracks for several decades. The ranch has been farmed over the past 60 years, growing a variety of crops including tomatoes, corn, milo, rice, and sunflower. The Upper Swanston Ranch Inc. water purchase agreement will temporarily fallow or leave idle (unfarmed) 696 acres of historically irrigated agricultural lands to reduce diversions and retain water in the Tule Canal and Toe Drain. This water purchase agreement will be in place until Upper Swanston Ranch, Inc., meets a total water volume commitment of 39,600 acre-feet in dry, below normal, and above normal water year types (middle WYTs). By ceasing irrigation diversions of water in middle WYTs, approximately 3,300 acre-feet of water that would have been diverted to fields to grow crops would flow through the Tule Canal and Toe Drain in the Yolo Bypass to the lower Sacramento River and into the Delta. This will leave 696 acres of farmland that was previously irrigated between the months of April 1 and October 1 as fallowed land, resulting in a corresponding increase in the amount of water in the Tule Canal, Toe Drain and Sacramento River from April 1 through October 30, with the majority of flows retained instream from April 1 to June 30, consistent with reduced diversions during months reflecting historical irrigation practices and the terms of relevant water rights. By fallowing or leaving lands idled, only water resulting from natural hydrologic conditions will cover the 696 acres of farmland in the project location in middle WYTs from April 1 to October 30. The water remaining in the Tule Canal and resulting in waters remaining in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta is for the benefit of the aquatic and riparian ecosystems, to preserve and benefit sensitive aquatic biological resources, to promote ecological resilience, to provide climate change adaptation, and to provide other biological benefits to native species that utilize the aquatic environment.
